blocks.text: Introduction: A Master of Both Chan and Pure Land

inline.s: Surveying the whole course of Master Hanshan's life, we see that, like Master Yongming (the Sixth Patriarch of the Pure Land school) and Master Chewu (the Twelfth Patriarch of the Pure Land school), his cultivation and his propagation of both Chan and Pure Land were outstanding and shining, and his name is recorded in the Record of Sages of the Pure Land; thus he is both a Chan-lineage master and a Pure Land-lineage master. Only because Master Hanshan's bodily remains are enshrined side by side with those of Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of the Chan school, at Caoxi is he mistakenly taken to be merely a Chan patriarch. In truth, Master Hanshan, in order to bring students of Buddhism to freedom from birth and death in this very life, pointed them everywhere back to the Pure Land; all his life he advocated and spread the Pure Land Dharma-gate, perfect in both principle and fact. Moreover he led by example, seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and won brilliant success; he is a patriarch of the Pure Land school beyond any doubt.
The Record of Sages of the Pure Land states:
Ming dynasty
Deqing
, a holy monk of the Ming era)

Deqing, courtesy name Chengyin, in later life styled the Old Man Hanshan, was a son of the Cai family of Jinling. His mother dreamed that Avalokiteshvara brought her a boy and gave him to her, and so she conceived. When he was born
(he was born in the twenty-fifth year of the Jiajing era of the Ming Shizong emperor)
, he was wrapped in a white double membrane
(a white double-layered membrane)

. At the age of nineteen he left home and gave himself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation. One night in a dream he saw Amitābha Buddha manifest before him, standing in the sky where the sun sets; his face, eyes, light and marks were perfectly clear. From that time on the radiant sacred form
(from that time on the luminous sacred form of Amitābha Buddha)
was ever before his eyes. Before long
(before long)
he went to Mount Wutai to cultivate samādhi and awakened to his original nature
(a complete awakening to mind-nature)
. He pricked his finger to write the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood, and with every stroke of the brush he recited the Buddha's name once. In time, movement and stillness were one.

Awakening to the Original Nature: Concerning Master Hanshan's complete awakening to mind-nature at the age of thirty, the Record of the Autobiographical Chronological Account of the Old Man Hanshan in the Collection of Dream Wanderings relates: “I lived alone here (Longmen on the North Terrace of Mount Wutai), holding up a single thought; when people came I did not speak, I only looked at them. After a long time I looked upon people as so many tree stumps, until I reached the point of not knowing a single written character. At first the great winds that arose and howled through a thousand crevices, and the melting ice whose torrents rushed and thundered along the mountain gullies, made sounds in the stillness like a thousand armies and ten thousand horses marching forth, and I found this very disturbing. So I asked Master Miao (Master Miaofeng), and he said: ‘The realm arises from the mind; it does not come from outside. I have heard the ancients say: hear the sound of the water for thirty years without turning the root of the mind, and you will realize Avalokiteshvara's perfect penetration.’ Above the stream there was a single-log bridge, and every day I sat or stood upon it. At first the sound of the water was plainly there; after a long time, when a thought stirred I heard it, and when no thought stirred I did not hear it. One day, sitting on the bridge, I suddenly forgot my body, and the sound became utterly still; from then on all sounds were hushed and no longer troubled me. Each day I ate wheat bran mixed with wild greens and washed it down with a drink of rice gruel (one ge of rice). At first people sent me three dou of rice (ten ge make one sheng, ten sheng make one dou), and after half a year there was still some left. One day, when the gruel was finished and I was walking in meditation, I suddenly stood still, and saw neither body nor mind — only one great treasury of light, perfect and utterly still, like a great round mirror, in which the mountains, rivers, and the great earth appeared as reflections. When I came to, all was luminous; I looked for body and mind and could not find them at all. At once I spoke a verse: “A sudden thought, and the mad mind rests; / Inside and out, the senses and their objects are wholly clear. / I turn and strike the great empty space — / The myriad forms in their teeming array arise and cease with it.” From then on, within and without were utterly still, and sound, voice, form, and appearance no longer obstructed me; all my former doubt and bewilderment melted away on the spot. When I looked at the pot (the cooking pot), it had already gathered dust — because I was utterly without a companion, I did not know how long it had been.”
Movement and Stillness as One: At the age of thirty-two Master Hanshan resolved to prick his finger and write out in blood-ground gold
(to draw his own blood and mix it with gold dust for writing the sutras)

one copy of the Great Means and Vast Buddha Avatamsaka Sutra. When Empress Dowager Li learned of this, she bestowed gold paper on Master Hanshan for copying the sutra. In the fourth month of the following year Master Hanshan began to write. As he wrote, no matter whether the dot or stroke was large or small, with every stroke that fell he recited the Buddha's name once. When monks and laypeople touring the mountain came to the Master's quiet room, they would invariably exchange greetings and ask for instruction, and the Master answered and conversed with them while his hand never stopped copying. With certain eminent friends and old acquaintances the Master would invite them to sit on the meditation couch and discuss the Dharma, and all the while his hand still never stopped copying. Day after day the Master went on in this way: though people came and went and he received them and talked with them, his copying never ceased, and in his mind there was not the slightest trace of movement to be found. Many old scholars(elderly and deeply learned men) who heard of the Master's condition found it hard to believe. One day the old scholars led a great company of their disciples to the Master's quiet room, wishing to put the matter to the proof. Beside the Master they deliberately asked questions and made a clamor, using every means to disturb him; then, when the Master had finished a section, they took it and compared it with the original, and truly there was not the slightest error. Only then were they convinced that the Master's attainment was far from ordinary. Yet still they did not understand it, and they went to ask Master Miaofeng: “Why is Master Hanshan able to use one mind for many things at once?” Master Miaofeng answered: “My Dharma-brother's Buddha-recitation samādhi has reached utter purity!” (See the Collection of Dream Wanderings · Record of the Autobiographical Chronological Account of the Old Man Hanshan)
In the twenty-third year of the Wanli era
(the twenty-third year of the Wanli era of the Ming Shenzong emperor, when Master Hanshan was fifty)
, he dwelt in quiet at Mount Lao
(he withdrew to the Naluoyan grotto on Mount Lao by the Eastern Sea)
, and Empress Dowager Li ordered that gold be sent to build a monastery there
(Empress Dowager Li gave orders that gold and silver be sent to Master Hanshan to build a monastery there)
, bestowing on it the plaque-name Haiyin. At that time the Empress Dowager several times sent palace envoys
(envoys sent out from the palace, usually eunuchs)
to repair the various stupas and monasteries. When the powerful men at court who bore a grudge against the palace envoys
(bore resentment)
had the Eastern Depot
(the Eastern Depot, a Ming-dynasty secret police agency whose affairs could be reported directly to the emperor and whose power exceeded that of the Embroidered Uniform Guard)
send its agents
(runners, underlings)
disguised as Daoist priests
for at that time the emperor
Ming Shenzong
was a devout patron of Daoism
to strike the petition drum
(the drum hung outside the court, by which subjects were permitted to sound their appeals, whether in remonstrance or in search of redress)
, and laid information concerning embezzlement and occupation of land. The matter implicated Qing
(the affair implicated Master Hanshan; Qing is Deqing, that is, Master Hanshan)
, who was sentenced for
(found guilty of)
privately building a monastery, and was exiled to Leizhou
(sent into exile to serve as a soldier on the frontier garrison at Leizhou; Leizhou is the prefecture on the Leizhou Peninsula in the southwest of Guangdong province)
. Wherever Qing went, he preached the Dharma in cap and robes
(because the authorities had revoked his monastic registration, he preached wearing the cap and robes of a Confucian scholar)
, and again he made the vow to spread the great sutras, composing commentaries on the Lankavatara, the Shurangama, and other sutras.

The Matter Implicated Qing: The affair implicated Deqing (Master Hanshan). At that time Empress Dowager Li devoutly believed in Buddhism and performed many Buddhist works, while the Shenzong emperor, a believer in Daoism, had always detested the palace envoys who were constantly going about on Buddhist business. Once, when the Empress Dowager sent a palace envoy to Mount Lao by the Eastern Sea, the inner court angered Shenzong over some chance incident, and the Empress Dowager was drawn in as well. This gave the powerful courtiers who opposed the Empress Dowager just the opening they wanted: they planned first to do away with the envoy who had delivered the sutras, and then to use the old rumor of the Daoist adepts' mischief to strike at the Empress Dowager. So they had the runners of the Eastern Depot disguise themselves as Daoist priests, ascend the hall, strike the drum, and present a false accusation that Master Hanshan had embezzled the state treasury silver. When the emperor read it he flew into a rage and issued an edict for the arrest of the Master and the envoy who had delivered the sutras.
In the forty-second year
(the forty-second year of the Wanli era of the Ming Shenzong emperor, when Master Hanshan was sixty-nine)
, by gracious edict he resumed the monk's robe
(he resumed the monastic robe)
. On his way back he passed through Mount Lu and built a hermitage below Wuru Peak, where he followed Master Yuan
(Master Huiyuan)
in the six-period water-clock
(taking Buddha-recitation through the six periods as his fixed daily practice; the six periods correspond to twelve hours of our time)
, and his cultivation of the Pure Land karma grew ever more refined.
At that time a Chan practitioner from Haiyang asked to receive the precepts, and then asked about the essentials of cultivating the Pure Land. Qing
(Master Hanshan)
said:

The Buddha said that among the methods of practice for escaping birth and death the skillful means are many, but only Buddha-recitation and the seeking of rebirth in the Pure Land is the most direct and essential. This Dharma-gate the Buddha proclaimed unasked; it covers the three capacities equally and gathers in all four assemblies; it is not a provisional
(expedient)
device set up for those of lower faculties.

The sutra says: If one would purify the Buddha-land, one must first purify one's own mind. Now in cultivating the Pure Land karma, one must take a pure mind as the root. To purify one's own mind, the first thing is to keep the precept-root pure. The three of the body
(killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct)
, the four of the mouth
(false speech, idle talk, harsh speech, and divisive speech)
, and the three of the mind
(greed, anger, and ignorance)
— these ten evil karmas are the cause of suffering in the three evil paths. Now the essential of upholding the precepts is that the three karmas
(bodily, verbal, and mental karma)
must first be pure; then the mind is pure of itself. Within this pure mind, weary of the sufferings of Saha, make the vow to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Nourishment
(that is, the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
, and establish Buddha-recitation as your proper practice.

Yet in reciting the Buddha's name one must be deeply in earnest about birth and death: first cut off outward entanglements, take up the single thought alone, and take the one phrase “Amitābha Buddha” as your very root of life, never forgetting it in any thought, never breaking it in any mind. Throughout the six periods of the day, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, taking up the spoon or raising the chopsticks, turning and bowing, in movement or stillness, at leisure or in busyness, at all times, neither dull nor confused, with no extraneous condition
(the mind not reaching out after other things)

Working in this way, after long familiarity even dreams do not lose it, and waking and sleeping are one; then the practice becomes fine and close, beaten into a single piece, and this is the time of gaining power. If one recites to the point of single-mindedness without distraction, then at the end of life the realm of the Pure Land appears, one is naturally not detained by birth and death, and Amitābha Buddha is moved to release light and receive one — this is the sure proof of rebirth. Yet single-minded holding of the Name is indeed the proper practice.

One must further support this with visualization, and it becomes all the more steady and sure. For Vaidehi the Buddha set forth the sixteen wonderful contemplations, and by them one may accomplish the matter in a single life. Now from among the sixteen contemplations
(the sixteen kinds of visualization taught in the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life)

choose whichever one you will. Either contemplate only the wonderful marks of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas, or contemplate the realms of the Pure Land, such as the lotus flowers and jeweled pools described in the Amitābha Sutra, visualizing as you wish. If the visualization is clear, then throughout the six periods of the day the Pure Land is present before you, and at the end of life, in a single thought, you are at once reborn
(in a single instant, at once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)

. Working in this way, carefully upholding the precepts, forever cutting off evil thoughts and afflictions, and by this pure mind keeping contemplation and recitation joined without interruption — the true cause of the Pure Land is nothing beyond this.
There was also a Layman of Pure Mind who asked: My recitation of the Buddha's name never becomes a single piece; I beg you to instruct me. Qing instructed him, saying:

In cultivation, the first thing is to be deeply in earnest about birth and death. If the mind is not in earnest about birth and death, how can recitation of the Buddha become a single piece? Moreover, for measureless kalpas sentient beings have given rise to deluded thoughts in every thought, their roots of feeling firmly covered over. Even if in this life one would cultivate and transcend the world
(even if in this very life one would cultivate and leave the world)
, when has a single thought ever been in bitter earnest about birth and death? Day in and day out, thought after thought follows the affections
(ordinarily thought after thought follows the flow of feeling and consciousness)

, and one has never once turned back to examine oneself. Now with a shallow and floating faith you would cut off the birth and death of many kalpas — this is what is called “a cup of water to quench the fire of a cartload of firewood.” How could there be any such principle
(how could there be such a principle?)
If one is in truth deeply in earnest about birth and death, so that every thought is like putting out a fire on one's head
(burning)

, then one fears only that, having lost this human body, it will be hard to regain in a hundred kalpas. One must bite down hard on this one sound of the Buddha and be determined to overcome deluded thoughts. In every place, thought after thought present before one
(every single thought is the thought of the Buddha come before one)

, not veiled or obstructed by deluded thoughts. To practice with such bitter and earnest effort, after long familiarity one naturally comes into accord, and without seeking a single piece it becomes a single piece of itself.
In this matter everything depends on one's own effort. If one merely makes Buddha-recitation a face-saving show
(putting on an act)
, then in the year of the donkey one will have no benefit
(so that even in the year of the donkey one will find no time of benefit — that is, one will never find any benefit at all)
. One must be brave and fierce, and hesitate no longer.
“Like putting out a fire on one's head (burning)”: this describes a matter of such urgency that no delay is possible and it overrides everything else.
He dwelt at Mount Lu for several years, then went
(went to)

to Caoxi. In the tenth month of the third year of the Tianqi era he showed a slight illness. He said to those around him: “This old monk's worldly conditions are nearly exhausted.” He bathed and burned incense, sat upright
(sat erect and composed)
and passed away, with a light that illumined the sky
(a radiance lit up the whole sky)
, at the age of seventy-eight.
A Light That Illumined the Sky: In the Collection of Dream Wanderings a disciple records the scene of that time, saying:
(the tenth month of the third year of the Tianqi era)
on the eleventh day, at the si hour
(nine o'clock in the morning)
, he took leave of Lord Zhang
(Master Hanshan took leave of Governor Zhang of Shaoyang, who had come into the mountains to pay his respects)
. At the shen hour
(three o'clock in the afternoon)

he drank water, bathed, burned incense, and announced to the assembly: ‘All of you should bear in mind that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift.’ He sat upright with one mind and passed away. At that time a hundred birds cried out in grief, and the four assemblies wailed without ceasing. Through the starry night a fine radiance illumined the sky, and people across the mountains all suspected that the monastery had caught fire
(they all suspected that the monastery had caught fire)
. Three days later
(three days after his passing)
, his countenance was as in life, his hair had grown
(zhǎng, the hair continued to grow)
, his lips were red, there was a faint moisture at the tip of his nose, and his hands and feet were soft as silk.”

blocks.text: 1. The Ultimate Teaching

inline.s: Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream Wanderings
Preface to Master Yunqi's Ultimate Words says:

As for the single practice of the Pure Land — cultivating the samādhi of Buddha-recitation — this again gathers in the three capacities, wholly encompasses the sudden and the gradual, and is accomplished within a single lifetime; there is nothing that surpasses it.”

Here Master Hanshan clearly points out that the Pure Land Dharma-gate is the ultimate teaching (the perfectly complete Dharma-gate) of which it can be said that “there is nothing that surpasses it.” I now excerpt that essay as follows:

[The Three Capacities] The strength of sentient beings' roots of goodness is of three kinds: the high, the middling, and the low. [The Sudden and the Gradual] The sudden teaching and the gradual teaching. The sudden teaching is the Dharma that brings accomplishment at once and swiftly; the gradual teaching is the Dharma that brings accomplishment by stages.

As for the single practice of the Pure Land — cultivating the samādhi of Buddha-recitation — it gathers in the three capacities, wholly encompasses the sudden and the gradual, and is accomplished within a single lifetime; there is nothing that surpasses it. The Buddhas and patriarchs of old urged it with all their might, and did so more than once. But alas, later students, aiming at emptiness and mystery, take Chan as the highest and belittle the Pure Land so that they will not practice it. Now that we are in the Dharma-ending age, and sentient beings are heavy with defilement, how can everyone claim to be of the high faculty? Many deceive themselves, never measuring their own capacity, but merely echoing others in empty agreement and never making a real effort — is this not self-deception? Alas! The Chan school has long lacked a clear-eyed good teacher
(the Chan school has long been without a clear-eyed good teacher)
, and no one corrects this bias
(and so no one comes to correct this deviation)
. As for those given to doctrinal study
(the study of doctrine and theory)
, they busy themselves with empty and shallow talk, most of it contrary to reality
(mostly contrary to reality)
; not only do they have no Chan, but the eye of the teachings is not clear — and it has never been worse than today.
Master Yunqi
(that is, Master Lianchi)
, awakened early
(in ancient usage the same as “early”)

to mind-only, and therefore advocated the Pure Land with all his might, to remedy the ills of the Dharma-ending age. He built a monastery himself, taught his disciples by his own example, and never let a day or night go by in idleness for nearly
(almost)
forty years. Therefore throughout the land monks and laypeople
(clergy and laity)
trusted and followed him in great numbers. The Master's Commentary and Notes on the Amitābha Sutra expounded the matter to the utmost
(it gave a complete and thorough elucidation of the purport of the Pure Land)

. As for his ordinary words of instruction, he mostly raised mind-only to illuminate the meaning of the Pure Land. Mr. Zhu, the Layman of Empty Mind, was his inner-chamber disciple; the words he recorded he entitled The Ultimate Words. Truly it is the perfect mirror of the Chan school, the compass of the one mind, and the golden probe that directly scrapes away the film from the eyes of the Dharma-ending age

(it is precisely the golden probe that restores sight to the blind eyes of sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age. [Golden probe] an instrument of gold used to scrape the film from the surface of the eyeball so that the blind may see again)
In the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Ritual Manual for Transformation-Birth, Master Hanshan also says:
This
(rebirth in the nine grades)

— though one has not yet cut off afflictions, because once one is born in that land, sees the Buddha and hears the Dharma, and dwells in the stage of non-retrogression, one will never again fall into the birth and death of the three realms. From there one makes the vow to return to the three realms to save living beings, and so one comes and goes freely, no longer detained by the afflictions of birth and death. Therefore Master Yongming said: once you see Amitābha, what need to worry that you will not awaken? This is exactly so. This single practice can be accomplished within one lifetime of sincere, earnest effort; once one is born there, one suddenly escapes birth and death and forever leaves the cycle. Such a direct practice — why should one fear not to cultivate it, and even despise it? Yet to awaken through Chan investigation of the matter of birth and death is hard, while to settle birth and death through Buddha-recitation is easy — it only requires that the person have a single thought of true earnestness and bitter effort. From ancient times, those born in the Pure Land are countless and numberless; all these worldly people see with their own eyes yet do not believe — what then can be believed? I now exhort the wise of high intelligence to trust their own mind, and not to wrongly believe in false doctrines. Even within this practice, there are very many who cultivate both Chan and the Pure Land, as Master Yongming said: recite the Buddha and investigate Chan; investigate Chan and recite the Buddha. That is the so-called “having Chan and having the Pure Land, like a tiger with horns: in this present life a teacher of people, in the future a Buddha and patriarch.” This too is the highest practice.
[Ritual Manual for Transformation-Birth] The
gradual
and skillful means by which
beings are transformed
; that is, the rules of practice.

blocks.text: 2. Beginning with Buddha-Recitation

inline.s: Master Hanshan was ordained and left home at nineteen, and at once gave himself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation. In the Autobiographical Chronological Account the Master writes:
So I gave myself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation, day and night without interruption. Before long
(after reciting in this way for a short while)
, one night in a dream I saw Amitābha Buddha appear, standing in the sky where the sun had set. I saw his face and eyes, his light and marks, perfectly clear. I received his feet with my head
(I knelt and received the Buddha's two feet in my hands, touching them with my head)
, grieving and longing without end. I then vowed to see the two great bodhisattvas Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta
(I further vowed to see Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva)
, and at once they appeared half-length
(Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva at once showed themselves half-length)
. From that time on the Three Sages were ever radiant before my eyes
(from then on the Three Sages shone before his eyes at all times)
, and I was confident that my cultivation could be accomplished
(and so he believed that his own cultivation could attain the fruit)
[The Three Sages] The Three Sages of the West: Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva.

blocks.text: 3. Realizing the Way at Mount Wutai

inline.s: At the age of thirty Master Hanshan realized the Way at Mount Wutai. In the Autobiographical Chronological Account the Master writes:
One day, when the gruel was finished and I was walking in meditation, I suddenly stood still
(I suddenly stood rooted in samādhi)

, seeing neither body nor mind — only one great treasury of light, perfect and utterly still, like a great round mirror, in which the mountains, rivers, and the great earth appeared as reflections. When I came out of it
(when I emerged from samādhi)
, all was luminous
(all was one brightness)

, and I looked for body and mind and could not find them at all. At once I spoke a verse: ‘A sudden thought, and the mad mind rests; within and without, the senses and their objects are wholly clear. I turn and strike the great empty space — the myriad forms in their teeming array arise and cease with it.’ From then on, within and without were utterly still, and sound, voice, form, and appearance no longer obstructed me; all my former doubt and bewilderment melted away on the spot. When I looked at the pot (the cooking pot), it had already gathered dust.

(when he returned to the room he saw that a thick layer of dust had gathered on the rice pot; because he lived alone without a companion and had no one to ask the time, he did not know how long had passed)

blocks.text: 4. Spreading the Pure Land

inline.s: All his life Master Hanshan spread the Pure Land with all his might. Master Ouyi, the Ninth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, when teaching that the Pure Land is the Dharma-gate for transcending birth and death, said:

Moreover, in this age of decline, the false teachers who expound the Dharma are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the blind lead the blind, and all are drawn together into the pit of fire. Therefore Master Yongming said: “Without Chan but with the Pure Land, ten thousand practice and ten thousand arrive.” “With Chan but without the Pure Land, nine out of ten go astray.” And our Master Hanshan also said: “If in these times one has Chan but no Pure Land, why speak of nine out of ten going astray — I would venture to say that eleven out of ten are still here.” All these are words of deep compassion and great mercy, true words and real words. I bow and pray: good people all, do not fall into the wild wastes of the perverse and the shallow! You must simply and keenly bear in mind impermanence, believe and vow, recite the Buddha's name, and seek rebirth in the Pure Land. If this body is not delivered in this life, in what other life will this body be delivered?”
(“A Universal Discourse Delivered at the Renyi Cloister, Fengnan, Shexi”)
Master Ouyi himself also held Master Hanshan in the highest esteem. In the autobiography he wrote in his later years, Master Ouyi says:

At twenty-three... I resolved to leave home and investigate the great matter. At twenty-four I dreamed of bowing to Master Hanshan, and wept with regret that my karmic fortune was so poor and that we had met too late.... Within one month I dreamed of Master Hanshan three times. The Master was on his way to Caoxi, and I could not follow him so far. So I was ordained under Master Xueling, who gave me the name Zhixu. Master Xue was a disciple of Master Hanshan.”
At the same time, Master Hanshan and Master Lianchi, the Eighth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, shared a deep bond of Dharma friendship. Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream Wanderings
Autobiographical Chronological Account says:
In the fourth year
(the fourth year of the Wanli era)

, bingzi, I was thirty-one. In the third month of spring, Master Lianchi passed through Mount Wutai and came to visit; he stayed several days, and we talked heart to heart at night with great accord.”
In the forty-fifth year, dingsi, I was seventy-two. In the first month of spring I went down to Shuangjing to mourn at Yunqi
(Master Lianchi)

, where more than a thousand monastic and lay disciples had long awaited me in the mountains. I stayed twenty days, and every night at the minor gathering they heard the Dharma, each one rejoicing, as I set forth Master Lianchi's hidden practices through his whole life
(which shows how deeply Master Hanshan knew Master Lianchi)
. When the disciples heard it, some were moved to tears, saying that I had revealed what others did not know
(they thought that what I told was known to no one else)
, and they asked me to compose a stupa inscription
(the Stupa Inscription for Master Yunqi Lianchi Hong)
The Stupa Inscription for Master Yunqi Lianchi Hong, written by Master Hanshan, is deeply moving; its full text appears at the end of this piece.

blocks.text: 5. Reciting the Buddha and Copying the Sutras

inline.s: Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream Wanderings
Autobiographical Chronological Account says:
In the fifth year
(the fifth year of the Wanli era)
, dingchou, I was thirty-two. In spring I returned from Yanmen, and because I reflected that the boundless
(limitless)

kindness of my father and mother could never be repaid, and that in the Dharma I was beset by many obstacles, and because I had seen the vow-text of Master Si of Nanyue I resolved to prick my finger and write out in blood-ground gold one copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra, thus forming above a supreme prajñā-bond and below repaying the boundless kindness of my parents; in the spring of that year I conceived the plan. Before this, the holy Empress Dowager Cisheng
(the holy Empress Dowager Li, principal mother of the Ming Shenzong emperor, a devout Buddhist and most generous in giving, whom the people of the capital called the Buddha Old Lady)
had chosen monks to recite sutras for the protection of the nation, and I presumptuously
(jian
jiàn
, a term of self-deprecation)
had my name enrolled. When I arrived there
(when I got there)
, word reached the throne that I would copy the sutras
(the Empress Dowager heard that I intended to
prick my finger and write the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood-ground gold
, and at once she bestowed gold and paper to assist me. In the fourth month of the following year I began to copy the sutras
(began to write the sutras)

[Pricking the finger to write one copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood-ground gold] To draw the fresh blood from one's tongue, mix it with gold powder, and write out one copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra. Master Yinguang says: “When Master Hanshan wrote out the sutras, it was the Empress Dowager who supplied the paper and the gold. The paper for writing in gold must be blue for the characters to show; on white paper they do not show.... Thus Hanshan, at Miaode Hermitage on Mount Wutai, pricked his tongue, ground the blood with gold, and wrote out the Avatamsaka Sutra.” (Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, First Letter in Reply to Master Hongyi)
In the sixth year
(the sixth year of the Wanli era)
, wuyin, I was thirty-three. I applied my mind wholly
(with single-minded attention)
to copying the sutras; no matter whether the dot or stroke was large or small, with every stroke that fell I recited the Buddha's name once.”
Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Chan Practitioner Xingchu on Copying Sutras says:
In former days, when this old man
(Master Hanshan's self-reference)

dwelt at Mount Wutai, he pricked his finger and wrote out the great Avatamsaka Sutra in blood-ground gold. In the midst of that writing, regardless of the dots and strokes of the characters, their size or length, with every stroke set down he recited the Buddha's name once. Thus, dot after dot and stroke after stroke, the light of the mind streamed forth, thought after thought unbroken and unforgotten, without error and without omission. After a long time it no longer mattered whether he was writing or not, and even in dreams it all became one piece. From this, amid all the states of turmoil and clamor, his mind remained utterly still, and he attained the gate of liberation, sovereign and unobstructed in all states; indeed all that he saw and heard was nothing but the true sutra appearing before him.”

blocks.text: 6. The Essential Meaning of Buddha-Recitation

inline.s: Master Hanshan constantly instructed students in Buddha-recitation, and this is found everywhere in the Collection of Dream Wanderings. Especially in the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Reply to the Questions of Prince De he gives an instruction on how to recite the Buddha's name that is most penetrating; I now excerpt and annotate it as follows:

[Throughout the six periods of the day, simply place the one sound “Amitābha Buddha” across your chest, never forgetting it in any thought, never dull in any mind. Give no thought at all to the affairs of the world, but take this one phrase of the Buddha as your own root of life. Bite down with set teeth and never let it go, so that even in eating, drinking, rising, and resting, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, this one sound of the Buddha is ever present before you.]

The Buddha's name is the very root of life for ending birth and death and escaping the wheel of rebirth; it may not be parted from for even a moment. Walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, this one sound of the Buddha's name is ever present before you.
This is to say: first, attain an unbroken recitation of the Buddha.
[If you meet with states of adversity or favor, of joy, anger, or affliction, and your mind is not at peace, then take up this
(this)
one sound of the Buddha, raise it and press it home, and you will see the affliction vanish on the spot. For to think affliction
(to use thought to dwell on affliction)
is the bitter root of birth and death; now to use Buddha-recitation to dissolve affliction
(now to use the thought of the Buddha to dissolve affliction)
is precisely where the Buddha delivers beings from the suffering of birth and death
(it is precisely where Amitābha Buddha delivers beings from the suffering of birth and death)
. If Buddha-recitation can dissolve affliction, then birth and death can be ended, and there is no other method.]

What your thoughts are determines your next life. To dwell on affliction is to enter the wheel of birth and death; to recite the Buddha's name is to leave the wheel of birth and death. Bear it firmly in mind: “If Buddha-recitation can dissolve affliction, then birth and death can be ended, and there is no other method.”
[Press home (zā)] To squeeze and press.
Second, attain a recitation of the Buddha that dissolves affliction.

[If by reciting the Buddha's name you become master even in the midst of affliction, then you will be master in dreams; if you are master in dreams, then you will be master in sickness and pain; if you are master in sickness and pain, then at the end of life you will be clear and lucid and will know where you are going.]
Then, reciting the Buddha until you are master over affliction, master in dreams, and master in sickness and pain.

[This matter is not hard to practice; it only requires that one thought be in earnest about birth and death, and that you simply lean steadily on the one sound of the Buddha, seeking nothing else. After long familiarity you will naturally attain great peace, ease, and freedom, and gain great joy and benefit — by no means comparable to the pleasures of the five desires of the world.]

When the mind set on ending birth and death is earnest, there is naturally no hard matter. The point is to practice it gradually and to persevere; where sincere devotion reaches, stone and metal open.

[The five desires] Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form means beautiful appearances; sound means melodious sounds; smell means fragrant scents; taste means delicious flavors; touch means pleasing sensations of contact. Because these five can cause people to give rise to a mind of craving, they are called the five desires.

blocks.text: 7. Reciting the Buddha and Investigating Chan

inline.s: For a very long time the two sides, Chan and Pure Land, had contended without resolution, as incompatible as fire and water. Master Hanshan, standing at a higher vantage, unified Chan and Pure Land: Buddha-recitation is itself Chan investigation. Master Hanshan taught:
If we take mind-only Pure Land
(if we speak from the standpoint of mind-only Pure Land)

, then when the mind is pure the land is pure. Therefore, when one first investigates Chan and has not yet awakened, without Buddha-recitation there is no way to purify one's own mind — yet a purified mind is itself the awakened mind. The bodhisattva, having awakened, does not abandon Buddha-recitation; thus without Buddha-recitation there would be no way to attain perfect enlightenment. How do we know the patriarchs did not awaken the mind through Buddha-recitation? If one recites the Buddha's name to the point of single-mindedness without distraction, with afflictions dissolved and one's own mind clearly understood, that is called awakening — and so Buddha-recitation is itself Chan investigation. If one is like the bodhisattva, then one does not abandon Buddha-recitation after awakening. Hence all the patriarchs of old did not abandon the Pure Land. In this way, Buddha-recitation is itself Chan investigation, and Chan investigation is itself birth in the Pure Land.”
(Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Chan Practitioner Hui Jingxin)

[Buddha-recitation is itself Chan investigation] Chan investigation is meant to purify the mind so as to awaken it. The passage above says: “When one first investigates Chan and has not yet awakened, without Buddha-recitation there is no way to purify one's own mind.” “If one recites the Buddha's name to the point of single-mindedness without distraction, with afflictions dissolved and one's own mind clearly understood, that is called awakening — and so Buddha-recitation is itself Chan investigation.” “How do we know the patriarchs did not awaken the mind through Buddha-recitation?” Therefore, Buddha-recitation is itself Chan investigation. Moreover, the excellence of this kind of Chan investigation is that one need not cut off afflictions utterly in order to end birth and death. Hence Buddha-recitation is the ultimate teaching that gathers in the three capacities, wholly encompasses the sudden and the gradual, and is accomplished within a single lifetime.

Buddha-recitation is itself Chan investigation; there is no second Dharma. When reciting the Buddha's name, one must first set down all at once every affliction, deluded thought, greed, anger, and craving, and every kind of jumbled thought in one's breast. Set them down until there is nowhere left to set them down, then take up the single sound “Amitābha Buddha,” clear and distinct, unbroken in the mind, like a thread running through pearls, or like arrow-nocks fitted one to another with not the slightest gap between. Lean steadily upon it with such effort, and in all places you will not be dragged away or lose it to circumstances. Day in and day out, in the midst of activity, undefiled and undistracted, waking and dreaming as one — working in this way until at the end of life you are single-minded without distraction, that is the hour of transcending birth and death in the Pure Land.”
(Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Chan Practitioner Ning Xutong)
[Unbroken in the mind] The mind's recollection is unbroken. [Arrow-nocks fitted together] Arrow joined to arrow, head to tail. Nock (kuò): the end of an arrow.

In this Dharma-gate, first, one must have a settled resolve; second, one must be able to let go; third, one must be able to follow conditions — and to follow conditions is simply to be at peace with one's lot; fourth, one must recognize the truth, and to recognize the truth is to be free of doubt; fifth, one must be keenly weary of suffering — for when the weariness of suffering is keen, the thoughts of desire are of themselves removed, and one will not retreat or bend. With these five keys, hold to the single thought alone.”

(Translation: In this Dharma-gate, first, one must have a settled resolve; second, one must be able to let go; third, one must be able to follow conditions — and to follow conditions is simply to be at peace with one's lot; fourth, one must recognize the truth, and to recognize the truth is to be free of doubt; fifth, one must be keenly weary of suffering — for when the weariness of suffering is keen, the thoughts of desire are of themselves removed, and one will not retreat or bend. With these five keys, hold to the single thought alone.) (
Collection of Dream Wanderings
To the Two Masters Chen Jiannan)

blocks.text: 8. Diligent Cultivation of the Pure Karma

inline.s: Master Hanshan himself put this into practice, reciting the Buddha's name and attaining rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. In a letter from his later years the Master writes:

And I fear that I have not many days left, and my mind is in earnest about birth and death; so I have shut myself away and cut off all ties, holding to the single thought alone, waiting only for death
(to the end of my life)
. Yesterday, at the Mid-Autumn Festival, I had already begun this
(yesterday, the Mid-Autumn Festival, I had already entered retreat, cut off all ties, and taken up the single sound of the Buddha's name)

. For more than twenty years I have thought of the storms of the sea of suffering; green hills and white clouds have often been in my dreams. Now that I have suddenly obtained my wish, how could I be content to treat it lightly? Here in retreat
(within the retreat)
I have put aside all Chan talk and Dharma matters, shelving them high, and simply keep to my dull simplicity
(single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name; “keeping to dull simplicity” here means no longer investigating Chan or studying the teachings)

. I often think how the ancients recited Amitābha a hundred thousand times a day and night; now I am ashamed that, old and weak, my physical strength is insufficient, and when I test myself I can usually manage a little more than half. Therefore I follow the example of Master Yuan
(Master Huiyuan)
in the six-period lotus-clock
(the “lotus clock” was the water-clock devised with a lotus by Huiyao, a disciple of Huiyuan, the First Patriarch of the Pure Land school, for marking time at the Mount Lu Way-place)
, using incense in place of the flower
(I use burning incense to mark the time instead of a lotus water-clock)
. For several months now, body and mind have of themselves reached Ultimate Bliss. Knowing how deeply you care for me
(knowing how much you care for me)
, I venture to tell you of it
(and so I take the liberty of telling you)
(Collection of Dream Wanderings
Reply to the Hanlin Scholar Qian Shouzhi)
Please note the phrase “for several months now, body and mind have of themselves reached Ultimate Bliss” — this is a portrait of the Master's state of Buddha-recitation in his later years.

blocks.text: 9. Directing All to the Pure Land

inline.s: Master Hanshan not only recited the Buddha's name himself and sought rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, but also insisted with all his might that every Dharma-gate should point toward the Pure Land.

[Master Hanshan not only recited the Buddha's name himself and sought rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss] Master Hanshan entered nirvāṇa on the thirteenth day of the tenth month of the third year of the Tianqi era (
), at the age of seventy-eight. According to the Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan:
“At noon
the thirteenth day of the tenth month
at noon)
, Lord Zhang
(Governor Zhang Sanxing of Shaoyang, who had come into the mountains with a purple silk Chan robe as a birthday gift for the Master;
the twelfth day of the tenth month
was the Master's birthday)

took his leave, and at once the Master called an attendant to fetch pure water to rinse his mouth, saying: ‘Today I cut off the trailing vines.’ Then he called for hot water to bathe and change his robes, and
the assembly gathered around reciting the Buddha's name
. He instructed them: ‘Do not be alarmed. Follow the Buddha's rule: do not wear hemp or mourning, do not weep and wail, but
recite the Buddha's name with one mind
.’ At the third hour of the afternoon
(three o'clock in the afternoon)

the Master sat upright and passed away. That night a radiant light illumined the sky, flocks of birds cried out in grief, and monks and laity alike wailed in sorrow, their voices shaking the valleys. After his passing he sat upright for three days, his face fair, his lips red, his hands and feet soft, as though entered into samādhi.”
This shows that Master Hanshan attained rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
In the Collection of Dream Wanderings

Preface to Directing the Mind to the Pure Land, the Master writes: “As for the one gate of the Pure Land, it universally covers the three capacities, the sudden and the gradual enter it alike, and there is no capacity it does not gather in; this is what is called transcending the three realms horizontally, and it is the most supreme of Dharma-gates. Among all the patriarchs and those who have awakened the mind, there has never been one who did not take this as his final refuge — as with Nagarjuna (Nagarjuna Bodhisattva) and Ashvaghosha (Ashvaghosha Bodhisattva), who praised it with all their might.” “Among Chan practitioners of the highest faculties, there is none who does not return to the Pure Land.” I now excerpt and annotate that essay as follows:

[“Directing to the Pure Land” means directing the practitioner to return to the Pure Land. Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, gathering and transforming the multitudes of beings, taught Dharma-gates whose skillful means were not of one kind. Yet the essential purport from first to last comprises the two schools of nature and form. Because the capacities of beings are great or small, the teachings are set forth as sudden or gradual. In the end they are divided into the two gates of Chan and the teachings: the teachings draw in and gather the three capacities, while Chan suddenly awakens to the one mind. As with the whole Great Treasury of Sutras and the seventeen hundred koans, this has been so from ancient times.]

“Directing to the Pure Land” means guiding practitioners to return to the Pure Land. Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, gathered and transformed the multitudes of beings, teaching according to capacity, and the Dharma-gates he spoke were many and various. Yet the essential purport from first to last comprises the Dharma-nature school and the Dharma-form school. This is because the capacities of beings are great or small, and so the teachings are set forth as sudden or gradual. In the end they are divided into the two gates of Chan and the teachings. The gate of the teachings draws in and gathers the three capacities (high, middling, and low), while the gate of Chan suddenly awakens to the one mind. As with the whole Great Treasury of Sutras and the seventeen hundred koans, this has all along been the drawing in of the three capacities and the sudden awakening to the one mind.

[The two schools of nature and form] The Dharma-nature school (abbreviated the nature school) and the Dharma-form school (abbreviated the form school). [The one mind] Another name for the original nature, the Buddha-nature, the tathagata-garbha. Master Hanshan's Notes on the Lankavatara Sutra says: “Deluded as to the one mind, it becomes the eight consciousnesses.” It also says: “That which is quiescent is called the one mind; the one mind is called the tathagata-garbha.” This means: when the tathagata-garbha (the original nature) is deluded, it turns into the storehouse of consciousness (the habitual nature) and there arise the eight consciousnesses: alaya-consciousness, manas, mental consciousness, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says: “The self is the meaning of the tathagata-garbha. All beings possess the Buddha-nature; this is the meaning of self. This meaning of self has from the beginning been constantly covered by measureless afflictions, and so beings cannot see it.” It also says: “The true self spoken by the Tathagata today is called the Buddha-nature.”

[As for the one gate of the Pure Land, it universally covers the three capacities, the sudden and the gradual enter it alike, and there is no capacity it does not gather in; this is what is called transcending the three realms horizontally, and it is the most supreme of Dharma-gates. Among all the patriarchs and those who have awakened the mind, there has never been one who did not take this as his final refuge — as with Nagarjuna and Ashvaghosha, who praised it with all their might.]

As for this one gate of the Pure Land, it universally covers the three capacities, the sudden and the gradual enter it alike, and there is no capacity it does not gather in; this is what is called transcending the three realms horizontally, and it is the most supreme of Dharma-gates. Among all the patriarchs, those who have realized and awakened to the one mind, there has never been one who did not take this as his final refuge — Nagarjuna Bodhisattva and Ashvaghosha Bodhisattva, for example, both praised it with all their might.

[Transcending the three realms horizontally] The Pure Land Dharma-gate transcends the three realms horizontally to end birth and death, whereas other Dharma-gates leave the three realms vertically (by cutting off afflictions utterly) to end birth and death. Master Yinguang says: “If we speak of leaving vertically, nothing will do but the vigorous cultivation of the Way of precepts, concentration, and wisdom and the utter cutting off of affliction and delusion. If affliction and delusion are not entirely exhausted, the three realms still cannot be left. How much more so for beings in the Dharma-ending age, shallow in roots of goodness and short in lifespan: though those who practice number in the billions, those who escape are scarcely one or two in a million. Because they rely solely on self-power, they seldom gain real benefit. If we speak of transcending horizontally, one need only rely on the Pure Land Dharma-gate: give rise to faith, make the vow, recite the Buddha's name, and seek rebirth in the West. Together with honoring moral duty, fulfilling one's part, avoiding all evil, and practicing all good, then not one in ten thousand will be missed, and all will attain rebirth. Once reborn, one ends birth and death, transcends the ordinary and enters the sage, forever leaving all suffering and receiving only every joy. Those whose practice is mature surely ascend to the highest grade; those who recite only at the end of life also join the lowest ranks. This relies entirely on the Buddha's power, and its benefit is as far from that of relying solely on self-power as heaven is from an abyss.” (Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Preface to the Founding of the Hengchao Lotus Society)

[Those who speak of it suppose that it merely lifts up the middling and the low; they are not people who know the purport of the Pure Land. Why so? Because all beings in the worlds of the ten directions, in their primary and dependent retributions, though they differ as superior or inferior, pure or defiled, are all transformations sensed by the one mind. Hence it is said, “When the mind is pure, the land is pure” — this is what is called mind-only Pure Land. Thus the land is not outside the mind; purity comes from the one mind. If one is not a person who has awakened the mind, how could one purify one's land? This is why among Chan practitioners of the highest faculties there is none who does not return to the Pure Land.]

Those who discuss the matter suppose that the Pure Land Dharma-gate exists only to lift up those of middling and low capacity; this is because they do not know the purport of the Pure Land. Why? Because all beings in the worlds of the ten directions, in their dependent retribution (environment) and primary retribution (body and mind), though they differ as superior or inferior, pure or defiled, are all transformations sensed by the one mind. When the mind is pure, it senses and transforms into a superior, pure dependent and primary retribution; when the mind is defiled, it senses and transforms into an inferior, defiled dependent and primary retribution. Hence it is said, “When the mind is pure, the land is pure” — this is what is called mind-only Pure Land. Therefore the land is not outside the mind; the purity of the land comes entirely from the purity of the one mind. If one is not a person who has realized and awakened the one mind, how could one purify one's land? Hence among Chan practitioners of the highest faculties there is none who does not return to the Pure Land; this is the reason.

[Primary and dependent retribution] Primary retribution refers to the body and mind of sentient beings; this is the principal fruit of retribution summoned by past karmic causes, and so it is called primary retribution. Dependent retribution is the environment on which body and mind (primary retribution) depend; this too is a fruit of retribution summoned by past karmic causes, such as lands, mountains and rivers, the great earth, houses, and implements.

[Those of middling and low capacity keep the pure precepts, concentrate the mind single-mindedly, and continue contemplation and recitation without interruption; at the end of life they are certain to attain rebirth. Though there are marks of going and coming, the excellent marks of Amitābha, the jeweled trees and flower terraces, are in truth manifestations sensed by one's own mind — like the affairs of a dream, which do not come from outside. As for foolish men and women who merely cultivate the ten good deeds, carefully keep the five precepts, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name, at the end of life they too are certain to attain rebirth: this is because the Buddha's power adds its support, and the practitioner's thought and contemplation grow stronger. The practitioner brings superior contemplation, the Buddha brings his great vow; vow meets thought, and one's own mind and the Buddha silently respond to each other. Though the realm of the Pure Land has not yet appeared, the work of rebirth is already accomplished: it is in truth the power of the one mind's hidden resonance, and is not something external either. As for those of the ten evil deeds, at the end of life their karma is stronger, and the sufferings of hell already appear before them; but because suffering presses them to the extreme and the wish to escape suffering is keen, the mind of extreme suffering becomes the power of thought, and they exhaust their remorse. When remorse is at its utmost, at that very extreme the whole is transformed, and a single thought accords with the Buddha. Thus the Buddha's power adds its support, and it appears before them as they think: knife-mountains of hell are transformed into jeweled trees of the Pure Land, the cauldron of fire into a lotus pool, and so these evil ones too attain rebirth. Yet this realm of the Pure Land comes about through the work of the whole mind's transformation, and is in truth not obtained from outside.]

Those of middling and low capacity keep the pure precepts, concentrate the mind single-mindedly, and continue contemplation and recitation without interruption; at the end of life they are certain to attain rebirth. Though there are marks of going and coming, the excellent marks of Amitābha, the jeweled trees and flower terraces, are in truth manifestations sensed by one's own mind — like the affairs of a dream, which do not come from outside. As for foolish men and women who merely cultivate the ten good deeds, carefully keep the five precepts, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name, at the end of life they too are certain to attain rebirth: this is because the Buddha's power adds its support, and the practitioner's thought and contemplation grow stronger. The practitioner brings superior contemplation, the Buddha brings his great vow; vow meets thought, and one's own mind and the Buddha silently respond to each other. Though the realm of the Pure Land has not yet appeared, the work of rebirth is already accomplished: it is in truth the power of the one mind's hidden resonance, and is not something external either. As for those of the ten evil deeds, at the end of life their karma is stronger, and the sufferings of hell already appear before them; but because suffering presses them to the extreme and the wish to escape suffering is keen, the mind of extreme suffering becomes the power of thought, and they exhaust their remorse. When remorse is at its utmost, at that very extreme the whole is transformed, and a single thought accords with the Buddha. Thus the Buddha's power adds its support, and it appears before them as they think: knife-mountains of hell are transformed into jeweled trees of the Pure Land, the cauldron of fire into a lotus pool, and so these evil ones too attain rebirth. Yet this realm of the Pure Land comes about through the work of the whole mind's transformation, and is in truth not obtained from outside.

[Looking at it from this, among the ten thousand dharmas of the three realms there is not one dharma that does not arise from the mind; among the realms of purity and defilement there is not one realm that does not appear from the mind. Therefore the one gate of the Pure Land, whether one is awakened or not, whether of high wisdom or low folly, is such that all who practice it are certain to attain — all by virtue of their own mind. Thus the purport of mind-only Pure Land is as clear as looking at black and white. Because the Buddha's essence is like space and one's own mind is pure like space, one is silently one with the Buddha; only by borrowing the adornment of a single thought of vow-power does the realm of the Pure Land at once appear, without relying on merit and rank. This is the supreme of the supreme, and by no means within the reach of the shallow in wisdom and thin in faith.]

Looking at it from this, among the ten thousand dharmas of the three realms there is no dharma that is not a transformation sensed by the mind; among the realms of purity and defilement there is no realm that does not appear from the mind. Therefore the one gate of the Pure Land, whether one is awakened or not, whether of high wisdom or low folly, is such that all who practice it are certain to attain — all by virtue of their own mind. Thus the purport of mind-only Pure Land becomes perfectly clear (as clear as looking at black and white). Because the Buddha's essence is like space, and the reciter's own mind is pure like space and silently one with the Buddha, only by borrowing the adornment of a single thought of vow-power does the realm of the Pure Land at once appear, without relying on merit, fruit, or rank; this is the supreme of the supreme Dharma-gate, and by no means something the shallow in wisdom and thin in faith can comprehend.

[Mysteriously one] To be merged and indistinct, so that self and other cannot be distinguished, is called being mysteriously one. [Merit and rank] A Chan-forest term, referring to the fruits and stages of practice.

[Those of middling and low capacity, relying on the continuity of contemplation and recitation, are not toppled or carried off by the conditions of craving and the habits of karma; though their faculties are somewhat inferior, their resolve is truly supreme. Yet the practice of it is only difficult because cutting off the root of craving is difficult. For the evil, rebirth is even harder: though it is called “bringing karma along,” it too comes about through the inner perfuming of good roots habituated over many lives; their faculties, though evil and inferior, are such that a single thought of fierce courage surpasses the supreme. Compared with those who “put down the butcher's knife and at once do the Buddha's work,” they are a little ahead. Yet such a one is not found once in ten thousand thousand; if worldly people were certainly to wait for this before seeking rebirth, they would be greatly mistaken. As I see it, faculties are neither great nor small; in the end one must attain accomplishment through a single thought directed upward. How then could this Dharma-gate have been established provisionally only for those of middling and low capacity?]

Those of middling and low capacity, relying on the continuity of contemplation and recitation, are not toppled or carried off by the conditions of craving and the habits of karma; though their faculties are somewhat inferior, their resolve is truly supreme. Moreover the practice of it is only difficult because cutting off the root of craving is difficult. For the evil, rebirth is even harder: though it is called “bringing karma along,” it too comes about through the inner perfuming of good roots habituated over many lives; their faculties, though evil and inferior, are such that a single thought of fierce courage surpasses the supreme. Compared with those who “put down the butcher's knife and at once do the Buddha's work,” they are a little ahead. Yet such a one among the evil who attains rebirth at the end of life is not found once in ten thousand thousand; if worldly people were to rely on this method to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, they would be greatly mistaken. As I see it, faculties are neither great nor small; in the end one must attain accomplishment through a single thought directed upward (from delusion into awakening). How then could this Dharma-gate have been established provisionally only for those of middling and low capacity?

[The root of craving] Craving and desire as the root of affliction give rise to other afflictions, and so are called the root of craving. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “In the cycle of rebirth, craving is the root.” [A single thought directed upward] The turning of the mind from delusion into awakening.
In the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Pure Practitioner Xiyin, Who Devoted Himself to the Pure Land, Master Hanshan says:

[The people of the world know only that in the patriarchs' gate, awakening is held to be supreme. But the original intent of awakening the mind is to escape birth and death — is Buddha-recitation not then a Dharma for escaping birth and death? Those who investigate Chan mostly do not escape it, while those who recite the Buddha's name escape birth and death beyond doubt. The reason is that Chan investigation requires detaching from thought, while Buddha-recitation consists in focusing thought. Because
(because)

beings have long been sunk in deluded thought, detaching from it is truly hard; but to turn defiled thought into pure thought is to use poison against poison, a method of exchange. Hence Chan investigation is hard to awaken through, while Buddha-recitation is easy to accomplish. If one is truly in earnest about birth and death, and recites the Buddha with the mind of one investigating Chan, what fear is there that a single life will not end birth and death?]

The people of the world know only that in the patriarchs' gate, awakening the mind is held to be supreme. Yet the original intent of awakening the mind is to escape birth and death — is Buddha-recitation not then a Dharma for escaping birth and death? Those who investigate Chan mostly cannot escape birth and death, while those who recite the Buddha's name escape birth and death beyond doubt. The reason is that Chan investigation requires detaching from thought, while Buddha-recitation consists in focusing thought. Because beings have long been sunk in deluded thought through beginningless kalpas, to detach from deluded thought entirely is truly hard. But to turn defiled thought into pure thought is to use poison against poison, replacing deluded thoughts with the Buddha's name — a method of exchange, and so it is easy. Hence Chan investigation is hard to awaken through, while Buddha-recitation is easy to accomplish. If one is truly in earnest about birth and death, and recites the Buddha with the mind of one investigating Chan, what fear is there that a single life will not end birth and death?

blocks.text: 10. Auspicious Signs at Rebirth

inline.s: Master Hanshan's lifelong practice began with Buddha-recitation and ended with Buddha-recitation, and he took “various spiritual signs as the proof of rebirth.” (Master Chewu, the Twelfth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, says: “Take various spiritual signs as the proof of rebirth.” See the Bequeathed Collection of Master Chewu.)
The Praise of the Portraits of the Eighty-Eight Patriarchs records that Master Hanshan

in the dingsi year returned to Mount Lu and built the Dharma Cloud Temple below Wuru Peak, where he followed Master Yuan in the six-period water-clock and devoted himself to the Pure Land karma. In the renxu year of the Tianqi era he again dwelt at Caoxi. On the eleventh day of the tenth month of the guihai year he showed a slight illness, bathed and burned incense, and gathered the assembly to take his leave. Looking back at them he said: “Today I cut off the trailing vines.” He sat upright and passed away. He lived seventy-eight years and had sixty years of monastic seniority.... Earlier, in the yichou year, his coffin-shrine was returned to the stupa of Dharma Cloud Temple below Wuru Peak on Mount Lu and there enshrined. In the guiwei year of the Chongzhen era the people of Guangdong again received his shrine and brought it back to Caoxi. Twenty years having passed, he sat upright as if alive, and so his body was lacquered in gold and raised to the seat, where it faces the bodily remains of the Sixth Patriarch, and is enshrined and offered to in the old stupa court on Tianshi Ridge, under the name Hanshan Cloister, about half a li from Nanhua Temple.”

[Trailing vines] A Chan-forest term. It means that words and language spread and interweave like the trailing vine, originally meant to explain and clarify a matter, yet one ends up bound and entangled by them. To make idle interruptions and talk nonsense is called “pulling trailing vines.”

[Twenty years having passed, he sat upright as if alive, and so his body was lacquered in gold and raised to the seat] After Master Hanshan entered nirvāṇa, his countenance remained as fair and smooth as jade, his lips as red and lustrous as ever, and his hands and feet as soft as before, just as when he was in samādhi. After the disciples escorted the Master's bodily remains to Mount Lu, because the climate there is damp and overcast, the attendant Fushan built a stupa court and enshrined the Master's shrine upon the stupa.

Twenty years later the disciples of Lingnan went to Mount Lu to welcome the Master back to Caoxi. When they reached Caoxi, the disciples guarding the shrine, Guangcheng and Cili, saw a crack in the shrine (xià
a fissure), and privately bored a small hole in the crack to
peep inside
, and saw the Master's bodily remains sitting upright as if alive,
and so they told the assembly,
who opened the shrine room and saw the Master seated cross-legged, as solemn as in life, his nails and hair still growing, his complexion still
red and moist

, and the purple silk robe and the string of beads still brand new. Then a gust of wind came, and the garment suddenly scattered like clouds and stars, dancing away on the wind; the local people gathered them up as an auspicious sign. Just then a monk suddenly appeared and asked leave to use the Indian method of preserving
the body
to protect the Master's remains

With the assembly's consent, he smeared the Master's body with sandalwood powder from Hainan, so that outwardly it looked as if coated with a layer of lacquer. When the monk had finished, he simply went away. In his lifetime a devout woman of Caoxi had vowed to embroider a robe of a thousand Buddhas as an offering to the Master; fearing that her breath might be impure, she covered her mouth with yellow silk as she embroidered it
When the robe of a thousand Buddhas was finished, the Master had already
entered nirvāṇa

and been placed in the shrine, and the robe was stored in the jeweled treasury of the storehouse. Now it was brought out again and draped over the Master's bodily remains; though twenty years had passed, it shone brightly, as if newly made. When the sealing of the shrine was complete, the disciples enshrined the Master in the old stupa court and changed its name to Hanshan Temple, about half a li from Nanhua Temple, where the bodily remains of the Sixth Patriarch rest. Following the custom of making offerings to the Sixth Patriarch, each morning the disciples used a bowl of hot fragrant water to steam the Master's face until it perspired, then wiped it dry with a towel, and afterward made offerings of food and drink as in life. Once a year they also bathed him. (Excerpted from
The Life of Master Hanshan

blocks.text: 11. Returning on the Vow

inline.s: Master Yinguang says: “Hanshan's former vow was not yet fulfilled, and so he appeared again in the world as Jieliu
(Master Xingce)
. He rebuked those who cultivate human and heavenly blessing, calling them outright icchantikas and chandalas
(nothing but icchantikas and chandalas)

. The Buddha's mind-nature and mine are originally no different; the Buddha is one already accomplished, I am one not yet cultivated. If you would have mind and Buddha be two no longer, you must seek by remembering the Buddha and reciting his name.”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · Master Xingce of Puren Monastery on Mount Yu, the Tenth Patriarch of the Qing)

[Icchantika] The abbreviation of “one who has severed all roots of goodness”: one who does not believe in cause and effect, commits the five rebellious offenses and the ten evil deeds, cuts off all roots of goodness, and falls into the Avici hell. [Chanda (zhān)] The abbreviation of chandala; here it means an evil person.
Master Xingce
, the Tenth Patriarch of the Pure Land school)

, a native of Yixing in Jiangsu, whose secular surname was Jiang and whose courtesy name was Jieliu. His father Quanchang was thoroughly versed in Confucianism and Buddhism, and was a close friend of Hanshan Deqing
(a bosom friend of Master Hanshan)
. Five years after Deqing entered stillness, Quanchang dreamed that he came into the room leaning on his staff, and then Xingce was born
(Quanchang dreamed that Master Hanshan came into the room leaning on his staff, and so Xingce was born)
, and so he named him Menghan, “Dreaming of Hanshan.” When he grew up, his parents passed away one after another, and he resolved to leave the world. At twenty-three he went to the Ruo
(ruò)
Hermitage of Li'an Temple in Wulin to leave home under Master Wen. For five years he did not let his ribs touch the mat
(he sat long and did not lie down)

, and suddenly penetrated the source of the Dharma. After Master Wen passed away, the Master dwelt at Bao'en Temple; he met his fellow practitioner Master Xi'an Ying, who urged him to cultivate the Pure Land karma. He also met Master Qiaoshi of Qiantang, who guided him through the Tiantai teachings, and together they entered a pure chamber to cultivate the Lotus Samādhi, where his past-life wisdom opened at once and he fathomed the marrow of the teachings. In the second year of the Kangxi era he built a hermitage among the streams and islets of Xixi on Mount Fahua in Hangzhou, devoting himself to the Pure Land karma, and named his dwelling the Lianfu Hermitage
(fu
fū
, the calyx of a flower)
. In the ninth year he dwelt at Puren Cloister on Mount Yu, where he founded a Lotus Society, and students flocked
(xī)
to take him as their master
(the students all praised him with one voice and followed him)
He once
wrote the Essay Exhorting the True Faith, saying:
The Buddha-recitation samādhi has come down from long ago
(its origin is far distant)
. Though it is said to be of high merit and easy to enter, yet practitioners in the age of decline rarely obtain spiritual results, all because
(all because)
their faith and vow are not single-minded, and they cannot guide their good practices, taking rebirth in the Pure Land as the essential aim
(for lack of taking rebirth in the Pure Land as the essential aim)

[Guiding practice by faith and vow] Using faith and vow to guide practice, and to bring it to fulfillment in practice. [Taking rebirth in the Pure Land as the essential aim] For one who recites the Buddha's name, rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss should be taken as the foremost matter.

Now that we have widely invited good companions to cultivate together the cause of the Pure Land, if we do not carefully examine our own resolve, how shall we know the essential path out of suffering? All of us who join this Dharma assembly must possess true and genuine faith. Without true faith, then though one recites the Buddha's name, keeps the fasts, releases living beings, and cultivates blessings, one is merely a good person of the world, rewarded with birth in a good place and the enjoyment of pleasures. And while enjoying those pleasures one creates karma; having created karma, one must fall into suffering. Seen with right eyes, such a one is only one step removed from the icchantika and the chandala. Is such a faith as this true faith? What is called true faith

First, one must believe that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are three with no difference. I am a Buddha not yet accomplished; Amitābha is a Buddha already accomplished; the nature of awakening is not two. Though I am confused, inverted, and deluded, the nature of awakening has never been lost. Though I have turned through kalpas of rebirth, the nature of awakening has never moved. Hence it is said: “A single thought turns the light around, and one is one with what was originally attained.”

Second, one must believe that I am the Buddha in principle and the Buddha in name, while Amitābha is the ultimate Buddha. Though the nature is not two, the station is as far apart as heaven and an abyss. If one does not single-mindedly invoke that Buddha and seek rebirth in that land, one will inevitably follow karma in turning and receive measureless suffering. This is what is meant by “the dharmakāya turning through the five paths, no longer called a Buddha but called a sentient being.”
[The Buddha in principle and the Buddha in name] The first two of the six identities of Buddhahood.

[The six identities of Buddhahood] The six stages that mark the practice of an ordinary being up to the attainment of Buddhahood. 1. The Buddha in principle: all sentient beings, though they turn through the six paths and dwell day after day amid the weariness of dust and affliction, turned away from the substance of awakening, nevertheless still possess the merit of Buddha-nature in full; hence “the Buddha in principle.” 2. The Buddha in name: whether from a good and wise teacher or from the scriptures, one hears that this very mind is inherently possessed of the Buddha-nature that is neither born nor dies, and through names and words one comprehends and understands it, suddenly having an awakening; hence “the Buddha in name.” 3. The Buddha in contemplation and practice: not only understanding the names, but going further to cultivate contemplation according to the teaching, so that the contemplation of the mind becomes clear and principle and wisdom correspond; hence “the Buddha in contemplation and practice.” (Principle and wisdom corresponding: principle is the objective realm contemplated, wisdom is the subjective wisdom that contemplates; “corresponding” means matching, that is, realm and wisdom match and words and deeds are one.) 4. The Buddha in resemblance: at this stage the practitioner, in contemplation and practice, contemplates ever more clearly and stills ever more deeply; though he has not truly awakened and realized, he resembles the principle as though truly realized; hence “the Buddha in resemblance.” 5. The Buddha in partial realization: after the ten faiths, breaking one part of ignorance and realizing one part of the three virtues, one enters the initial abiding and realizes the dharmakāya, and from then on becomes a great being of the dharmakāya. From the initial abiding onward, each stage breaks ignorance and realizes the three virtues, and up to equal awakening there are forty-one stages in all, breaking forty-one parts; hence “the Buddha in partial realization.” 6. The Buddha in ultimate realization: from equal awakening one breaks the last part of ignorance, so that delusion is exhausted and truth is pure, and one thoroughly realizes the tathagata-nature of true suchness inherently possessed by this very body, enters the station of wonderful awakening, and becomes a Buddha; hence “the Buddha in ultimate realization.”
[The three virtues]
1. The virtue of the dharmakāya
2. The virtue of prajñā
3. The virtue of liberation.

Third, one must believe that though I am deep in obstruction and heavy in karma, long dwelling in the realm of suffering, I am a sentient being within Amitābha's mind. And though Amitābha is adorned with ten thousand virtues and dwells far beyond a hundred thousand kotis of lands, he is the Buddha within my mind. Since mind and nature are not two, response and resonance naturally meet. It is as a magnet draws iron; there can be no doubt of it. This is what is meant by “remembering the Buddha and reciting the Buddha's name, one shall in the present or the future surely see the Buddha, and not be far from the Buddha.”
[The meeting of response and resonance] The response of sentient beings and the resonance of Amitābha Buddha mutually intersect.
