For one who possesses the true faith described above, even a hair’s-breadth of goodness, a mote of blessing, may be dedicated to the West and adorn the Pure Land — how much more so keeping the fast, upholding the precepts, releasing living creatures, giving in charity, reading and reciting the Great Vehicle, and making offerings to the Three Jewels: surely such deeds of goodness suffice to fill the provisions for the Pure Land.
(namely, all the good one does)
, and the merit will not be wasted.
Leaked-out (yǒu lòu)

Here it means a leaked-out cause: the karmic cause that brings about rebirth in the three realms (the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm). [Wasted (táng juān)] Thrown away to no purpose.
Once he held a seven-day intensive retreat, and wrote a piece to instruct the assembly, saying:

In the seven days of holding the Name, what matters is single-mindedness and no confusion — unbroken and unmixed. It is not that rapid or copious recitation is necessarily the better. Simply, neither hurried nor slow, densely hold the Name, so that within the mind the Buddha’s name stands out clear and distinct. Whether dressing or eating, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one line of the great Name continues densely without interruption, just like breathing; then the mind is neither scattered nor sunk in dullness. Holding the Name thus may be called single-minded diligence in practice.
(a man of the Way, one of the company of those who study the Way)
, one can directly realize that all dharmas are suchness
(“suchness,” along with dharma-nature and the real limit, are all alternative names for the true aspect of all dharmas)

, and are without duality. This is what is meant by: birth and Buddha are non-dual, self and other are non-dual, direct and circumstantial retribution are non-dual, pure and impure are non-dual, suffering and joy are non-dual, delight
(the same as “joy”)

and aversion are non-dual, taking up and letting go are non-dual, bodhi and affliction are non-dual, birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are non-dual. All these pairs of dharmas share one single mark; one path, pure. No need to force and arrange them
(to arrange)
; simply realize them as they truly are
(one simply realizes them as they truly are: all dharmas are suchness, without duality)

. When such realization is carried to its utmost, one suddenly merges with one’s original mind. Then one knows that dressing and eating are always samādhi; that laughter, anger, cursing, and scolding are nothing but Buddha-work; that the one mind and the distracted mind are, in the end, but idle talk. Through the six periods of the day and night, one looks and finds not so much as a hair’s breadth of any mark of difference; and though one recites
(the same as “recite”)

with the utmost sincerity, it is still the same as cursing aloud; though one cultivates with diligence, it is still asceticism within a dream. Understanding and penetrating thus is what makes one a true student of the Way, holding the Name with single-minded diligence.
The first single-mindedness
(single-mindedness in practice)
seems difficult but is easy; the latter single-mindedness
(single-mindedness in principle)

seems easy but is difficult. One who can attain only the former may be certain of rebirth in the Pure Land; one who can attain both may reach the highest grade. Yet both kinds of single-mindedness are matters within the reach of ordinary mortals
(both are things that ordinary beings can practice)
; all who have a mind may study them. Monastic and lay together in this hall
(monastics and laity)

, do not exalt the sage’s realm too high nor settle contentedly for what is base. Each of you must diligently spur body and mind: whether near, within seven days, or far, through a whole lifetime, always give rise to this faith and always cultivate this practice. Even if you do not attain
(even if you do not attain the state of merging with your own mind)
, the causes you plant are still strong, and you will be lodged in a grade
(the grade of being born transformationally within a lotus calyx)
in the lotus palace, certainly not in the middle or lower grades. But if after the seven days you set it aside as though you had never heard it, so that old familiar habits
(the habits of emotional clinging)
after all do not arise in you, while the new ground
(namely, Buddha-recitation)

remains hard to make familiar, and ignorance and karmic habit draw you and entangle you along, if you merely wish to claim merit from seven days, and those seven days have not even reached the field of single-mindedness — this is precisely what is meant by “scant roots of goodness, merit, and causal conditions.” How can you hope to be reborn in that land? You will cause the Buddha’s golden-mouthed and truthful words to be doubted as lies. Whose fault is that? You pure assembly of the seven days, I beg each of you to examine yourselves, and to admonish and encourage one another.

[Matter within the reach of ordinary mortals of the broad earth Matter belonging to this side of the ordinary mortal of the broad earth. The ordinary mortal of the broad earth is also called the ordinary mortal of the thin earth, meaning one in the stage of an ordinary being. [Broad earth (bó dì)] “Broad” means pressed upon; “broad earth” is the position of being pressed upon by all kinds of suffering, and it refers to the state of an ordinary being. The Pure Mind Precepts and Contemplation says: “The ordinary mortal of the broad earth, with a foul and vulgar body, has base and inferior karmic retribution.”

He dwelled at Puren for thirteen years; on the ninth day of the seventh month of the twenty-first year of Kangxi he passed away, aged fifty-five. At that time a man named Sun Han had died of illness, and after a day and a night came back to life, saying: “I was seized by the officers of the underworld and bound before King Yama. In the darkness I suddenly saw light blazing to the heavens and fragrant flowers filling the sky, while King Yama bowed to the ground to welcome the Master of the Western Return. I asked: who is this Master? He said: Jieliu
(that is, Master Xingce)
. Because the Master’s light shone upon me, I was released and sent back.” On that same day, a son of the Wu family died of illness, and after the second night
(the second night)
revived, telling in full what he had seen, just as Han had said.

A eulogy says: Master Hanshan, because his former vow was unfulfilled, returned to save living beings and appeared in birth as Master Jieliu. He spread the Pure Land teaching and urged people to rely solely on faith and vow to guide their practice, to hold the Name with diligence, and to understand the supreme truth. His sorting and selecting of Dharma-gates, and the regulations he set for the seven-day period of single-minded, diligent Buddha-recitation, exhausted the full range of Pure Land teaching in both understanding and practice, and are enough to serve later generations as a ford and a bridge. At his return to the West he was honored by the underworld authorities, an event like that of Yongming
(a great monk of the Song dynasty, the sixth patriarch of the Pure Land school)
. Truly, first patriarch and later patriarch — their measure
kuí
is one and the same
(their measure is one and the same)

[The supreme truth The highest and unsurpassed principle — that is, the supreme middle-way principle of neither emptiness nor existence, of true emptiness and wondrous existence. [Sorting and selecting the Dharma-gate] Master Jieliu wrote a piece called “Sorting and Selecting the Dharma-gate.” [Sorting and selecting] It is also written as “sorting out and sifting,” meaning to select. In the scriptures and treatises, “sorting and sifting” often means being well able to discern and choose the true Dharma. [Ford and bridge] A crossing and a bridge; here it is a metaphor for the methods and paths by which one may be saved.

blocks.text: Main Text: Selected Instructions of Master Hanshan, with Notes

inline.s: Note: the title of each instruction below was added by the annotator for ease of understanding and reference, and is not part of the original text.

blocks.text: 1. Resolving the Will to Renounce

inline.s: (from The Dream-Wandering Collection
, Instruction for the Chan Monk Wusheng Lu)

[When the ancients first aroused the mind, it was truly for the great matter of birth and death, and they resolved their will upon renunciation. Therefore they cut off love and took leave of kin, sought out teachers and visited friends, and endured every hardship. Mind after mind, thought after thought, it was only that the matter beneath their own feet was not yet clear; their grief and sorrow were urgent, as though they had lost father and mother. When they met a knower of the Way, it was like an infant finding its mother. If they obtained a word or half a phrase that opened and guided the ground of the mind, it was like the sick obtaining medicine. If a single thought matched, and the mind understood within, it was like the poor obtaining a treasure. They gave up body and life, and buried themselves unknown in base servitude, never shrinking from toil. Such were the Second Patriarch’s setting his mind at ease and cutting off his arm, the Sixth Patriarch’s carrying a stone at his waist, Baizhang’s taking on labor, Yangqi’s serving the assembly. All who have their names recorded in the lamp-transmission histories and whose light shines through a thousand ages came to it through bitter toil. Even the Buddhas of the past, seeking unsurpassed bodhi, gave up body and life as many times as there are motes of dust; there was no kind of body they did not take, and no body in which they did not practice austerities.

For a hundred kalpas they cultivated causes, and so attracted boundless offerings in the heavens and among men. Even the sons and grandsons of the Dharma-ending age still enjoy a single share of the merit in the white-hair light without exhausting it.
How could there be a Maitreya born so, or a Śākyamuni come about of itself!]

When the ancients first aroused the mind, it was truly in order to be freed from the great matter of birth and death, and they resolved their will to escape the round of rebirth. So they cut off love and took leave of kin to leave home, sought out teachers and visited friends in quest of the Way, and endured every hardship and bitterness. Mind after mind, thought after thought, it was only that their own great matter of birth and death was not yet clear; their grief and sorrow were urgent, as though they had lost father and mother. When they met a good and wise teacher, it was like an infant finding its mother. If they gained a word or half a phrase that opened and guided the ground of the mind, it was like the sick obtaining medicine. If a single thought corresponded, and the mind understood within, it was like the poor obtaining a treasure. They gave up body and life, and unknown and unnoticed took on base servitude, never once fearing hardship or weariness. Examples are the Second Patriarch Huike’s setting his mind at ease and cutting off his arm, the Sixth Patriarch’s carrying a stone at his waist to hull rice, Baizhang’s taking on labor, and Yangqi’s serving the assembly. All who have their names recorded in the lamp-transmission records and the Chan histories of the generations, whose light shines through a thousand ages, came to it through bitter toil. Even the Buddhas of the past, seeking unsurpassed bodhi, gave up body and life as many times as there are motes of dust; there was no kind of body they did not take, and no body in which they did not practice austerities. For a hundred kalpas they cultivated causes, and so attracted boundless offerings in the heavens and among men. Even the sons and grandsons of the Dharma-ending age all still enjoy a single share of the merit in Śākyamuni Buddha’s white-hair light without exhausting it. How could there be a Maitreya born so, or a Śākyamuni come about of itself!

[As though they had lost father and mother Grieving and broken-hearted as though one’s parents had died. Kǎo means father; bǐ means mother. [Giving up (pàn) body and life] To stake body and life. Here “pàn” is the ancient form of “pīn,” meaning to cast away. [Buried unknown] Also written as “land-sunken,” buried and unknown to others. [Never shrinking from toil] “Dàn” means to fear. [Setting the mind at ease and cutting off the arm] Huike (originally named Shenguang) studied the inner scriptures of the Tripiṭaka with great depth, and wished to seek Bodhidharma’s setting of his mind at ease, praying for the Way with the utmost earnestness. He stood all night in the snow, and when day broke was still not permitted to enter the chamber; thereupon he cut off his own left arm to show the sincerity of his seeking of the Way, and so was granted an audience with the Patriarch and awakened. Afterwards he received Bodhidharma’s robe and bowl and inherited the lineage of the Chan school as the Second Patriarch. [Baizhang’s taking on labor] Chan Master Baizhang established an agricultural Chan system of self-sufficiency, put forward the motto “A day without work is a day without food,” and practiced it himself: whenever there was work to be done, he always went before the assembly. The monk in charge, seeing that he took the lead in labor even in his old age, could not bear it, and urged him not to go down to the fields again, hiding his tools. When he could not find his tools anywhere, he would not eat, so as to carry through the principle of “A day without work is a day without food.” [Yangqi’s (qí) serving the assembly] Yangqi was the founding patriarch of the Yangqi branch of the Linji school in the Northern Song. Beneath the seat of Chan Master Ciming Yuan, the sixth patriarch of the Linji line, he personally took on duties, enduring a hundred thousand hardships and never shrinking from toil. [As many as motes of dust] A metaphor for an extremely great number. [Still enjoy a single share of the merit in the white-hair light without exhausting it] In the Scripture of the Buddha’s Treasury, the Buddha says: “There may be monks who, having left home and received the precepts under my Dharma, practice with diligence within this Dharma. Though the gods and men do not think of them, one who can single-mindedly and diligently walk the Way will in the end have no thought for what he needs in clothing and food. Why so? The Tathāgata’s treasury of merit is boundless and hard to exhaust. Śāriputra, after the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, of the hundred billion shares of the white-hair mark, a single share is offered to the śarīra and the disciples. Śāriputra, suppose all the people in the world should leave home and follow the Dharma in practice: of the hundred billion shares of the white-hair mark, not one would be exhausted. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s merit is thus boundless, and whatever food and drink and necessities the monks obtain are all sufficient. Śāriputra, the monks should think thus, and should not, for the sake of necessities, practice evil dharmas of wrong livelihood.”

[Grieving over the Dharma-ending age: far are we from the sages, and the model of the Dharma-gates has been swept away. We who have left home do not know what it is we are really about. From birth we have known only to fear hunger and cold and to seek fullness and warmth. Once inside the gate of emptiness, we drift along with vulgar habits, gossiping all day, holding our bellies and giving free rein to our feelings, letting the six senses run loose and piling up every kind of evil. We do not plow, yet eat fine food; we do not spin, yet wear good clothes. We consume the gifts of the faithful to no purpose and waste our time for nothing. We do not even know where birth comes from or where death goes. How should we know that cause and effect are hard to escape, that offense and blessing bring their exact return? When the day of the great limit comes, it is like a stone thrown into water. In the three evil paths the suffering is terrible; one retribution lasts five thousand kalpas, and when one may raise one’s head again, who knows on what day? Saying this, the pain is bitter and grieving. Looking at the people of the present, it is so in a ceaseless stream. Of those of our number whom one would hope to be true cultivators, they are like gold sifted from sand: it is not that there are none at all, but they are few indeed.]

Mourning the Dharma-ending age: far are we from the sages, and the model of the Buddha-gate has been swept away. We who have left home do not know what it is we have really left home for. From birth we have known only to fear hunger and cold and to covet fullness and warmth. Once inside the gate of emptiness, we still follow vulgar worldly habits, gossiping all day, laughing and giving free rein to our feelings, letting the six senses run loose and piling up every kind of evil. We do not plow, yet eat fine food; we do not spin, yet wear good clothes. We consume to no purpose the goods given by the faithful and waste our precious time for nothing. We do not even know where birth comes from, or where death goes. How should we know that cause and effect are hard to escape, and that offense and blessing bring their exact return, without the least error? When the day of the great limit (death) comes, it is like a stone thrown into water, sinking to the very bottom. In the three evil paths the suffering is terrible; one retribution lasts five thousand kalpas, and when one may raise one’s head again, who knows in what year or month! Speaking of this, the heart aches and grief is bitter. Such people are seen everywhere, one after another. And of those among us who would be true cultivators, they are like gold sifted from sand: it is not that there are none at all, but they are very few.

[Model The norms handed down. Gui Youguang in his Colophon on the Portrait of the Seventy Disciples of Confucius says: “Though the years are far distant, the model is fully preserved.” Master Hanshan in The Dream-Wandering Collection

Instruction for the Supervisor of the Monastery of Guizong says: “Only Baizhang’s ‘A day without work, a day without food’ became for a thousand ages the model of the monastery.” [Swept away] Lost completely. [Drift along] To keep to old habits. [Holding their bellies] Holding their bellies — describing loud laughter; for example, “holding their bellies with laughter,” “making one hold one’s belly.” [The three evil paths] The path of blood, the path of knives, and the path of fire. The path of blood is the animal realm, because animals are constantly being killed or devouring one another; the path of knives is the hungry ghost realm, because hungry ghosts are constantly pressed by hunger or by swords and staves; the path of fire is the hell realm, because hells are constantly places of freezing ice or of fierce fires and boiling cauldrons. “The three paths” is another name for the three evil realms. [In the three paths the suffering is terrible; one retribution lasts five thousand] A verse says: “In the three paths one retribution lasts five thousand kalpas; when will one raise one’s head again?”

[Alas! The three realms are a prison; the four kinds of birth are fetters; burned by the great fire, in the perilous house of birth and death, how can one ever quench the fierce flames and leave all suffering, to reach the place of fearlessness? Unless one is a man of true mettle, endowed with a spiritual root and bearing past-lives’ bones, one cannot rouse oneself to fierce courage and leap straight in at one bound. You are fortunate to be born in an age when the Buddhadharma exists, to have your form clothed in the robe of the sangha, to have met a clear teacher early, with the six senses complete. If you do not urgently bear in mind impermanence, deeply ponder the great matter, think on the sufferings of the hells, arouse the bodhi mind, mend the past and cultivate the future, and day and night press on with diligence, seeking early to escape — but instead drift through the days, indulging body and mind — when the great limit comes, what use will regret be? Alas, go forth! Do not forget the words I earnestly enjoin on you at this parting, so as to betray my own hopes for you.]

Alas! The three realms are a prison; the four kinds of birth are fetters; burned by the great fire, in the perilous house of birth and death, how can one ever quench the fierce flames and leave all suffering, to reach the place of fearlessness? Unless one is a man of true mettle, endowed with a spiritual root and bearing past-lives’ bones, one cannot rouse oneself to fierce courage and leap straight in at one bound. You are fortunate to be born in an age when the Buddhadharma exists, to put on the robe of the sangha, to have met a clear teacher early, with the six senses complete. If you do not urgently bear in mind impermanence, deeply ponder the great matter of birth and death, think on the many sufferings of the hells, arouse the bodhi mind, mend the past and cultivate the future, and day and night press on with diligence, seeking early to escape, but instead drift through the days and indulge body and mind, then when the great limit comes, what use will regret be?
Alas, farewell!
Do not on any account forget the words I earnestly enjoin on you at this parting, so that you betray me and betray yourself as well!

blocks.text: 2. The Mind of Loyalty and Rightness

inline.s: (Excerpted from The Dream-Wandering Collection
, Urging the Young Master Dayi to Return to the Mountain to Attend His Parents)

[When I was young and read the histories, I privately admired the characters of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu. I thought: one who holds such a mind and serves as a subject or a son may be said not to have brought shame to his parents
hóng

. When I grew up and left home, I said: my Buddha is the Dharma-king of the three realms and the compassionate father of the four kinds of birth; if one can hold the hearts of those two men and be a disciple, one may be said not to betray one’s own spiritual nature. And when I read the “opportune encounters” of the patriarchs in the lamp-transmission records, and saw Shenguang’s cutting off his arm, the Boatman’s overturning his boat, Baizhang’s conduct toward Mazu, and Yangqi’s toward Ciming, I sighed and said: if one forgets oneself for the Dharma, with a heart like those old masters’, what fear is there that the patriarchs’ Way will not flourish, or that the Dharma-gate will not rise?]

When I was young and read the histories, I privately admired the characters of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu. I thought to myself: one who holds this heart of loyalty and rightness and serves as a subject and a son may be said not to have failed this life. Later, when I had grown up and left home, I said again: my Buddha is the Dharma-king of the three realms and the compassionate father of the four kinds of birth; if one can hold the loyal and righteous heart of those two men (Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu) and be a disciple of the Buddha, one may be said not to have betrayed one’s own spiritual nature (one’s own nature). And when I came to read the accounts of the patriarchs’ attainment of the Way in the lamp-transmission records, and saw Shenguang’s cutting off his arm, the Boatman’s overturning his boat, Baizhang’s conduct toward Mazu, and Yangqi’s toward Ciming, I sighed and said: if all disciples of the Buddha forget themselves for the Dharma, with a heart of loyalty and rightness like the patriarchs’, what fear is there that the Chan school (the patriarchs’ Way) will not flourish, or that the Dharma-gate will not rise?

[Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu In the time of Duke Ling of Jin, the military minister Tu’an Gu was at odds with the civil minister Zhao Dun, and so falsely accused Zhao Dun of rebellion. More than three hundred members of Zhao Dun’s household were executed; only his son, the imperial son-in-law Zhao Shuo, and the princess escaped. Later Tu’an Gu, falsely claiming the Duke’s command, forced Zhao Shuo to take his own life. The princess, imprisoned in the mansion, gave birth to a son and entrusted him to the Zhao family’s retainer Cheng Ying, then hanged herself. Cheng Ying hid the infant in a medicine chest and carried him away secretly; the general Han Jue, who was in charge of the guard and pitied the Zhao family, let Cheng Ying and the Zhao orphan go, and then cut his own throat. Cheng Ying took the infant to Zhao Dun’s old friend Gongsun Chujiu. At that time Tu’an Gu, eager to pull up the roots and cut them off, falsely claimed the Duke of Jin’s command in order to search out the orphan, and ordered that all infants in the land under half a year and over one month old be killed.

Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu discussed what should be done. Gongsun Chujiu asked Cheng Ying: “Which is harder — to set up the orphan and preserve him, or to die with him?” Cheng Ying said: “Dying is easy; setting up the orphan is very hard.” Gongsun Chujiu then said: “The late lord of Zhao treated you generously; you must exert yourself in the hard task, and I will do the easy one!” Cheng Ying then decided to substitute his own son, and denounced Gongsun Chujiu to Tu’an Gu for secretly hiding the Zhao orphan. Tu’an Gu believed it, sent men to search out the infant, threw him to the ground, and ran him through with several sword thrusts. Cheng Ying watched his own son die horribly and held back his grief in silence. Gongsun Chujiu, after cursing Tu’an Gu loudly, dashed his head against the steps and died. His mind now set at ease, Tu’an Gu took Cheng Ying as a retainer. Everyone in the world cursed Cheng Ying as one who sold his lord for favor, while Cheng Ying, his heart bleeding, endured disgrace and bore the burden of raising the Zhao orphan. Fifteen years later, when the child had grown to manhood, Cheng Ying told him the truth. The Zhao orphan was filled with grief and fury, and resolved on vengeance. By then Duke Ling of Jin was dead and Duke Dao of Jin was on the throne; Cheng Bo reported to him how Tu’an Gu had monopolized power and run amok, destroying the loyal and good, and Duke Dao of Jin commanded him to arrest Tu’an Gu and put him to death. The Zhao family’s great vengeance was repaid, and the Zhao orphan, restored to his own surname, was granted the name Zhao Wu.

When Cheng Ying saw that the great matter was done, he took his leave of the various ministers, and then said to Zhao Wu: “At the time of the calamity of the lower palace, everyone was able to die for it. It was not that I could not, but that I had to set up the Zhao orphan. Now you have grown to manhood, inherited the family’s work, and been restored to your former rank; now I must go below the earth to report to Gongsun Chujiu.” Zhao Wu wept and knocked his head on the ground, insisting: “I would rather endure every hardship myself and repay you for life; can you bear to leave me?” Cheng Ying said: “No. Gongsun Chujiu believed I could accomplish the great matter, and so died before me; if I do not now go to report, he will think my task has still not succeeded.” With that he cut his own throat and died. The loyal and righteous deeds of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu were widely celebrated by later ages, and were made into the play The Orphan of Zhao.

[The four kinds of birth Womb birth, egg birth, moisture birth, and transformation birth. [Lamp-transmission] To transmit the Dharma to others, as lamp is passed to lamp, mind to mind. Here “lamp-transmission” refers to the Lamp-Transmission Records and the Chan histories of the generations. [Shenguang’s cutting off his arm] Huike, the Second Patriarch of Chan, was originally named Shenguang. When Master Bodhidharma was dwelling at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, Shenguang prayed for the Way with the utmost earnestness. On a snowy night he cut off his left arm, and Bodhidharma, moved, consented; his name was changed to Huike. Afterwards he received Bodhidharma’s robe and bowl and inherited the lineage of the Chan school as the Second Patriarch.

[The Boatman’s overturning his boat The Boatman is Chan Master Decheng, who received the Dharma from Yaoshan (Chan Master Weiyan) and attended him for thirty years. Later he went to Huating, wishing to obtain a Dharma heir to repay his teacher’s kindness, and so drifted in a small boat, crossing people as conditions came, waiting for one who would come; hence he was called the Boatman Monk. Later he transmitted the Dharma to Jiashan, and in order to strengthen Jiashan’s faith he resolutely gave up his life as a guarantee, overturning the boat and entering the water to pass away. The Five Lamps’ Extended Records says: “Later Daowu (the Boatman’s elder Dharma-brother) arrived at Jingkou and encountered Jiashan ascending the hall. A monk asked: ‘What is the Dharma-body?’ Shan said: ‘The Dharma-body has no mark.’ He asked: ‘What is the Dharma-eye?’ Shan said: ‘The Dharma-eye has no flaw.’ Daowu could not help laughing. Shan then descended from the seat and asked Daowu: ‘What I have just said to this monk must have been wrong, to make the elder laugh. I beg the elder not to begrudge his compassion!’ Wu said: ‘You are in one respect the same, but you have no teacher.’ Shan said: ‘Wherein am I (speaking of himself) wrong? I beg you to point it out.’ Wu said: ‘I will never tell you; please, you had better go to the Boatman at Huating.’ Shan said: ‘What sort of man is he?’ Wu said: ‘Not a tile above his head, not a foot of ground beneath his feet. If you go, you must change your clothes and go.’ Shan then dismissed the assembly, packed his things, and went straight to Huating. As soon as the Boatman saw him he asked: ‘Great Virtue, in what temple do you dwell?’ Shan said: ‘I do not dwell in a temple; dwelling is not resembling.’ The Master said: ‘If not resembling, what do you resemble?’ Shan said: ‘It is not a dharma before the eyes.’ The Master said: ‘Where did you learn that?’ Shan said: ‘It is not something the ears and eyes can reach.’ The Master said: ‘A single phrase that fits the tune — ten thousand kalpas a stake to tether a donkey.’ (A phrase that brings awakening, if one clings to it without truly practicing and realizing, turns instead into an obstruction.) The Master asked again: ‘Letting down a line a thousand feet long, the intent is in the deep pool. Three inches above the hook — why do you not speak?’ Shan was about to open his mouth when the Master struck him with the oar and knocked him into the water. As soon as Shan had climbed back into the boat, the Master said again: ‘Speak! Speak!’ Shan was about to open his mouth, and the Master struck him again. Shan was suddenly greatly awakened, and nodded three times. The Master said: ‘The pole-tip and the silk line are yours to play with; not stirring the clear waves, the meaning is of itself distinct.’ Shan then asked: ‘Casting away the line and throwing aside the hook — what is the Master’s meaning?’ The Master said: ‘The silk hangs in the clear water, floating to fix the meaning of being and non-being.’ Shan said: ‘The words carry the profound yet have no road; the tongue speaks and does not speak.’ The Master said: ‘Having fished out all the river’s waves, at last I meet the golden-scaled one.’ Shan then covered his ears. The Master said: ‘So it is! So it is!’ And he enjoined him: ‘Where you go hereafter (from now on), you must hide yourself where there is no trace, and where there is no trace, do not hide your body. For thirty years I was at Yaoshan and understood only this matter. Now that you have obtained it, do not hereafter dwell in cities and towns; only in the deep mountains, by a hoe (a farming tool for digging earth, like a pick), find one or half a one to continue the line, and do not let it be cut off.’ Shan then took his leave, turning back again and again. The Master called out, ‘Ācārya (that is, ācārya)!’ Shan turned his head, and the Master raised his oar upright and said: ‘Do you take it that there is something else? (Do you imagine there is some dharma more ultimate than this?)’ And he overturned the boat and entered the water, passing away (giving his life as a guarantee: this is the ultimate dharma!).” [Dharma heir] One who inherits the Dharma lineage. [Ācārya] A master of propriety and model, one able to teach disciples the forms of the Dharma.

[Baizhang’s conduct toward Mazu The Diamond Scripture says: “One should not give rise to a mind dwelling on forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling on sounds, scents, tastes, tangible things, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing whatsoever.” The Blue Cliff Record records: Mazu and his disciple Baizhang were walking together when they saw a flock of wild ducks fly past. The Patriarch said: “What is that?” Zhang said: “Wild ducks.” The Patriarch said: “Where have they gone? (testing whether Baizhang’s mind was dwelling on forms)” Zhang said: “They have flown away.” The Patriarch then twisted Baizhang’s nose, and Zhang cried out in pain. The Patriarch said: “When did they ever fly away?” At these words Zhang had a realization. Baizhang’s first answer, “wild ducks,” was like a mirror reflecting an object — that was right; but the second answer, “they have flown away,” was a mind dwelling on forms, following the object and chasing after it, failing to guard the original mind (losing right mindfulness). That is why Mazu twisted his nose, to make him turn back and guard the original mind. In the midst of the pain Baizhang heard his teacher say, “When did they ever fly away? (the ducks are illusory — how could there be coming or going?)” and was suddenly enlightened: “Thus should one give rise to a pure mind.” (Mazu twisted Baizhang’s nose precisely to make him never forget to guard the original mind, and never to follow objects and chase after them.) “Whatever has marks is all delusion.” If one does not depart from marks, it is hard to awaken to the Way; hence Mazu used the thunderbolt method, swift as lightning that leaves no time to stop the ears, to strike at Baizhang’s unawakened mind. The Five Lamps’ Extended Records says: “Once, when the Master (Baizhang) was attending Mazu on a walk, they saw a flock of wild ducks fly past. The Patriarch said: ‘What is that?’ The Master said: ‘Wild ducks.’ The Patriarch said: ‘Where have they gone?’ The Master said: ‘They have flown away.’ The Patriarch then twisted the Master’s nose, and he cried out in pain. The Patriarch said: ‘And you still say they have flown away.’ At these words the Master had a realization. He returned to the attendant’s quarters and wept bitterly. A colleague asked: ‘Are you thinking of your parents? (in ancient usage the same as ‘yé,’ a questioning particle)’ The Master said: ‘No.’ He said: ‘Has someone scolded you?’ The Master said: ‘No.’ He said: ‘Then why are you crying?’ The Master said: ‘My nose was twisted by the Great Master and still aches.’ The colleague said: ‘What circumstance did not accord?’ The Master said: ‘Go and ask the Master.’ The colleague asked the Great Master: ‘What circumstance of the attendant Hai does not accord, that he cries in his quarters? I beg the Master to tell me.’ The Great Master said: ‘He understands. Go and ask him yourself.’ The colleague returned to the quarters and said: ‘The Master says you understand, and told me to ask you myself.’ The Master then laughed heartily. The colleague said: ‘A moment ago you were crying; why are you laughing now?’ The Master said: ‘A moment ago I cried; now I laugh.’ The colleague was bewildered. The next day Mazu ascended the hall, and when the assembly had just gathered, the Master came forward and rolled up the mat. The Patriarch then descended from the seat. The Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters. The Patriarch said: ‘I had not yet spoken, so why did you roll up the mat?’ The Master said: ‘Yesterday the Master twisted my nose and it ached.’ The Patriarch said: ‘Where were you directing your attention yesterday?’ The Master said: ‘My nose does not ache today.’ The Patriarch said: ‘You deeply understand yesterday’s matter.’ The Master bowed and withdrew.” [Yangqi] Chan Master Fanghui of Mount Yangqi in Yuanzhou in the Song dynasty, together with Huinan of Mount Huanglong, were both Dharma heirs of Chan Master Ciming Yuan, the sixth patriarch of Linji; each established a branch, called the Yangqi and Huanglong lines.

[Alas! When a true man lives in the world, if he cannot exhaust his strength in serving a ruler to win renown and honor his parents, then he should be a loyal subject of the Dharma-king and a filial son of the compassionate father. The principle is the same in either place — why should he stoop to petty and sordid affairs? Therefore I know of myself that ever since there has been the matter of the upward path, this mind of mine has soared, bearing thoughts that transcend the world. Even when confined in a cage or wandering the marketplace, I have never failed to place myself amid ice and snow, among a thousand cliffs and ten thousand ravines.]

Alas! When a true man lives in the world, if he cannot exhaust his strength in serving a ruler to win renown and honor his parents, then he should be a loyal subject of the Dharma-king (the Buddha) and a filial son of the compassionate father of the four kinds of birth (the Buddha). The principle is the same in either case: whether at home in government or having left home in the service of the Buddha, one must have the loyal and righteous heart of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu. Why then stoop, petty and sordid, to those selfish and unrighteous dirty dealings? Therefore I know of myself that ever since I set my will on the upward path, this mind has been lofty, bearing thoughts that transcend the world. So whether shut in prison or in the midst of a busy market, I have never failed to place myself amid ice and snow, among a thousand cliffs and ten thousand ravines.

[The principle is the same in either place “Changing place” means changing position. “The principle is the same in either place” means: so long as a person’s faith is firm, even if his position is changed and he is placed in a different environment (changing place), his conduct will be the same (the same in every case). [The upward path] The search for the ultimate and most profound principle of the Buddha-Way is called the matter of the ultimate upward, the latch of the upward, the matter of the upward. [Cage] A cage to shut in birds and beasts, used as a metaphor for a condition of bondage and unfreedom. In the case of Master Hanshan’s own experience, it means prison. [Market (
chán
) place] The marketplace, where shops are gathered together.

blocks.text: 3. The Two Kinds of Lay Practitioners

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
, Instruction for the Upāsakas of Xiangtan)

[While the Buddha dwelt in the world and taught the Dharma, there were four assemblies that constantly attended him: two assemblies of those who had left home, called bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; and two assemblies of those still at home, called upāsakas, which means “near-serving men,” and upāsikās, meaning “near-serving women.” Because they can keep the five precepts while at home, they are able to serve the Three Jewels from near at hand and are fit to receive the benefits of the Dharma. Therefore, when the Buddhadharma came east, those of the two lay assemblies who received its teaching as conditions allowed were never lacking in any generation, and some even clarified the mind and saw the nature and entered the patriarchs’ chamber.]

While the Buddha dwelt in the world and taught the Dharma, there were four assemblies that constantly attended him. The two assemblies of those who had left home are the bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇīs. The two assemblies of those still at home are the upāsakas (meaning near-serving men) and the upāsikās (meaning near-serving women). Because they can keep the five precepts while at home, they can serve the Three Jewels from near at hand and obtain the benefits of the Buddhadharma. Therefore, when the Buddhadharma came east to China, the two lay assemblies who received its teaching as conditions allowed appeared in every generation, and some even clarified the mind and saw the nature, entered the patriarchs’ chamber, and received the Dharma.

[The five precepts Not killing living beings, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking alcohol. Not killing living beings means not taking the life of any living creature; not stealing means not taking what belongs to others; not committing sexual misconduct means not engaging in sexual relations outside of husband and wife; not speaking falsely means not speaking words that deceive and cheat people; not drinking alcohol means not consuming alcoholic drinks or drugs that cloud human nature.

[Of late the way of the Dharma has long been buried, and teachers have no eye for choosing heirs: people bow three times at random and as a matter of course obtain a name, and at once call themselves disciples. In truth they have not yet spat out the reek of meat and pungent herbs, and their former conduct is unchanged, so that they draw mockery and slander, gain no benefit at all, and become a great source of the Dharma’s ruin. Therefore in all my life I have not dared lightly to accept disciples. Now, observing the disciples of Xiangtan, their faith is sincere and deep, and they are not of the sort that drift with the common stream; so I have forced myself to grant their request.]

Of late the way of the true Dharma has long been buried. Teachers take disciples without discernment: three bows at random, and by convention one becomes an upāsaka or upāsikā and calls oneself a disciple of the Buddha. In truth the pungent herbs are not yet given up and the meat is not yet spat out, and one’s former evil conduct is unchanged, so that one draws the mockery and slander of others, gains no benefit at all, and truly becomes a source of the Dharma’s ruin. Therefore this old man (Master Hanshan’s own designation of himself) has in all his life not dared lightly to accept lay disciples. Now, observing the disciples of Xiangtan, their faith is sincere and deep, and they are not of the sort that drift along with the common stream; so I have with difficulty consented to their request.

[Pungent The five pungent herbs, also called the five pungent vegetables: five vegetables with a pungent flavor — garlic, wild garlic, scallion, Chinese leek, and asafoetida. The reason students of the Buddha must abstain from the five pungent vegetables is that they are intensely stimulating: eaten cooked they can set the fires of lust blazing in the body, and eaten raw they easily increase anger. Once a student of the Buddha has desire and anger, wisdom is obscured, delusion grows, ignorance stirs blindly, and every kind of evil karma is committed. [Reek] Refers to eating meat. [Not yet spat out the reek] Here “spat out” means to spit out in disgust.

[But considering that you have never before heard the Dharma, though you may be called good people, you do not know what goodness is. Now, following the Consciousness-Only treatise, which sets out fifty-one mental factors, of which only eleven are wholesome dharmas while the rest are all unwholesome mental factors: the eleven dharmas are faith, diligence, shame, remorse, non-greed, non-anger, non-delusion, pliancy, non-heedlessness, equanimity of activity, and non-harming. When these eleven dharmas are complete, one is a purely good person. Lack but one, and one is wanting in virtue. If you can simply receive the teaching and uphold these wholesome dharmas, each of you investigating and clarifying them, constantly observing and keeping them alert, then whatever dharma is not yet fully matured in you, apply more of the work of mutual polishing, and strive to make it wholly good and only then stop: to use the mind thus is to be a truly good person.]

But considering that you have never before heard the Buddhadharma, though you may be called good people, you do not know what goodness is. Now, following the Consciousness-Only treatise: there are altogether fifty-one mental factors, of which only eleven are wholesome mental factors and the rest are all unwholesome mental factors. The eleven wholesome mental factors are faith, diligence, shame, remorse, non-greed, non-anger, non-delusion, pliancy, non-heedlessness, equanimity of activity, and non-harming (not vexing living beings). When these eleven dharmas are complete, one is a purely good person. Lack but one, and one is wanting in virtue. If you can simply receive the teaching and uphold these wholesome dharmas, each of you investigating and clarifying their principles and requirements, constantly observing and keeping them alert, then whatever dharma is not yet fully matured in you, apply more of the work of mutual polishing, and strive to make it wholly good and only then stop: to use the mind thus is to be a truly good person.

[Mental factors An abbreviation of “dharmas belonging to the mind,” that is, the various mental phenomena that belong to the mind. There are altogether fifty-one dharmas: five universally pervasive, five object-determining, eleven wholesome, six root afflictions, twenty secondary afflictions, and four indeterminate. [Equanimity of activity] Xing means cultivation and she means to let go: the cultivator should let go of the mark of self and the mark of dharmas — that is, to cultivate goodness one step and let go one step. [Keeping alert] To rouse oneself, stir oneself up, and keep right mindfulness.

[What is called the good mind is the pure true mind. Because all living beings each inherently possess the Tathāgata’s pure true mind, but are defiled by evil thoughts, they follow their feelings and create karma without knowing it. If one can now observe the good mind, then all evil dharmas of themselves no longer appear before one, and the mind is of itself pure.]

What is called the good mind is the pure true mind. Because all living beings each inherently possess the Tathāgata’s pure true mind, but are defiled by evil thoughts, they follow their feelings and create karma without knowing it. If one can now observe the good mind, then all evil dharmas of themselves no longer appear before one, and the mind is of itself pure.

[If one can but have the will to contemplate deeply and gradually, and simply investigate the koan in which the Sixth Patriarch instructed Huiming: “Without thinking of good, without thinking of evil — at this very moment, what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?” — investigating it at all times and in all places, this is what is called the upward path. At your heels, who among you lacks a foot of ground? Press forward with effort, and you will surely not be cheated. If you are willing to take refuge in the Pure Land, then follow this method and recite the Buddha’s name with one mind; then in this present life you may cut off birth and death and forever end your sinking down. But I fear that a thieving mind deceives itself and cannot undertake true practice. This old man has forced himself to speak thus for you: for pity of a three-year-old child, grudging not his two eyebrows. Do not on any account take this as a worldly, commonplace remark.]

If one can but have the will to contemplate deeply and gradually, and simply investigate the koan in which the Sixth Patriarch instructed Huiming: “Without thinking of good, without thinking of evil — at this very moment, what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?” — investigating it at all times and in all places, this is what is called the upward path. At your heels, who among you lacks a foot of ground? Press forward with effort, and you will surely not be cheated (deceived). If you are willing to take refuge in the Pure Land, then follow this method and recite the Buddha’s name with one mind; then in this present life you may cut off birth and death and forever end your sinking down. But I fear that a thieving mind deceives itself and cannot undertake true practice. This old man has forced himself to speak thus for you: for pity of a three-year-old child, he exhausts an old grandmother’s heart. Do not take this as an old platitude.

[The upward path The ultimate point of the Chan school (beyond sages and ordinary beings, beyond birth and death) is called the upward path, the same meaning as “the one step upward.” Master Hanshan says: “The purport of the Buddha’s teaching takes the one mind alone as its foundation. Originally this mind is inherently perfect, luminous and vast, utterly without a speck of dust, pure and without anything at all; within it there is originally no delusion or awakening, no birth or death; sages and ordinary beings are not established, living beings and Buddhas are of one substance, without two and without difference. This is precisely what Bodhidharma brought from the West, directly pointing to this inherent true mind as the Chan school; so he said to Emperor Wu (Emperor Wu of Liang): ‘Vast and open, there is no sage.’ If one can suddenly awaken to this mind, then birth and death are forever ended; it lies solely in the present person’s single thought of sudden awakening, which is then named the Tathāgata of suchness — not belonging to the ranks of cultivation and realization, not belonging to the gradual stages of the three vehicles. This the Chan school regards as the upward path. What the patriarchs of old transmitted was precisely this mind, taken as the ultimate of the school, and this is called Chan.” (The Dream-Wandering Collection, Reply to Prince De’s Questions) He says further: “Therefore Bodhidharma, coming from the West, did not establish words and letters; he only concerned himself with awakening to one’s own mind, taking this mind as the root of all sages and ordinary beings, of the ten realms, of direct and circumstantial retribution. To awaken to this mind wholly is to be a supreme sage of the Great Vehicle; to awaken partially is to be of the two vehicles; not to awaken is to be an ordinary being. If one awakens yet does not dwell in it, realizes yet gains nothing, that is the upward path beyond sages and ordinary beings, beyond birth and death.” (The Dream-Wandering Collection, Instruction for the Seat-Master Miaozhan) [Beyond sages and ordinary beings, beyond birth and death] The birth and death spoken of here are segmental birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death. [Segmental birth-and-death] Living beings within the three realms and six paths, because of the good and evil karma they have attracted, have lifespans that are limited and bodies that are divided into segments; hence their birth and death is called “segmental birth-and-death.” One who ends segmental birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. [Transformational birth-and-death] The sages of the three vehicles have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended segmental birth-and-death. In the course of cultivating the Way, deluded conceptions gradually cease and realized understanding gradually increases; each stage of this shifting from delusion to awakening differs, and the passage from an earlier stage into a later one is just like passing through one birth and death. Hence it is called “transformational birth-and-death.” One who ends transformational birth-and-death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. [An old grandmother’s heart] A grandmother’s heart — meaning the Chan master’s heart of repeated, earnest urging and urgent instruction of others. [Grudging not his two eyebrows] Not grudging any bitter effort.

blocks.text: 4. All Ten Realms Are Mind Only

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
, Instruction for Xu Qingzhi)

[The Buddha says: “The dharmas above and below the three realms are made by one mind alone.” By “above the three realms” are meant the four holy ones who have transcended the world: Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. By “below the three realms” are meant the ordinary beings of the six paths: the three good paths of gods, humans, and asuras, and the three evil paths of hells, animals, and hungry ghosts. Thus within the ten dharma-realms, all sages and ordinary beings, the causes and effects of good and evil, and the adornments of direct and circumstantial retribution, are all made by one mind. Yet this one mind is nothing else: it is the very mind by which we, in our daily use and present activity, discriminate and know.]

The Buddha says: all dharmas above and below the three realms are made by one mind alone. By “above the three realms” are meant the four holy ones who have transcended the world: Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. By “below the three realms” are meant the ordinary beings of the six paths: the three good paths of gods, humans, and asuras, and the three evil paths of hells, animals, and hungry ghosts. Therefore within the ten dharma-realms, all sages and ordinary beings, the causes and effects of good and evil, and the adornments of direct and circumstantial retribution, are all made by one mind. Yet this one mind is nothing else: it is the very mind by which we, in our daily use and present activity, discriminate and know.

[The ten realms The ten dharma-realms: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary realms; the last four are the four holy realms. [Direct and circumstantial] Circumstantial retribution and direct retribution. The lands, houses, and implements of the world, being that on which the body depends, are called “circumstantial retribution”; the body, falsely assembled from the five aggregates and attracted by past karma, is called “direct retribution.” [Adornment] The word “adornment” here means embellishment. To adorn lands with what is good and beautiful, or to adorn the body with merit, is called adornment; to pile up evil deeds upon the body is likewise called adornment. For example, the Buddha Speaks of Amitābha Buddha Sutra says: “adorned with merit”; the Contemplation Sutra on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says: “Such a foolish person steals the goods of the sangha, steals the goods of the present sangha, teaches the Dharma impurely, and has no shame or remorse, adorning himself with all manner of evil karma.”
[Mind

In Buddhist study the word “mind” is used extremely widely and has very many meanings, so one must be clear about what the “mind” spoken of in a given sentence contains; otherwise, an error of a hairsbreadth leads one astray by a thousand miles. Master Hanshan here points out plainly that the “mind” of “the ten realms are mind only”
is the very mind by which we, in our daily use and present activity, discriminate and know

[The three realms The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world inhabited by living beings who have the two desires of sex and food, and includes the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below; the form realm is the world inhabited by living beings who are without the two desires of sex and food but still have a material body, and includes the four dhyānas and the eighteen heavens; the formless realm is the world inhabited by living beings who are without a material body and dwell with their mind-consciousness in deep and wondrous dhyāna, and includes the four formless heavens (the heaven of boundless space, the heaven of boundless consciousness, the heaven of nothing whatsoever, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all the domain of the birth and death and rebirth of ordinary beings.
[The dharmas above and below the three realms are made by one mind alone Ultimately, in which of the

ten dharma-realms one is born, and what direct and circumstantial retribution one receives, is entirely brought about by the karma created by the thoughts of one’s own mind. So the karma created by the thoughts of one’s own mind is
the cause
, while which dharma-realm one is born into, and what kind of direct and circumstantial retribution one receives, is
the effect
. The “making” of “
made by one mind alone
” is the karmic cause of creating karma. As the text below says:
“Thus within the ten dharma-realms, all sages and ordinary beings, the causes and effects of good and evil,
the adornments of direct and circumstantial retribution
, are all made by one mind. Yet this one mind is nothing else: it is the very mind by which we, in our daily use and present activity,
discriminate and know
. Since everything is made by the mind, and is not made in successive stages, but is rather the karma created by the thoughts of our daily use and present activity,
the karma created by thought after thought
we revolve through the ten dharma-realms

. If a single thought, arising from greed, anger, and delusion, creates the ten evil deeds — three of body, four of speech, and three of mind — that is the cause of the painful destinies of the three evil paths; if a single thought turns the ten evil deeds into the ten good deeds, that is the cause of the wondrous bliss of humans and gods; if a single thought forgets both good and evil, so that inwardly one sees no self and outwardly one sees no other, the mind being utterly still, that is the cause of the śrāvaka’s escape from suffering; if one contemplates that present suffering and joy, adversity and favor, arise and cease from causes and conditions, revolving and returning to cessation, that becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha; if a single thought comprehends that persons and dharmas are without self, that causes and conditions are empty of nature, that there is no maker and no receiver, and yet one goes on practicing giving, upholding precepts, patience, and the six pāramitās, transforming and saving living beings, that is the cause of the bodhisattva; if a single thought suddenly awakens to one’s own mind, which is originally luminous and vast, excluding nothing, saving nothing that it does not save, with not a single dharma standing before it, living beings and Buddhas equal, that is the cause of Buddhahood.”

[Since everything is made by the mind, and is not made in successive stages, but is rather the karma created by the thoughts of our daily use and present activity, we revolve through the ten dharma-realms. If a single thought, arising from greed, anger, and delusion, creates the ten evil deeds (three of body, four of speech, and three of mind), that is the cause of the painful destinies of the three evil paths; if a single thought turns the ten evil deeds into the ten good deeds, that is the cause of the wondrous bliss of humans and gods; if a single thought forgets both good and evil, so that inwardly one sees no self and outwardly one sees no other, the mind being utterly still, that is the cause of the śrāvaka’s escape from suffering; if one contemplates that present suffering and joy, adversity and favor, arise and cease from causes and conditions, revolving and returning to cessation, that becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha; if a single thought comprehends that persons and dharmas are without self, that causes and conditions are empty of nature, that there is no maker and no receiver, and yet one goes on practicing giving, upholding precepts, patience, and the six pāramitās, transforming and saving living beings, that is the cause of the bodhisattva; if a single thought suddenly awakens to one’s own mind, which is originally luminous and vast, excluding nothing, saving nothing that it does not save, utterly without any discriminatory view of feeling and consciousness, living beings and Buddhas equal and without two, that is the cause of Buddhahood.]
Although all dharmas are made by the mind, they are not made one after another following the thoughts; rather, the karma created by the thoughts of our daily use and present activity
is taken as the cause

, and we receive its retribution as we revolve through the ten dharma-realms. If a single thought, arising from greed, anger, and delusion, creates the ten evil deeds (three of body, four of speech, and three of mind), this is the cause of the painful destinies of the three evil paths; if a single thought turns the ten evil deeds into the ten good deeds, that is the cause of the wondrous bliss of humans and gods; if a single thought forgets both good and evil, so that inwardly one sees no self and outwardly one sees no other, the mind being utterly still, that is the cause of the śrāvaka’s escape from suffering; if one contemplates that present suffering and joy, adversity and favor, arise and cease from causes and conditions, revolving and returning to cessation, that becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha; if a single thought comprehends that persons and dharmas are without self, that causes and conditions are empty of nature, that there is no maker and no receiver, and yet one goes on practicing giving, upholding precepts, patience, and the six pāramitās, transforming and saving living beings, that is the cause of the bodhisattva; if a single thought suddenly awakens to one’s own mind, which is originally luminous and vast, excluding nothing, saving nothing that it does not save, utterly without any discriminatory view of feeling and consciousness, living beings and Buddhas equal and without two, that is the cause of Buddhahood.

[Karma created Karma is of two kinds: shared karma and individual karma. Shared karma is the karmic cause common to living beings, able to attract the world of mountains, rivers, and earth that they use in common; this is the karma of circumstantial retribution. Individual karma is the karmic cause by which an individual living being attracts his own retribution, such as differences of body and differences of suffering and joy; this is the karma of direct retribution. [Karma] All our thoughts, words, and deeds of good and evil are called karma: thoughts, words, and deeds of good are called “good karma,” and thoughts, words, and deeds of evil are called “evil karma.” [Revolving and returning to cessation] To create karma and receive the fruit of birth and death is called revolving; to cultivate the Way and realize nirvāṇa is called returning to cessation. “Returning to cessation” means returning to stillness and extinction, that is, cultivating the Way and realizing nirvāṇa.

[Therefore this one mind is vast, with nothing outside it, originally pure, perfect and luminous. If in one’s daily use one awakens to this thought after thought, then though one dwells amid the toil of the dust, one is a person who has transcended the world; this is why Vimalakīrti called it the gate of non-duality. If the lay disciple can embody this and practice it, then all grievances and kindnesses, right and wrong, self and other, the roots of affliction and feeling, will at a single thought be transformed into the treasury of light. With every circumstance of daily use, try watching in this way, aware thought after thought. If you cannot patiently accept and are obstructed by affliction, then as soon as you see an arising, at once raise the Sixth Patriarch’s line “originally there is not a single thing,” and it will be like the vajra-king’s precious sword: all affliction will instantly melt like ice, and body and mind will be transformed into a cool pool. Practicing with effort in this way, if you can be diligent without retreating, you will suddenly realize the great field of liberation — why seek the Buddhadharma elsewhere besides this!]

Therefore this one mind is vast, with nothing outside it, originally pure, perfect and luminous. If in one’s daily use one awakens to this thought after thought, then though one dwells amid the toil of the dust, one is a person who has transcended the world; this is the gate of non-duality spoken of in the Vimalakīrti Sutra. If you can embody this and practice it, then all grievances and kindnesses, right and wrong, self and other, the roots of affliction and feeling, will at a single thought be transformed into the treasury of light. With every circumstance of daily use, try watching in this way, aware thought after thought. If you cannot patiently accept and are obstructed by affliction, then as soon as you see a deluded thought arise, at once raise the Sixth Patriarch’s line “originally there is not a single thing,” and it will be like the vajra-king’s precious sword: all affliction will instantly melt like ice, and body and mind will be transformed into a cool pool. Practicing with effort in this way, if you can be diligent without retreating, you will suddenly realize the great field of liberation — why seek the Buddhadharma elsewhere besides this!

[The gate of non-duality The teaching that transcends all relative distinctions and reaches the one absolute, equal truth; that is, the teaching above the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates of Buddhism by which one may directly see the holy Way. The Vimalakīrti Sutra, chapter nine, “Entering the Gate of Non-Duality,” records thirty-three kinds of gate of non-duality. [Originally there is not a single thing] The Sixth Patriarch says: “Bodhi is originally no tree, and the bright mirror is not a stand; originally there is not a single thing — where could dust ever cling?” (The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch) [The vajra-king’s precious sword] The sharp sword that cuts through all the tangled vines of emotional clinging; see the Records of Linji.

blocks.text: 5. Stilling the Mind and Cutting Off Delusion

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
, Instruction for Zhong Hengying)

[Zhong Mingsheng of Chaling came from a family of poetry and ritual. In the past, because of misfortune, he traveled to Guangdong and paid his respects to me at Caoxi. This old man enlightened him with the teaching of cause and effect and the retribution of good and evil, and set his mind at ease so that he returned home, and his trouble was unexpectedly resolved. The reason it was resolved could not have been reached by any reckoning: it was a chance meeting of conditions, coming of itself without intent. Thereupon Zhong’s property was unharmed and he entered a state of peace and quiet, with nothing to trouble him. Yet he remained utterly unaware of why this was so, and was still reckoning on the things of his life that had not yet pleased and satisfied his heart, intending to expend his mental effort in pursuit of them, as though reaching into a bag and picking up a mustard seed.]

Zhong Mingsheng of Chaling (a place name) came from a family of poetry and ritual. In the past, because he fled disaster, he came to Guangdong and paid his respects to this old man (Master Hanshan’s own designation of himself) at Caoxi. This old man enlightened him with the teaching of cause and effect and the retribution of good and evil, and set his mind at ease so that he returned home, and his disaster was unexpectedly resolved. The reason it was resolved could not have been anticipated by any thought: it was a chance meeting of conditions, coming of itself without intent. Thereupon Zhong’s family property was safe and unharmed, and he entered a state of ease and quiet, with nothing to trouble him. Yet he remained utterly unaware of the reason his disaster had been resolved, and was still reckoning on the fame and fortune of his life that had not yet been achieved (the things that would please and satisfy his heart), intending to expend his mental effort in pursuit of them, thinking it as easy as reaching into a bag and picking something up.

[Reaching into a bag and picking up a mustard seed To reach into a bag and take something, to stoop and pick up a mustard seed — a metaphor for being able to accomplish something with the greatest ease. Bag: a pouch. Mustard: a small grass.

[On the last day of the year jiayin, Liu Cunzhi came from far away to comfort me and to keep me company through the turning of the year. This old man sighed deeply and said: what you aspire to is like crossing seas and rivers to seek sweet spring water to drink: the spring may never be found, while your thirst grows ever more burning, and you suffer all the toil of the journey besides. In the past I enlightened you with the principle of cause and effect and retribution — have you forgotten it? Good and evil attract their response as swiftly as shadow follows form, as echo answers sound: when the sound is harmonious the echo follows, when the form is straight the shadow is upright. Therefore the sages did not speak of cause and effect, but said, “For the good, a hundred blessings descend; for the evil, a hundred calamities.” Thus they took settling one’s lot and fixing one’s will as their admonition. Hence it is said: “He who does not know his lot cannot be a noble man.”]

On the last day of the year jiayin, Liu Cunzhi came from far away to comfort me and to keep me company through the turning of the year. This old man sighed deeply and said: what you plan is like crossing seas and rivers to seek sweet spring water to quench your thirst. If you do so, the sweet spring may never be obtained, while the long journey makes your thirst burn ever more fiercely, and you suffer the hardship of the road to no purpose. In the past I enlightened you with the principle of cause and effect and retribution — can it be that you have forgotten it? Good and evil attract their response, and the retribution is as swift as shadow following form, as echo answering sound: when the sound is harmonious the echo follows, when the form is straight the shadow is upright. Therefore the Confucian sages, though they did not plainly speak of cause and effect, said, “For the good, a hundred blessings descend; for the evil, a hundred calamities,” and so took settling one’s lot and fixing one’s will as their admonition. Hence it is said: “He who does not know his lot cannot be a noble man.”

[The sages taught people to settle their lot; the Buddha taught people to follow conditions: the principle is one. To settle one’s lot is to have not the least need to force anything; to follow conditions is to leave no room in a single thought for deluded thinking. Therefore the Buddhadharma teaches people to take the cutting off of deluded thinking as the root, for deluded thinking is the root of all the many evil karmas of greed, anger, and delusion. Even the bodhisattva’s cultivation up to Buddhahood, and the reward of the most excellent, adorned, vast and fruitful field among gods and humans, all begin from cutting off deluded thinking. When deluded thinking is cut off, evil karma dissolves; when evil karma dissolves, a hundred blessings gather: this is what is meant by seeking abundant blessings for oneself.]

The sages taught people to settle their lot; the World-Honored One taught people to follow conditions: the principle is one. To settle one’s lot is to have not the least need to force anything; to follow conditions is to leave no room in a single thought for deluded thinking. Therefore the Buddhadharma teaches people to take the cutting off of deluded thinking as the root, because deluded thinking is the root of all the many evil karmas of greed, anger, and delusion. Even the bodhisattva’s cultivation up to Buddhahood, and the reward of the most excellent, adorned, vast and fruitful field among gods and humans, all begin from cutting off deluded thinking. When deluded thinking is cut off, evil karma dissolves; when evil karma dissolves, a hundred blessings gather: this is seeking abundant blessings for oneself!
[Seeking abundant blessings for oneself The Classic of Poetry says:
“Forever matching the mandate of Heaven, one seeks abundant blessings for oneself.”

(The Classic of Poetry says: forever matching the mind of Heaven, one seeks abundant blessings for oneself.) [Forever matching the mandate] Forever in accord with the mandate of Heaven. [Forever] Forever, always. [Matching] To accord with. [Mandate] The mandate of Heaven.

[Therefore he showed him a verse: “Worldly affairs all arise from deluded thinking; where the deluded mind dissolves, the karma-conditions grow light. No need to seek further for the road of bodhi — just let the man step back.” This stepping back is the highest work of stilling the mind and cutting off delusion. Because the human mind is originally luminous and vast, the source of ten thousand blessings, but is obscured by deluded thinking and evil karma, calamity grows day by day and blessing decreases day by day. If now delusion dissolves and karma is cut off, then the one nature is perfect and bright, enjoyment is boundless, and where there is enjoyment, that is true blessing. Thus one knows that blessing is made by oneself, and is precisely
(the same as “precisely”)
not something that cleverness, artfulness, or scheming can bring about. Moreover, the Buddha taught that cutting off the deluded mind attracts the blessings of gods and humans.]

Therefore he showed him a verse: “Worldly affairs all arise from deluded thinking; where the deluded mind dissolves, the karma-conditions grow light. No need to seek further for the road of bodhi — just let the man step back.” This stepping back (not grasping at conditions, not seeking) is the highest work of stilling the mind and cutting off delusion. Because the human mind is originally luminous and vast, the source of ten thousand blessings, but is obscured by deluded thinking and evil karma, calamity grows day by day and blessing decreases day by day. Now if deluded thinking dissolves and evil karma is cut off, then the one nature is perfect and bright, enjoyment is boundless, and where there is enjoyment, that is true blessing. Thus one knows that blessing is made by oneself, and is by no means something that cleverness, artfulness, or scheming can bring about. Moreover, the Buddha taught that cutting off the deluded mind attracts the blessings of gods and humans.
[Stilling the mind and cutting off delusion To still the mind that grasps at conditions and seeks, and to cut off deluded thinking.

[Zhong was originally endowed with the talent and resource for fame and fortune. If he can at once still his mind, and go over the karma he has created in his life from the beginning, examining it carefully point by point, then wherever there is a single thought that wrongs the conscience and injures principle, not according with the great Way, all of it is a root of suffering: spit it all out together. Establish a new foundation afresh and do a new round of work, taking “still the mind, cut off delusion, accept your lot, and await your time” as the one standard, and devote your mind to the work you inherently have, without needing to seek further after a single thought of deluded thinking. In this way make up for the faults of your former conduct.]

Zhong was originally endowed with the talent and resource for fame and fortune. If he can at once still his mind, and go over the karma he has created in his past life from the beginning, examining it carefully point by point, then wherever there is a single thought that wrongs the conscience and injures principle, not according with the great Way, all of it is a root of suffering: cast it all aside together. Establish a new foundation afresh and do a new round of work, working only at the one thing: “still the mind, cut off delusion, accept your lot, and await your time.” Take “still the mind, cut off delusion, accept your lot, and await your time” as the standard of your thought and action, devote your mind to the work you inherently have, and do not need to seek further after a single thought of deluded thinking. In this way make up for your former faults.
[Talent and resource (zī jī) Talent and capacity. [Await (
sì
To wait.

[Once calamity dissolves and blessing arrives, then fame and fortune press in upon you, and even if you wished to avoid them there would be nowhere to avoid them. Why then use all kinds of deluded thinking and grasping at conditions to seek elsewhere! If Zhong can truly believe without doubt, hold to it and practice it, then the fruit of Buddhahood may be awaited — how much more so worldly fortune? Strive at it! Strive at it!]

Once calamity dissolves and blessing arrives, then fame and fortune press close upon you, and even if you wished to avoid them there would be nowhere to avoid them. Why then use all kinds of deluded thinking and grasping at conditions to pursue them! (This means: blessing is not something that deluded thinking and grasping at conditions can pursue and obtain; one must cut off the roots of suffering and cultivate the causes of blessing. Once the causes of blessing bear fruit, the reward of blessing descends of itself.) If Zhong can truly believe without doubt, hold to it and practice it, then the fruit of Buddhahood may be awaited — how much more so the fame and fortune of the world? Strive at it! Strive at it!

blocks.text: 6. The Essentials of Cultivation and Awakening

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
, Reply to Censor Zheng Kunyan)
Cultivation

: to follow the outflow of one’s own mind and purity away the habitual tendencies of deluded thinking and of greed, anger, and delusion. Awakening: to see through wholly that one’s own mind is originally perfect, luminous, vast, pure by nature, and utterly without a single thing.
[The outflow of one’s own mind The stream of presently active thought.]

[When we speak of this great matter of the one great cause, it is inherently present in everyone and complete in each, wanting not a hairsbreadth. But alas, since beginningless kalpas the seeds of the root of craving, of deluded thinking and emotional reckoning, and of habitual defilement have grown deep and thick, obscuring the wondrous brightness, so that one cannot obtain true benefit. One has always made a living only within the deluded shadows of body, mind, and world, and so drifts on through birth and death. The Buddhas and patriarchs appeared in the world and spoke a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, using all kinds of skillful means, teaching Chan and teaching the scriptures; all of it is but an implement for breaking clinging, suited to the capacity at hand, and fundamentally there is no substantial dharma to give to anyone.]

When we speak of this great matter of the one great cause (opening, revealing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision), it is inherently present in everyone and complete in each, wanting not a hairsbreadth. But alas, since beginningless kalpas the seeds of the habitual tendencies of craving, of deluded thinking and emotional reckoning, and of habitual defilement have grown deep and thick, obscuring the wondrous bright true mind, so that one cannot obtain true benefit. One has always made a living only within the deluded shadow of body, mind, and world, and so drifts on through birth and death. The Buddhas and patriarchs appeared in the world and spoke a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, using all kinds of skillful means, teaching Chan and teaching the scriptures; all of it is but an implement for breaking living beings’ clinging to self and clinging to dharmas, suited to the capacity at hand, and fundamentally there is no substantial dharma to give to anyone.

[The great matter of the one great cause Opening, revealing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
