These two words “empty” and “illusory” should be viewed in the light of each other, and then one suddenly sees their wonder. What is called empty is viewing the substance as originally empty through the appearance of illusory existence (this is named “true emptiness”). What is called existence is the illusory existence that is originally nothing (this is named “wondrous existence”). Because of true emptiness, the mind is not annihilated; because of wondrous existence, states are unborn. Since states are unborn, what can the mind grasp? Since the mind grasps nothing, where can deluded thoughts abide? If deluded thoughts do not abide, with what mind will one grasp states? States are themselves illusory; with what states will they entangle the mind? The mind simply does not grasp states, and the mind is not annihilated; states do not entangle the mind, and states are of themselves thus. Mind and states thus, the two not disturbing each other, in what is one not happy? This is what is meant by “the mind is originally unborn but exists because of states; if the states before it are not, the mind too is not.”

[Mind and states thus] The term “thus” (rúrú) usually describes that which does not change and is not different. Here “thus” means that mind and states each go their own way, without disturbing or entangling each other. [The mind is originally unborn but exists because of states; if the states before it are not, the mind too is not] This is the transmission verse of the Buddha Visvabhu (the third of the seven Buddhas of the past): “Borrowing the four great elements, one takes them for a body; the mind is originally unborn but exists because of states. If the states before it are not, the mind too is not; offense and merit are like illusions, arising and ceasing as well.”

[But simply see through the illusory and unreal, and it is named “as if not”; while the spirit-mind shines alone and deluded mind suddenly rests, and it is named “also not.” What is not is deluded mind; how could it be that the true mind is utterly not! What is deluded mind? That which clings to states and does not melt away. What is true mind? That which does not grasp the marks of body, mind, and states, which is clearly and constantly aware, spiritual and still-illumining. Using the mind thus, what hindrance is there? Hence it is said: “The self-mind grasps the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharma. Not grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory. The non-illusory does not even arise — how can illusory dharmas stand?” And as it is said: “States and conditions have no good or ugly; good and ugly arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcefully name them, from what do love and hate arise?”]

In the line “if the states before it are not, the mind too is not,” one sees through the states before one as illusory and unreal, and so it is named “as if not”; while the spirit-mind shines alone and deluded mind suddenly rests, and so it is named “also not.” What is called “not” means that deluded mind is not; how could it mean that even the true mind is not! What is deluded mind? That which clings to states and does not melt away is deluded mind. What is true mind? That which does not grasp the marks of body, mind, and states, which is clearly and constantly aware, spiritual and still-illumining, is true mind. Using the mind thus (using the true mind), what hindrance is there in states? Hence the Surangama Sutra says: “The self-mind grasps the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharma. Not grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory. The non-illusory does not even arise — how can illusory dharmas stand?” And it is just as the Fourth Patriarch of Chan, Daoxin, said: “States and conditions have no good or ugly; good and ugly arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcefully name them, from what do love and hate arise?”
[The self-mind grasps the self-mind] The Surangama Sutra says:
“When knowing and seeing set up a knowing, that is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are without seeing, that is nirvāṇa, taintless and truly pure.”

[If thus the feelings do not attach to things, how can things obstruct a man? Since things cannot obstruct a man, how does a man obstruct things? The reason worldly men cannot be free is only that they do not understand that mind and states are unborn and illusory and unreal. If one understands that a single thought is unborn and like an illusion, then all suffering and joy, care and calamity, gain and loss, love and hate, grasping and rejecting, melt away like ice on the spot. Hence it is said: “Knowing the illusory, one is at once free, without using expedients; free of the illusory, one is at once awake, and there are no stages either.” This is what is meant by “a single thought arrives at the Buddha’s home at once”; it is no idle word.]

In this way, so long as the feelings do not attach to things, how can things obstruct a man? Since things cannot obstruct a man, how does a man obstruct things? The reason worldly men cannot be free is only that they do not understand that mind and states are both unborn (originally non-existent) and illusory and unreal. If one understands that a single thought is unborn and like an illusion, then all suffering and joy, care and calamity, gain and loss, love and hate, grasping and rejecting, melt away like ice on the spot. Hence the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Knowing the illusory, one is at once free, without using expedients; free of the illusory, one is at once awake, and there are no stages either.” This is what is meant by “a single thought arrives at the Buddha’s home at once”; it is no idle word.

[You need only contemplate the place where all deluded thoughts arise and cease, the place where all states arise and cease: all of it is illusory and unreal. Then the mind of itself will not run after states, and states of themselves will not entangle the mind. Coming and going, meeting conditions, a single thought is empty and bright, spirit-like and illumining alone, seeing the body and mind before one as illusory and magical, as the moon in water, as an image in a mirror, as a cloud in the sky, as a mirage and a shimmering haze. Holding the adamantine eye thus, do not move again; let all states come as they will — touched, they vanish at once. Whatever deluded mind there be, one glance and it is gone. Using the mind thus, what deluded mind is there to trouble oneself? What deluded state is there that can entangle the mind?]

You need only contemplate the place where all deluded thoughts arise and cease, the place where all states arise and cease: all of it is illusory and unreal. Then the mind of itself will not run after states, and states of themselves will not entangle the mind. Coming and going, meeting conditions, a single thought is empty and bright, spirit-like and illumining alone, seeing the body and mind before one as illusory and magical, as the moon in water, as an image in a mirror, as a cloud in the sky, as a mirage and a shimmering haze. Holding the adamantine eye thus, do not move again; let all states come as they will — touched, they vanish at once. Whatever deluded mind there be, one glance and it is gone. Using the mind thus, what deluded mind is there to trouble oneself? What deluded state is there that can entangle the mind?

[Shimmering haze] In full, “the horse of the wilds” (yěmǎ): a vapor or a haze of dust that appears far off in the desert or the open plain under the heat — an illusion. When one draws near, the illusion vanishes. [Mirage] A vapor that arises under the blazing sun; from afar it looks like water, and the thirsty long to drink, but in the end it cannot be obtained.

blocks.text: 10. Intimate Seeing-Through

inline.s: (From the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Attendant Qi on the Boat Bound for Leiyang)

[The Buddhas and patriarchs taught men, amid birth and death, to realize at once the non-birth dharma-patience, and again and again they wondered that men, within the unborn, falsely see birth and ceasing. These words are like telling a man in the marketplace about the events of a dream: the hearer is not one who does not open his eyes wide and pluck up courage, but he has not yet verified it for himself. In short, what is spoken is not what is heard, and what is heard is not what is seen. The ancients valued actual realization because they wished simply, within the dharmas of birth and death, to see through intimately — there is no other extraordinary place. I once saw a child afraid of ghosts: walking in the night, he fancied that something followed him, and great terror arose. Though his kind mother reasoned with him that originally there was nothing, he did not believe her; he had to wait until he himself believed beyond doubt before he stopped. If he came of himself to the place of no doubt, then even if a ghost were sent to frighten him, he would laugh and let it go.]

The Buddhas and patriarchs taught men, amid birth and death, to realize at once the non-birth dharma-patience. And again and again they sighed over why men, within the unborn (the originally unborn), falsely see birth and ceasing. Those who hear these words cannot but be moved and stirred, yet they have not verified them for themselves; it is just like telling a man on the street about some strange event in a dream — it is truly hard to believe. In short, the principle that is spoken of, that “birth is yet non-birth,” is not what they have ever heard before; and even what they have heard is not what they have seen with their own eyes. Hence it is hard truly to believe. The ancients esteemed those who actually realized the unborn dharma because they wished simply, within the dharmas of birth and death, to see through intimately with their own eyes — there is no other extraordinary place. I once saw a child afraid of ghosts: often, walking alone at night, he always felt that something followed behind him, and was terribly frightened. Though his kind mother reasoned well with him that there was originally nothing following him, he would not believe it. He had to wait until he had verified it himself and truly believed there was nothing, and knew it was all the working of his own mind, his own frightening of himself, before he would no longer feel that something followed him at night. If he had come to the place of complete and undoubting belief in “no ghost follows me,” then even if someone dressed up as a ghost and followed behind him to frighten him, he would laugh it off.

[Non-birth dharma-patience] In brief, non-birth patience: true wisdom resting securely upon the principle of true suchness, which is neither arising nor ceasing. “Neither arising nor ceasing” means: all dharmas are like things in a dream — originally unborn, and therefore also not ceasing. The Diamond Sutra says: “Whatever has marks is false and delusive.”

[In former days I traveled on the frontier, and rode by night with a sturdy fellow. Beside the road was a stone; the horse suddenly saw it and was greatly startled, and nearly threw him to the ground. He then reined in the horse, whipped and urged it mightily, and made it walk round the stone several dozen times; then he led it to look closely at the stone for a long while, and only then let it go loose and gallop off. From that time on, the horse was never startled by anything it met. From this I knew that a man who travels the perilous road of birth and death, testing his mind through states as they come, must do the same and only then be done. Therefore the Avatamsaka uses Sudhana to represent realization. The hundred cities he passed through, the many good friends he consulted — even at the mountain of knives and the mass of fire he still hung back and waited to be urged before entering. And when he entered, he truly attained the gate of cool and great liberation. Is this not what is meant by “urging the horse round the stone and making it look closely”?]

In former days, when I traveled on the frontier, I rode by night with a sturdy fellow. Beside the road was a great stone; his horse suddenly saw it, took it for some monstrous beast, and was greatly startled, and nearly threw him to the ground. He then reined in the horse, and whipped and urged it mightily, making it walk several dozen circles round the stone; then he stopped and led the horse to gaze at it closely for a long while, until it knew there was nothing to fear, and only then let the reins go and galloped off. From that time on, that horse was never startled by anything it met. From this I knew that a man who comes and goes on the perilous road of birth and death, testing his mind through states as they come, must do the same and only then be done (urging the horse round the stone, making it look closely, until it no longer doubts or fears and only then stops). Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra uses Sudhana’s fifty-three visits to make clear how actual realization is won. Sudhana passed through more than a hundred cities and consulted many good friends; and when he came to the Brahmin Shantacitta and faced the mountain of knives and the mass of fire, he was still alarmed and doubtful. Only after repeated urging did he dare to enter. And when he entered, he truly attained the gate of cool and great liberation (personally realizing that the mountain of knives and the mass of fire are an illusion). Is this not precisely “urging the horse round the stone and making it look closely,” so as to see through intimately?
[Frontier] A strategic place on the border. [Sudhana’s fifty-three visits] The Avatamsaka Sutra

, “Entering the Dharma Realm,” relates how the youth Sudhana journeyed south in succession and consulted fifty-three good friends. [The mountain of knives and the mass of fire] This is the ninth of Sudhana’s fifty-three visits, his visit to the Brahmin Shantacitta. When Sudhana came before the Brahmin Shantacitta, he saw on all four sides masses of fire, and in their midst a mountain of knives, high and steep beyond measure. The Brahmin Shantacitta climbed this mountain of knives and then threw himself into the great mass of fire. At that time Sudhana bowed to him, stood with palms joined, and said reverently: “Holy One, I have already brought forth the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, but I do not know how to learn the bodhisattva’s practices or how to cultivate the bodhisattva’s way. I have heard that you, Holy One, are skilled in instructing, and I beg you to speak for me.” The Brahmin Shantacitta said: “Good man, if you can now climb this mountain of knives and throw yourself into the mass of fire, then all the bodhisattva’s practices will be purified.” Sudhana’s mind gave rise to doubt: “If I throw myself in, will I not lose my life? Can it be that a demon has taken the form of a bodhisattva to lure me into the evil paths and obstruct my study?” So he was frightened beyond measure. At that time ten thousand great Brahma kings, ten thousand Paranirmita-Vasavartin kings, ten thousand Sunirmita kings, ten thousand Tushita kings, ten thousand Yama kings, ten thousand Shakra kings (lords of the Trayastrimsha heaven), ten thousand naga kings, ten thousand yaksha kings, ten thousand gandharva kings, ten thousand asura kings, ten thousand garuda kings, ten thousand kinnara kings, and measureless gods of the desire realm appeared one after another, crying out in the air, telling Sudhana not to doubt, and testifying for him that the Brahmin Shantacitta was a great good friend. Only after the gods had urged him in turn did Sudhana give rise to faith. “At that time the youth Sudhana, hearing all these various teachings, was greatly delighted, and leaped for joy beyond measure. Before the Brahmin he gave rise to the thought that this was a true good friend. Bowing his head to his feet, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke thus: ‘Toward the great holy good friend I gave rise to disbelief and harbored doubt. I pray only that the Holy One permit me to repent my fault.’ Then the Brahmin spoke a verse for Sudhana: ‘If there are bodhisattvas who follow a good friend’s teaching, without any doubt or fear, abiding with a mind unmoved, they shall surely attain the Buddhas’ natural wisdom, subdue Mara, sit at the place of enlightenment, and broadly save beings beyond measure.’ At that time Sudhana at once climbed the mountain of knives and threw himself into the mass of fire. Before he reached the middle, he attained the bodhisattva’s samādhi of good abiding; and the moment he touched the flames, he attained the bodhisattva’s samādhi of serene bliss and spiritual power.”
[Seen from this, the Buddhas and patriarchs have no other strong point at all; they were simply men who could look closely at the marks of the world
(the world)

. What worldly men dread — is it not birth and death and calamity? Yet the Buddhas and patriarchs wish to make men realize non-birth patience amid these very things, and moreover declare plainly that within the unborn one falsely sees birth and ceasing. Ah! What does this really mean? If one does not look closely until one comes of oneself to the place of no doubt, then in my view, though the compassionate Honored One reason with one well, one will hardly escape dread.]

Seen from this, the Buddhas and patriarchs have no other strong point at all; they were simply able to see clearly that the marks of the world are illusory, and in the midst of what is so plainly birth and ceasing to see only non-birth. What worldly men dread is nothing but birth and death and calamity. Yet the Buddhas and patriarchs wish to make men actually realize non-birth dharma-patience amid birth and death and calamity, and moreover declare plainly: living beings, within the utterly still and unborn, falsely see birth and ceasing. Ah! What does this really point to? If one does not look closely with one’s own eyes until one comes to the place of no doubt, then in my view, though the greatly compassionate World-Honored One instruct one earnestly, when faced with the calamity of birth and death one will probably hardly escape dread.

[Of late, because I spread the Dharma, I met with calamity: it reached even to the sage’s anger, like thunder on a bright day, at which hearers stopped their ears. From the time I was arrested until I came out, more than two hundred days, I passed through bitter things beyond all words. From first to last, I looked within and found that a single thought of joy was not in the least diminished from former days, and those who saw it were all astonished, taking it for something quite out of the ordinary. Yet the calamity of birth and death — others were astonished on my account; and when they saw that my joy was not diminished, they were astonished again. I am not astonished at what astonishes them, while they are astonished at what does not astonish me; perhaps there is a Way in it!]

Of late, because I spread the Dharma, I met with persecution, and it reached even to the sage’s (the emperor’s) anger (the Master, being slandered for spreading the Dharma, enraged the emperor, was arrested and cast into prison, tortured for confession, his life or death unknown), like thunder on a bright day, at which hearers stopped their ears. From the time I was arrested until my exile left the capital, for more than two hundred days, I passed through bitter things beyond all words. From first to last, I looked within and found that a single thought of joy was not in the least diminished from usual, and those who saw it were all greatly astonished. Yet the sudden calamity of birth and death — others were astonished on my account; and when they saw that my joy was not diminished from usual, they were all the more astonished. I am not astonished at the calamity of birth and death at which men are astonished, while men are astonished that I am not astonished; perhaps there is some principle in it!

[Attendant Qi, not grudging three thousand li, came to share my calamity and questioned me in the dark prison. Afterwards, by the grace of the sage’s favor, I was exiled to Lingnan. Qi then accompanied me on the boat, and so I write this in farewell. Alas! The perilous road of birth and death is precisely what men dread; will he not hear of my mind of joy as a thing in a dream? Another day, when I am tested in the field of stillness and cessation, do not take today’s words for the talk of a dream.]

Attendant Qi (an attendant whose surname was Qi) came from three thousand li away to rescue me from danger, and questioned me in the great prison. Before long, by the grace of the emperor’s favor, I was not sentenced to death but exiled to Lingnan. Attendant Qi then accompanied me along the way, as far as the boat bound for Leiyang. Now that he was going back, I wrote these words in farewell. Alas! At the very edge of birth and death — this is precisely what men dread. Yet to hear that I, my body suffering cruel punishment and facing death, had a mind of joy not in the least diminished from usual — is it not like hearing tell of some strange event in a dream? Another day, in the field of stillness and cessation, you will of yourself verify that what I have said is true speech, and will not take today’s words for the talk of a dream.

[Attendant] One who waits at the side of a master or elder, obeying his commands and serving him. [Field of stillness and cessation] The state of realizing non-birth dharma-patience — delusion exhausted and the real revealed, stillness and cessation manifest before one.

blocks.text: 11. True Cultivation and Real Awakening

inline.s: (From the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Seat-Master Miaozhan)
To let no single thought slip past is true cultivation; to see through every single thought is real awakening.

[To let no single thought slip past] Do not let any deluded thought slip by (do not be deceived by it). [To see through every single thought] Do not be shrouded by any deluded thought, do not follow its tricks, do not take it for something real.

[From of old the ancients left home for the sake of the great matter of birth and death. Even the Buddhas’ appearing in the world was specially to reveal this matter and nothing more. It is not that apart from birth and death there is a separate Buddhadharma, nor that apart from the Buddhadharma there is a separate birth and death. It is as said: deluded, birth and death begin; awakened, the wheel of rebirth ceases. From this one knows that the ancients’ investigation and seeking was only to get to the bottom of things and seek the ultimate at the head of the road of birth and death; it was not that apart from this, in paper, ink, and letters, or in the three vehicles and twelve teachings, there was something extraordinary to be made of it.]

From of old the ancients left home for the sake of the great matter of escaping birth and death. Even the Buddhas’ appearing in the world was specially to reveal this matter (escaping birth and death) and nothing more. It is not that apart from the great matter of escaping birth and death there is a separate Buddhadharma, nor that apart from the Buddhadharma there is any separate escaping of birth and death. (This means: the Buddhadharma is precisely about escaping birth and death; only what escapes birth and death is Buddhadharma. The birth and death spoken of here means the birth and death of delimited rebirth and the birth and death of transformation.) It is as said: deluded, birth and death begin; awakened, the wheel of rebirth ceases. (“The wheel of rebirth ceases” is the escape from delimited birth and death. Here Master Hanshan especially stresses escaping delimited birth and death, because this is the cultivator’s urgent task.) From this one knows that the ancients’ investigation and seeking was only to find an ultimate way out at the crucial juncture of birth and death, and not, apart from this, to find something extraordinary in paper, ink, and letters, or in the three vehicles and twelve teachings.

[The great matter of birth and death] The great matter of escaping birth and death. The birth and death spoken of here means the birth and death of delimited rebirth and the birth and death of transformation. [The bottom of things] The details, the root cause. [The twelve teachings] All the sutras and teachings. The content of the teachings is divided into twelve classes altogether, and so they are called the twelve divisions of the teaching, also known as the twelve divisions of the sutras.

[Therefore Bodhidharma came from the West, established nothing in words, and only awakened to his own mind, taking this mind as the root of all the dependent and principal retributions of the ten realms of sages and ordinary beings. Awakening to this mind wholly, one is the supreme Mahāyāna; awakening to it in part, one is of the two vehicles; not awakening to it, one is an ordinary being. If one awakens without keeping it, and realizes without attaining, then one is on the road that goes beyond, transcending sages and ordinary beings and escaping birth and death.]

Therefore Patriarch Bodhidharma came from India (ancient India) and established his guiding principle: establish nothing in words, point directly at the human mind. Cultivation lies only in awakening to one’s own mind, because this mind is the root of all the dependent and principal retributions of the ten dharma realms of sages and ordinary beings. Awakening to this mind wholly, one is the supreme Mahāyāna; awakening to it in part, one is of the two vehicles; not awakening to it, one is an ordinary being. If one awakens without keeping it in mind, and realizes without counting it as an attainment, then one is on the road that goes beyond, transcending sages and ordinary beings and escaping birth and death.

[Establish nothing in words] In Chan, awakening to the Way does not involve words and phrases, but single-mindedly transmits mind to mind by its profound purport; this is called “establishing nothing in words, a separate transmission outside the teachings.” The Five Lamps Meeting at the Source, “Chapter on the World-Honored One,” says: “When the World-Honored One was at the Vulture Peak assembly, he held up a flower before the assembly. At that time the men and gods, a million of them, were all at a loss; only the golden-haired ascetic (Mahākāśyapa) broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the subtle Dharma gate of the mark of reality that is no mark, which establishes nothing in words and is a separate transmission outside the teachings; I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa.”

[Students in recent times are farther from the sages than ever, and have not seen the ancients’ true conduct of practice — passing through, one by one, the states that appear daily before them and the shore of birth and death. In this very daily use, not departing from a single dharma and not abiding in a single dharma, never lightly letting a thing slip past anywhere: this is true and genuine work. In this very present moment, wherever one sees through, one by one, all the states of sound and form, of adverse and favorable, of love and hate, there is the true gate of awakening. In this very place of awakening, each thing and each dharma is the true Buddhadharma. It is not that the Buddhadharma is only when one listens to a seat-master strike the bell and beat the drum, ascend the flower seat, open his mouth wide and learn the howl of the jackal, or when one inclines the ear, bows the head, shuts the eyes, and dons the robe. Therefore the youth Sudhana journeyed south through a hundred cities and paid respects to good friends as numerous as dust-motes in a Buddha-land, and so awakened to the Dharma gates of liberation in every dust-mote and every Buddha-land.]

Students in recent times are far from the sages, and have not seen the ancients’ true conduct of practice — passing through, one by one, the states that appear daily before them and the shore of birth and death. In this very daily use, not departing from (not avoiding) a single dharma and not abiding in (not clinging to) a single dharma, never lightly letting a thing slip past anywhere: this is true and genuine work. In this very present moment, wherever one sees through, one by one, all the states of sound and form, of adverse and favorable, of love and hate — seeing through to the place where one is not deceived and not turned by them — there is the true gate of awakening. In this very place of awakening, each thing and each matter is the true Buddhadharma. It is not that the Buddhadharma is only when one listens to a preacher of sutras strike the bell and beat the drum, ascend the dharma seat, open his mouth wide and imitate the howl of the jackal (falsely speaking the truth), or when one inclines the ear, bows the head, shuts the eyes, and dons the robe (the motions by which a seat-master draws out and awakens a student). Therefore the youth Sudhana journeyed south through more than a hundred cities and paid respects to good friends as numerous as dust-motes in a Buddha-land, and in practice awakened to the Dharma gates of liberation in every dust-mote and every Buddha-land.

[Seeing through] Not being entangled and manipulated by the dusts of states. [Each thing] Every single matter, every single item. [Seat-master] One who preaches the sutras and speaks the Dharma. [Flower seat] The lotus seat; here it means the dharma seat from which one preaches the sutras and speaks the Dharma. [Jackal] A kind of fox. “The howl of the jackal” is the counterpart of “the lion’s roar,” used to liken one whose practice has not yet ripened but who falsely speaks the truth. [As numerous as dust-motes in a Buddha-land] A figure for an extremely great number. [Every dust-mote and every Buddha-land] A state spoken of in the Avatamsaka Sutra: within each single dust-mote appear countless Buddha-lands (Buddha realms), and in each Buddha-land there are countless dust-motes, and within each dust-mote again appear countless Buddha-lands, layer upon layer without end. Here “every dust-mote and every Buddha-land” is used to describe an extremely great number.

[Yet of Dharma gates there is no need to speak; but as for good friends, how could there be as many as dust-motes in a Buddha-land? Little does one know that “every Buddha-land and every dust-mote” is simply the deluded thoughts, calculations, and emotional dust of our daily use. If one can, at the place where thought arises and moves in daily use, at the place where the roots of feeling are knotted fast, at the place where love and hate cross and are hard to untie, at the place where the habitual tendencies of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride are hard to wear away, — if at the root’s sorest point one drives in the awl
(same as “pricks”)

and sees through them one by one, passes through them one by one, then this is the true good friend, and on the spot one ascends the supreme Dharma gate of unobstructed freedom and great liberation. Apart from this, what other good friend is there to consult? What more extraordinary Dharma gate is there to enter?]

Yet let us leave the Dharma gates aside; to speak of good friends, how could there be as many of them as dust-motes in a Buddha-land, so many that they cannot be counted? Little does one know that what is called “every Buddha-land and every dust-mote” means the deluded thoughts, calculations, and emotional dust of our daily life. If one can, at the place where thought arises and moves in daily life, at the place where the roots of feeling are knotted fast, at the place where love and hate cross and are hard to untie, at the place where the habitual tendencies of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride are hard to wear away, — if at the root’s sorest point one drives in the awl, sees through them
(as a dream or an illusion)
, and passes through them
(cutting off deluded thoughts)

one by one, then this is your true great good friend, and on the spot you attain the supreme Dharma gate of unobstructed freedom and great liberation. Apart from this, what other good friend is there to consult? What more extraordinary Dharma gate is there to enter?

blocks.text: 12. Returning Home Along the Road

inline.s: (From the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Instructions to the Chan Man Zhenyu)

[The Chan man Zhenyu was born in Luling. He abandoned wife and children and left home, delighting in the practice of remoteness, his aspiration set on the famous mountains, to consult good friends. The illusory man, carried astray to Linghai by illusory karma, was thus visited by the Chan man. A short while ago he took leave to go to Putuo to pay respects to Master Daguan, who gave him the verse of the Buddha Visvabhu; and again he brought it here to Wuyang.]

The Chan man Zhenyu (this Chan man was named Zhenyu) was born in Luling; he abandoned wife and children and left home, delighting in the practice of distant wandering, and set his resolve to travel all the famous mountains of the world and pay respects to the good friends. The illusory man (Master Hanshan’s name for himself), because the illusory karma of his own transformation carried him into exile at Linghai, was thus visited by the Chan man. Before long he took leave to go to Putuo to pay respects to Master Daguan (that is, the Venerable Zibai, who often taught people with the verse of the Buddha Visvabhu), who gave him the verse of the Buddha Visvabhu; and again he brought this verse to Wuyang (Guangzhou) to seek instruction from me.

[Linghai] The region of Guangdong and Guangxi. Its land leans north upon the Five Ranges and faces south upon the South Sea; hence the name “Linghai.” [The verse of the Buddha Visvabhu] The Buddha Visvabhu is the third of the seven Buddhas of the past. The verse of the Buddha Visvabhu runs: “Borrowing the four great elements, one takes them for a body; the mind is originally unborn but exists because of states. If the states before it are not, the mind too is not; offense and merit are like illusions, arising and ceasing as well.” This means: body, mind, and world are all illusory.

[The illusory man, in the field of illusion, performs illusory Buddha-work, opens the assembly of the illusory, and speaks the illusory Dharma gate. The Chan man bowed and sought instruction, and the illusory man, relying on the samādhi of illusion, spoke for him of all dharmas as states of illusion and dream, and instructed him, saying:]

The illusory man (I, Master Hanshan), in the field of illusion, performs illusory Buddha-work, instructs the assembly of the illusory, and speaks the illusory Dharma gate. The Chan man bowed and sought teaching; and so the illusory man, relying on the samādhi of illusion that the World-Honored One sets forth in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, explained for him that all dharmas are states of illusion and dream, and instructed him, saying:

[Excellent, son of the Buddha! You should consider it well. All Buddhas manifest by the power of illusion; all bodhisattvas cultivate by the power of illusion; all of the two vehicles advance toward stillness by the power of illusion; all non-Buddhists fall into confusion by the power of illusion; all living beings undergo birth and death by the power of illusion. And as for the heavenly palaces and pure lands, they are established by the power of illusion; the jeweled groves and precious trees flourish by the power of illusion; the iron beds and copper pillars are furnished by the power of illusion; the cauldrons of boiling water and the furnaces of coals seethe by the power of illusion; the scaled, the shelled, the feathered, and the furred fly and dive by the power of illusion; the crawling, the wriggling, the shelled, and the winged move and rest by the power of illusion. Even to the utmost, what the Buddhas of the three ages have realized and what the six generations of patriarchs have transmitted is nowhere beyond this samādhi of the illusory net. How could the Chan man escape it?]

Excellent, son of the Buddha! You should consider it well. All Buddhas manifest by the power of illusion; all bodhisattvas cultivate by the power of illusion; all of the two vehicles advance toward stillness by the power of illusion; all non-Buddhists fall into confusion by the power of illusion; all living beings undergo birth and death by the power of illusion. As for the heavenly palaces and pure lands, they are all established by the power of illusion. The jeweled groves and precious trees all flourish by the power of illusion; the iron beds and copper pillars are all furnished by the power of illusion; the cauldrons of boiling water and the furnaces of coals all seethe by the power of illusion; the scaled, the shelled, the feathered, and the furred all fly and dive by the power of illusion; the crawling, the wriggling, the shelled, and the winged all move and rest by the power of illusion. Even to the utmost, what the Buddhas of the three ages have realized and what the six generations of patriarchs have transmitted is nowhere beyond this samādhi of the illusory net. How could the Chan man be outside the illusory net?

Throughout this book, Master Hanshan constantly instructs students in the true character of all dharmas. Hence it is best to read it after finishing the five courses of the “Prajñā Breaking Delusion” stage at the
“Practice as Taught” Online Buddhist Academy

: the Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra, the Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra, the Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the Selected Annotations on the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury, and the Detailed Explanation of Direct Pointing at the True Mind — and then it will be easy to understand.

[Try to consider carefully: for what cause do you fall into birth and death? For what cause do you enter a mother’s womb? For what cause are you drowned in the entanglement of craving? For what cause do you wish to escape the sinking? For what cause do you set out and cross beyond the region? For what cause do you consult good friends? For what cause do you tread famous mountains and climb blessed lands, pass through the thicket of the assembly and enter the community of the bound? This year the South Sea, next year Mount Wutai, the year after Mount Emei — you would travel all within the realm, and though you pass through dust-mote kalpas and exhaust the dust-mote lands of the ten directions, serving all the great good friends of the ten directions, it is all nowhere beyond the doorway of illusion; it is not the ultimate and true place.]

Think about it seriously: why do you have birth and death? For what cause did you enter your mother’s womb? For what cause do you drown in craving and the entanglement of love? For what cause do you wish to escape saṃsāra? For what cause do you wander abroad in every direction? For what cause do you call upon and visit spiritual benefactors? For what cause do you tread famous mountains and climb blessed lands? You pass through the monastery groves, cross the villages, go to Nanhai this year, roam Mount Wutai next year, visit Mount Emei the year after — even if you travel the whole world over, even if you pass through dust-mote kalpas, exhausting lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, and serve the great spiritual benefactors of the ten directions, still you never get beyond the gate of illusion; and so this is not the ultimate, true place.

[Drowning (gǔ)] To be buried and lost, to sink. [Entanglement of love] The Yoga Sutra says: “Craving that arises inwardly and outwardly, within the activity of love — one should know its mark; this is called the defilement of the entanglement of love.” [Beyond the ordinary sphere] This uses the allusion “his traces filled the land, yet his aspiration transcended the ordinary sphere,” meaning: his feet covered the four seas, his mind transcended the dusty world. The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wude of Fenyang says: “If one does not advance, there can be no natural Śākyamuni or natural Maitreya; therefore set out beyond the ordinary sphere and enter the stairway of the sages.” [Protective society] A kind of folk organization in old rural villages; because it was established on the basis of the bao (the hundred-household unit), it was called a protective society. [Within the realm] The world, all under heaven. [Dust-mote kalpas] That is, “dust-mote kalpa” or “three-thousand dust-mote kalpa,” meaning: grind all things within three thousand great thousand-worlds into ink, and every time one passes through a three-thousand great thousand-world, let fall one drop; when the ink is gone, all the worlds passed through are again shattered into motes of dust, and each mote of dust is counted as one kalpa — this is a simile for an extremely long span of time.

[Yet though it be so, this is called mistaking the head and clutching at its reflection. There is no harm in going home along the road one came; if one can cut through the knot of illusion with a single step, then the boundless net of illusion is in one instant rent asunder; the shoreless ocean of illusion is in one instant dried up; the measureless karma of illusion is in one instant dissolved; the boundless practices of illusion are in one instant attained; the measureless beings of illusion are in one instant ferried across. This is what is called practicing illusion by means of illusion — as it is said, the illusory mind of sentient beings is still extinguished in dependence on illusion. If it be otherwise, then even though one pass through three lives and sixty kalpas, with Mañjuśrī as father, Avalokiteśvara as mother, and Samantabhadra as teacher, and would rely on these intimate causes to seek the matter of escaping birth and death, one is far, far away! Consider this well; do not say that I am a phantom person and that what I speak are not true words. Investigate! Investigate!]

Though you toil and rush about in this way, worn out in body and mind, it is still called “mistaking the head and clutching at its reflection, running madly without cause,” and it is not the ultimate, true place. You ought rather to go home along the road you came (and not toil and rush about seeking spiritual benefactors); if you can go home along the road you came (doing the work right where your mind stirs and thoughts arise) and cut through the knot of illusion with a single step, then the boundless net of illusion is in one instant rent asunder; the shoreless ocean of illusion is in one instant dried up; the measureless karma of illusion is in one instant dissolved; the boundless practices of illusion are in one instant attained; the measureless beings of illusion (illusory sentient beings) are in one instant ferried across. This is what is called practicing illusion by means of illusion — as it is said, “the illusory mind of sentient beings is still extinguished in dependence on illusion.” If you do not practice thus (going home along the road you came, cutting through the knot of illusion), then even though you pass through three lives and sixty kalpas, with Mañjuśrī as father, Avalokiteśvara as mother, and Samantabhadra as teacher, and would rely on this intimate cause to settle birth and death, that is far, far indeed! You must earnestly ponder these principles, and on no account think that I am a phantom person and that what I speak are not true words. Investigate! Investigate!

The Chan practicer Zhenyu placed his hopes for his own cultivation and realization upon spiritual benefactors; and so, sparing himself no hardship, he roamed the four seas and visited famous teachers everywhere. Master Hanshan, taking the verse of Viśvabhu Buddha that he had brought to ask about, instructed him with the samādhi of illusion, telling him to go home along the road he came (doing the work right where his mind stirs and thoughts arise) and to cut through the knot of illusion. And he especially roused him, saying: to say nothing of famous teachers and great spiritual benefactors — even if you relied on the intimate causes of Mañjuśrī as father, Avalokiteśvara as mother, and Samantabhadra as teacher in order to escape birth and death, that would be utterly impossible; only by doing the work yourself right where your mind stirs and thoughts arise, and cutting through the knot of illusion, can you escape birth and death.

[Mistaking the head and clutching at its reflection] To lose one’s own head and take up the reflection in a mirror instead. It is a metaphor for losing one’s true nature and failing to see one’s own original face. This uses the simile recorded in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra

Fascicle Four: In the city of Śrāvastī there was a man named Yajñadatta who one day looked at his face in a mirror, and, seeing in the mirror the brows and eyes of his own head, was delighted; but when he turned to look at his own head, he could not see the brows and eyes, and so gave rise to great rage, thinking himself possessed by a demon, and thereupon ran madly about without cause. Here one’s own head is a simile for the true nature, and the head in the mirror a simile for delusive appearance. Delight at seeing brows and eyes on the head in the mirror is a simile for falsely seizing the illusory state as real and clinging to it without letting go; rage at one’s own head for not showing brows and eyes is a simile for delusion and falsehood turning away from the true. The Five Lamps Meeting at the Source

Chan Master Hongying of Letan says: “The patriarchs succeeded one another, until Bodhidharma came from the West, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha, setting up no reliance on words or language — was this not the ancient sages’ skillful means? Yet people today do not believe it; instead they mistake the head and clutch at its reflection, running wild upon a mad path, so that they are left utterly alone (líng píng, solitary and shadowless), wandering through birth and death.” Master Hanshan here uses this allusion to point out the error of the Chan practicer Zhenyu, who did not do the work right where his own mind stirs and thoughts arise, but sought the Dharma outside the mind and rushed about in all directions. [Going home along the road one came] The Old Man Wansong says: “If one can go home along the road one came, one turns about and returns to the father. Do you not see the saying: a single thought turned back to the light is the same as attaining the original.” [Knot of illusion] A knot means binding; it is another name for affliction. Because affliction can bind the body and mind of sentient beings so that they cannot be freed but forever sink into birth and death, it is called a “knot.” The knot of illusion means that the knot is an illusion. [Three lives and sixty kalpas] The time required by the Śrāvaka Vehicle to cultivate and realize the fruit. The quickest realize the highest fruit in three lives; the slowest realize the highest fruit in sixty kalpas.

blocks.text: 13. The Wondrous Practice of Freedom from Desire

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practicer Ruoliang)

[The Buddha said: “To shave off the beard and hair and become a śrāmaṇera, to be free of desire and still — this is foremost.” From this we know that desire is the foremost great matter at the head of the road of birth and death. Therefore he sharply rebuked it and strictly warned against it; being free of it, one attains peace
(the same character as “steady”)
and happiness. The reason sentient beings sink into the sea of suffering and cannot quickly reach the other shore is none other than the fault of desire.]

The Buddha said: “To shave off the beard and hair and become a śrāmaṇera, to be free of desire and still — this is foremost.” From this we know that desire is the foremost great matter at the head of the road of birth and death. Therefore the Buddha sharply rebuked it and strictly warned against it; being free of desire, one attains peace and happiness. The reason sentient beings sink into the sea of suffering and cannot quickly reach the other shore is entirely the fault of desire!

[The Buddha said: “The cause of all suffering is craving, which is the root.” If craving is extinguished, there is nothing to rely on. Moreover, the three realms are the house in which all sentient beings take refuge, and desire is its foundation. The clamor of the dust of affliction — all of it is this making noise. If one once departs from this reliance, then there is no longer any question of breaking the three poisons, leaving the three realms, and shattering the net of Māra; at such a time the Tathāgata is greatly delighted. From this we know that if the five desires are not abandoned, the three realms are hard to break, and our Tathāgata’s sorrow may be known; to seek still liberation will be difficult.]

The Buddha said: “The cause of all suffering is craving, which is the root.” If craving is extinguished, then suffering has nothing to rely on. Moreover, the three realms are the house in which all sentient beings take refuge, and desire is its root. The reason why affliction clamors and disturbs, so that one cannot be still, is entirely because of desire! Once desire is let go, affliction and all suffering have nothing to rely on, and then there is no longer any question of breaking the three poisons, leaving the three realms, and shattering the net of Māra; at such a time the World-Honored One is greatly delighted. From this we know that if the five desires are not abandoned, the three realms are hard to break, and our Buddha’s sorrow may be known; and to seek still liberation will be difficult!

[Foundation] Basis, root. [Dust of affliction] The mind toiling over the objects of dust — another name for affliction. [Five desires] Form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Form means beautiful appearances; sound means melodious voices; fragrance means fragrant scents; taste means delicious flavors; touch means pleasant sensations of the body. These five can cause the mind of craving to arise, and so they are called the five desires.

[Ruoliang left home young and wandered on pilgrimage in many places. Now he has met this old man, aroused the bodhi mind, and received the śrāmaṇera precepts. To resolve to cultivate the practice of freedom from desire — this is the foremost wondrous practice of one who wishes to escape birth and death. The only fear is that the resolve be unsteady and the practice lacking in strength. The Buddha said: “Only after long endurance of hardship can one attain it.” One should settle a firm resolve and not stop until one has become Buddha; this is truly resolving to cultivate the practice of freedom from desire.]

Ruoliang left home young and wandered on pilgrimage in many places. Now he met this old man, aroused the bodhi mind, and received the śrāmaṇera precepts. To resolve to cultivate the practice of freedom from desire — this is the foremost wondrous practice of one who wishes to escape birth and death. But out of fear that his resolve might be unsteady and his practice lacking in strength, the old man gave the instruction above. The Buddha said: “Only after long endurance of hardship can one attain it.” Therefore one should settle a firm resolve and not stop until one has become Buddha; this is truly resolving to cultivate the practice of freedom from desire.

blocks.text: 14. Patience as a Robe

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practicer Fajin)

[Fajin said of himself that his nature had much habit of anger; the old man therefore tamed him by skillful means and showed him the Dharma gate of patience. He further instructed him, saying: Master Yongjia has said: “My teacher saw the Lamp-Lighting Buddha; for many kalpas he was the Patient Immortal.” From this we know that the single practice of patience is the foremost wondrous practice for becoming Buddha.]

Fajin said of himself that the habit of anger was very heavy; the old man (Master Hanshan referring to himself) therefore tamed him by skillful means and showed him the Dharma gate of patience. He further instructed him, saying: Master Yongjia says in the Song of Realizing the Way: “My teacher saw the Lamp-Lighting Buddha; for many kalpas he was the Patient Immortal.” From this we know that the single practice of “patience” is the foremost wondrous practice for becoming Buddha.

[Therefore our teacher, the old Śākyan, life after life was slandered and harmed by Devadatta, down to his appearance in this present life. Devadatta’s various devices to destroy the Dharma stopped at nothing, and more than once he even tried to take his life. Yet at the Lotus assembly the Buddha predicted for him that he would become a Buddha, saying: my thirty-two marks and eighty excellences, my supreme and wondrous virtues, were all brought to accomplishment through the good friend Devadatta. Was this not because the single practice of patience is an essential practice for becoming Buddha? He also said: formerly, when King Kali cut my body to pieces, at that time I had no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life; if I had had the mark of a self, of a person, of a being, or of a life, the Lamp-Lighting Buddha would not have given me the prediction.]

Therefore our World-Honored One, life after life, was slandered and harmed by Devadatta, down to this present life. Devadatta’s various devices to destroy the Dharma stopped at nothing, and more than once he even sought to take the World-Honored One’s life. Yet at the Lotus assembly the World-Honored One predicted for him that he would become a Buddha, and said: the reason I have realized the thirty-two marks and eighty excellences, my supreme and wondrous virtues, is that they were brought to accomplishment through the persecution of the good friend Devadatta. Does this not show that the single practice of “patience” is an essential practice for becoming Buddha? The World-Honored One also says in the Diamond Sūtra: formerly, when King Kali cut my body to pieces, at that time I had no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life; if I had had the mark of a self, of a person, of a being, or of a life, the Lamp-Lighting Buddha would not have given me the prediction.

[Devadatta] The Buddha’s cousin, who left home and studied supernormal powers; his body bore thirty marks. He persecuted the Buddha again and again. [My teacher saw the Lamp-Lighting Buddha; for many kalpas he was the Patient Immortal] The World-Honored One (my teacher) came to see the Lamp-Lighting Buddha and receive the prediction of becoming a Buddha, all because of the tempering he underwent through many kalpas as the Patient Immortal. Utterly contrary to worldly people, the Buddha took being humiliated as a good thing, for only through a hundred refinings does iron become steel, and only through patience can the marks of self, person, being, and life be worn away — as it is said, “hardship and adversity bring you to completion.” [Seeing the Lamp-Lighting Buddha] In the past, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva of the seventh ground, he met the Lamp-Lighting Buddha and heard the Dharma, realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, and rose to the eighth ground; the Lamp-Lighting Buddha then gave him the prediction, saying: after ninety-one kalpas, in the kalpa called Bhadra, you shall become a Buddha with the name Śākyamuni. [Prediction] The Buddha’s advance naming of a bodhisattva: after how many ages, in such-and-such a place, in such-and-such a country, one will become what Buddha. [Bhadra kalpa] The past great kalpa is called the Adornment kalpa, the future great kalpa is called the Constellation kalpa, and the Bhadra kalpa is the present great kalpa; because a thousand Buddhas appear in this great kalpa, it is called the “Bhadra kalpa.”

[From this we see: for all sentient beings, the implements of the suffering of birth and death are all accomplished through having a self; the unsurpassed bodhi, the adornment of merit and wisdom, is all reached through having no self. Because the self is set in opposition to things, right and wrong arise; right and wrong arising, love and hate are established; love and hate established, joy and anger proliferate; the self-nature grows turbid and the mind-ground grows dim; the mind-ground dim, all evils grow; all evils growing, all suffering gathers; all suffering gathered, birth and death are prolonged! All of this is brought about by the self. How grave is the harm done by the self! It is like a heavily fortified city with strong soldiers — how could it be broken easily?]

From this we see: the reason all sentient beings have birth, death, and suffering is that these are established through having a self; the unsurpassed bodhi, the adornment of merit and wisdom, is all realized through having no self. Taking the self as the center, one stands opposed to others, and so right and wrong arise; right and wrong arising, love and hate are established; love and hate established, joy and anger breed. Then the self-nature grows turbid and the mind-ground grows dim; the mind-ground dim, all evils grow; all evils growing, all suffering gathers; all suffering gathered, birth and death roll on without end! All of this is brought about by the presence of a “self.” How grave is the harm done by the self! Yet to break the attachment to self is like attacking a fortress closely guarded by picked troops — how could it be broken easily!

[Having a self] To take the physical body (the four great elements) as one’s own body and thoughts (the shadowy reflections of the six dusts) as one’s own mind. [No self] Not to take the physical body (the four great elements) as one’s own body or thoughts (the shadowy reflections of the six dusts) as one’s own mind, but to take the dharma-body as one’s own body and the numinous awareness as one’s own mind. [Setting the self in opposition to things] To take the self as the center and stand opposed to others. Here “things” means people other than oneself.

[Laozi has a saying: “The soft overcomes the hard; the weak overcomes the strong.” This is the first stage of the practice of patience. Sentient beings rely on their view of self, which is firm and hard to break; and so a single contrary word cannot be borne, a single contrary matter cannot be tolerated, a single hunger or cold cannot be endured, a single thought of desire cannot be purified — all because they do not know the method of patience, and only increase their clinging to the view of self! Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the practice of harmony. He also said: the patience of the truth of suffering, the wisdom of the truth of suffering. And he also said: the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is attained only at the eighth ground. From this we know that from the patience of dharmas as born, enduring on until no-birth, the wondrous practice is perfected and the Buddha-fruit accomplished! How could the single practice of patience be a shallow thing! Therefore it is said: in whatever you do, you should endure.]

The Daodejing of Laozi says: “The soft overcomes the hard; the weak overcomes the strong.” This is the first stage of the practice of patience. The view of self that sentient beings hold is firm and hard to break; and so a single contrary word cannot be borne, a single contrary matter cannot be tolerated, a single hunger or cold cannot be endured, a single thought of desire cannot be purified — all because they do not know the method of the practice of patience, and only keep strengthening their clinging to the view of self! Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the practice of harmony. He also says: “The patience of the truth of suffering, the wisdom of the truth of suffering.” And he also says: “The patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is realized only by a bodhisattva of the eighth ground.” From this we know that enduring on from the patience of dharmas as born until nirvāṇa (no-birth) is attained, the wondrous practice is perfected and the Buddha-fruit accomplished! How could the single practice of “patience” be a trifling matter! Therefore it is said: in whatever you do, you should be able to endure.

[View of self] Also called attachment to self. Falsely clinging to the five aggregates of body and mind as oneself. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all kinds of inversions, like a deluded person who changes his directions (for example, taking east as west, south as north, and so on), falsely acknowledging the four great elements as the marks of their own body and the shadowy reflections of the six dusts as the marks of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons! The sky truly has no flowers; the diseased one falsely clings to them. Because of this false clinging, he is confused not only about the self-nature of this emptiness, but also about where the real flowers arise. Hence he falsely has the revolving of birth and death; this is called ignorance.” [Four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, wind has motion as its nature. All material forms in the world possess these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion, and so are called “great.” [Shadowy reflections of the six dusts] The various thoughts produced when the six sense-faculties come into contact with the six dusts; and since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadowy reflections of the six dusts — the illusory shadows conditioned by the six dusts.

[A single contrary word cannot be borne, a single contrary matter cannot be tolerated, a single hunger or cold cannot be endured, a single thought of desire cannot be purified] This speaks of those who cannot be patient. Patience means being able to do this: to bear a contrary word, to tolerate a contrary matter, to endure hunger and cold, to purify desire when it arises.

[Harmony] Harmony is of two kinds: harmony in principle and harmony in affairs. Harmony in principle is the realization of cessation-by-choice — that is, all together cultivating and realizing this commonly chosen principle of quiescence. Harmony in affairs has six items, the so-called six reverent harmonies: 1. Harmony of body in dwelling together — peaceful coexistence of the body; 2. Harmony of speech in being without contention — speech that does not give rise to argument; 3. Harmony of mind in sharing joy — shared gladness of mind; 4. Harmony of precepts in cultivating together — common observance of the precepts; 5. Harmony of view in understanding alike — complete agreement of views; 6. Harmony of benefit in sharing equally — benefits enjoyed as one body. [The patience of the truth of suffering] With regard to the sufferings of the desire realm, the mind of wisdom abides in the principle of suchness. [The wisdom of the truth of suffering] The undefiled wisdom obtained by contemplating the truth of suffering in the desire realm. [The patience of dharmas as born] The various kinds of patience prior to the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas are called the patience of dharmas as born.

[Thus, wherever the mind stirs and a thought arises, test it with patience; wherever a foot is raised and a step taken, let patience go before; in every movement and every change of countenance, hold to patience; in joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, verify with patience. In this way the mind dares not stir wildly, the body dares not act wildly, in affairs one dares not do wildly, in feelings one dares not erupt wildly. Therefore Laozi says: “Not daring to be first in the world.” “Not daring” is another name for patience. Because of “not daring to be first in the world,” patience is the first practice for becoming Buddha.]

Therefore, wherever the mind stirs and a thought arises, examine it with patience; wherever a foot is raised and a step taken, let patience walk ahead; in dealing with people and handling matters, meet them with patience; in joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, test them with patience.

In this way the mind dares not stir wildly, the body dares not act wildly, in affairs one dares not do wildly, in feelings one dares not erupt wildly. Therefore Laozi says in the Daodejing: “Not daring to act willfully (at whim), one becomes the highest in the world.” “Not daring” is another name for patience. Since not daring (patience) is the highest in the world, patience is the foremost practice (the first practice) for becoming Buddha.
[Movement and turning] Bearing and conduct. [Change of countenance] The appearance of an expression on the face.

[In this way patience is great and the self is small; and so patience can clothe and cover me, and can also clothe and cover others. There is no virtue of benefiting self and others that surpasses this. Hence it is said, the robe of gentleness and patience — for this reason. The Chan practicer asked for a Dharma word, and so I have entitled it: Patience as a Robe. Let the Chan practicer strive to practice it; let him not take it as mere talk of the lips, and let him not use it to win himself a meal.]

In this way patience is great and the self is small; and so patience, like a warm garment in deep winter, can shelter me and can shelter others too. There is no virtue of benefiting self and others that surpasses patience. Hence the saying that one should take gentleness and patience as one’s robe — this is the very reason. The Chan practicer Fajin came to ask for a Dharma word, and so I have entitled this instruction: Patience as a Robe. Fajin, you must strive to practice it! Do not think it a commonplace, and do not use it as a tool to win fame and profit, but carry it out in your own person.

[Robe of patience] The mind of patience, because it can ward off all outer obstructions, is likened to a robe. [Talk of the lips] Set phrases always hanging on the lips. [Win] To exchange for. [Not to use it to win himself a meal] Master Hanshan here warns with weighty earnestness: to study and understand the principle is to practice it in one’s own person; one must never fail to do it oneself while using it to teach others, making it a tool to win fame and profit. The Analects

Xian Wen says: “The learning of the ancients was for themselves; the learning of people today is for others.” The Analects with Commentary and Sub-commentary says: “The learning of the ancients was to tread and practice it — this was for themselves. The learning of people today is merely to speak of it to others, while they cannot practice it themselves — this is for others. Fan Ye says: ‘To be for others is to display oneself to things by means of reputation; to be for oneself is to meet the Way by means of the mind.’” [To display oneself to things by means of reputation] To appear to others (things) by means of reputation — that is, to fish for fame and reputation. “Feng” is in ancient usage the same as “ping” — to rely on, to depend on. “Things” means people other than oneself.

blocks.text: 15. Shattering the Dream and Escaping the Peril

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practicer Mingzhe)

[In the fourth year of my banishment, in the summer of the jǐhài year, I was lecturing on the New Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra in the Traveler’s Rest Hermitage at Qingmen in Wuyang. The Chan practicer came from several thousand li away to call on me in this land of miasma. Seeing his careful and honest manner, I appointed him to oversee the temple meals, intending thereby to let him know the three virtues and harmonize the six flavors, gathering in the one mind while cultivating the ten thousand practices. The Chan practicer obeyed my instructions in all things and worked diligently for more than half a year. Then he happened to breathe the miasmic vapors and was gradually infected with illness. He felt that the four great elements could no longer support him and that he could not bear the many duties. So he begged to cross north of the ranges and seek a pleasant place to rest and recover. When he came to take his leave, the old man therefore urged him, saying: Do you think that suffering and joy are different places, and that death and life have a here and a there? You do not realize that the four great elements are something borrowed, that suffering and joy are a stage of illusion, that death and life are night and morning; nor do you know that the mind is the source of all evils and the body the root of all suffering.]

In the fourth year of my banishment, in the summer of the jǐhài year, I was lecturing on the New Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra in the Traveler’s Rest Hermitage at Qingmen in Wuyang (Guangzhou). The Chan practicer Mingzhe came from several thousand li away to call on me in this land of miasma. Seeing his solid and honest manner, I appointed him to oversee the temple meals, and further instructed him, letting him understand that overseeing the meals, with the three virtues and the six flavors, is likewise gathering in the one mind while cultivating the ten thousand practices. The Chan practicer strictly followed my teaching and had worked diligently for more than half a year. Then, because of the miasma, he was gradually infected with illness. He felt that his physical body could no longer support him and that he could not bear the many duties. So he asked to go north of the ranges and seek a place of peace and comfort to rest and recover. He came to take his leave, and I therefore urged him, saying: How could you think that a land of suffering and a land of joy are different places, and that death and life have a this and a that? You do not realize at all that this is borrowing the four great elements for a body, that the land of suffering and the land of joy are an illusory stage, and that death and life are but the alternation of night and day upon that stage; nor do you know that the mind is the source of all evils and the body the root of all suffering.
[Land of miasma] A place in the south with miasmic vapors. [Miasma] The damp, hot, stifling vapor in the mountain forests of the tropics that causes people to fall ill. Abbreviated as
zhàng,” as in “zhàng-lì (miasmic fever),” “dú-zhàng (poisonous miasma),” “zhàng-yǔ mán-yān (miasmic rain and barbarian smoke).” [Careful and honest] Solid and plain; the character is read “
què”

, pronounced as in the word for “certain.” [Oversee] To be in charge of. [The three virtues and harmonizing the six flavors] When the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, the upāsakas prepared all kinds of food and drink for the Buddha and the Saṃgha; the food was sweet and fine, possessing the three virtues and six flavors. In later ages this became the offering verse recited at temple meals: “Three virtues, six flavors, offered to the Buddha and the Saṃgha; sentient beings of the Dharma realm, all equally receive the offering.” The three virtues: light and soft, pure and clean, in accord with the Dharma. The six flavors: bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland.

[Originally, because the mind was deluded it became consciousness, and one clung to the false as the body, inverting birth and death, appearing and disappearing in the path of suffering, for who knows how many thousands of ten-million kalpas. It is like racing through a perilous road in a dream, terrified and panicked, seeking escape and unable, wishing to get away and not permitted. Sorrowful and wretched, one looks for rescue with no door to turn to; the spirit is worn out, with no means of rest even for a moment. One thinks that one will at last fall into the depths, and so one resigns oneself to drowning. How could one know that by calling out with all one’s might and leaping up with a sudden start, one greatly awakens — and then all the former sorrow and bitterness become a laughingstock. Since one is now awake, how different that is from the former seeking of escape — as different as heaven from earth!]

Sentient beings originally, because they were deluded about the one mind and it became the eight consciousnesses, falsely cling to the four great elements as the body; and so they invert birth and death (taking the illusory as real), appearing and disappearing in the path of suffering, and no one knows for how many thousands of ten-million kalpas this has gone on. This is like racing through a perilous road in a dream, terrified and flustered, wishing to shake it off and unable, wishing to get away and not permitted. Sorrowful and wretched, one looks for rescue with no door to turn to; one can only flee with all one’s might, utterly exhausted, with no way even to catch one’s breath. Thinking there is no way out, one can only accept one’s fate. How could you know that if you but call out with all your might and leap up with a sudden start, the dream will be broken, and all the sorrow and bitterness of the dream will become a laughingstock. Comparing the joy of the nightmare now ended with the suffering of fleeing in the nightmare, there is truly the difference between heaven and hell!
[And so] Thereupon. [Drowning (gǔ)] To sink.

This passage says: sentient beings, from beginningless kalpas, have revolved in birth and death because of delusion and inversion, appearing and disappearing in the path of suffering. This is like having a nightmare: one thinks that these terrors and sufferings cannot be utterly escaped, and so one can only flee helplessly, and when one cannot flee, one can only endure. Yet one does not know that if one but cries out loudly and leaps up with a sudden start, the dream will break — what need then for fleeing and enduring? Once the dream is broken, you discover that all the terror in the dream, the suffering, and the resignation to enduring when rescue was sought in vain, were truly laughable. The joyous state of a mind at ease after waking, compared with the suffering state of desperately fleeing in the dream and enduring when escape was impossible — truly the difference between heaven and an abyss!
Therefore the way of liberation is not to dodge and flee this way and that within the dream of saṃsāra, but to wake from the deluded dream!

[Looking at it from your present state, this groaning in sickness and this thought of going or staying, of seeking release, are just like things in a dream. You cannot cry out yourself and wake; I cry out loudly for you, and still you do not know it. Then in this worn-out long night there will never be a time of opening your eyes. Why should you, for the sake of illusion and falsehood, be content with bitterness and toil, taking the dream house as your true home? Now that you have met with one who calls and still do not wake, if you abandon this, who else will call to you? Alas, alas! In the dark, inverted long night, to wish to see the light of the wisdom sun, with an opportunity such as today’s — that is difficult beyond difficulty! Try to think it over: if you suddenly rouse yourself, turn your head and shift your mind, and the pass of birth-and-death emotion bursts open at once, that is the time of shattering the dream house and escaping the perilous road.]

Judging by your present plan, this groaning in sickness, and this thought of going or staying (“going” meaning leaving this land of miasma and crossing north of the ranges; “staying” meaning finding another pleasant place to rest) and of seeking release (seeking to escape the suffering state of illness), are just like things in a dream. You cannot cry out loudly and wake up with a start yourself, and though I cry out loudly to wake you, you still do not know it. In this way you can only struggle wearily and helplessly through the long, long night, and there will never come a time when you open your eyes and wake. Why should you cling to the illusory state as real and be content to be tormented by it, taking the dream house as your true home? Now that you have met me crying out loudly to you and still do not wake, if you abandon this, who else will cry out to wake you? Alas, alas! In this dark, inverted, long, long night, to wish to see the light of the wisdom sun, with an opportunity such as today’s, is difficult beyond difficulty! Think it over carefully: if you suddenly rouse yourself, turn your head and shift your mind, then the pass of birth-and-death emotion bursts open at once, and this is the time of shattering the dream house and escaping the perilous road.
[Worn out (ěr)] Weary and exhausted. [Naihe] The same as the usual “naihe”; here it means: why.

blocks.text: 16. Only Purify the Mind

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practicer Shu Zhong’an on Dwelling in the Mountains)

[The Chan practicer Shu Zhong’an was about to clear the thatch on the Southern Peak and asked for the essentials of the Dharma for dwelling in the mountains. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: The Way is not in the mountains, yet to dwell in the mountains one must first see the Way. To see the mountain and forget the Way — the mountain becomes the root of obstruction. To see the Way and forget the mountain — wherever the eye falls and conditions are met, there is nothing that is not the Way. This is a famous saying of the ancient worthies and the true instruction of Yongjia. Now you intend to dwell in the mountains: is it that you will see the Way and then dwell, or dwell and afterwards see the Way? If you see the Way and then dwell, then in dwelling there is abiding, and where there is abiding the Way is not the true Way. If you wish to dwell in the mountains and afterwards see the Way — the Way is originally without abiding, and where there is abiding the Way is not in the mountain. What then will you take as the Way, and where will you dwell?]

The Chan practicer Shu Zhong’an was about to build a thatched hut on the Southern Peak to cultivate the Way, and asked for instruction on the essentials of dwelling in the mountains. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: The Way is not in the mountains, yet to dwell in the mountains one must first see the Way. To see the mountain and forget the Way — the mountain becomes the root of obstructing the Way. To see the Way and forget the mountain — wherever the eye falls and conditions are met, there is nothing that is not the Way. This is a famous saying of the ancient worthies and the true instruction of Master Yongjia. Now you intend to dwell in the mountains: will you see the Way and then dwell, or dwell and afterwards see the Way? If you see the Way and then go to dwell in the mountains, then in dwelling there is attachment, and where there is attachment the Way is not the true Way. If you wish to dwell in the mountains and afterwards see the Way — the Way is originally without attachment, and where there is attachment the Way is not in the mountains either. What then will you take as the Way, and where will you dwell?

[Clearing the thatch] That is, cutting away the cogongrass; by extension, building a hut and settling down to cultivate the Way. [Southern Peak] Also written with a variant character; one of the Five Peaks, namely Mount Heng, in the central part of Hunan Province.

[You alone take the mountain as a mountain, not realizing that in daily life before you, body, mind, and the objects of mind are all mountains. The teachings say: birth, old age, sickness, and death are pressed upon by four mountains.
