They also say: the mountain of the five aggregates; the mountain of self and others; the mountain of nirvāṇa. Yet nirvāṇa is the mind; self and others are the object; the five aggregates of body and mind are the den of birth, old age, sickness, and death. The Sanskrit word nirvāṇa is rendered here as “quiescent extinction.” The illusory body, mind, and objects of mind all belong to movement and disturbance; but tracing them to their root, the true and the false are not two, and movement and stillness are both suchness. It is only because of the division between delusion and awakening that there is the distinction between sage and ordinary being. Deluded, nirvāṇa becomes birth and death; awakened, birth and death realizes nirvāṇa. From this we know that the mountain of the five aggregates and of self and others is originally the peaceful abode of nirvāṇa. Thus all sages and ordinary beings, in birth and in death, have never failed to dwell on this mountain — and you have long been lying and dwelling upon it through the long night. Why then do you now wish to go and dwell in the mountains?]

You alone take the Southern Peak as a mountain, not realizing that in daily life before you, body, mind, and the objects of mind are all mountains. The teachings say: “Birth, old age, sickness, and death are pressed upon by four mountains.” They also say: “the mountain of the five aggregates”; “the mountain of self and others”; “the mountain of nirvāṇa.” Yet nirvāṇa is mind; self and others are object; the five aggregates of body and mind are the den of birth, old age, sickness, and death. The Sanskrit word “nirvāṇa” means in Chinese “quiescent extinction.” The illusory body, mind, and objects of mind all belong to movement and disturbance; tracing them to their source, the true and the false are not two, and movement and stillness are both suchness. It is only because of the division between delusion and awakening that there is the distinction between sage and ordinary being. Deluded, nirvāṇa becomes birth and death; awakened, birth and death realizes nirvāṇa. From this we know that the mountain of the five aggregates and of self and others is originally the peaceful abode of nirvāṇa. Therefore all sages and ordinary beings, in birth and in death, have never failed to dwell on this mountain of the five aggregates and of self and others; and you, lying and dwelling in the long night of saṃsāra, have been dwelling on this mountain all along — why then do you still wish to go and dwell in the mountains?

[If one takes delight and aversion, taking up and casting off, as the resources for entering the Way, that is like fleeing from drowning and throwing oneself into fire. Hence it is said: I wish to escape it, yet cannot escape; beyond the great square all is blocked and filled. It is also said: the mad mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi. The essentials of entering the Way lie only in resting the mad mind, blotting out seeing and hearing, cutting off knowing and understanding, forgetting subject and object, stilling right and wrong, and quiescing this mind. It is not at all a matter of fleeing the body into mountain valleys, eating one’s fill and lying about, indulging in sloth and idleness, and increasing one’s arrogance, and taking that as the wonder of the Way. The Sanskrit word dhūta is rendered here as “shaking off,” because it can shake off the afflictions of guest-dust. To simply purify one’s mind — this is the Way of all Buddhas. Do strive after it.]

If one takes the mind of delight and aversion, of taking up and casting off, as the resource for entering the Way, that is like fleeing from drowning and throwing oneself into fire. Hence it is said: “I wish to escape it, yet cannot escape; beyond the great square all is blocked and filled.” It is also said: “The mad mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi.” Therefore the essentials of entering the Way lie only in resting the mad mind, blotting out seeing and hearing, cutting off knowing and understanding, forgetting subject and object, stilling right and wrong, and quiescing this mind. It is precisely not a matter of fleeing the body into mountain valleys, eating one’s fill and lying about, indulging in sloth and idleness, and increasing one’s arrogance, while thinking this is the wonder of the Way. The Sanskrit word “dhūta” means in Chinese “shaking off,” because one is able to rouse the spirit and rid oneself of the afflictions of guest-dust. To simply purify one’s mind — this is the Buddha Way! May you practice it with diligence.

[I wish to escape it, yet cannot escape; beyond the great square all is blocked and filled] “The mad mind does not rest; when it rests, that is bodhi.” Therefore the essentials of entering the Way lie only in resting the mad mind, and not in fleeing the body into mountain valleys. If the mad mind does not rest, then even if you flee beyond the great earth, that place too is filled and blocked with affliction. The Song-dynasty monk Shi Chongxian, in his poem “Seeing Off the Chief Seat Shanxian,” says: “I fear that if I wish to escape it, I cannot escape; beyond the great square there is no outside, all is blocked and filled. Vast and chaotic, who knows where it ends; on every side the fragrant wind (the mood of extravagance and indulgence) catches the hem of the robe (the lapel).” [Great square] The ancients held that heaven is round and earth square, and so “great square” refers to the great earth.

blocks.text: 17. Only Detach from the Mind’s Defilement

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to Liu Cunchi)

The sūtra says: Ordinary beings, worthies, and sages are equal, with no higher or lower; it is only that the mind’s defilement is extinguished, and then the realization is attained as easily as turning over one’s palm.

[Recently I retired in my old age to the Southern Peak. At the end of winter in the jiǎyín year, Liu Jizi of Chaling came from afar to call and inquire. On a snowy night we sat around the stove, a cold lamp lighting us. I therefore asked him: How have you been applying your mind all along? He replied: Formerly I received your instruction, reverend sir, in a verse: “The lotus is born within the fire — the world calls this rare; yet it is not that fire gives birth to the lotus, but only that the mind is free of defilement.” Whenever I read these words, I gain much benefit from the last line. The old man was deeply pleased, and therefore instructed him, saying: That you have gained strength from the line “only that the mind is free of defilement” — these words are not empty, yet they are not easy to reach. The sūtra says: Ordinary beings, worthies, and sages are equal, with no higher or lower; it is only that the mind’s defilement is extinguished, and then the realization is attained as easily as turning over one’s palm.]

Not long ago, in my old age, I retired to the Southern Peak. At the end of winter in the jiǎyín year, Liu Cunchi of Chaling came from afar to call and inquire. The two of us sat around the stove on a snowy night, a cold lamp lighting us. So I asked him: How have you been applying your mind all along? He answered: “Formerly I received your instruction, reverend sir, in a verse: ‘The lotus is born within the fire — the world calls this rare; yet it is not that fire gives birth to the lotus, but only that the mind is free of defilement.’ Each time I read this verse, I gain much benefit from the last line, ‘only that the mind is free of defilement.’” Hearing this I was very glad, and therefore instructed him, saying: That you have gained strength from the line “the mind is free of defilement” — these words are true and substantial, yet also not easy to accomplish. The sūtra says: Ordinary beings, worthies, and sages are equal, with no higher or lower; it is only that the mind’s defilement is extinguished, and then the realization is attained as easily as turning over one’s palm.

[Reverend sir] Meaning “my teacher”; it is the honorific used by monks for their own preceptor. [The lotus is born within the fire, the world calls this rare; yet it is not that fire gives birth to the lotus, but only that the mind is free of defilement] A lotus growing out of fire is thought by worldly people to be exceedingly rare and precious; yet what is rarest and most precious is not a lotus born in fire, but the mind’s freedom from illusory defilement.
[From
(in ancient usage written with the character for “you”)

this we see: sentient beings and Buddhas are originally not two; as it is said, mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction. But when the mind is pure, that is Buddha; when the mind is defiled, that is sentient being. The distance between sentient being and Buddha is not far; it lies only in whether the mind’s defilement is extinguished or not. Because this mind is originally pure, and only through craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, the five desires, and afflictions — all kinds of karmic illusions — is it obscured by defilement and turbidity, it is therefore called a sentient being. If this defilement is purified, one is then called a Buddha — how could this depend on any other power!]

From this we see: sentient beings and Buddhas are originally not two; as it is said, mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction. Only, when the mind is pure one is a Buddha; when the mind is defiled one is a sentient being. The road by which sentient beings become Buddhas is not far; it lies only in whether the mind’s defilement is extinguished or not. Because this mind is originally pure, and only through craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, the five desires, and other afflictions — all kinds of illusory karma — is it obscured by defilement and turbidity, it is therefore called a sentient being. If this defilement is purified, one is then called a Buddha — how could this depend on any other power!

[Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction] Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings: these three dharmas are fundamentally without distinction. When the mind is pure (the mind is purified), this mind is Buddha; when the mind is defiled (the mind is tainted), this mind is sentient being. [Affliction] “Fan” means to disturb, “nao” means to disorder; whatever can disturb the body and mind of sentient beings and make the mind fretful and confused is called “affliction.” There are six root afflictions: craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, doubt, and wrong view. Craving is craving for the five desires; anger is wrath without forbearance; delusion is foolish ignorance; arrogance is haughty self-importance; doubt is suspicious misgiving; wrong view is incorrect views, including the view of the body, the extreme view, deviant view, the view of grasping views, and the view of grasping precepts. Craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, and doubt, together with the five wrong views, make ten root afflictions, also called the ten delusions or the ten messengers. Craving, anger, delusion, arrogance, and doubt are called delusions of thought; the five wrong views are called delusions of view. Together they are called the delusions of view and thought, or the afflictions of view and thought. [Ten messengers] Also called the ten delusions, or the ten root afflictions: 1. Craving — craving for the five desires; 2. Anger — wrath without forbearance; 3. Delusion — foolish ignorance; 4. Arrogance — haughty self-importance; 5. Doubt — suspicious unbelief; 6. View of the body — clinging to the five aggregates as the root body; 7. Extreme view — clinging to the two views of permanence and annihilation; 8. Deviant view — denying cause and effect, destroying all good works; 9. The view of grasping views — holding to one’s own opinion, taking the non-fruit as fruit; 10. The view of grasping precepts — holding to incorrect precepts, taking the non-cause as cause. The first five are called the five dull messengers, the latter five the five sharp messengers. “Messenger” is another name for affliction, because affliction can cause sentient beings to fall into birth and death.

[But there is no help for it: all sentient beings have deep and heavy karmic obstructions from beginningless time, and firm afflictions, and it is hard for them to attain purity; they must rely on the work of polishing and refining. Hence there are Chan investigation, Buddha-recitation, huatou-contemplation, and various other skillful means — all of them medicines for treating the mind. For example, the light of a mirror is originally bright, but because of grime it is dimmed, and it must rely on the medicine of polishing. Yet the medicine is itself grime; because it is used to remove the grime, when the mirror is bright the medicine is no longer there. Again, when true gold is in the ore, with sand and stone and filth, there must be a method of smelting; when the gold is pure, the smelting is no longer needed. The mind’s defilement of sentient beings is hard to detach from, and one must work with diligence and refine and treat it; when the defilement is gone and the mind is bright, it is said that sentient beings are originally Buddhas — not that while dwelling all along amid the turbidity of affliction one may recklessly call oneself a Buddha.]

There is no help for it: all sentient beings, from beginningless kalpas, have deep and heavy karmic obstructions and firm afflictions, and it is hard for them to attain purity; they must rely on the work of polishing and refining. Hence there are Chan investigation, Buddha-recitation, huatou-contemplation, and various other skillful means — all of them medicines for treating the mind. For example, the light of a mirror is originally bright; because of grime it is dimmed, and it must rely on the medicine of polishing (in ancient times bronze mirrors were polished with a polishing compound to remove grime). Yet the medicine is itself grime; it is used only because it can remove the grime. Therefore, when the mirror is bright the medicine is no longer used. Again, when true gold is in the ore, the sand, stone, and filth must be removed before pure gold can be obtained, and so a method of smelting must be used. Once the pure gold has been refined, the method of smelting is no longer used. Because the mind’s defilement of sentient beings is firm and hard to detach from, one must work at it, refining and treating it with diligence. When the defilement is gone and the mind is bright, the work too need no longer be done; and so it is said that sentient beings are originally Buddhas. It is not that while dwelling all along amid the turbidity of affliction one may recklessly call oneself a Buddha.

[The one path of Chan investigation and huatou-contemplation is the most essential for illuminating the mind, yet in recent times those who take it in hand are few. On the one hand, their faculties are dull, and they lack the death-ground resolve of the ancients; on the other, they have no true spiritual benefactor to decide and select for them, and most fall into deviant views. Therefore the practice of cultivating Buddha-recitation and Chan investigation together is an extremely reliable Dharma gate. If one takes a single sound of Buddha-recitation and stores it in the breast, thought after thought pursuing and verifying where it arises and where it falls, determined to see a precise landing place — after a long, long time, suddenly the defilement is purified and brightness appears, and the mind-ground opens through. This is no different from contemplating a koan or huatou, and one must press on with unremitting effort to succeed. If one drifts up and down on delusive thoughts and passes the days idly, taking this as a matter of no importance, then to the end of one’s years one will gain no benefit. If one takes idly letting delusive thoughts run as one’s benefit, then one deceives oneself — not merely for this one life: from now on, even to the end of kalpas, there will be no time when one is not deceived.]

The one path of Chan investigation and huatou-contemplation is the most essential for illuminating the mind (removing the mind’s defilement), yet in recent times those who can take it in hand are very few. On the one hand this is because their faculties are dull and they lack the death-ground resolve of the ancients; on the other hand it is because they have no true spiritual benefactor to guide them correctly, and most fall into deviant views. Therefore the practice of cultivating Buddha-recitation and Chan investigation together (the investigation of Buddha-recitation) is an extremely reliable Dharma gate. Its method is: recite one sound of the Buddha’s name and store it in the breast, pursuing and verifying where the Buddha-name arises and where it falls, thought after thought, determined to see a precise landing place. After a long time, suddenly the defilement is purified and brightness appears, and the mind-ground opens through. This is no different from the Chan school’s contemplation of a koan or huatou, and one must press on with dense and unremitting effort. If one drifts up and down on delusive thoughts and passes the days idly, taking this investigation of Buddha-recitation as a matter of no importance, then one will gain no benefit in a whole lifetime. If one takes idly letting delusive thoughts run as one’s benefit, then one deceives oneself — not merely in this life: from now on, even to the end of kalpas, there will be no time when one is not deceived.
[This is no different from contemplating a koan or huatou] This is no different from the Chan school’s contemplation of a koan or huatou. In the Dream-Wandering Collection

Instructions to the Chan Practicer Zhaofan Yong, Master Hanshan says: “It is like the monk asking Zhaozhou whether a dog has the Buddha-nature; or like Yongming teaching people to verify who it is that recites the Buddha’s name. This one word ‘no’ or this one word ‘who’ is precisely the sharp sword that cuts off the life-root of birth and death. Yet this investigation and verification is only a matter of peering at this word ‘no’ or ‘who’ — from where does it arise, and to where does it fall? Just watch where this single thought arises and falls, and you must see the root of its arising and ceasing. If you investigate to the ultimate point, you will burst apart the delusive thoughts of a single thought’s arising and ceasing, smash the lacquer barrel, and suddenly see your original face.” (For details see
Investigating Buddha-Recitation
) [Pressing close] Closely arrayed. Here it means doing the work densely and with unremitting effort.

[You have long had a karmic affinity with the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation; try to investigate and verify it in earnest. If, amid the defilement and turbidity of affliction, a single sound of the Buddha-name is like a water-clearing pearl, then you gain benefit from it — but this is not yet a thoroughgoing penetration to the source. The sūtra says: It is like settling turbid water; the sand and earth sink of themselves, and clear water appears — this is called first subduing the afflictions of guest-dust. When the mud is gone and the water is pure, this is called forever cutting off fundamental ignorance. Do but test this Buddha-word silently for yourself, and there will be no failure. If you reach the place of true freedom from defilement, then, as the sūtra says, the mark of brightness is pure and undefiled, and one is no longer obstructed by the afflictions of guest-dust. In that way, not only will Amitābha come to receive and guide you, but the Buddhas of the ten directions will all praise you with one voice!]

You have long had a karmic affinity with the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation; simply recite with this method of earnest investigation and verification. When the work is deep, then amid the defilement and turbidity of affliction, a single sound of the Buddha-name is like a water-clearing pearl: as soon as the Buddha-name is raised, delusive thoughts all vanish. In this way you gain considerable benefit — but this is not yet a thoroughgoing penetration to the source. The sūtra says: “It is like settling turbid water; the sand and earth sink of themselves (the same as ‘sink’), and clear water appears — this is called first subduing the afflictions of guest-dust. When the mud is gone and the water is pure, this is called forever cutting off fundamental ignorance.” Do but test this passage of the Buddha’s words silently for yourself, and there will be no failure. If you reach the place of true freedom from defilement, then, as the sūtra says: “The mark of brightness is pure and undefiled, and one is no longer obstructed by the afflictions of guest-dust.” Having reached this state, not only will Amitābha Buddha come to receive and guide you, but the Buddhas of the ten directions will all praise you with one voice!

[Water-clearing pearl] The Threefold Recitation of Zhongfeng says: “In the Western Heaven there is a treasure called the clearing pearl. It is said that when this pearl is thrown into turbid water, for every inch it enters, an inch of the turbid water at once becomes clean. As this pearl enters the water, from inch to foot, even to the bottom, the turbid water becomes clear and limpid along with it. You should know that the clearing pearl is a simile for the pure thought of Buddha-recitation; the turbid water is a simile for the confused and deluded mind.”

[Happily I have spent with you the year’s end and a snowy night, and this plain and cool family style is rare in the world. If you do not betray this fine gathering, then from now on, never parting from it thought after thought, in this plainness and coolness there is a path of freedom from defilement. Press on with effort at every step, and there will surely come a time of reaching home and true liberation.]
I am very glad to have spent with you, at the year’s end and on this snowy night, this stretch of
plain
and cool
family style, which is rare in the world. If you would not betray this fine gathering, then from now on you must not part from it thought after thought; investigate and verify in earnest, and
in that plainness
and coolness
there is a shortcut to freedom from the mind’s defilement. Press on with effort at every step of the work, and there will surely come a time of reaching home and true liberation.
[“Líng”
(líng)
] Cool and refreshing. [“Líng
dàn”
] Cool, quiet, and plain.

blocks.text: 18. The Wisdom Sun Removes Transgression

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to Dong Zhiguang)

Delusive thought is the cause of all karma; if one is not driven by delusive thought, there is no cause of karma-making. If one can sever it with a single thought at the place where delusive thought arises, then the long-accumulated root of karma is dissolved on the spot.

[The student Dong Sizhang grew up in a house of wealth and honor, and early aroused the mind that seeks to escape birth and death — this is the power of the inner permeation of the supreme condition of prajñā cultivated in former lives. He first called on Master Yunqi, who taught him the Pure Land Dharma gate. Recently he called on the old man at Shuangjing and wished to receive the upāsaka precepts. He further disclosed that his karmic offenses were deep and heavy, and wished to learn the essentials of escaping suffering: by what cultivation should he extinguish his transgressions? The old man therefore instructed him, saying:]

Dong Sizhang grew up in a house of wealth and honor and early aroused the mind to escape birth and death — this is the power of the inner permeation of the supreme condition of prajñā cultivated in former lives. He first called on Master Lianchi, who taught him the Pure Land Dharma gate. Not long after, he came to call on me at Shuangjing and wished to receive the upāsaka precepts. He further disclosed that his karmic offenses were deep and heavy, and wished to learn the essentials of escaping suffering: how should he cultivate in order to extinguish his transgressions? Therefore I instructed him, saying:

[Upāsaka precepts] “Upāsaka” means a male lay devotee. The upāsaka precepts are the five precepts: not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to speak falsely, and not to drink alcohol.

[Since the student knows that the root of his transgressions is deep and heavy — the ancient worthies teach people: “At all times dissolve old karma; on no account create new calamity.” For sentient beings heavy in karma, the Buddha opened the one gate of repentance, which is the most skillful means of escaping suffering. The verse says: “All transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark.” This is the primary practice; all else is auxiliary skillful means.]

The ancient worthies teach people: “At all times dissolve old karma; on no account create new calamity.” The one gate of repentance that the Buddha opened for sentient beings heavy in karma is the most skillful means of escaping suffering. The verse says: “All transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark (the later text says, ‘the mind that has no thing is the true mark’).” This is the primary practice; all else is auxiliary practice.

[All transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them] Just as the sun melts frost and dew, so contemplating the true mark (the wisdom sun) can dissolve all transgressions. The Sūtra of the Method of Contemplating Bodhisattva Samantabhadra says:

“The sea of all karmic obstructions arises entirely from delusive thought. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark. All transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them.”
[Sea of karmic obstructions] Karmic obstructions as deep and vast as the great ocean. [Sit upright and contemplate the true mark] The later text says:
“The mind that has no thing — this is the true mark.”

[The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to the Buddha’s, originally undefiled, and without the marks of birth and death, coming and going. But because of the initial non-awakening, one is deluded about one’s own self-nature — hence it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, all delusive thoughts arise, with every kind of inversion, creating every kind of karma and falsely seizing the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not understanding one’s own mind, one turns with delusive thought. It is like a person deep asleep having all kinds of evil dreams — every kind of state, every kind of terror, every kind of suffering hard to bear. When he wakes, he seeks the things of the dream and cannot find them at all. Therefore sentient beings fall into the dream of ignorance, follow delusive thought and inversion, create all kinds of karma, and seize all kinds of suffering for themselves. Seen with awakened eyes, how could those inverted states be had?]

The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to the Buddha’s, originally without defilement, and without the marks of birth and death, coming and going. But because of the initial non-awakening, one is deluded about one’s own self-nature (entering the dream of ignorance) — this is ignorance. Because of ignorance, all delusive thoughts arise, and so with every kind of inversion one creates every kind of karma and falsely seizes the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not awakening to one’s own mind, one is turned along by delusive thought. It is like a person in deep sleep having all kinds of evil dreams — every kind of state, every kind of terror, suffering beyond bearing. When he wakes, he seeks the things of the dream and cannot find them at all. Sentient beings are the same: fallen into the dream of ignorance, they follow delusive thought and inversion, create all kinds of karma, and seize all kinds of suffering for themselves. Seen with awakened eyes, where are all those inverted states?

[Now, while present in the dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve old karma? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and firmly believe that one’s own mind is originally pure, and not be driven by delusive thought and inversion; then all karma is without cause, because delusive thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? Because from beginningless time one has been deluded about one’s own original mind, and life after life has created all kinds of karma with the delusive mind. The habitual tendencies of that karma accumulate within the field of the eighth consciousness, and are irrigated with the water of ignorance, causing those evil seeds to put forth the sprouts of karma — this is the root of transgression, from which all evil karma arises.]

Then, now that one is already in the dream of ignorance, how can old karma be dissolved? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and firmly believe that one’s own mind is originally pure, and not be driven by delusive thought and inversion; in this way there is no cause of karma-making, because delusive thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? Because from beginningless kalpas one has been deluded about one’s own original mind, and life after life has created all kinds of karma with the delusive mind. These karmic habits accumulate in the ālaya consciousness (the eighth consciousness), and are then irrigated with the water of ignorance, causing those evil seeds to put forth the sprouts of karma — this is the root of transgression, from which all evil karma arises.

[Now, if one wishes to dissolve old karma, one must first arouse the great light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and not permit delusive thoughts to sprout and quietly grow in the dark. If one can sever them with a single thought at the place where delusive thought arises, then the long-accumulated root of karma is dissolved on the spot. As it is said: do not fear the arising of a thought; fear only that awareness comes late. If awareness and illumination are even slightly late, one is turned about by it. If one can, in daily life, at every place where the mind stirs and a thought arises, become aware of each thought and dissolve each thought, this is what is called “all transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them.” Since the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is called wisdom’s dissolving them.]

Now, if one wishes to dissolve old karma, one must first arouse the great light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and not permit delusive thoughts to sprout and quietly grow in the dark. If one can sever them with a single thought at the place where delusive thought arises (a chilling moment of awareness), then the root of karma accumulated in former days is dissolved on the spot. As it is said, “Do not fear the arising of a thought; fear only that awareness comes late.” If awareness and illumination are even slightly late, one is turned about by it (delusive thought). If one can, in daily life, at every place where the mind stirs and a thought arises, become aware of each thought and dissolve each thought, this is what is called “all transgressions are like frost and dew; the wisdom sun can dissolve them.” Since the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is what is meant by wisdom’s dissolving all transgressions.

[If, day and night without letting go, one diligently observes and does not let it pass, but simply, at the place where delusive thought arises, investigates exhaustively until there is no mark of arising at all — looking and looking again, in the end it cannot be found. When after a long time one is thoroughly familiar with this, then one’s own mind is pure and without thing; and the mind that has no thing is the true mark. If one constantly contemplates this mind, what delusive thought can be admitted, what accumulated karma can lodge there? Applying the mind in this way is called the samādhi of contemplation.]

You must, day and night without letting go, diligently observe and not let it pass, but simply, at the place where delusive thought arises, investigate exhaustively until there is no mark of arising at all. Looking and looking again, delusive thought in the end cannot be found at all. When after a long time you are thoroughly familiar with this, then your own mind is pure and without thing, and the mind that has no thing is the true mark. If you constantly contemplate this pure mind, what delusive thought can be admitted, what accumulated karma can lodge there? Applying the mind in this way is called the samādhi of contemplation.

[“If, day and night without letting go, one diligently observes”] Here “if” (ruò) means “you.” For example: “Change your duty of catching snakes, restore your taxes — what would you think of that?” (This line comes from Liu Zongyuan’s “The Snake-Catcher’s Discourse”; the meaning is: if one changed your job of catching poisonous snakes and restored your tax levy, what would you think of it?)

[If one’s own afflictions are coarse and heavy, and at the places where ignorance obstructs one is not aware of it — in such a case the ancient worthies had a method of investigation they taught people: take the koan of verifying Buddha-recitation and apply your strength there. Raise a single sound of the Buddha-name and set it across your breast, and at once investigate: who, after all, is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Thus, as you raise it you investigate it, never letting it go empty. Set this mass of doubt across your breast, like your own life-root, and never let it go. In all movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, coming and going, sitting and standing, there is only this one matter and nothing else. Applying the mind in this way, as soon as you see a delusive thought arise, give the huatou a single thrust, and it is shattered on the spot; all delusive thoughts of themselves are swept away without trace. For this huatou is like the sun’s disc in the sky, illuminating every dark place. The only fear is that one’s mental strength slackens and one will not earnestly rouse oneself, and so cannot stand against delusive thoughts. If one can stand against them, then where delusive thoughts vanish is the time when old karma is dissolved. Abandon this one stroke and seek elsewhere outside the mind, and even if all the Buddhas were to appear in the world, there would be no place for repentance. This rests on one’s own power; no other power can substitute for it.]

If one’s own afflictions are coarse and heavy, and at the places where ignorance obstructs (when delusive thoughts arise) one is unable to be aware of it — if this is one’s situation, then the ancient worthies had a method of investigation they taught people: take the koan of verifying Buddha-recitation (who is it that recites the Buddha’s name) and use it to cut off delusive thoughts. The method is: raise a single sound of the Buddha-name and set it across your breast, then at once investigate: who, after all, is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Thus, as you raise it you investigate it, never letting it go empty. Set this mass of doubt across your breast, like your own life-root, and never let it go. In all movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, coming and going, sitting and standing, there is only this one matter and nothing else. Only by applying the mind in this way, as soon as you see a delusive thought arise, do you give the huatou a single thrust, and delusive thought is shattered on the spot. Investigating in this way, all delusive thoughts of themselves are swept away without trace. For this huatou is like the sun’s disc in the sky, illuminating every dark place. The only fear is that one’s mental strength slackens and one will not earnestly rouse and hold to it, and therefore cannot stand against delusive thoughts. If one can stand against them, then where delusive thoughts vanish is the time when old karma is dissolved. Abandon this one stroke and seek elsewhere outside the mind, and then even if all the Buddhas were to appear in the world, there would be no place for repentance. This matter depends entirely on one’s own effort; no other power can substitute for it.

[Rousing and holding] To rouse oneself and bestir oneself, to keep right mindfulness. It also refers to concentrating on the work of investigation while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. The Gateless Gate of the Chan School says: “Take the three hundred and sixty bones and joints and the eighty-four thousand hair-pores, raise a mass of doubt through the whole body, and investigate the word ‘no,’ rousing and holding it day and night.” The Complete Works of Master Zhu

Preserving and Nourishing says: “One need only constantly rouse and hold it oneself; accumulating little by little, after a long time it will naturally continue without interruption and be beaten into one piece.” For example, the monk Ruiyan every day used to ask himself: “Master! Are you clear and awake?” and then answer himself: “I am clear and awake.” [Clear and awake] Alert and clear-minded.

[If evil habits are strong and one’s strength cannot stand against them, then formerly the Buddha gave a clear instruction: if a cultivator’s habitual tendencies are not removed, he should single-mindedly recite the heart-mantra spoken by me, the unconditioned Mind-Buddha. This is truly an extraordinary skillful means. Because each person’s storehouse consciousness flows on hidden currents, and habitual tendencies are deep and thick, the power of wisdom does not reach there. Where it does not reach, one must rely on the Buddha’s mind-seal to break through it secretly. It is like a bandit hard to subdue: one must request the imperial sword. For this, one should take the two periods of morning and evening, arrange them as suits one’s convenience, and recite the set lesson. In sum, the work of investigation is to be taken as the primary principle.]

If evil habits are strong and investigation cannot stand against delusive thoughts, then formerly the Buddha gave a clear instruction: “If a cultivator finds it hard to uproot his habitual tendencies, he should single-mindedly recite the heart-mantra spoken by me, the unconditioned Mind-Buddha.” This is truly an extraordinary skillful means. Because each person’s storehouse consciousness flows on hidden currents, and habitual tendencies are deep and thick, the power of wisdom does not reach there. Where it does not reach, one must rely on the Buddha’s mind-seal to break through it secretly. It is like a bandit hard to subdue: one must request the imperial sword. For this, one must take the two periods of morning and evening, arrange the time according to one’s own situation, and recite the set lesson. In sum, the work of investigation is to be taken as the main thing.
[Heart-mantra] A general term for dhāraṇī. A dhāraṇī is the supreme Dharma within the Tathāgata’s mind, and so it is called a heart-mantra.
In the Śūraṅgama Sūtra the Buddha says:

If there are former habits that cannot be extinguished, you should teach that person to single-mindedly recite the unsurpassed spirit-mantra of the Buddha’s summit light, Mahā-sitātapatra. This is the heart-mantra spoken by the Tathāgata of the invisible summit, the unconditioned Mind-Buddha, who radiates light from the summit and sits upon a jeweled lotus.
This heart-mantra is:
“Mahā-sitātapatra.”

[Imperial sword] A sword specially made by the Imperial Household Office for the emperor’s own use. In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven sent a minister to handle a grave case, he would often bestow the imperial sword, signifying the grant of full authority to execute first and report afterward.

[The old man’s instruction here is much like giving a blind man a staff; in truth the practice lies with oneself, and no teacher or friend can take one’s place. Because the layman’s aspiration turns toward the Dharma gate, I have named him Fujue (Blessed Awakening), intending that he take awareness and illumination as the foundation of his practice. His courtesy name is Zhiguang (Light of Wisdom), for without the light of wisdom, how could the darkness of delusion be broken? One need only keep awareness and illumination undimmed and the light of wisdom present, and that is the time when karmic obstructions are ended and birth and death escaped.]

This instruction of mine is like giving a blind man a staff; the actual practice lies with oneself, and no teacher or friend can take one’s place. Because you have resolved to cultivate, I have given you the name Fujue (Blessed Awakening), meaning that you should take awareness and illumination as the foundation of your practice. Your courtesy name is Zhiguang (Light of Wisdom), for without the light of wisdom, how could the darkness of delusion be broken? One need only keep awareness and illumination undimmed and the light of wisdom present, and that is the time when karmic obstructions are ended and birth and death escaped.

[One’s own person] To do it oneself. [Courtesy name] A style name, an alternate name for a person, expressing the meaning of the given name or the person’s character and virtue. For example: surname Liu, given name Bei, courtesy name Xuande. In usage, one refers to oneself by the given name, expressing humility, and refers to others by the courtesy name, expressing respect.

blocks.text: 19. The Dharma of Prajñā

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to Deng Sizhi)

[The Buddhas and patriarchs appear in the world and speak the Dharma of prajñā. They teach people to cultivate, and one must take prajñā as the foundation. Prajñā is Sanskrit; in Chinese it means wisdom. This wisdom is the Buddha-nature we originally possess; it is also called the self-mind, and also called the self-nature. This essence is originally undefiled, and so it is called pure. Originally undimmed, and so it is called bright. Originally vast and all-embracing, and so it is called empty space. Originally without falsehood, and so it is called the one true. Originally unmoving and unchanging, and so it is called suchness, and also called thusness. Originally perfect and complete, illuminating all, and so it is called perfect enlightenment. Originally quiescent and extinguished, and so it is called nirvāṇa.]

The Buddhas and patriarchs appear in the world and speak the Dharma of prajñā. They teach people to cultivate, and one must take prajñā as the foundation. Prajñā is Sanskrit; in Chinese it means wisdom. Because this wisdom is the Buddha-nature we originally possess, it is also called the self-mind and also called the self-nature. This mind-essence is originally undefiled, and so it is called pure. Originally undimmed, and so it is called bright. Originally vast and all-embracing, and so it is called empty space. Originally without falsehood, and so it is called the one true. Originally unmoving and unchanging, and so it is called suchness, and also called thusness. Originally perfect and complete, illuminating all, and so it is called perfect enlightenment. Originally quiescent and extinguished, and so it is called nirvāṇa.

[In the Buddhas this is perfectly realized, and so it is called great enlightenment, and also bodhi; the Buddhas use it, and so it becomes spiritual penetrations and wondrous functioning. Bodhisattvas cultivate it, and it is called wondrous practice. The two vehicles attain it, and it is called liberation. Ordinary beings are deluded about it, and it becomes delusive thought and karmic consciousness. Aroused and put to use, it becomes craving, anger, delusion, love, arrogance, flattery, and deceit. Made into karma, it becomes lust, killing, stealing, and falsehood. The fruit reaped is knives, saws, iron, and grinding stones, and even the boiling cauldron, the glowing coals, and all kinds of implements of suffering — all of them are transformed and manifested from this mind.]

This mind-essence, the Buddhas have perfectly realized, and so it is called great enlightenment, and also bodhi; the Buddhas use it, and so it becomes spiritual penetrations and wondrous functioning. This mind-essence, bodhisattvas cultivate it, and it is called wondrous practice; the two vehicles realize it, and it is called liberation. This mind-essence, ordinary beings are deluded about it, and it becomes delusive thought and karmic consciousness. Aroused and put to use, it becomes craving, anger, delusion, love, arrogance, flattery, and deceit. Made into karma, it becomes lust, killing, stealing, and falsehood. The fruit reaped is knives, saws, iron, and grinding stones, and even the boiling cauldron, the glowing coals, and all the various implements of hell — all of them are transformed and manifested from this mind-essence.

[Implements of suffering] The instruments of torture used in hell. [All transformed and manifested from this mind] All are dream-states manifested because this mind establishes knowing upon knowing and so enters the dream of ignorance.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“To establish knowing upon knowing is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are without seeing, that is nirvāṇa, undefiled and truly pure.”

[It is just as when a person awake and at ease has all kinds of pleasant states before his eyes. After a little while he falls into deep, heavy sleep, and suddenly dreams that he is in hell, where all kinds of implements of suffering and all its affairs are endured at once, with sourness and bitterness and poison beyond bearing. Just when he seeks rescue and cannot get it, the guests seated in the hall are still clamoring without pause. Then he starts awake and rises with a groan. He looks at that state of mirth and pleasure — it is still there before his eyes, the wine still warm, the dishes still hot. He has not left his pillow and mat, yet the states of suffering and joy are suddenly different. In short, joy comes from outside, suffering comes from within. From this we see that the doctrines of heaven and hell appear plainly within one’s own mind — how could they be strange illusions! They are all brought about by delusion about one’s own mind. The sūtra says: The self-mind seizes the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharmas. It also says: The dharmas above and below the three realms are all made by the one mind.]

It is just like a person awake who roams at ease with all kinds of pleasant states before his eyes. After a little while he falls into a heavy sleep, and suddenly dreams that he is in hell, where all kinds of implements of torture and all its affairs are endured at once, with sourness and bitterness and poison beyond bearing. Just when he seeks rescue and cannot get it, the guests in the hall are still chatting and laughing. Suddenly he starts awake and rises with a groan. He looks at that state of mirth and pleasure — it is still there before his eyes, the wine still warm, the dishes still hot. He has not left his pillow and mat, yet the states of suffering and joy are utterly different. In short, joy comes from outside, suffering comes from within. From this we see that to say heaven and hell appear plainly within one’s own mind — what is there in that hard to understand! All of this is brought about by delusion about one’s own mind. The sūtra says: “The self-mind seizes the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharmas.” It also says: “The dharmas above and below the three realms are all made by the one mind.”
[The self-mind seizes the self-mind] The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“To establish knowing upon knowing is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing are without seeing, that is nirvāṇa, undefiled and truly pure.”
Master Hanshan says:

“What is the deluded mind? It is the one that clings to objects and does not dissolve. What is the true mind? It is the one that does not seize the marks of body, mind, and objects, but is clearly and constantly aware, numinously still and illuminating. Applying the mind in this way, what obstruction is there? Hence it is said: ‘The self-mind seizes the self-mind; the non-illusory becomes illusory dharmas. If one does not seize, there is nothing that is not illusion. When the non-illusory does not even arise, how can illusory dharmas stand?’ And as it is truly said: ‘Objects and conditions have no beauty or ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, from what can love and hate arise?’”
(The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to Zhou Ziyin)
[The dharmas above and below the three realms are all made by the one mind] In which of the

ten dharma realms one is ultimately born, and the direct and dependent rewards one receives — all of these are fashioned by the karma made by one’s own mind in thought after thought. Therefore, the karma made by one’s own mind in thought after thought is the
cause
, while which dharma realm one is born into and what kind of direct and dependent rewards one receives are the
effect
All made by the one mind
” — the word “made” means the karma-cause of creating karma. Master Hanshan instructs, in the Dream-Wandering Collection: Instructions to Xu Qingzhi:

“The Buddha says: ‘The dharmas above and below the three realms are all made by the one mind.’ What is above the three realms are the four holy ones beyond the world, namely Buddha, bodhisattva, śrāvaka, and pratyekabuddha. What is below the three realms are the ordinary beings of the six paths, namely the three good paths of gods, humans, and asuras, and the three evil paths of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts. Thus within the ten dharma realms, all sages and ordinary beings, the causes and effects of good and evil,
the adornments of direct and dependent reward
, are all made by the one mind. Yet this one mind is none other than the mind of
discriminating cognition
that is present before us in daily life. Since all is made by the mind, not made in stages, it is present before us in daily life as
the karma made in thought after thought
circulating through the ten dharma realms

. If a single thought, through craving, anger, and delusion, performs the ten evil deeds — the three of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind — then that is the cause of the three evil paths of suffering; if a single thought turns the ten evil deeds into the ten good deeds, then that is the cause of the wondrous bliss of humans and gods; if a single thought forgets both good and evil, so that inwardly one does not see a self and outwardly does not see a person, and the one mind is still — then that is the cause of the śrāvaka’s escape from suffering; if one contemplates that the suffering and joy, adversity and favor before one arise and cease, revolve and return to cessation, by cause and condition — then that becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha; if a single thought understands that persons and dharmas are without self, that causes and conditions are empty of nature, and that there is no doer and no receiver, and yet one does not hinder the manifest practice of giving, precept-keeping, patience, and the six pāramitās, transforming and ferrying sentient beings — then that is the cause of the bodhisattva; if a single thought suddenly awakens to one’s own mind, originally bright and vast, embracing all, saving all, with not a single dharma before the mind, with sentient beings and Buddhas equal — then that is the cause of becoming Buddha.”

[Seen in this way, it is not the Buddhadharma alone that speaks of the one mind. From the sages and worthies of old down to all the nine schools and strange arts, all speak of it to the utmost. As for sentient and insentient beings, none is not established from this one mind; there is only the difference of great and small, many and few, good and evil, deviant and upright, bright and dim, and the variety of its uses. Hence it is said: Mountains, rivers, and the great earth wholly reveal the Dharma-king’s body; scales, shells, feathers, and fur universally manifest the samādhi of the body of form. All of these are the true light of prajñā, the shadow-events of our own mind. The essence of mind that we originally possess is originally vast and all-embracing, pure and bright as this. And the crisscrossing, jumbled, crowded things displayed on every side before our eyes — all those various states and appearances — are again manifested by our mind as that. That we possess this and do not know it is truly pitiable.]

Seen in this way, it is not the Buddhadharma alone that speaks of the one mind. From the sages and worthies above down to all the nine schools and strange arts, all proclaim it with all their might. As for sentient beings and insentient things, none is not established from this one mind; there is only the difference of great and small, many and few, good and evil, deviant and upright, bright and dim, and this is because the uses of the mind-essence are each different. Hence it is said: “Mountains, rivers, and the great earth wholly reveal the Dharma-king’s body; scales, shells, feathers, and fur (fish, turtles, birds, and beasts) universally manifest the samādhi of the body of form.” All of these are the true light of prajñā, the illusory shadows of our own mind. The essence of mind that we originally possess is originally vast and all-embracing, pure and bright as this. And the crisscrossing, jumbled, crowded things displayed on every side before our eyes — all those various states and appearances — are again manifested by our mind as that. That we possess this all-capable mind-essence and do not know it is truly pitiable and lamentable!

[Nine schools] From the pre-Qin period to the early Han there were nine academic schools: Legalism, Names, Mohism, Confucianism, Daoism, Yin-Yang, Vertical and Horizontal Alliance, Miscellaneous, and Agriculture; later it refers generally to all kinds of schools. [Strange arts] Refers to different doctrines.

[Moreover, one mistakenly seizes one’s own mind and takes it as a pleasant ground of craving and love. The eye delights in beautiful forms, the ear delights in licentious sounds, the nose delights in fragrance, the tongue delights in flavors, the body delights in touch, the mind delights in dharmas — and all of these come forth from one’s own mind. One seizes them again and makes them into joy and pleasure, into craving, anger, and delusion, into lust, killing, stealing, and falsehood, creating all kinds of illusory karma, and thereby summoning the fierce suffering of the three evil paths in the future. Is this not like a person wandering in a dream without waking? Must it not be greatly lamented!]

We not only fail to know the mind-essence we inherently possess, but further falsely seize the illusory shadows within our own mind and take them as a pleasant ground of craving and love. The eye delights in the dust of form, the ear in the dust of sound, the nose in the dust of fragrance, the tongue in the dust of flavor, the body in the dust of touch, the mind in the dust of dharmas — delighting in all these illusory appearances manifested by our own mind. And we seize them to make joy and pleasure, to make craving, anger, and delusion, to make lust, killing, stealing, and falsehood, creating all kinds of illusory karma, and thereby summoning the fierce suffering of the three evil paths in the future. Is this not like a person lost in a dream without waking? How lamentable indeed!
[The particle
yú
] expresses an exclamatory tone.

[Because this mind is of one substance with all Buddhas, not two; and though the patriarchs of every generation have awakened to it and made it clear, it is no different in them — yet we alone possess it in full and do not know it, deluded as though by an illusion. The child runs away and forgets to return home, and the parents long for him and search him out. That is why Śākyamuni appeared in the world, why Bodhidharma came from the West, and why all that Caoxi taught over more than thirty years, and the seventeen hundred cases that have since spread through every quarter to point the way for people — all of it is this one matter, and not Old Lu alone. What I, the old man, say to you today, Director Si, is this matter too. What you, Director Si, together with all those present here who hear and see it, is this matter too. The sutra says: “This alone is the one reality; the other two are not true.” From this we know that outside this one matter, all is the talk of Māra, mere idle debate. Therefore, if the Buddhas, who are fully awakened, did not appear in the world, they would fail living beings. If the patriarchs, having awakened, did not expound the Dharma, they would fail the Buddhas. And all who hear it but do not believe, do not understand, do not receive, and do not practice fail themselves. To fail living beings is pride; to fail the Buddhas is downfall; to fail oneself is delusion. Thus the Buddhas and patriarchs may be failed, but oneself must not be failed — for to possess this mind originally and not seek it, to be complete in all virtues and not use them well, is like one who carries a wish-fulfilling pearl and yet goes begging. Could this not be called the greatest of sorrows?]

The mind-substance of living beings is no different from the mind-substance of the Buddhas. The patriarchs of every generation have awakened to this, and only we, though complete in it, do not know that we are lost in illusion. It is like a child who runs away and forgets to return, while the parents search for him everywhere. That is why Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world, why Bodhidharma came from the West, and why the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi taught for more than thirty years — and why the seventeen hundred kōans that have spread through every quarter to point the way for people are all like parents seeking back their own child, and not the Sixth Patriarch Huineng (Old Lu) alone. What I say to you today is this matter too (bringing you home). What you and all those present hear and see is this matter too. The sutra says: “This alone is the one reality; the other two are not true.” From this we know that apart from this one matter, everything is the talk of Māra and idle debate. Therefore, if the Buddhas, who have perfectly realized this mind-substance, did not appear in the world, they would fail living beings. If the patriarchs, who have awakened to this mind-substance, did not expound the Dharma, they would fail the Buddhas. And whoever hears it but does not believe, does not understand, does not receive, and does not practice fails himself. To fail living beings is pride; to fail the Buddhas is backsliding; to fail oneself is delusion. Thus the Buddhas and patriarchs may be failed, but oneself must not be failed — for to set aside this mind-substance, originally ours and capable of all things, and not seek it, to be complete in all powers and virtues and not use them well, is like carrying a wish-fulfilling pearl and yet going begging. How truly pitiable!

[You, Director Si, are now caught in the sea of dust, your mind fallen into a wrong road. Suddenly you wake with a start and turn back to seek this matter — like the child who holds the pearl and is ashamed to keep company with beggars, his every thought set on asking others for the way to be self-sufficient. I, the old man, at once point this Dharma straight at him, as though pointing out the wondrous pearl sewn in the hem of his garment: it was yours from the beginning, Director Si; it is not something I hand over as a favor, nor a matter of social courtesy.]

You, Director Si, are now tangled in the sea of dust, your mind fallen into a wrong road. Suddenly you wake with a start and turn back to seek this matter — like one who carries a wish-fulfilling pearl but is ashamed to keep company with beggars, his every thought bent on asking others how to be self-sufficient. I at once point this prajñā-Dharma straight at the mind-substance, as though pointing out the wondrous pearl sewn in the hem of your garment: it was yours from the very beginning; it is not something I offer as a favor.

[Qú] He — here it means the originally inherent mind-substance. [The wondrous pearl in the garment] A man had a priceless pearl sewn inside his garment without knowing it, and so wandered the four directions, living in hardship and poverty. The story is told in the Lotus Sutra
Chapter 3, “Parable.”

[Yet this wish-fulfilling pearl responds to whatever is sought; in all undertakings and in every realm of enjoyment, nothing is lacking. As for the way to make it respond, that lies in your own mind's skill and diligence, Director Si — in the power of
(here the same as “kè”)

bitter effort. If you can truly affirm it yourself and seek it with all your might, then one day, suddenly and thoroughly awakened, you will swallow in a single gulp the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the scaly, shelled, feathered, and furry creatures, the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of every generation, and the deeds of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius — without relying on any other power. Otherwise you remain a dreaming, deluded living being — how then could you be called a great man!]

Yet this wish-fulfilling pearl responds to whatever is sought; in all undertakings and every realm of enjoyment there is nothing it does not supply. As for how to make it respond, that again lies in your own mind's skill and diligence — in the power of bitter effort (kèkǔ, “to toil hard”). If you can truly resolve and seek with all your might, then one day, suddenly and thoroughly awakened, you will swallow in a single gulp the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the scaly, shelled, feathered, and furry creatures; the Buddhas of the three times; the patriarchs of every generation; and the deeds of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius — without relying on any other power. Otherwise you remain a dreaming, deluded living being — how then could you be called a great man!

[Bitter effort (kèkǔ)] To toil hard. The variant character here is equivalent to the usual one, and the phrase means the same as “to toil.” [Swallowing it all in a single gulp] This is the state of thorough awakening. Master Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way: “In dream, the six realms appear most clear; awake, the vast thousand worlds are void.” The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp relates: “Pang Yun, the layman of Xiangzhou, called on Mazu and asked, ‘What sort of person is one who keeps company with not a single dharma?’ The Patriarch said, ‘When you can swallow the West River in a single gulp, then I will tell you.’ At these words the layman was suddenly awakened.”

[Director Si, Director Si — better to fail the Buddhas and patriarchs above and to fail this old man below than to fail yourself, your lord, or your parents. The prajñā I speak today comes entirely from the mind-ground Dharma-gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs above, and it differs not a single word from what the Sixth Patriarch first taught. Only you alone were the first to hear it. Since one man now stands in place of the twelve hundred of old, I cannot contain my joy, and so I have also taught the Dharma of prajñā. As our Buddha and patriarchs have said: “As for one man, so for many.” If Deng holds to this for his own benefit and the benefit of others, he will surely not fail to have a broad and long tongue.]

Director Si, Director Si — better to fail the Buddhas and patriarchs above and this old man below than to fail yourself, your lord, or your parents. The prajñā I speak today is the mind-ground Dharma-gate handed down from the Buddhas and patriarchs of old, and it differs not one word from what the Sixth Patriarch first taught. But the first to hear it was you alone. Since one man could stand in place of the twelve hundred hearers of old, I cannot contain my joy, and so I speak the Dharma of prajñā for you as well. As our World-Honored One said: “As for one man, so for many.” If you hold to these words for your own benefit and the benefit of others, you will surely not fail to have a broad and long tongue.

[The twelve hundred hearers] The twelve hundred constant followers who were present whenever the Buddha taught the Dharma. [Broad and long tongue] One of the Buddha's thirty-two marks: the Buddha's tongue is broad and long, soft, red, and thin, able to cover his face up to the hairline. Here it is a metaphor for skill in expounding the Buddha-Dharma.

blocks.text: 20. Cutting Off the Root of Birth and Death

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to Feng Yanling)

[For a student turning toward the Way, the first thing is to fear birth and death; the second is to know the root of birth and death. The root of birth and death is simply the various deeds of aversion and craving, of taking and rejecting, of pride, of greed, anger, and delusion that arise before you in daily life. Since this is the bitter root of birth and death, and you have resolved to cut it off, there is no other method: simply, the moment it arises, illuminate it, and by no means allow it to arise. Where it does not arise, it is extinguished right there; once extinguished, let it not continue. With such effort, thought after thought is not let slip, mind after mind is not beclouded. Let the knowing be aware of itself; if the knowing is aware, then when it meets objects the objects do not drag the mind away, and when it contemplates the mind the mind does not cling to objects. When mind and objects do not meet, birth and death has nowhere to lodge. With such effort, there is no need to seek anything else mysterious!]

When a student resolves to cultivate the Way, the first thing is to fear birth and death; next, to know the root of birth and death. The root of birth and death is simply the deeds of aversion and craving, taking and rejecting, pride, greed, anger, and delusion that you create before you in daily life. Since this is the bitter root of birth and death, and you have resolved to cut it off, there is no other method: simply, when it arises, illuminate it at once and by no means allow it to arise. When it does not arise, it is extinguished on the spot; once extinguished, it must not be allowed to continue. With such effort, thought after thought is not let slip, mind after mind is not beclouded. You must know that your own nature (the self-awake) is yourself; if you know that your own nature is yourself, then meeting objects, objects do not drag the mind away, and contemplating the mind, the mind does not cling to objects; mind and objects cannot be tangled together, and so birth and death has nowhere to lodge. With such effort, there is no need to seek anything else mysterious!

[Not beclouded] Not muddled. [Let the knowing be aware of itself] You must know your own nature (the self-awake). The word “its” here has the force of an imperative. Living beings revolve in birth and death because they deludedly cling to the five aggregates and the four marks as “I,” and so create all the deeds of aversion and craving, taking and rejecting, pride, greed, anger, and delusion. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “What is ignorance? Good sons, all living beings, from beginningless time, have fallen into every kind of inversion, like a man who has lost his way and mistakes east for west. They deludedly take the four elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects as the mark of their own mind — like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons, the sky truly has no flowers; it is the sick man who deludedly clings to them. Because of this deluded clinging, he is confused not only about the self-nature of emptiness but also about where the real flowers arise. From this deluded existence comes the turning round in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.” If one sees through the five aggregates of body and mind as not being oneself, and knows that the self-nature alone is oneself, then all aversion and craving, taking and rejecting, pride, greed, anger, and delusion have no way to arise. [If the knowing is aware] Know that your own is aware. Here “if” (ruò) means “you, your,” as in “your kind.” [The five aggregates] Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Question: The passage above says, “You must know that your own nature alone is yourself.” Who is this “you”?

Answer: This “you” is the self-nature. From beginningless kalpas the self-nature has been deluded and has deludedly clung to the five aggregates of body and mind as itself, and so it creates all the deeds of aversion and craving, taking and rejecting, pride, greed, anger, and delusion, and undergoes the turning round of birth and death, imprisoned in the jail of the three realms. Now, if the self-nature is to cut off birth and death and be freed from the three realms, it must no longer think and act from the standpoint of the five aggregates of body and mind, but think and act from the standpoint of the self-nature's liberation.

[The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by living beings who have the two desires of sex and food; it includes the six heavens of desire above, the four continents where humans and animals dwell in the middle, and the uninterrupted hell below. The realm of form is the world inhabited by living beings who are free of the two desires of sex and food but still have form; it includes the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas. The formless realm is the world inhabited by living beings who have no form at all but abide with their consciousness in profound and subtle samādhi; it includes the four heavens of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These three realms are all the territory through which ordinary beings come and go in birth and death, and so Buddhist practitioners take escape from the three realms as their aim.

blocks.text: 21. Affairs Do Not Obstruct the Way

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to Zhu Suchen)

[Scholars who study the Way mostly take reading as an obstacle. The old man says: How does reading hinder the Way? It is only that when you are not reading, you are mostly disturbed by groundless idle thoughts. If in your leisure you can gather the mind to one place, cut off idle thoughts so that they do not run on, and keep mind after mind on the Way, thought after thought without forgetfulness — then you will spend much time studying the Way and little time reading.]

Men of letters who study the Way mostly think that reading gets in the way of practice. The old man says: How could devoted reading hinder the cultivation of the Way? The trouble is that when you are not reading, you are mostly disturbed by groundless idle thoughts, and that is the main thing that hinders the Way. If in your free time you can gather your mind to one place, cut off idle thoughts so that they do not continue, and keep mind after mind on the Way, thought after thought without forgetfulness — then the time you spend studying the Way will be much and the time you spend reading will be little.
[Shi ren] A Confucian scholar, a man of letters.

When you read, your mind is focused on one place. Moreover, in the course of a day the time when you are not reading is greater than the time when you are reading; if only you can gather your mind to one place during the hours when you are not reading, so that idle thoughts do not continue, then the time you spend studying the Way will again be greater than the time you spend reading with single-minded attention. Generally speaking, when you work, work with single-minded attention, and at all other times be wholly in cultivation — always keeping the mind fixed in one place, and the work of the Way will naturally be accomplished.

[The old man once instructed his students: The moment a thought arises, see through it at once. When a matter has not yet come, do not stir it up groundlessly. If you can truly apply your mind in this way, then idle thoughts cut themselves off, outer affairs naturally do not disturb you, the power of the Way strengthens of itself, and your practice will surely be easily accomplished.]

The old man once instructed his students, saying: The moment a thought arises, you should see through it at once. When a matter has not yet come, do not stir things up groundlessly. If you can truly apply your mind in this way, idle thoughts cut themselves off, outer affairs naturally do not disturb you, the power of the Way strengthens of itself, and your practice will surely be easily accomplished.

blocks.text: 22. The Essential Method of Investigation

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to Shen Zhizhi)

[The Way does not want clutter; with clutter there is much, with much there is disturbance, with disturbance there is anxiety, and with anxiety one does not enter. The ancients said: ‘In studying the Way, the aim should be gathered into one.’ What I call the one is simply the gathering of the aim. Now that you know the work of investigation, take up the case you are investigating and lay it across your chest. Whether busy or at leisure, moving or still, receiving guests and entertaining visitors, in all your daily words and deeds, raise it to mind everywhere and never let it slip. Let it slip, and you are disturbed by circumstances; disturbed, you grow weary; weary, and you have only a mind that seeks idleness and no mind that remembers the Way.]

Studying the Way should not be complicated. When it is complicated there are many threads; with many threads the mind becomes scattered and troubled; when the mind is scattered and troubled there is entanglement and anxiety; and with entanglement and anxiety in the mind, one cannot enter the Way. The ancients said: “In studying the Way, the aim should be gathered into one.” The one is simply the gathering of the aim. Now that you know the work of investigation, you must lay the case you are investigating across your chest. Whether busy or at leisure, moving or still, receiving guests and entertaining visitors, in your everyday speech and conduct, you must raise it to mind everywhere and never let it slip. Let it slip, and you are disturbed by circumstances; disturbed by circumstances, you grow weary; and once weary, you have only a mind that seeks idleness and no mind that remembers the Way.

[The aim should be gathered into one] “Aim” here means intent. The Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters says: “Aim is intent.” [Words and deeds] Speech and conduct. [Kōan, huatou] The original meaning of “kōan” is a case in which a government office judges right and wrong. The Chan school recorded the words and deeds of the eminent monks of every generation to serve as guidance for practitioners, and in time these too became objects of thought, or the mottoes of practitioners. Such records of words and deeds are like the official proclamations of a government: dignified and inviolable, yet also able to stir thought, to be studied by others, and to serve later generations as models to rely on — hence they are called kōans. This custom began in the Tang dynasty and became widespread in the Song. In most kōans there is a single word or single phrase for students to investigate, and this is called a “huatou.” For example: “Question: Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Answer: No!” This exchange is one kōan, and the word “no” is the huatou. When one works at the huatou of a kōan in Chan practice, it is called investigating the huatou; when a teacher gives a kōan with words to a student, it is called a huatou kōan. Generally speaking, kōans cannot be explained by logical reasoning or ordinary common sense, because the spirit of the Chan school transcends verbal expression and conceptual thought; hence teachers often use the “illogicality” of a kōan to trigger in the student a deep intuition beyond discriminating consciousness, helping the student to realize the true nature. The use of kōans has five aspects: (1) as a tool for awakening to Chan, (2) as a method of testing, (3) as an authoritative model, (4) as a seal of confirmation, and (5) as a definitive pointer. [Teacher] A Chan master of learning and virtue who can serve as a guide for practicing monks.

[When mind and aim are gathered into one, all things can be done. Wherever you apply the mind, work only at the place where thoughts arise. When they arise, see through them; seeing through them, they vanish on the spot and no longer continue to play with you — this is the essential method of investigation. Hence it is said: Plan for the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. This is precisely taking hold at the easy place and the small place, and you will find it saves effort. If you set this aside and wait for leisure and quiet before doing the work, then to the end of this life there will be no time for you to enter the Way.]

When mind and aim are gathered into one, all things can be done. Wherever you apply the mind, work only at the place where thoughts arise. If a deluded thought arises, see through it at once; seeing through it, it disappears; by no means let it continue and be toyed with by it — this is the essential method of investigation. Hence it is said: Plan for the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. This is precisely taking hold at the easy place and the small place, and you will find it saves effort. If you set this aside and wait for leisure and quiet before doing the work, then to the end of this life there will be no time for you to enter the Way.

[Plan for the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small] This refers to the passage above, “work only at the place where thoughts arise.” To remove habitual tendencies and break through ignorance is difficult, and to cultivate and realize the fruit is a great matter; yet “work only at the place where thoughts arise” is easy and small in itself — and if you now work only at the place where thoughts arise, you will of yourself be able to remove habitual tendencies, break through ignorance, and realize the fruit of practice. Therefore it is said, “Plan for the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small.”

[Chen Sheng, simply work on this one thought; there is no need to seek outside yourself. Even when you bow to the Buddha or recite mantras, do it only on the faith-power of a single thought. In short, all skillful means are merely methods of gathering in the mind.]

Chen Sheng (that is, the student Shen Zhizhi to whom Master Hanshan gave this instruction), work only on this one thought; there is no need to seek outside yourself. Even when you bow to the Buddha or recite mantras, do it only on the faith-power of a single thought. In short, all skillful means are merely methods of gathering in the mind.

[Faith-power] One of the five powers. [The five powers] When the five roots become firm and generate power, they are called the “five powers”: the powers of faith, vigor, mindfulness, samādhi, and wisdom.
