The power of faith is the growth of the root of faith, which can destroy all wrong beliefs; the power of vigor is the growth of the root of vigor, which can destroy sloth of body; the power of mindfulness is the growth of the root of mindfulness, which can destroy all wrong thoughts; the power of samādhi is the growth of the root of samādhi, which can destroy all scattered thinking; the power of wisdom is the growth of the root of wisdom, which can destroy all the delusions of the three realms. [The five roots] Here the “five roots” means the roots of faith, progress, mindfulness, samādhi, and wisdom. These five dharmas are the root from which the noble path is born, and so they are called the “five roots.”

blocks.text: 23. Who Is It That Recites the Buddha's Name?

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to the Chan Monk Xingjue)

[The ancients left a great many occasions for investigation, but among them the one huatou that is honest and true — “Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?” — is the easiest to work with. Now that you, Chan monk, have resolved to investigate, simply raise this one kōan to mind at all times.]

The ancients left a great many occasions for investigation, but only the one huatou that is honest and true — “Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?” — is the easiest to work with. Now that you, Chan monk, have resolved to investigate, take this one kōan and raise it to mind at all times.

[First set down together all the idle and tangled thoughts inside and outside your body and mind. When you have set them down to the point where there is nothing left to set down, then deeply raise up one utterance of Amitābha Buddha. The four syllables are distinct and clear; urgently bring them before your gaze. If after a while you find it lacks power, raise the Buddha's name again.]

First set down together all the idle and tangled thoughts inside and outside your body and mind. When you have set them down to the point where there is nothing left to set down, then deeply raise up one utterance of Amitābha Buddha: the four syllables distinct and clear, urgently brought before your gaze. If after a while you find it lacks power, raise the Buddha's name again. And so continue. (This is the preliminary to investigation.)

[When it has power, then bring down the mass of doubt and ask: Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Ask again and again — after all, who is it? If you see drowsiness or distraction come before you, at once rouse your spirit to the utmost: raise it again, look again, ask again, doubt again. When the doubt reaches the place where doubting is no longer possible, and your chest feels like a silver mountain and an iron wall standing between mind and eye — this is the time when the huatou has power. If you reach this place of power, this is just the time to bring down the mass of doubt once more, so that through all the times and all the places of daily life it does not shift from thought to thought, until even in long sleep it is just as when you are awake. If your effort reaches this point, you must on no account retreat or fall back. Then of a sudden the mass of doubt bursts asunder, and you naturally see your original face in a flash.]

If the work of reciting and looking has already gained power, then bring down the mass of doubt within the no-thought: ask, who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Ask again and again — after all, who is it? If you see drowsiness or distraction come before you, at once rouse your spirit to the utmost: raise it again, look again, ask again, doubt again. When the doubt reaches the place where doubting is no longer possible, and your chest feels like a silver mountain and an iron wall standing between mind and eye — this is the time when the huatou has power. If you reach this place of power, this is just the time to bring down the mass of doubt once more, so that through all the times and all the places of daily life it does not shift from thought to thought, until even in long sleep it is just as when you are awake. If your effort reaches this point, you must on no account retreat or fall back. Then of a sudden the mass of doubt bursts asunder, and you naturally see your original face in a flash.

[If you are willing to set forth this determined resolve and hold to a mind that does not retreat, then simply go straight on with this one thought. By no means seek quick results, and by no means use the mind to wait for awakening. If your practice is close and continuous, the time of breaking through will come of itself.]

If you are willing to set forth this determined resolve and hold to a mind that does not retreat, then simply go straight on with this one thought. By no means seek quick results, and by no means use the mind to wait for awakening. If your practice is close and continuous, the time of breaking through will come of itself.

[The investigation described above is the easiest and most economical of effort. The essential thing is to be able to set it down, to take it up, to lean on it steadily, and to doubt it keenly; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whether moving or still, at leisure or busy, every moment is a time for applying the mind. The Sixth Patriarch said, “If we speak of this matter, one may do it even with sword whirling in battle” — this is what he meant. Chan monk, if you have the resolve and truly act for the sake of birth and death, then set your foot on this one road.]

The investigation described above is the easiest and most economical of effort. The essential thing is to be able to set it down, to take it up, to lean on it steadily, and to doubt it keenly; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whether moving or still, at leisure or busy, every moment is a time for applying the mind. The Sixth Patriarch said, “If we speak of this matter, one may do it even with sword whirling in battle” — this is what he meant. Chan monk, if you have the resolve and truly act for the sake of birth and death, then set your foot on this one road.

blocks.text: 24. Instructions on Practicing Pure Land

inline.s: (Excerpted from The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation on the Practice of the Pure Land Dharma-Gate)

[The sutra says: “If one would purify the Buddha-land, one should purify one's own mind.” Therefore, in practicing the Pure Land work today, one must take a purified mind as the foundation. To purify one's own mind, the first thing is to purify the roots of the precepts. For the ten evil deeds — three of body, four of speech, and three of mind — are the cause of suffering in the three evil paths.]

The sutra says: “If one would purify the Buddha-land, one should purify one's own mind.” Therefore, in practicing the Pure Land work today, one must take a purified mind as the foundation. And to purify one's own mind, the first thing is to purify the roots of the precepts. For the three of body (
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct
), the four of speech (
lying, frivolous talk, divisive speech, harsh speech
), and the three of mind (
desire, anger, and delusion
) — these ten evil deeds are the cause of suffering in the three evil paths (the three destinies).
[The ten evil deeds] Deeds of body: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct. Deeds of speech: lying, frivolous talk, divisive speech, harsh speech. Deeds of mind: greed, anger, delusion.

[The essential point of keeping the precepts today is that the three karmas must first be purified, and then the mind is of itself pure. If the body does not kill, steal, or commit sexual misconduct, the karma of body is pure. If one does not lie, speak frivolously, divide others by gossip, or speak harshly, the karma of speech is pure. If the mind is not greedy, not angry, and not deluded, the karma of mind is pure. In this way the ten evil deeds are forever cut off and the three karmas are clear as ice — this is the essential point of purifying the mind.]

The essential point of keeping the precepts today is that the three karmas of body, speech, and mind must first be purified, and then the mind is of itself pure. If the body does not kill, steal, or commit sexual misconduct, the karma of body is pure. If one does not lie, does not speak frivolously, does not divide others by gossip, and does not speak harshly, the karma of speech is pure. If the mind is not greedy, not angry, and not deluded, the karma of mind is pure. In this way the ten evil deeds are forever cut off and the three karmas are clear as ice — this is the essential point of purifying the mind.

[Within this purified mind, turn away from the sufferings of the Sahā world, make the vow to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Nurture, and establish the primary practice of reciting the Buddha's name.]

Then, within this purified mind, turn away from the sufferings of the Sahā world, make the vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and establish the primary practice of reciting the Buddha's name.

[Yet in reciting the Buddha's name, the resolve for birth and death must be keen. First cut off outer entanglements, then raise aloft a single thought: take the one phrase Amitābha Buddha as your very root of life, never forgetting it from thought to thought, never breaking it from mind to mind. Throughout the twelve hours of the day, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, lifting the spoon and raising the chopsticks, turning and bowing, moving or still, at leisure or busy, at all times be neither muddled nor beclouded, and let there be no other entanglements.]

Yet in reciting the Buddha's name, the resolve to be free of birth and death must be genuine and keen. First, do not let the mind reach out after conditions; then raise aloft a single thought, taking the one phrase Amitābha Buddha as your very root of life, never forgetting it from thought to thought, never breaking it from mind to mind. Throughout the twelve hours of the day, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, lifting the spoon and raising the chopsticks (that is, while eating), turning and bowing (that is, in every movement), moving or still, at leisure or busy, at all times do not be toyed with by idle thoughts (not muddled) and do not be deceived by them (not beclouded), and let there be no reaching out after other conditions (no other entanglements).

[A keen resolve for birth and death] A genuine and keen resolve to be free of birth and death. People in the world may be divided into three kinds. The first do not know that one can be free of birth and death, and have no wish to be; they have no resolve for birth and death at all. The second know that one can be free of birth and death and wish to be, but are unwilling to undertake hard practice, and still less willing to give up the enjoyments of worldly desire; their resolve for birth and death is not keen. The third are willing to undertake hard practice and to give up the enjoyments of worldly desire, and regard freedom from birth and death as the foremost matter, as the meaning and mission of life; their resolve for birth and death is keen. [First cut off outer entanglements] First, do not let the mind reach out after conditions. [Turning] Turning the body. [Bowing and raising] Lowering and lifting the head, and by extension every movement. [Neither muddled nor beclouded] Not toyed with by idle thoughts, and not deceived by them.

[With such effort, after long practice it becomes wholly familiar, until even in dreams it is not forgotten. When waking and sleeping are one, your practice is close and continuous, beaten into a single piece — this is the time of power.]

With such effort, after long practice it becomes wholly familiar, until even in dreams it is not forgotten. Day and night are alike; your practice becomes close and continuous, beaten into a single piece — this is the time of power.

[Wù mèi] Waking and sleeping; commonly used to mean day and night. For example: “The modest, retiring, virtuous young lady — waking and sleeping he sought her.” (Book of Songs, Odes of Zhou and the South, “Guan Ju”)

[If you recite until you reach single-mindedness without distraction, then at the approach of death the realms of the Pure Land appear before you, and you are naturally no longer held back by birth and death; you will move Amitābha Buddha to emit light and come to receive you. This is the sure proof of rebirth there.]

If you recite until you reach single-mindedness without distraction, then at the approach of death the realms of the Pure Land appear before you, and you are naturally no longer held back by birth and death; and so you move Amitābha Buddha to emit light and come to receive you. This is the sure proof of rebirth there.

blocks.text: 25. The Essentials of Reciting the Buddha's Name

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation on the Essentials of Reciting the Buddha's Name)

[The single gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land was originally meant for the great matter of settling birth and death. Hence it is said: recite the Buddha's name and settle birth and death. When people today arouse the resolve, it is because they want to settle birth and death that they are willing to recite; they merely say that the Buddha can settle birth and death. But if you do not know the root and trunk of birth and death, where after all will you recite? If the mind that recites cannot cut off the root and trunk of birth and death, how can birth and death be settled?]

The single gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land was originally meant for the great matter of settling birth and death. Hence it is said: reciting the Buddha's name settles birth and death. When people today arouse the resolve, it is because they want to settle birth and death that they are willing to recite, and they merely say that reciting can settle birth and death. But if you do not know the root of birth and death, where after all will you recite? If the mind that recites cannot cut off the root of birth and death, how can birth and death be settled?
[Root and trunk] The root and main stem of a plant — a metaphor for the foundation of a thing.

[What is the root and trunk of birth and death? The ancients said: “If one's karma were not heavy, one would not be born in the Sahā world; if one's craving were not cut off, one would not be born in the Pure Land.” From this we know that the root of craving is the root and trunk of birth and death. For all living beings suffer the pain of birth and death through the fault of craving and desire. Trace this root of craving: it is not something that exists only in this life, nor only in one, two, three, or four lives; it is that from beginningless time, ever since birth and death first began, life after life, casting off one body and receiving another, all has been the turning round of craving and desire, right down to today. Reflect on the past: was there ever a single thought that briefly left this root of craving? Such seeds of craving, accumulated deep over kalpas, are why birth and death is endless.]

What is the root of birth and death? The ancients said: “If one's karma were not heavy, one would not be born in the Sahā world; if one's craving were not cut off, one would not be born in the Pure Land.” From this we know that the root of craving is the root of birth and death. For all living beings suffer the pain of birth and death through the fault of craving and desire. Trace this root of craving: it is not something that exists only in this life, nor only in one, two, three, or four lives; it is that from beginningless time, ever since birth and death first began, life after life, casting off one body (dying) and receiving another (being reborn), all has been the turning round of craving and desire, right down to today. Reflecting on the past, was there ever a single thought that briefly left this root of craving? Such seeds of craving, accumulated deep over beginningless kalpas, are why birth and death is endless.
[The root of craving] Craving produces the fruit of karma; hence it is called the root of craving.

Yang Cigong said: “If one's craving is not heavy, one is not born in the Sahā world; if one's mindfulness is not single, one is not born in the Pure Land.” Elder Master Guangqin said: “If the clinging of affection is not cut off, then even while reciting the Buddha's name with the mouth, thought after thought still falls into the Sahā world. But if one is earnest and utterly sincere and lets go of the ten thousand conditions, then in the space of a single thought one can reach the West. If the ten thousand conditions drag at one and cannot be relinquished, then for a hundred years or ten thousand years one is still within the three realms.” Therefore the essential key to being born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is: cut off craving and make the mindfulness single.

[Yang Cigong] Yang Jie, courtesy name Cigong, style name Wuweizi. A man of the Song dynasty. He was at first fond of the Chan school and was greatly awakened while studying under Chan Master Tianyi Huai. At the end of the Xining era he returned home on account of his mother's death (his mother having passed away), and in retirement read the Buddhist canon; thereupon he turned his heart to the Pure Land, advocated it vigorously, and had a sixteen-foot image of Amitābha Buddha painted to keep with him for visualization. At the time of his death a golden terrace appeared from the sky, and he spoke a verse and passed away. [Cut off craving and make the mindfulness single] Cut off the root of craving and make the thought of reciting the Buddha's name single and undivided.

Question: At the time of his death, Yang Cigong spoke a verse: “In life there is nothing to cling to; in death there is nothing to forsake. In the vast empty space — zhi, hu, zhe, ye (idle classical particles) — take the wrong for the wrong: the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.” What does “take the wrong for the wrong” mean in this verse?

Answer: On this point Master Yinguang gave instruction in his Dharma Words for the Shanghai Dharma Assembly for Protecting the Nation and Averting Disaster: “As for ‘take the wrong for the wrong': if one has thoroughly realized the true nature, then there is no need to seek rebirth in the West — seeking rebirth would still be one wrong. But since one has not realized it and must seek rebirth in the West, it is said, ‘take the wrong for the wrong: the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.’ After the ‘Biography of Master Yang’ in Master Lianchi's Record of Rebirths, the praise reads: ‘I would that all the clever scholars of the world would all commit this one wrong.’”
Master Xing'an said: “To recite the Buddha's name is no hard thing — the hard thing is a single mind. A single mind is no hard thing — the hard thing is to cut the root of craving behind.”
Master Youxi said: “In the Sahā world, if there is a single craving that is not lightened, then at the moment of death one is dragged by that craving and cannot be reborn; how much more so with
shěn

(that is, ‘how much more’) many cravings? In the Pure Land, if there is a single thought that is not single, then at the moment of death one is turned about by that thought (turned about by that unsingle thought) and cannot be reborn; how much more so with many thoughts? For craving has its light and heavy, its thick and thin, in both the direct and the circumstantial retribution. To list its items (its kinds) one by one: parents, wife and children, elder and younger brothers, friends, fame and wealth, essays and poems, arts and crafts, clothing and food, house and fields, woods and springs, flowers and plants, treasures and playthings — they cannot be counted one by one (there is no end to the listing). To be unable to forget a single thing is craving; to be unable to let go a single thought (unable to relinquish it) is craving. If one craving remains in the breast, the mindfulness is not single; if one thought does not return to the one, one cannot be reborn.”

[You have only today begun to recite the Buddha's name, and you simply gaze into emptiness seeking rebirth in the West, not even knowing the name of craving, the root of birth and death — how could a single thought have cut it off? Since you do not know the root of birth and death, then while you recite on one side, the root of birth and death only grows on the other. Reciting in this way, recitation and birth and death have nothing to do with each other. In such a case, recite however you like: when death approaches, you will only see the root of craving for birth and death appear before you, and only then will you know that the Buddha's name had no power at all. To complain then that recitation is without efficacy — regret will come too late.]

You have only today begun to recite the Buddha's name, and you simply gaze into emptiness seeking rebirth in the West, not even knowing that craving is the root of birth and death — how could a single thought have cut it off? Since you do not know what the root of birth and death is, then while you recite on one side, the root of birth and death (the root of craving) is left to grow as it will. Reciting in this way, recitation and the settling of birth and death have nothing to do with each other. By such a method, recite however you like: when death approaches, you will only see the root of birth and death (the root of craving) appear before you, and only then will you know that reciting the Buddha's name had no power at all. To complain then that recitation is without efficacy — regret will be too late.

[Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha's name today first to know that craving is the root of birth and death. And now as you recite, let thought after thought cut off this root of craving. Take the case of a householder reciting at home: in your eyes you see your children and grandchildren, your family ties and property, and there is not one thing that is not craved; then there is no affair and no thought that is not the business of birth and death, and you are like one whose whole body is in a pit of fire. You do not know that while you are reciting, not a single thought in your mind has let go of the root of craving. It is just that when you recite you only say your recitation is not keen, not knowing that craving is the master and recitation the surface. Reciting in this way, the Buddha is merely recited while craving is merely left to grow. And when the affection for children comes before you, turn the light around and look: can this one utterance of the Buddha's name really stand against this craving? Can it really cut off this craving? If it cannot cut off this craving, how after all will birth and death be settled? Because the ties of craving have been made familiar through many lives, while recitation has only just been taken up and is quite unfamiliar, and is not yet genuine and solid — for this reason it has no power.]

Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha's name today first to know that craving is the root of birth and death. Now, as you recite, let thought after thought cut off this root of craving. Take the case of reciting at home right before you: in your eyes you see your children and grandchildren, your family ties and property, and there is not one thing that is not craved; then there is no affair and no thought that is not the business of birth and death, and you are like one whose whole body is in a pit of fire. Yet you do not know that while you are reciting, not a single thought in your mind has let go of the root of craving. It is just that when you recite you only say your recitation is not keen, not knowing the reason within — that craving is the master and recitation the surface. Reciting in this way, the Buddha is merely recited while craving is merely left to grow. Moreover, when the affection for children comes before you, turn the light around and look: can this one utterance of the Buddha's name really stand against this craving? Can it really cut off this craving? If it cannot cut off this craving, how after all will birth and death be settled? Because the ties of craving have been made familiar through many lives, while recitation has only just been taken up and is quite unfamiliar, and is not yet genuine and solid — for this reason it has no power.
[The ties of craving] The ties of affection and desire. The Ratnakūṭa Sutra says: “Among all the afflictions, those joined by the ties of craving are the heaviest.”

[If before you now you cannot take charge of the realm of craving, then at the moment of death you will certainly not be able to take charge. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha's name: first, know that the resolve for birth and death must be keen; know that the cutting off of birth and death must be keen; you must cut it off thought after thought at the very root and trunk of birth and death — then thought after thought is the time of settling birth and death. Why wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month to settle it? That would be late beyond late! As it is said: “Before you now, all is the business of birth and death; settle it before you now, and birth and death is empty.” If you apply your mind in this way, thought after thought genuine, every cut drawing blood, and still do not escape birth and death, then all the Buddhas would have fallen into lying speech. Therefore, whether householder or monastic, whoever has the mind that knows birth and death — that is the season of escaping birth and death. How could there be any other wonderful method!]

If before you now you cannot take charge of the realm of craving, then at the moment of death you will certainly not be able to take charge. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha's name: first, know that the resolve to cut off birth and death must be keen. Knowing that the resolve to cut off birth and death must be keen, you must cut it off thought after thought at the very root of birth and death, and then thought after thought is the time of settling birth and death. Why wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month (the end of life) to settle birth and death? If only then do you think of settling it, it will be late beyond late! As it is said: “Before you now, all is the business of birth and death; settle it before you now, and birth and death is empty.” If you apply your mind in this way, thought after thought genuine, every cut drawing blood, and still do not escape birth and death, then all the Buddhas would have fallen into lying speech. Therefore, whether householder or monastic, so long as you have the mind that knows birth and death, that is the season of escaping birth and death. Where else would there be a more wonderful method!

[Before you now, all is the business of birth and death; settle it before you now, and birth and death is empty] Before you now is all the business of birth and death; to settle these affairs of birth and death before you now is precisely to be settling birth and death (birth and death being empty).

blocks.text: 26. The True Practice of the Pure Land

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to the Chan Monk Ningxu Tong)

[The essentials of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' practice lie in only two gates, Chan and Pure Land, adorned besides by the ten thousand practices — this is the true path of practice. Of late, students who investigate Chan have mostly been led astray by false teachers, drawn into a thicket of wrong views, fallen into the demon of pride, and increased the seed of the outsiders. This is gravely to be feared. And of ten such “teachers,” not one has attained liberation. In this way they not only ruin themselves but ruin others as well — should one not be afraid! For this reason I, the old man, urge with all my strength the true practice of the Pure Land.]

The essentials of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' practice lie in only two gates, Chan and Pure Land, adorned besides by the ten thousand practices — this is the true path of practice. Of late, among students, those who investigate Chan have mostly been misled by false teachers, drawn into a thicket of wrong views, fallen into the demon of pride, and increased the seed of the outsiders; this is deeply to be feared. What is more, of ten such “teachers,” not one has himself attained liberation. For people like this to instruct students who investigate Chan is not only to ruin themselves but also to ruin others — should one not be afraid! (To be misled and so cut off the life of the Dharma-body and wisdom is a most fearful thing; and those who, without having realized it, rashly set themselves up as teachers not only cut off their own life of Dharma-body and wisdom but must also bear the karma of misleading living beings — this is still more to be feared.) For this reason I urge with all my strength that students should truly practice the Pure Land Dharma-gate (the true practice of the Pure Land).
[Of late] Recently. [Led astray] The sense is to act improperly; here it is extended to mean misleading.

[People in the world do not understand, and all take it lightly as something common; they do not know the wonder of reciting the Buddha's name, and so they make many mistakes. Moreover, reciting the Buddha's name is itself the investigation of Chan — there is no second Dharma. When you recite, you must first set down together all the afflictions and idle thoughts in your breast — greed, anger, delusion, and craving, and every kind of tangled thought. When you have set them down to the point where there is nothing left to set down, then singly raise up one utterance of Amitābha Buddha, distinct and clear, unbroken in the mind, like a thread stringing pearls, or like arrow-nocks joined end to end, with not the least gap between. Lean on it with such strength that in every place you are not dragged off and lost by conditions and circumstances.]

People in the world do not understand the Pure Land Dharma-gate, and all take it lightly as something common; they do not know the wonder of reciting the Buddha's name, and so they make many mistakes. Moreover, reciting the Buddha's name is itself the investigation of Chan — there is no second Dharma. When you recite, you must first set down together all the afflictions and idle thoughts in your breast — greed, anger, delusion, and craving, and every kind of tangled thought. When you have set them down to the point where there is nothing left to set down, then singly raise up one utterance of Amitābha Buddha, distinct and clear, unbroken in the mind, like a thread stringing pearls, or like arrows joined head to tail, with not the least gap between. Lean on it with such strength that in every place you are not dragged off and lost by conditions and circumstances.
[Arrow-nocks joined] Arrow joined to arrow, head to tail. Kuò (nock) is the end of an arrow.

[In this way, amid the movements of daily life you are neither mixed nor disordered, and sleeping and waking are one. With such effort, when you recite to the point of death with a single mind undistracted, that is the season of transcending birth and death and reaching the Pure Land. If you only speak of reciting with the mouth while the ground of the mind is impure and idle thoughts are not removed, and merely say that recitation is without efficacy — then even after three lives and sixty kalpas you will have no share in getting out. You must exert yourself!]

In this way, amid the movements of daily life you are neither mixed nor disordered, and sleeping and waking are one. With such effort, when you recite to the point of death with a single mind undistracted, that is the season of transcending birth and death and reaching the Pure Land. If you only speak of reciting with the mouth while the ground of the mind is impure and idle thoughts are not removed, and merely say that recitation is without efficacy — then even after three lives and sixty kalpas you will have no share in getting out. You must exert yourself!

blocks.text: 27. Truly for the Sake of Birth and Death

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to the Chan Monk Wuzhi Jian)

[A monastic must first know that leaving home, cutting off affection, and taking leave of kin is originally for the sake of escaping birth and death. If it is for the great matter of birth and death, you must know that all the dharmas of the world are the root of suffering, that the body is a mass of suffering, and that you must arouse the resolve to practice. To seek the way out of suffering, you must first see through the present state of body and mind. You should contemplate this body: it is earth, water, fire, and wind, formed by the false union of the four elements. When the four elements separate, where will this false body be? Seeing through it in this way, you will not seek for this body all kinds of enjoyments.]

A monastic must first know that leaving home, cutting off affection, and taking leave of kin is originally for the sake of escaping birth and death. If it is for the great matter of birth and death, you must know that all the dharmas of the world are the root of suffering, that the body is a mass of suffering, and that you must arouse the resolve to practice. To seek the way out of suffering, you must first see through the present state of body and mind. You should contemplate this physical body: it is earth, water, fire, and wind, formed by the false union of the four elements. When the four elements separate, where will this false body then be? Seeing through it in this way, you will not seek for this body all kinds of enjoyments.

[Next you must see through the present seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as entirely the work of idle thought, and never the true mind. With this false mind one creates all kinds of karma; every stirring of the mind and every movement of thought is nothing but karma, nothing but offense. This very single thought is the bitter root of birth and death; by no means follow it as idle thought turns and flows. Observe closely through the day: where idle thought arises, see through it at once, and it perishes on the spot; by no means let it continue, reaching out after conditions and going on without return. If your observation is unsettled and you have nothing to hold to, then simply take the one utterance of Amitābha Buddha as your huatou, clasp it tight, and never forget it from thought to thought. With this huatou as your master, whenever you see idle thought arise, at once raise up the Buddha's name: this is the right mindfulness coming before you, and the idle thoughts vanish of themselves without needing to be driven out.]

Next you must see through the present seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as entirely the work of idle thought, and never the true mind. With this false mind one creates all kinds of karma; every stirring of the mind and every movement of thought is nothing but karma, nothing but offense. This very single thought is the bitter root of birth and death; by no means follow it as idle thought turns and flows. Observe closely through the day: where idle thought arises, see through it at once, and it perishes on the spot; by no means let it continue, reaching out after conditions and drifting on without return. If your observation is unsettled and you have nothing to hold to, then simply take the one utterance of Amitābha Buddha as your huatou, clasp it tight, and never forget it from thought to thought. With this huatou as your master, whenever you see idle thought arise, at once raise up the Buddha's name: this is the right mindfulness coming before you, and the idle thoughts vanish of themselves without needing to be driven out.
[Nothing to hold to] No place to take hold.

[In this way, through the twelve hours of the day, apply the mind closely, taking this one thought alone as master and all other idle thoughts as guests. Once guest and master are distinguished, after long familiarity the idle thoughts vanish of themselves and the true mind manifests of itself. Chan monk, if you truly have the resolve for the great matter of birth and death, then take this one thought alone as true. As for the various other skills of the world — writing poems, practicing calligraphy, and even reaching out after conditions, keeping company, and giving yourself up to license — all are matters of inversion and delusion. If you do not admire real practice but devote yourself to the superficial and the empty, giving free rein to the six senses, roaming and chattering without root, vainly wasting your time, then you will not only live and die in vain but will also, I fear, find evil karma hard to escape: for a thousand lives and a hundred kalpas there will be no time of getting out.]

In this way, through the twelve hours of the day, apply the mind closely, taking this one thought (the thought of reciting the Buddha's name) alone as master and all other idle thoughts as guests. Once guest and master are distinguished, after long familiarity the idle thoughts vanish of themselves and the true mind manifests of itself. Chan monk, if you truly have the resolve for the great matter of birth and death, then take this one thought alone as true. As for the various other skills of the world — writing poems, practicing calligraphy, and even reaching out after conditions, keeping company, and giving yourself up to license — all are matters of inversion and delusion. If you do not admire real practice but devote yourself to the superficial and the empty, giving free rein to the six senses, wandering east and west and chattering of everything under heaven (roaming and chattering without root), vainly wasting your time, then you will not only live and die in vain but will also, I fear, find evil karma hard to escape: for a thousand lives and a hundred kalpas there will be no time of getting out.

[The six senses] That is, the six roots. In the old translations of the sutras and treatises the six roots are often rendered as the six senses, because the six roots — eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — all possess sentient awareness, and so they are called the six senses.

blocks.text: 28. One Must Know the Inherently Possessed

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to the Practitioner Kuanliang)

[The people of old went on pilgrimage for the sake of birth and death; the people of today merely go on pilgrimage without knowing birth and death. This is deeply to be pitied — this is what is meant by “using it daily and not knowing it.” Their fault lies in not knowing the inherently possessed. If a person knows what he possesses, he knows to respect himself. Knowing to respect himself, he does not follow things as they turn but can turn things instead. The Book of Songs has it: “My heart is not a stone; it cannot be turned.” You must know that unless it is the mind-ground of diamond, nothing but is turned by things. And once turned by things, one goes along with them — can such a one be called a pilgrim monk?]

The people of old went on pilgrimage for the sake of escaping birth and death; the people of today merely go on pilgrimage without knowing escape from birth and death. This is deeply to be pitied — this is what is meant by going on pilgrimage every day yet not understanding what it is about! Their fault lies in not knowing the inherently possessed diamond mind. If a person knows the inherently possessed diamond mind, he knows to respect himself. Knowing to respect himself, he does not follow things as they turn but can turn things instead. The Book of Songs says: “My heart is not a stone (my heart is not stone), it cannot be turned.” You must know that whoever does not have the diamond mind is turned by things without exception. And once turned by things, one goes along with them — can such a one be called a pilgrim monk?
[Going on pilgrimage] A Chan monk's walking journey on foot everywhere in search of the Way. [The inherently possessed] That is, the diamond mind. Master Hanshan's The Dream-Wandering Collection

Postscript to the Prayer of the Bodhi Mind says: “All saints and ordinary beings alike originally dwell in the mind-ground of diamond, complete in the Buddha's inconceivable wisdom.” In his commentary on the Diamond Sutra (Resolving Doubts About the Diamond Sutra), Master Hanshan says: “The diamond mind is the fundamental mind in which the Buddha cultivated the cause and realized the fruit. Appearing in the world today to teach living beings, he uses this mind entirely. He now teaches bodhisattvas to take the diamond mind as the root of their cultivation, as the initial gate of entry into the Great Vehicle.” “Now, in order to lead those formerly of the Small Vehicle to arouse the Great Vehicle mind, he takes this diamond mind-ground as the root of cultivation.” [Fei] Is not. [Nazi] Also called the nazi monk: another name for a Chan monk, because Chan monks often wear a patchwork robe and wander in all directions.

[Kuanliang has come from the north to the south to comfort me several times. Not turned by the hardships of the road or by hunger and cold, hardship and suffering, I, the old man, know only that your heels are strong, and so I call you Iron Feet. Now I see that your mind does not shift, and so I further praise you with the two words “Iron Guts.” Yet that you are iron-guts is what I, the old man, know; the matter of your pilgrimage is certainly not something you know. Had you the least knowledge of pilgrimage, you would not go on so blankly, straight ahead. I, the old man, pity your foolishness, and fearing what you do not know, I send you this letter again, and you shall go on pilgrimage again. If after this you still cannot grope for your own nostrils, then in other days and at another time we shall surely find it hard to meet as we do today.]

The Chan monk Kuanliang has come from the north to the south to pay his respects to me several times already. You are not turned by the hardships of the road or by hunger and cold, hardship and suffering, and I, the old man, know that your heels are strong beyond the ordinary, and so I call you Iron Feet. Now I see that your mind is unshifting, and so I further praise you as Iron Guts. Yet that you are iron-guts and unshifting is what I, the old man, know; but the principle of pilgrimage you certainly do not know. For had you the least knowledge of the principle of pilgrimage, you would not just go back and forth in this way. I, the old man, pity your benightedness, and fearing that you do not know what pilgrimage means, I have written this letter and send it to you, that you may go on pilgrimage again. If after this you still cannot grope for the inherently possessed, then in other days and at another time we shall surely find it hard to meet as we do today (saints and ordinary beings being separated).
[Nostrils] Refers to the inherently possessed. The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo says: “Before your parents were born, where are your nostrils?”

blocks.text: 29. The Single Thought Before You

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to Sun Shenbai)

[The root and trunk of ignorance and birth and death lies only in the single thought before you. It is like a man who travels all ten directions, exhausting the strength of his whole life without stopping, and thinks he has covered a thousand, ten thousand leagues — never knowing that he has not moved one step from where his heels stand. From this we know that the idle thoughts that shift and flow over kalpas, and the turning round of birth and death, have never in fact left this person's single thought.]

The root of ignorance and birth and death lies only in the single thought before you. It is like a man who travels all ten directions, exhausting the strength of his whole life without rest, and supposes that he must by now be near his destination, having covered a thousand, ten thousand leagues — never knowing that the destination has never left his own heels by a single step. From this we know that the idle thoughts that shift and flow over kalpas, and the turning round of birth and death, have never left this person's single thought.
[Bodhi] Chinese translation: the Way, awakening. That is, the principle of cutting off affliction and accomplishing nirvāṇa.

[If in daily life, before you now, in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, at the place where thought after thought arises, you apply your strength and pierce through it, so that the place of arising does not arise — then the root of the feeling of birth and death accumulated over kalpas is cut off at once, and in truth without relying on any other power. The Buddha said, “If the mad mind does not rest, when it rests, that is bodhi” — how could this be an empty saying! The old man points you to the phrase “before your parents were born”; apply your strength and look into it. One day you will have a time of believing for yourself.]

If in daily life, before you now, in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, at the place where thought after thought arises, you can apply your strength and pierce through it, so that the place of arising does not arise, then the root of the feeling of birth and death accumulated over kalpas is cut off at once, and in truth without relying on any other power. The Buddha said, “If the mad mind does not rest, when it rests, that is bodhi” — how could this be an empty saying! The old man points you to the phrase “before your parents were born, what is your original face?” Apply your strength and look into it. One day you will have a time of believing for yourself.

[Before your parents were born] In the round of rebirth, before taking a womb, one is in the intermediate existence. But “before your parents were born” as spoken here means before the very first taking of birth.

blocks.text: 30. Breaking the Black Lacquer Bucket

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to the Chan Monk Zhaofan Yong)

[Chan monk Yong, you once came to study with me at Wuyang, and I instructed you in the purport of no-birth. Recently you came to visit me at Mount Kuang, and I saw that your resolve for the Way has grown more firm, but that your work of investigation is not yet pure — simply because you have not taken it as one truly great matter. So I instructed him, saying: When the ancients studied the Way, the first thing was that their minds should be keen for birth and death; it was not a matter of seeking mysterious and wonderful principles. What is this thing called birth and death? It is simply, in our daily life before us, amid all the states of worldly toil — meeting circumstances and encountering conditions, whether adverse or favorable — when the habitual tendencies within give rise and bring them into activity, and there arise craving and aversion, taking and rejecting, and all the various thoughts of idle discrimination.]

Chan monk Yong, in former days you came to study with me at Wuyang, and I once instructed you in the purport of no-birth. Before long you came again to visit me at Mount Kuang, and I saw that your resolve for the Way has grown more firm, but that your work of investigation is not yet pure — this is because you have not taken investigation as one truly great matter. I therefore instructed you, saying: When the ancients studied the Way, the first thing was that their minds should be keen for birth and death, and not that they should pursue mysterious and wonderful principles. What then is birth and death? Birth and death is simply, in our daily life before us, amid all the states of worldly toil, meeting circumstances and encountering conditions — adverse circumstances and adverse conditions, or favorable circumstances and favorable conditions — when the habitual tendencies within give rise and bring them into activity, and there arise craving and aversion, taking and rejecting, and all the various thoughts of idle discrimination.

[Through thought after thought of reaching out after conditions, there arise all kinds of karma, good and evil, and all of them become the root and trunk of future birth and death. Because idle thought has no boundary, birth and death has no limit. Thus living beings turn round through long kalpas in the bitter sea of birth and death with no time of getting out — all because they do not know the fault of their own minds. Hence it is said: If one does not understand one's own mind, how can one know the right Way? Students of the Way in every age who have the resolve to escape birth and death seek only to understand their own minds. Because this mind has always been coarse and buoyant, like boiling water and leaping flame, never for a single thought clear and cool, the ancients set up a provisional means: they took one kōan and taught students to raise it and investigate it thought after thought.]

Because of reaching out after conditions thought after thought, the good and evil karma that arises is all the root of future birth and death. Since idle thought has no boundary, birth and death has no limit. Thus living beings turn round through long kalpas in the bitter sea of birth and death with no time of getting out — all because they do not know the fault of their own minds. Hence it is said: If one does not understand one's own mind, how can one know the right Way? Students of the Way in every age who have the resolve to escape birth and death seek only to understand their own minds. Because this mind has always been coarse and buoyant, like boiling water and leaping flame, never once clear and pure for a single thought, the ancients set up a provisional means: they took one kōan and taught students to raise it and investigate it thought after thought.

[For example, a monk asked Zhaozhou, “Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?” Or again, Yongming taught people to examine truly, “Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?” This one word “no,” this one word “who,” is the sharp sword that cuts off the very root of the life of birth and death. Yet this investigation and true examination is only to watch this word “no,” this word “who”: from where does it arise, and to where does it fall? Just look at the place where this single thought arises and falls, and you must see the root of its arising and ceasing. If you investigate to the ultimate point, you will burst asunder the idle thoughts of a single thought's arising and ceasing, break open the black lacquer bucket, and suddenly see your original face. When you reach this, the Buddha's and patriarchs' nostrils that face upward are all at once entirely in your own hands. From this you will know the original person, and no longer doubt whether it is Zhang San or Li Si — it turns out to be precisely your own original endowment. In such a case, what mystery is there to seek, and why seek it in another's house?]

For example, “a monk asked Zhaozhou, Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?”; or again, Master Yongming taught people to examine truly, “Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?” This one word “no,” this one word “who,” is the sharp sword that cuts off the very root of the life of birth and death. Yet this investigation and true examination is only to watch this word “no,” this word “who”: from where does it arise, and to where does it fall? Just look at the place where this single thought arises and falls, and you must see the root of its arising and ceasing. If you investigate to the ultimate point, you will burst asunder the idle thoughts of a single thought's arising and ceasing, break open the black lacquer bucket, and suddenly see your original face. When you reach this, the essential purport of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' Dharma (the nostrils that face upward) is all at once grasped entirely in your own hands. From this you will know the original person, and no longer doubt whether it is Zhang San or Li Si — it turns out to be precisely your own originally possessed nature (your own natal star). In such a case, what mystery is there to seek, and why seek it in another's house?

[Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?] The Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind says: “If you are a true man, look at a kōan. A monk asked Zhaozhou, ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhou said, ‘No.’ Simply go through the twelve hours of the day looking at this word ‘no.' Investigate by day and investigate by night; walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, when putting on clothes or eating, when shitting or pissing — mind watching mind, rousing your spirit to the utmost, keep to this one word ‘no.' As days and months deepen, it is beaten into a single piece; then of a sudden the mind-flower bursts forth, you awaken to the mechanism of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and you are no longer deceived by the tongues of the old monks of the world. Then you will open your big mouth: ‘Bodhidharma came from the West — no wind, yet waves arise; the World-Honored One twirled a flower — one scene of defeat.' When you reach this, what is King Yama to you? Even a thousand sages can do nothing with you! You would not believe it: there is really such a marvel! Why is it so? A matter fears a person of intent! The verse says: ‘To shed the dust of toil is no common thing; grip the rope's end and make your stand. Without one piercing turn of bone-chilling cold, how could plum blossoms scent the nose?' [Gripping the rope's end] A metaphor drawn from herding an ox.

[Breaking the black lacquer bucket] Breaking open the black lacquer bucket means breaking through fundamental ignorance (beginningless ignorance). [The nostrils that face upward] The essential purport of the Buddha-Dharma. [The natal] A person's natal star. [The original endowment] A person's birth year.

[Yet as for this one stroke: unless from the very first you have aroused the resolve keenly for birth and death, then do as you like, exhaust every trick — it is all the business of ghosts. Even if you have a bit of knowing and half a view, it is all the talk of Māra; whatever you do is all the karma of Māra. What a pity, for a great matter and a great cause that is hard to meet in a hundred thousand million kalpas! If you, Chan monk, truly have the resolve for this matter, you must simply fold up together all the worldly truths, the clever and sharp knowing and views, and all kinds of idle thoughts that have been in your breast, and turn them all toward working at the single thought. Take one huatou and make it a sword that sweeps the sky, cutting off all former idle thoughts like cutting through tangled silk. If you can truly lay on your hand so ruthlessly and do the bitter, urgent work, and there is no genuine place of awakening — then all the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old would have fallen into lying speech. What is most to be avoided is simply the lack of a genuine mind, merely making Chan practice a face and speaking fine-sounding words.]

Yet as for this one stroke (breaking the black lacquer bucket and suddenly seeing your original face): unless from the very first you have aroused the resolve truly and solidly for the sake of escaping birth and death, and investigate in earnest (rather than making Chan practice a face and speaking fine-sounding words), then do as you like, exhaust every trick — it is all the business of ghosts. Even if you have a bit of knowing and half a view, it is all the talk of Māra; whatever you do is all the karma of Māra. What a pity, for the cause and conditions of a great matter (escaping birth and death) that is hard to meet in a hundred thousand million kalpas! If you, Chan monk, truly have the resolve for this matter, you must simply fold up together all the worldly truths, the clever and sharp knowing and views, and all kinds of idle thoughts that have been in your breast, and turn them all toward working at the single thought. Take one huatou and make it a sword that sweeps the sky, cutting off all former idle thoughts like cutting through tangled silk. If you can truly lay on your hand so ruthlessly and do the bitter, urgent work, and there is no genuine place of awakening — then all the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old would have fallen into lying speech. What is most to be avoided is simply the lack of a genuine mind, merely making Chan practice a face and speaking fine-sounding words.
[Worldly truth] The truth of the world, also called conventional truth or worldly truth.

blocks.text: 31. How to Recite Mantras

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to the Chan Student Xuanji)

[The Chan monk took the holding of mantra as his exclusive practice, and had devoted himself to it for thirty years, yet his mind-ground had not opened to understanding. He begged the old man for instruction.]
The Chan monk took the holding of mantras as his exclusive practice, and had already devoted thirty years to it, yet had still not awakened. He begged the old man for instruction.
[Ming] Another name for dhāraṇī; “holding ming” means to receive and hold a true word, that is, to recite mantras.

[The old man therefore instructed him, saying: The Buddha taught that on the path of practice there are many gates of skillful means, but the source to which they return is not two. Thus investigating Chan and raising a huatou, reciting the Buddha's name, and holding mantra are all not two dharmas. It is only that those who are not skilled in applying the mind do not know to use them to grind away habitual tendencies and break through idle thoughts, but instead, with a clinging mind, lend support to ignorance — and so they use much effort and reap little result!]

The old man therefore instructed him, saying: The Buddha taught that on the path of practice there are many gates of skillful means, but the destination is the same for all (the source to which they return is not two). Thus investigating Chan and raising a huatou, reciting the Buddha's name, and holding mantra are all for returning to the origin. But those who are not skilled in applying the mind do not know to use the huatou, the Buddha's name, or the mantra to grind away habitual tendencies and break through idle thoughts; instead, with a clinging mind, they investigate the huatou, recite the Buddha's name, or hold mantra, and so lend support to ignorance — and therefore they use much effort and reap little result!
[Returning to the source] Returning to the root and going back to the source. [Di] Only, but.

[This matter is like using a tile to knock on a door: you only want the door to open, and need not consider what the tile in your hand is like. For from beginningless kalpas we have accumulated the defiled seeds of greed, anger, delusion, and craving, hidden within the storehouse consciousness, deep, firm, and remote, so that no one can break them. The sage set up a provisional means and taught people to raise one kōan as a huatou, to bring down the mass of doubt heavily, and to cut off the gate of idle thought, not letting the least through. After long effort gains power, like pressing a dog until it leaps the wall, of a sudden the storehouse consciousness bursts asunder, the original face is revealed, and this is called awakening to the Way. If it were merely a matter of pressing idle thought so that it does not run on, why would a huatou be needed? Even an old woman counting charcoal briquettes, single-minded and undivided, can awaken; how much more so reciting the Buddha's name and holding mantra — are these two dharmas?]

This matter is like using a tile to knock on a door: you only want to knock the door open, and need not concern yourself with what the tile in your hand looks like. For from beginningless kalpas we have accumulated the defiled seeds of greed, anger, delusion, and craving, hidden within the ālaya consciousness, deep, firm, and remote, so that no one can break them. The Buddha set up a provisional means and taught people to raise one kōan as a huatou, to bring down the mass of doubt heavily, and to cut off the gate of idle thought (cutting off the gate of idle thought — this is the key), not letting the least through. After long effort gains power, like pressing a dog until it leaps the wall, of a sudden the ālaya consciousness bursts asunder, the original face is revealed, and this is called awakening to the Way. Since it is merely a matter of pressing idle thought so that it does not run on, why must there be a huatou? Even an old woman counting charcoal briquettes, so long as she is single-minded and undivided, can also awaken; how much more so reciting the Buddha's name and holding mantra?

[Storehouse consciousness] The consciousness that contains and stores all seeds of good and evil, that is, the ālaya consciousness. [Are these two dharmas?] How could there be two dharmas? It means that reciting the Buddha's name and holding mantra are, like the huatou, all for pressing idle thought so that it does not run on.

[That you, Chan monk, have held mantra for thirty years without seeing any effect is not because the mantra has no efficacy, but only because the mind that holds the mantra has never gained power. Ordinarily it is like pushing an empty cart downhill: you just let it roll along — where have you ever applied strength? Applying the mind in this way, not only will there be no proof in this life; to the end of kalpas it will be only thus. And when the dark realms appear before you and birth and death arrive, you will still be dazzled and confused, and then you will blame your practice for having no outcome — is this not to mislead and mistake yourself?]

That you, Chan monk, have held mantra for thirty years without seeing any effect is not because the mantra has no efficacy, but only because the mind that holds the mantra has never gained power. Rather, you have taken holding mantra as an ordinary matter, like pushing an empty cart downhill, just letting it roll along — where have you ever applied strength? Applying the mind in this way to hold mantra, not only will there be no proof in this life; to the end of kalpas there will be no proof either. When the end comes and birth and death arrive, you will still be dazzled and confused, and then you will blame your practice for having no outcome — is this not to mislead and mistake yourself?

[From now on you need not change to another practice, Chan monk. Simply take the mind that holds the mantra as your huatou: word by word, mind by mind, apply your strength and grind away, like pushing a heavy cart uphill, exhausting every ounce of strength in your body, not daring to relax the least bit, inch by inch, step by step, never letting the heel land on emptiness. When you exert yourself in this way, you press the flow of idle thought until you block off the very root of life and let it through no further. When you reach this point, then right at the place where you are applying strength, bring down the mass of doubt once more, look deeply, and ask: this very one who applies strength to hold the mantra — what after all is it?]

From now on you need not change to another practice, Chan monk. Simply take the mind that holds the mantra as your huatou: word by word, thought by thought, apply your strength and grind away, like pushing a heavy cart uphill, exhausting every ounce of strength in your body, not daring to relax the least bit, inch by inch, step by step, never letting the heel land on emptiness. When you exert yourself in this way, you press the flow of idle thought until it stops, and block off the mind-root's reaching out after mental objects (you cut off the very root of life) and let it through no further. When you reach this state of not a single thought arising, then right at the place where you are applying strength, bring down the mass of doubt once more, look deeply, and ask: this very one who applies strength to hold the mantra — what after all is it?

[The flow of idle thought] The arising, ceasing, and shifting on of idle thought. [Cutting off the very root of life] Blocking off the mind-root (the manas consciousness) from reaching out after mental objects. [When you reach this point] That is, when your practice has already brought you to the point where not a single thought arises — which is precisely the “just at such a time” of “not thinking of good, not thinking of evil” spoken by the Sixth Patriarch in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. Then bring down the doubt once more and look deeply: “Which one is the original face of Upāsaka Ming?”

[Looking on and on, doubting on and on, like a mouse entering a cow's horn, until you reach the place where you cannot turn around or draw breath. This is precisely the time of power; by no means entertain the thought of resting, and do not take this as hardship and give rise to thoughts of retreat or stopping. And when you are pressed to the point where a single thought opens out — this is the samādhi of lightning — by no means entertain thoughts of mystery and rejoicing. From here rouse your spirit still more, throw your life into it, and do not let go until of a sudden the storehouse consciousness bursts asunder and empty space is shattered. If you can hold mantra in this way, how can it be two dharmas from investigating Chan? Hence it is said: ‘Juzhi only recited three lines of mantra, and so came to be called one who surpasses all people.' This is proof. Even if you were to meet the Buddhas and patriarchs face to face, they would not alter the old man's words.]

Looking on and on, doubting on and on, like a mouse entering a cow's horn, until you reach the place where you cannot turn around or draw breath. This is precisely the time of power; by no means entertain the thought of resting, and do not take this as hardship and give rise to thoughts of retreat or stopping. And when you are pressed to the point where a single thought opens out — this is the samādhi of lightning — by no means entertain thoughts of mystery and rejoicing. From here rouse your spirit still more, throw your life into it, and do not let go until of a sudden the ālaya consciousness bursts asunder and empty space is shattered. If you can hold mantra in this way, how can it be two dharmas from investigating Chan? Hence it is said: ‘The monk Juzhi only recited three lines of mantra, and so came to be called one who surpasses all people.' This is proof. Even if you were to meet the Buddhas and patriarchs face to face, the truth they speak would be entirely in accord with the old man.

[A mouse entering a cow's horn] A mouse bores into a cow's horn, gnawing its way layer by layer; the more it gnaws, the narrower it gets, until it cannot turn its body around — there is advance but no retreat. [Juzhi] Refers to the monk Juzhi of Mount Jinhua in Wuzhou in the Tang dynasty. Because he constantly recited the dhāraṇī of Cundī, the mother of the Juzhi Buddhas (the Cundī mantra), people addressed him by this name. [Three lines of mantra] These three lines of mantra are:
Namo saptānāṃ samyaksaṃbuddha.
namo saptānāṃ samyaksaṃbuddha,
Koṭīnāṃ. Tadyathā.
koṭīnāṃ tadyathā,
Oṃ. Cale cule. Cundī svāhā.
oṃ cale cule cundī svāhā.

Master Hanshan's instruction here sets forth the common pattern by which investigating Chan, reciting the Buddha's name, and holding mantra lead to understanding the mind and seeing the nature. There are three stages. In the first stage, the ten thousand thoughts return to one: that is, for one investigating Chan there is only the huatou, for one reciting the Buddha's name there is only the Buddha's name, for one holding mantra there is only the mantra, and no other thought — this is commonly called the resting of coarse thoughts, also called practice becoming a single piece. In the second stage, the one returns to nothing: one enters the state where not a single thought arises, still and yet illumining, illumining and yet still — this is called the resting of subtle thoughts, also called practice settling into the hall. In the third stage, the extremely subtle thoughts cease, and one understands the mind and sees the nature. The practice of the third stage is: before a single thought has arisen, look deeply — what is the original face? Chan Master Tiantong Yuanwu's verse on investigating Chan says: “Before a single thought arises, try to see what it looks like.” In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the Sixth Patriarch says: “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, just at such a time — which one is the original face of Upāsaka Ming?” Do it with all your might in this way, and once the extremely subtle thoughts cease, the original face appears completely, and you understand the mind and see the nature.

[Coarse, subtle, and extremely subtle thoughts] Thoughts are of three kinds: coarse, subtle, and extremely subtle. For example, for one who recites the Buddha's name, an idle thought is a coarse thought and the thought of reciting is a subtle thought. Ordinarily, when coarse and subtle thoughts have both ceased, it is called no-thought — this is no-thought as commonly spoken of. Further, if the extremely subtle thoughts also come to rest, this is ultimate no-thought, and at this time the self-nature manifests its intrinsic state. [Extremely subtle thought] The extremely subtle arising, ceasing, and shifting on of the consciousness-mind, which is the mark of the ālaya consciousness.

blocks.text: 32. Reciting the Buddha's Name and Seeing the Nature

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Reply to Commissioner Yuan Cangru)

[I know that you, layman, have resolved most urgently on the one stroke concerning your own person. This is the thought that the matter of birth and death is great — it is right to be urgent. Yet as for the work of investigation, it has always been said that one raises a kōan as huatou, as Chan Master Dahui urged with all his strength. From this we know that those in former times who awakened to the mind through Chan all did so by the work of raising a huatou. But within this, the ways of applying the mind differ greatly. To speak of raising the huatou as people do today is still more mistaken, and the application of mind is far from the mark, because they know only how to raise it up and do not know that letting it go is the essential wonder.]

I know that you, layman, have resolved most urgently on the one stroke concerning your own person (settling birth and death for yourself). This is the thought that the matter of birth and death is great — it is right to be urgent! Yet as for the work of investigation, it has always been said that one raises a kōan as huatou, as Chan Master Dahui urged with all his strength. From this we know that those in former times who awakened to the mind through Chan all did so by the work of raising a huatou. But within this, the ways of applying the mind differ greatly. To speak of raising the huatou as people do today is still more mistaken, and the application of mind is far from the Way, because they know only how to raise it up and do not know that letting it go is the essential wonder.
[Chan Master Dahui (

)] The Chan master Buddha-Sun of Mount Jing in Hangzhou in the Song dynasty, whose dharma name was Zonggao. After his great awakening he succeeded to the Dharma of Chan Master Yuanwu, and was given a seat to expound the Dharma; thereupon the monastic forest came to revere him, and his fame shook the capital. In the first year of Jingkang (
), he was granted the purple robe and the honorific title “Great Master Buddha-Sun.” In the seventh year of Shaoxing (

), at the invitation of the minister Zhang Jun, he became abbot of Nengren Temple on Mount Jing, and monks and laity gathered from every quarter, so that the school's wind greatly flourished. In the eleventh year of Shaoxing, the vice minister Zhang Jiucheng came to Nengren Temple to study Chan under him, and happened to discuss government affairs; at that time Qin Hui was in power and strove for peace with the Jin, while Zhang Jiucheng was of the war party at court. Qin Hui, holding all power, did his utmost to root out those who differed from him, and the master did not escape either: in the fifth month of that eleventh year his robe and ordination certificate were stripped away and he was exiled to Hengzhou (present-day Hengyang in Hunan). During this time he collected the pivotal sayings of ancient worthies and the recorded sayings and kōans of his discussions with his disciples, compiling them into the six fascicles of The Treasure of the True Dharma Eye. In the twentieth year of Shaoxing he was banished further to Meizhou (present-day Meizhou in Guangdong), a region of miasmic plague and poor soil, where more than half of his hundred-odd disciples died; yet the master still conducted himself by the ordinary Way and joyfully saved the local people. In the twenty-fifth year of Shaoxing he received a pardon, and the next year resumed the monk's robe. In the twenty-eighth year he was commanded to reside at Mount Jing, and monks and laypeople gathered to him as of old, so that he was known as “Zonggao of Mount Jing.” The master's eloquence was unbridled, and he advocated with all his strength the Chan method of kōans; his Chan method was called “Chan of looking at the huatou” (that is, the Chan method of examining kōans and huatous in search of awakening), which shone alongside Hongzhi Zhengjue's “Chan of silent illumination.” In his later years he lived at Mount Jing, and monks and laypeople of every quarter gathered at the news, so that under his seat there were always several thousand. Emperor Xiaozong of the Song took refuge in him and granted him the title “Chan Master Dahui.” In the eighth month of the first year of Longxing he fell slightly ill; on the tenth day he wrote his farewell memorial in his own hand, then wrote a farewell verse, threw down the brush, and peacefully entered quiescence. He was seventy-five years old and had been a monk for fifty-eight years.

[The ancients' one stroke of letting go is the most essential thing to be said about entering the Way. From this we know that the word ‘raise' means raising at the place of letting go, and not that merely thinking about the huatou is raising. Aśvaghoṣa says: “The essence of mind is free of thought, equal to the realm of space.” He also says: “The state beyond thought is only met with through realization.” Because the essence of mind is originally free of thought, and people today do not know that freedom from thought is right mindfulness, they cling to and raise up a single mind, and so only increase their confusion.]

The ancients' one stroke of letting go is the most essential thing to be said about entering the Way. From this we know that the word ‘raise' means raising at the place of letting go (this is the key!), and not that merely thinking about the huatou is raising. In the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa says: “The essence of mind is free of thought. The mark of being free of thought is equal to the realm of space and pervades everywhere.” He also says: “The state beyond thought is only met with through realization.” Because the essence of mind is originally free of thought, and people today do not know that freedom from thought is right mindfulness, they cling to and raise up a single mind, and so only increase their confusion.

[Why is it that letting go is raising? Take Amitābha Buddha as your huatou. When you have not yet raised the Buddha, you must first let go of outer objects, then let go together of all the idle thoughts within, then let go even of this one thought of letting go. When you have let go to the point where there is nothing left to let go, then within this, apply your strength and raise up one utterance of the Buddha. Then look at this one utterance of the Buddha: from where does it come, and where does it now fall? Fix the diamond eye, gaze steadily, and gaze until there is nowhere to land; then raise again and gaze again, and pursue it to the place where a single thought is unborn — and you will see your original face.]

Why is it that letting go is raising? Take Amitābha Buddha as your huatou. When you have not yet raised the Buddha's name, you must first let go of outer objects, then let go together of all the idle thoughts within, then let go even of this one thought of letting go. When you have let go to the point where there is nothing left to let go, then within this, apply your strength and raise up one utterance of the Buddha's name. Then look at this one utterance of the Buddha's name: from where does it come, and where does it now fall? Fix the diamond eye, gaze steadily, and gaze until there is nowhere to land; then raise again and gaze again, and pursue it to the place where a single thought is unborn — and you will see your original face.
[At first one uses the mind to gaze and pursue; pursuing until the single thought is severed at both ends, the middle
(the space between)

is of itself alone. Then, from this lone place, rouse your spirit and pursue straight on: of a sudden the mass of doubt bursts apart, and one's original face of itself manifests — this very thing is the single thought of the true meaning of no-birth. If the student but has this single thought of no-birth appear before him, then in every place he gains great benefit, and this is the very time of escaping birth and death.]

At first you use the mind to gaze and to pursue. When the work of gazing and pursuing has deepened, there appears the state in which the former thought has ceased and the latter thought has not yet arisen, and the middle is a lone, clear awareness. Then toward this no-thought place, rouse your spirit and pursue straight on: of a sudden the mass of doubt bursts apart, the original face appears of itself, and this very thing is the single thought of the true meaning of no-birth. If the student but has this single thought of no-birth appear before him, then in every place he gains great benefit, and this is the very time of escaping birth and death.
[The single thought of no-birth appearing before one] Master Hanshan's The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation on the Essentials of Reciting the Buddha's Name and Investigating Chan says:

“When you look to the place where not a single thought arises, then the reaches of before and after are cut off, and the middle is of itself alone. Of a sudden you break open the black lacquer bucket and at once see your original face
(thoroughly see the intrinsic nature)
. Then body, mind, and world all at once sink away, like the shadows of sky-flowers falling
(the empty flowers' phantom shadows cease)

, and the ten directions are perfectly bright, becoming one great treasury of light. Only thus is it the season of reaching home: in daily life before you, bright and perfectly clear, with nothing further to doubt. Only then do you believe that your own mind was originally thus. The Buddhas and patriarchs from of old, in their own place of enjoyment, are not two and not different.”
[Sinking away] Also written “sinking away”: to sink, to disappear.

[People in recent times do not know to seek, at the place of letting go, the one stroke of freedom from thought; they cling rigidly to the huatou, and so only increase their obstacles. Add to this that they further stir up all kinds of thinking and harbor mysterious and wonderful views beforehand — this is the very root that obstructs the Way. It is simply that you, layman, though your mind for investigation is keen, have not yet had the one stroke of letting go pointed out to you, and so, obstructed by the shadow of the habitual tendency toward the mysterious and wonderful, you gain no benefit. Among hundreds and thousands of skillful means, only the one stroke of letting go saves the most effort.
