Do your work at this place that saves effort, and then thought after thought in daily life will be true benefit. I beg you, wise one, to examine this.]

People in recent times do not know to seek, at the place of letting go, the one stroke of freedom from thought, but cling rigidly to the huatou, and so only increase their obstacles. Add to this that they further stir up all kinds of thinking and harbor mysterious and wonderful views beforehand — this is the very root that obstructs the Way. Even though you, layman, investigate with a keen mind, it is because the one stroke of letting go has not been pointed out to you that, obstructed by the shadow of the habitual tendency toward the mysterious and wonderful, you gain no benefit. Among hundreds and thousands of skillful means, only the one stroke of letting go saves the most effort. Do your work at this place that saves effort, and then thought after thought in daily life will be true benefit. I have spoken these words; I beg you, wise one, to consider them.

blocks.text: 33. The Wondrous Medicine for Body and Mind

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to Wang Ziyong (
yóng

[People in the world have always done their business on the states of the illusory body and mind, and from birth to death have never once turned to awaken to the original face of their own minds. Because they are not awake, they do not know where their root of illness lies. When water and fire are at odds and the four elements attack one another, this is illness of body. Idle thought reaching out after conditions, craving and aversion, taking and rejecting, this is illness of mind. Yet illness of body can be treated with medicines, while illness of mind has no medicine that can cure it. The Buddha is the king of physicians for the world; and in treating living beings' illness of mind, among all his skillful means the ultimate one is simply to awaken to the fact that idle thought has no nature of its own — this is the wondrous medicine that brings one back to life.]

People in the world have always done their business on the states of the illusory body and mind, and from birth to death have never once turned to awaken to the original face of their own minds. Because they themselves are not awake, they do not know where their own root of illness lies. When water and fire are at odds and the four elements attack one another, this is illness of body. Idle thought reaching out after conditions, craving and aversion, taking and rejecting, this is illness of mind. Yet illness of body can be treated with medicines, while illness of mind has no medicine that can cure it. The Buddha is the king of physicians for the world, and in treating living beings' illness of mind, among all his skillful means the ultimate one is simply to awaken to the fact that idle thought is illusory (without self-nature) — this is the wondrous medicine that brings one back to life.
[Medicine and stone] Medicines and stone needles, a general term for remedies. [Stone needle] A stone needle or stone blade used in ancient times to treat illness.

[If a student wants a Dharma-gate of peace and joy, he must first see through the fact that the body is not his own. Simply look: before your parents were born, was there ever this body of blood and flesh? And when the four elements separate, where will this present body be established? Observing in this way at all times, after long practice a single thought will of a sudden awaken and pierce through, and then you are no longer afflicted by this body — this is the wondrous medicine for illness of body.]

If you want a Dharma-gate of peace and joy, you must first see through the fact that the physical body is not inherently yours. The method is: simply look — before my parents bore me, was there ever this body of blood and flesh? And when death comes and the four elements separate, where will this present physical body go to be established? Observing in this way at all times, after long practice a single thought will of a sudden awaken and pierce through, and then you are no longer afflicted by this physical body; this is the wondrous medicine for illness of body.

[All illness has its source in idle thought, so you need only observe thought after thought through the day. Wherever any good or evil thought arises, that is the root of illness showing itself. You must apply your strength right at that thought: observe at the very place of arising, and see from where after all it arises, and who after all it is that arises and ceases. And when the idle thought ceases, you must pursue and examine where after all it ceases. When you have pursued it in this way to the point where arising has no place of arising and ceasing has no place of ceasing, this is called arising and ceasing having no basis; then the mind-essence is at peace and you attain great freedom.]

All illness of mind has its source in idle thought, so you need only observe thought after thought through the day. Wherever any good or evil thought arises, that is the root of the illness of mind showing itself. You must apply your strength right at that thought: observe at the very place of arising, and see from where after all it arises, and who after all it is that arises and ceases. And when the idle thought ceases, you must pursue and examine where after all it ceases. When you have pursued it in this way to the point where arising has no place of arising and ceasing has no place of ceasing, this is what is meant by arising and ceasing having no basis; then the mind-essence is at peace and you attain great freedom.

[When you cut off the crucial gate in this way, then before and after no longer continue, and the single thought in the middle stands alone of itself. At this place where the single thought stands alone, after long familiarity the very root of the illness of idle thought is pulled out by itself. All defilements of mind, too, have nowhere to lodge. This is the wondrous medicine for illness of mind.]
In this way

you cut off the crucial gate, and then the former thought and the latter thought no longer continue into one another, and the stretch in between stands naturally alone. At this stretch where it stands alone (the gap of no-thought), after long familiarity (the gaps of no-thought join into a piece and a stretch, until for long not a single thought arises and movement and stillness are one), the very root of the illness of idle thought is pulled out by itself. All defilements of mind, too, have nowhere to lodge. This is the wondrous medicine for illness of mind

[Ziyong has earnestly set his will on the matter that faces upward, but his error lies in seeking it in words and letters, and not knowing to seek it in his own mind-ground. Since his own idle thoughts are already the root of illness, to take others' words as a real dharma only adds one more layer of obstruction. From today on, simply pierce through your own idle thoughts and do not be dragged around by them. Just look at where idle thought arises, and by no means let it continue. The Buddha said: ‘If the mad mind rests, when it rests, that is bodhi.' The supremely pure and bright mind is not to be obtained from outside. If you apply your mind in this way without retreating, then this very mind before you is the great Dharma-gate of peace, joy, and liberation.]

Ziyong has earnestly set his will on the matter that faces upward, but his error lies precisely in seeking it in words and letters, and not knowing to seek it in his own mind-ground. Seeking it in words and letters with his own idle thoughts is already the root of illness, and to take others' words as a real dharma adds one more layer of obstruction. From today on, simply pierce through your own idle thoughts and do not be dragged around by them. The method is: just look at where idle thought arises, and by no means let it continue. The Buddha said: ‘If the mad mind rests, when it rests, that is bodhi.' The supremely pure and bright mind is not obtained from outside. If you apply your mind in this way (just looking at where idle thought arises and by no means letting it continue) without retreating or resting, then this very mind before you is the great Dharma-gate of peace, joy, and liberation.

[The matter that faces upward] To seek out the ultimate and most profound principle of the Buddha-Way is called the matter of the ultimate that faces upward, the latch that faces upward (liè), the matter that faces upward.
[The supremely pure and bright mind] The Essentials of Cultivating the Mind says:

“And this pure, empty, and still mind is the supremely pure and bright mind of the Buddhas of the three times, and is also the source-enlightenment nature of living beings. One who awakens to it and keeps to it sits in the one suchness, unmoving and liberated; one who is deluded about it and turns away from it goes to the six destinies and turns round for long kalpas.”
(For details, see
The Detailed Explanation of the Essentials of Cultivating the Mind
[Because he asked for further instruction, the old man gave him the name Fujue — Blessing-Awakening — since awakening is the foremost and measureless blessing. Exert yourself!]

Because Ziyong came to ask for instruction, I gave him the dharma name Fujue (Blessing-Awakening), since awakening is the foremost and measureless blessing. You must exert yourself with all your strength on the matter that faces upward!

[Ming] In ancient usage the same as “name,” to name, to give a name. [Dharma name] The name given by one's master when one leaves home to become a monk or takes refuge in the Three Jewels. [Exert] To do with all one's strength. Example: “You must exert yourself.” (Zuo Commentary
Duke Zhao, Twentieth Year)

blocks.text: 34. The One Stroke of Freedom from Thought

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation to the Chan Monk Liaoxin Hai)

[We leave home solely for the great matter of birth and death. To travel the roads on pilgrimage, to study under teachers and visit friends, is only to decide and choose the one road that faces upward for oneself, and not to rest until it is clear; therefore the good teacher points people to this matter alone. Of late the Dharma-gate has fallen desolate, and in every quarter this wind is seldom heard; wherever one goes on pilgrimage, there is nothing but the breath of porridge and rice. The old man was staying at the Luminous Lake Hermitage when the Chan monk Liaoxin came to study. Entering the gate, I saw that he had a pilgrim monk's grip on things and was evidently no ordinary eater of porridge and rice. Now, as he was about to return to Mount Funiu, he burned incense and asked for further instruction.]

We leave home solely for the great matter of birth and death. To wander the roads on pilgrimage, to study under teachers and visit friends, is only to find the road by which one understands one's own mind and sees one's nature — and not to rest until one has found it; therefore the good teacher, too, points people to this matter alone (the road of understanding the mind and seeing the nature). Of late the Dharma-gate has fallen desolate, and in every quarter this wind is seldom heard (it is rare to hear a good teacher instruct students in the road of understanding the mind and seeing the nature); wherever one goes on pilgrimage, there is nothing but the breath of porridge and rice. The old man was staying at the Luminous Lake Hermitage when the Chan monk Liaoxin came to pay his respects. Entering the gate, I saw that he had a pilgrim monk's grip on things and was evidently no ordinary eater of porridge and rice. Now, as he was about to return to Mount Funiu, he burned incense and asked for instruction.

[Grip] Means a place to take hold. [Eater of porridge and rice] One who merely eats porridge and rice without practicing earnestly. It is said: “Censor Lu entered the monks' hall and asked, ‘So many teachers and monks here — are they monks who eat porridge and rice, or monks who investigate Chan?'” (The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lingyou of Weishan in Tanzhou) [Burning incense] Lighting incense.

[The old man instructed him, saying: Among the Chan communities within the seas today, the foremost is the ascetic practice of Mount Niu, which no other quarter can match. If a student of the Way can throw away body and life, his one life will certainly not be spent in vain. Yet in daily practice, the raising of a single thought as huatou is the most close and continuous. The reason one cannot transcend and attain great freedom is that one has always clung rigidly to the huatou, never letting it go from thought to thought, and does not know that in investigating Chan the first thing is to be free of body and mind within and to leave the world behind without, in the one stroke of freedom from thought. That is why the tied thought is instead bound by thought, and one cannot transcend into great freedom.]

The old man instructed him, saying: Among the seas' Chan communities today, we are fortunate to have the ascetic practice of Mount Funiu, which no other quarter can match. If a student of the Way can throw away body and life, his one life will certainly not be spent in vain. Yet in daily practice, the raising of a single thought as huatou is the most close and continuous. The reason one cannot transcend and attain great freedom is that one has always clung rigidly to the huatou, never letting it go from thought to thought, and does not know that in investigating Chan the first thing is to be free of body and mind within and to leave the world behind without, and to work at the one stroke of freedom from thought. That is why the tied thought is instead bound by thought, and one cannot transcend into great freedom.

[On this visit to the mountain, Chan monk, you are fortunate to rely on the rules and the support of the great assembly, and it is just the time to enter the field and apply your strength. Simply, within thought after thought, look to the place where thought has not yet arisen. Because you are working at the one stroke of freedom from thought, after long practice the thought will of a sudden burst asunder, and mind and objects will both be forgotten
(in the old usage, “to perish”)
, like a lion escaped from its rope, roaming at ease. When you meet the old man again another time, you will certainly not be as you are today, with your eyes and brows shifting without command.]

On this return to Mount Funiu, Chan monk, you are fortunate to be able to sharpen yourself by the ascetic rules of Mount Funiu and the assembly of ascetics, and it is just the time to enter the field and apply your strength. Simply, within thought after thought, look to the place where thought has not yet arisen. Because you are working at the one stroke of freedom from thought, after long practice
(only the single thought of looking remains)
, the thought will of a sudden
(the single thought of looking)

burst asunder, mind and objects both perish, and you will be like a lion escaped from its rope, roaming at ease. When you meet the old man again another time, you will certainly no longer be as you are now, with movement and stillness having no master.

[Rules and plumb line] Rules and the carpenter's ink line — a metaphor for standards and norms. [Mind and objects both forgotten (in the old usage, “to perish”)] Mind and objects both perish. This is the state in which subject and object both perish: the mind that looks and the objects looked at are extinguished together, which is precisely the state of understanding the mind and seeing the nature.

blocks.text: 35. The Essentials of Investigating Chan

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Exhortation on the Essentials of Investigating Chan)

[The Chan school as a tradition exists to transmit the Buddha's mind-seal — this is no small matter. It began when Bodhidharma came from the West and established the purport of the single transmission, sealing the mind with the four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra. Thus, although Chan is a special transmission outside the teachings, it in fact uses the teachings to correspond and verify, and only then is the Buddha's and patriarchs' non-dual Way seen.]

The Chan school as a tradition exists to transmit the Buddha's mind-seal — this is no small matter. It began when Bodhidharma came from the West and established the purport of the single transmission, sealing the mind with the four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra. Thus, although Chan is a special transmission outside the teachings, it in fact uses the teachings (the Tathāgata's words) to verify, and only then is the Buddha's and patriarchs' non-dual Way seen.

[Mind-seal] “Mind” is the Buddha-mind; “seal” means to approve or to seal and confirm. The Chan school does not establish words and letters and does not rely on speech, but only transmits mind to mind, sealing the minds of living beings with the Buddha-mind and realizing the mark of non-duality. [Single transmission] The meaning of transmitting singly, transmitting purely and solely. In transmitting its teaching the Chan school does not rely on words or speech, but takes one person facing one person, striking when the moment is ripe, to transmit the Dharma of the mind-seal; this is called “the single transmission of the mind-seal.”
The Blue Cliff Record says:
“Bodhidharma, gazing from afar at this land
(China)
, saw that it had the faculties for the Great Vehicle, and so crossed the sea and came, and singly transmitted the mind-seal.”
[A special transmission outside the teachings] It means a special transmission apart from the Tathāgata's verbal teachings.

[The work of investigation likewise comes forth from the teachings. The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “Sitting in meditative ease in mountain forests, cultivating in the upper, middle, and lower stages, one can see the flow of one's own idle thoughts.” This is truly the World-Honored One's clear instruction on the essential method of doing the work. It also says: “The mind, manas, and consciousness, and the delusive marks of the self-nature's own realms projected by one's own mind; the ocean of existence, karma, craving, and not-knowing — from all such causes one is wholly carried across.” This is the Tathāgata's clear instruction on the wondrous purport of awakening to the mind. It also says: “The sages from of old, transmitting one to another, [taught that] idle thought has no nature.” This again is his clear instruction on the secret mind-seal. This is the essential point where the yellow-faced old fellow taught people to investigate.]

The work of investigation likewise comes forth from the sutras and teachings. The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “Sitting in meditative ease in mountain forests, cultivating in the upper, middle, and lower stages, one can see the flow of one's own idle thoughts.” This is truly the World-Honored One's clear instruction on the essential method of doing the work. It also says: “The mind, manas, and consciousness, and the delusive marks of the self-nature's own realms projected by one's own mind; the ocean of existence, karma, craving, and not-knowing — from all such causes one is wholly carried across.” This is the World-Honored One's clear instruction on the wondrous purport of awakening to the mind. It also says: “The sages from of old, transmitting one to another, [taught that] idle thought is illusory (idle thought has no nature).” This again is the World-Honored One's clear and definite instruction on the secret mind-seal. This is the essential point where Śākyamuni Buddha taught people to investigate.

[The yellow-faced old fellow] Refers to Śākyamuni Buddha, because Śākyamuni Buddha's bodily appearance was of golden hue. [From all such causes one is wholly carried across] This passage of the sutra reads:

“Sitting in meditative ease in mountain forests, cultivating in the lower, middle, and upper stages, one can see the flow of one's own idle thoughts. Buddhas of immeasurable buddha-lands pour water on one's head; one gains the powers of mastery, the superknowledges, and samādhi, together with good teachers, buddha-sons, and followers. The mind, manas, and consciousness, and the delusive thoughts of the self-nature's own realms projected by one's own mind; the ocean of existence, karma, craving, and not-knowing — from all such causes one has already been wholly carried across.”

[And when Bodhidharma instructed the Second Patriarch, he said: “You need only let outer conditions rest, keep the mind within without gasping, and make the mind like a wall — then you may enter the Way.” This was Bodhidharma's first essential method of instructing people in investigation. When the transmission reached Huangmei and he sought an heir to the Dharma, the Sixth Patriarch had only to say “originally there is not a single thing,” and he received the robe and bowl — this is the precise purport of the mind-seal transmitted from one to another. And when the Sixth Patriarch went back south and instructed Daoming, he said: “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, just at such a time — which one is the original face of Upāsaka Ming?” This is the Sixth Patriarch's first precise formula for instructing people in investigation.]

And when Bodhidharma instructed the Second Patriarch Huike, he said: “You need only let outer conditions rest, keep the mind within without gasping, and make the mind like a wall — then you may enter the Way.” This was Bodhidharma's first essential method of instructing students in investigation. When the transmission reached the Fifth Patriarch of Huangmei and he sought an heir to the Dharma, the Sixth Patriarch had only to say “originally there is not a single thing,” and he received the robe and bowl — this is the precise purport of the mind-seal transmitted from one to another. And when the Sixth Patriarch went back south and instructed Huiming, he said: “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, just at this very time — which one is your (Upāsaka Ming's) original face?” This is the Sixth Patriarch's precise formula for instructing people in investigation, opening the very source of investigation.

[Let outer conditions rest, keep the mind within without gasping, make the mind like a wall — then you may enter the Way] This means: outwardly, let go of the ten thousand conditions; inwardly, do not let the mind reach out after objects; and the mind must be like a wall without a crack or gap, so that no dharma can enter — that is, objects cannot move the mind. Only thus may one enter the Way. [Huangmei] Refers to Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch of the Chan school, so called because he lived at the East Chan Temple on Mount Huangmei. [Daoming] That is, Huiming in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, who was greatly awakened through the Sixth Patriarch's instruction, honored Huineng as his teacher, and changed his name to Daoming to avoid the taboo on the character “Hui” in his teacher's name. [Source] The Book of Rites, “Record of Learning”: “When the three kings sacrificed to the rivers, they always sacrificed first to the Yellow River and afterward to the sea.” In ancient times the Yellow River was held to be the source of the sea, and when emperors sacrificed they first sacrificed to the Yellow River and then to the sea. Later, “source” came to mean the first thing to initiate something.

[From this we know that the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old only taught people to awaken to their own minds and to know themselves — there was never any talk of kōans and huatous. From Nanyue and Qingyuan onward, the patriarchs instructed according to circumstance, mostly striking at the place of doubt, so that a person turned his head around and that was enough. Even for those who did not understand, though they applied the tongs and hammer, they only left it to the person's own season and conditions. It was Huangbo who first taught people to look at a huatou, and only with Chan Master Dahui was it urged with all his strength, teaching students to investigate one ancient's kōan as a grip, calling it a huatou, and requiring people to raise it to mind earnestly.]

From this we know that the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old only taught people to awaken to their own minds and to know themselves — there was never any talk of kōans and huatous. From Nanyue and Qingyuan onward, the patriarchs instructed according to circumstance, mostly striking at the place of doubt, so that a person turned his head around and that was the end of it. Even for those who did not understand (did not awaken), though they were struck and polished, it was only left to their own season and conditions. It was Chan Master Huangbo who first taught people to look at the huatou of the word “no,” and only with Chan Master Dahui was it urged with all his strength, teaching students to investigate one ancient's kōan as a grip, calling it a huatou, and requiring people to raise it to mind earnestly.

[Nanyue and Qingyuan] From the Sixth Patriarch Huineng there came two great dharma lineages: Nanyue (Chan Master Huairang) and Qingyuan (Chan Master Xingsi). From Nanyue's stream came the Linji school, and from Qingyuan's stream came the Caodong school. [Tongs and hammer] Tools for forging iron; cultivation is often compared to refining iron a hundred times into steel; “refining” here means hammering. Through repeated hammering the impurities in the iron blank are removed and its structure improved, so that it becomes steel of fine quality.
A precious sword that cuts iron like mud and severs a hair blown against its edge is made in this way, through a thousand hammerings and a hundred refinings.

[Huangbo] Chan Master Xiyun of the Tang dynasty, known as Duanji. He left home as a boy on Mount Huangbo in Fuzhou, and later studied under Chan Master Hai of Baizhang in Jiangxi, attaining the Way. He afterward lived at Da'an Temple in Hongzhou, and the assembly gathered to him in crowds. When the minister Pei Xiu was governing Wanling, he built a great Chan monastery and invited the master to teach; the master was deeply fond of Mount Huangbo, and so named it after the mountain. His Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind has come down to us. The Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind says:

“If you are a true man, look at a kōan. A monk asked Zhaozhou, ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhou said, ‘No.’ Simply go through the twelve hours of the day looking at this word ‘no.' Investigate by day and investigate by night; walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, when putting on clothes or eating, when shitting or pissing — mind watching mind, rousing your spirit to the utmost, keep to this one word ‘no.' As days and months deepen, it is beaten into a single piece; then of a sudden the mind-flower bursts forth, you awaken to the mechanism of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and you are no longer deceived by the tongues of the old monks of the world. Then you will open your big mouth: ‘Bodhidharma came from the West — no wind, yet waves arise; the World-Honored One twirled a flower — one scene of defeat.' When you reach this, what is King Yama to you? Even a thousand sages can do nothing with you! You would not believe it: there is really such a marvel! Why is it so? A matter fears a person of intent! The verse says: ‘To shed the dust of toil is no common thing; grip the rope's end and make your stand. Without one piercing turn of bone-chilling cold, how could plum blossoms scent the nose?'”

[Zhaozhou] Chan Master Congshen of Zhaozhou in the Tang dynasty. [Rousing your spirit to the utmost] Shaking off sluggishness. “Spirit” means vitality, energy. [Gripping the rope's end] A metaphor drawn from herding an ox. [Grip] Means a place to take hold.

[Why is this so? Simply because in the students' field of the eighth consciousness, the seeds of evil habit from beginningless kalpas inwardly perfume them thought after thought and flow on continuously, so that idle thoughts never cease, and there is no help for it. Therefore one takes a phrase with no flavor of meaning and makes you bite down on it, so that you first set down together all the idle thoughts of mind and objects, within and without. Because you cannot set them down, you are taught to raise this huatou, like cutting through tangled silk — one cut and all is cut, no longer continuing — cutting off the consciousness and letting it through no more. This is precisely Bodhidharma's rule of “let outer conditions rest, keep the mind within without gasping, make the mind like a wall.” Without taking hold in this way, you will never see your own original face. It is not that you are taught to ponder over the words of the kōan and take that as the mass of doubt, hoping to get an explanation from it.]

Why is this so? Simply because in the students' field of the eighth consciousness, the seeds of evil habit from beginningless kalpas inwardly perfume them thought after thought and flow on continuously, so that idle thoughts never cease, and there is no help for it. Therefore one takes a phrase with no flavor of meaning and makes you bite down on it, so that you first set down together all the idle thoughts of mind and objects, within and without. Because you cannot set them down, you are taught to raise this huatou
with this one thought opposing the ten thousand thoughts)

, like cutting through tangled silk — one cut and all is cut, no longer continuing — cutting off the consciousness and letting it through no more. This is precisely Bodhidharma's rule of “let outer conditions rest, keep the mind within without gasping, make the mind like a wall.” Without taking hold in this way, you can never see your own original face. It is not that you are taught to ponder over the words of the kōan and take that as the mass of doubt, hoping to get an explanation from it.

[For example, Dahui taught people exclusively to look at the huatou and to lay on a ruthless hand, only wanting you to kill the stealing mind. As he said in addressing the assembly: “In investigating Chan you need only empty out the mind, and paste the two words ‘birth and death' on your forehead, as though you owed someone ten thousand strings of cash. Three hours by day and three by night, in tea and in rice, walking and standing, sitting and lying down, when exchanging courtesies with friends, in quiet and in noise — raise a huatou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhou said: No.' Just look at it this way and that. When it has no flavor, it is like butting against a wall; when you come to the knot, it is like a mouse entering a cow's horn, and then you will see the outcome. I want you to prepare a long-enduring body and mind and wrestle with it. Of a sudden the mind-flower blazes forth, illumining buddha-lands in the ten directions, and one awakening goes through to the bottom.” This above
(the passage just quoted)

is the tongs and hammer that old man Dahui habitually used, and its meaning is simply that you should use the huatou to dam up the flow of idle thought beneath the mind-root so that it does not run on, and right at the place where it does not run on, look into and grasp your original face. It is not that you are taught to ponder over the kōan and take it as the mass of doubt, seeking an explanation. As for the words “the mind-flower blazes forth,” how could that be obtained from anywhere else?]

For example, Dahui taught people exclusively to look at the huatou and to lay on a ruthless hand (laying a ruthless hand on greed, anger, delusion, and idle thought), only wanting you to kill off the stealing mind (the mind that reaches out after conditions) entirely. As for example he said in addressing the assembly: “In investigating Chan you need only empty out the mind, and paste the two words ‘birth and death' on your forehead, as though you owed someone ten thousand strings of cash. Three hours by day and three by night, in tea and in rice, walking and standing, sitting and lying down, when exchanging courtesies with friends, in quiet and in noise — raise a huatou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: No.' Just look at it this way and that. When it has no flavor, it is like butting against a wall; when you come to the knot, it is like a mouse entering a cow's horn, and then you will see the outcome (like a mouse entering a cow's horn, there is advance but no retreat, and you will see the end). I want you to prepare a long-enduring body and mind and wrestle with it (making long-term plans, resolving firmly, investigating with your whole body and mind, never apart from it for a moment, not resting until you awaken. The Gateless Gate of the Chan School says: “Take the three hundred and sixty joints and the eighty-four thousand pores, raise a mass of doubt through the whole body, and investigate the word ‘no,' raising it to mind day and night.”). Of a sudden the mind-flower blazes forth, illumining buddha-lands in the ten directions, and one awakening goes through to the bottom.” The passage above is the tongs and hammer that old man Dahui habitually used, and its meaning is simply that you should use the huatou to dam up the flow of idle thought beneath the mind-root so that it does not run on, and right at the place where it does not run on, look into and grasp your original face. It is not that you are taught to ponder over the kōan and take it as the mass of doubt, seeking an explanation. As for the words “the mind-flower blazes forth,” how could that be obtained from anywhere else (from the place of thought)?

[The stealing mind] What is called the stealing mind is the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects, also called the consciousness of feeling, that is, the consciousness-mind. Chan Master Zhongfeng says: “What is the stealing mind? It is another name for the consciousness of feeling, because it can rob one of one's own supreme Dharma-wealth.” (The Extensive Record of Zhongfeng) [The six periods] In ancient India the day and night were divided into six periods: three by day and three by night. The three by day are morning, midday, and sunset; the three by night are early night, middle night, and late night. One such period equals four modern hours, so six periods make twenty-four hours. [To see the outcome] To clarify the causal relations or the outcome of a matter. [The flow of idle thought] The arising, ceasing, and shifting on of idle thought. [The flow of idle thought does not run on] The flow of idle thought comes to rest.

[As the Buddhas and patriarchs have one by one instructed above, they want you to investigate yourself, not to go seeking in mysterious and wonderful words and phrases. When people today investigate Chan and do the work, everyone speaks of looking at the huatou and bringing down the mass of doubt, but they do not know to investigate at the root; they only seek on the huatou. Seeking and seeking, of a sudden they think up a certain scene and say they are awakened; then they speak verses and present praises, treat it as rare merchandise, and think they have attained — never knowing that they have fallen entirely into the net of idle thought and views. In investigating Chan like this, do they not put out the eyes of people for generations to come?]

As the Buddhas and patriarchs have one by one instructed above, they want you to investigate yourself, not to go seeking in mysterious and wonderful words and phrases. When people today investigate Chan and do the work, everyone speaks of looking at the huatou and bringing down the mass of doubt, but they do not know to investigate at the root; they only seek on the huatou (pondering and guessing). Seeking and seeking, of a sudden they think up a certain scene and say they are awakened; then they speak verses and present praises, treat it as rare merchandise, and think they have attained — never knowing that they have fallen entirely into the net of idle thought and views. In investigating Chan like this, do they not put out the eyes of people for generations to come?

[Young people today have not yet sat steadily on the cushion before they claim to have awakened to the Way; they show off their tongues, play with the spirit-soul, take it for swift and sharp repartee, think up a few lines of groundless nonsense, and call it “praising the ancients.” All of it comes from your own idle thought — when did you ever dream of the ancients being present? If awakening to the Way were as easy for people today as this, then comparing them with the ancients' conduct — how Changqing sat until he wore out seven cushions, how Zhaozhou for thirty years did not let his mind stray — the ancients would be the dullest-rooted of people, not fit even to carry your straw sandals. People of overweening pride, claiming to have attained what they have not attained — should one not be afraid!]

Young people today have not yet sat steadily on the cushion before they claim to have awakened to the Way; they show off their tongues, play with the spirit-soul (the consciousness-spirit), take it for swift and sharp repartee, think up a few lines of groundless nonsense, and call it “praising the ancients.” All of it comes from your own idle thought — when did you ever dream of the ancients being present? If awakening to the Way were as easy for people today as this, then comparing them with the ancients' conduct — for example, Chan Master Hui Leng of Changqing in Fuzhou, who sat until he wore out seven cushions, and Chan Master Zhaozhou, who for thirty years did not let his mind stray — the ancients would be the dullest-rooted of people, not fit even to carry straw sandals for you people of today. These people of overweening pride, claiming to have attained what they have not attained — should one not be afraid!

[Conduct] Practice and bearing. [Claiming to have attained what one has not attained — should one not be afraid!] To claim to have attained what one has not attained is a great lying speech. In the noble path, to say one has attained when one has not, to say one has realized when one has not, and so to deceive the foolish and gain profit and offerings — all of this is called “great lying speech”; its offense is most heavy, and after death one falls into the great hells.

[In investigating Chan and looking at the huatou, bringing down the mass of doubt is absolutely indispensable. It is said: small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening; no doubt, no awakening. The point is only to use the doubt well: once the mass of doubt is broken, the Buddha's and patriarchs' nostrils are naturally strung through on one thread. Take the kōan of looking at reciting the Buddha's name: you only examine truly who it is that recites the Buddha's name, not doubt who the Buddha is. If you doubted who the Buddha is, then you need only hear a lecturer say that Amitābha Buddha is named Infinite Light, and you would thereby be awakened and produce a few verses on Infinite Light. If that were called awakening to the Way, then those who awaken to the mind would be as numerous as hemp and millet. How bitter! How bitter!]

In investigating Chan and looking at the huatou, bringing down the mass of doubt is absolutely indispensable. It is said: small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening; no doubt, no awakening. The point is only to use the doubt well: once the mass of doubt is broken, then you and the Buddha's and patriarchs' nostrils are naturally strung through on one thread. Take the kōan of looking at reciting the Buddha's name: you only examine truly “who it is that recites the Buddha's name,” not doubt who the Buddha is. If you doubted who the Buddha is, then you need only hear a lecturer say that Amitābha Buddha is named Infinite Light, and you would thereby be awakened and produce a few verses on Infinite Light. If that were called awakening to the Way, then those who awaken to the mind would be as numerous as hemp and millet. How bitter! How bitter!

[The ancients said: “A huatou is like a tile for knocking on the door; you only knock the door open to see the person inside, you do not do your business outside the door.” From this it is amply clear that when you raise doubt by means of the huatou, the doubt does not lie in the huatou — it must be at the root. Take the case of Jiashan studying under Chuanzi. Chuanzi asked: “A thousand feet of line let down, the intent is in the deep pool; three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the master struck him with the oar and knocked him into the water. Jiashan had just climbed back into the boat when the master said again, “Speak! Speak!” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the master struck him again. Jiashan was greatly awakened, and nodding three times, said: “The silk line at the pole's tip is yours to play with; not stirring the clear waves, the meaning is of itself apart.” If Jiashan had done his business on the hook and line, how could Chuanzi have given his life for him? This is how the ancients, quick and ready, were good at finding a way out.]

The ancients said: “A huatou is like a tile for knocking on the door; you only knock the door open to see the person inside (the intrinsic nature), you do not do your business outside the door.” From this it is amply clear that when you raise doubt by means of the huatou, the doubt does not lie in the huatou — it must be at the root. Take the case of Jiashan (Chan Master Shanhui) studying under Chuanzi (Chan Master Decheng). Chuanzi asked: “A thousand feet of line let down, the intent is in the deep pool; three inches from the hook — what do you say?” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, Chuanzi struck him with the oar and knocked him into the water. Jiashan had just climbed back into the boat when Chuanzi said again, “Speak! Speak!” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, Chuanzi struck him again. Jiashan was greatly awakened, and nodding three times, said: “The silk line at the pole's tip is yours to play with; not stirring the clear waves, the meaning is of itself apart.” If Jiashan had done his business on the hook and line, how could Chuanzi have given his life for him? This is how the ancients, quick and ready, were good at finding a way out.

[Three inches from the hook] In his Dream-Wandering Collection, “Miscellaneous Words from Mount Jing,” Master Hanshan says: “Biting down on the huatou is not for the sake of understanding the huatou; you only borrow the huatou to raise doubt and cut off idle thought. Your investigation must be carried on at the place apart from the huatou; only when doubt is raised does it gain power. The ancient worthy said, ‘Three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?' Those before us have already marked it out (the ancients have already pointed it out). When the doubt reaches the point where feeling and consciousness do not arrive and words do not reach, and you are pressed to the utmost, a little glimmer of light bursts out — this is called the samādhi of lightning. This is just the time to advance; do not rejoice. If you take this as it, you will be satisfied with little, and your whole person will be covered over by this bit of light, unable to emerge again. When it comes out afterward, you will be entirely at its command.” [How could Chuanzi have given his life for him?] See in full the note on Chuanzi in “2. The Mind of Loyalty and Righteousness” above.

[In former times, when the Chan Way flourished, there were clear-eyed good teachers everywhere. Many pilgrim monks throughout the land investigated, and everywhere there was opening and awakening. Moreover it is said: it is not that there is no Chan, only that there are no teachers. Today the Chan community has been desolate for a long while. How fortunate that at this time many have aroused the resolve to investigate! Yet although there are good teachers, some measure the faculties and advance them provisionally, and confirm them according to sentiment. Students' minds are shallow, and they take it for attainment; and they do not believe the Tathāgata's noble teachings, do not seek the true road, but only do things muddledly, and so take the winter-melon seal as the final confirmation. Not only do they mislead themselves — they mislead others as well. Should one not be afraid!]

In former times, when the Chan Way flourished, there were clear-eyed good teachers everywhere. Many pilgrim monks throughout the land investigated, and everywhere there was awakening. Moreover it is said: it is not that there is no Chan, only that there are no teachers. Today the Chan community has been desolate for a long while. How fortunate that at this time many have aroused the resolve to investigate! Yet although there are good teachers, they instead measure the faculties and advance them provisionally, and confirm them according to sentiment (confirming by feeling and consciousness). Students' minds are shallow, and they take it for attainment; and they do not believe the Tathāgata's noble teachings, do not seek the true road, but only do things muddledly, and so take the winter-melon seal as the true confirmation (as the final decision). Not only do they mislead themselves — they mislead others as well. Should one not be afraid!

[Nazi] Also called the nazi monk: another name for a Chan monk, because Chan monks mostly wear a patchwork robe and wander in all directions. [Opening and awakening] Bringing the mind-ground to understanding, that is, awakening. [Winter-melon seal] A seal carved from winter-melon rind — a metaphor for a false and unreal confirmation. [Seal] A stamp used as a credential. [Final decision] The sense is to pass sentence; here it means a teacher's confirmation of a student's level of realization.

[Even among the officials and laymen of old, those recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp are only a few. Among the people of toil today, they do not keep even the coarse precepts, and their idle thoughts are turbid and confused. Relying on their own cleverness, they read a few occasions of the ancient worthies, and each one prides himself on being of the very highest faculties; on seeing a monk they at once contend in sharp repartee, and also take themselves to be awakened to the Way. Though this is the fault of the times, it is truly because we of the Sangha are one blind man leading a crowd of blind men. The old man now follows the true and essential points of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' work, and discusses them with you all; the wise and accomplished will of themselves have a way to set it right.]

Moreover, even among the officials and laymen of old, those recorded in the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp are only a few. Among the laypeople of today (people of toil), they do not keep even the coarse precepts, and their idle thoughts are turbid and confused. Relying on their own small cleverness, they read a few occasions of the ancient worthies, and so each one prides himself on being of the very highest faculties; on seeing a monk they at once contend in sharp repartee, and also think themselves truly awakened to the Way. Though this is the fault of the present age, it is also because we and others are one blind man leading a crowd of blind men. The old man now follows the true and essential points of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' work and discusses them with you all; the wise and accomplished will of themselves have a way to set it right.

[Minister-officials (zǎi guān)] Originally officials subordinate to the Grand Steward in the Zhou dynasty; later a general term for government officials. [Grand Steward (zhǒng zǎi)] An office of the Zhou dynasty, first among the six ministers, also called the Grand Administrator. [Sharp repartee (jī fēng)] A Chan term. It refers to speech in question and answer that is swift and piercing, leaves no trace, and carries profound meaning. The original sense of jī fēng is the trigger mechanism and arrow-point of a crossbow; Chan uses it as a metaphor for agile and profound thought and speech. Chan practitioners often used such repartee to test the depth of another’s awakening in dialogue.

blocks.text: 36. Illness of the Body, Illness of Chan

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions for the Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng (zhuān))

[The upward path is the monk’s own proper concern. When the ancients set out and wandered beyond the regions, it was only to make this matter clear. In recent times people no longer know at all what leaving home is for — how could one expect them to match the ancients?]

The upward path is the monk’s own proper concern. When the ancients went on pilgrimage, roaming the whole world, it was only to make this matter clear. In recent times monks no longer know what leaving home is for — how could one expect them to reach the realm of the ancients?

[The Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng first studied under Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai, hearing and learning the scriptures and treatises. After a long time he cast all of it aside, took up a single thought, and earnestly investigated his own proper concern. He journeyed ten thousand li southward in search of instruction, passed through Caoxi, and called upon the Elder to ask for guidance. The Elder said: In this matter, if one does not put down body and mind and grind out the investigation with bitter effort to the place where the waters run dry and the mountains end, there will in the end be no landing place. Even when one reaches the place where waters run dry and mountains end, the ancients called it ‘still, sunken, dead water,’ and again ‘the burrow of the mysterious and wondrous.’ If one does not turn the head and shift the brain, then what stands before one is like an iron wall and a silver mountain: it is only the time of gaining power, not the place of use. The ancients’ use of mind was not to die all the way to the bottom; one must come alive within death — the key lies in turning the mechanism and shifting the position. Therefore it is said: ‘The one who does not move at the top of a hundred-foot pole
(having already reached the point where not one thought arises)
, though he may enter, has not attained the real; let him step forward once more from the top of the hundred-foot pole, and the great thousand-world will appear in his body
(personally realizing the original nature)

. ’ When a student reaches this, he has no choice but to turn around and walk another road; only so will he not be obstructed by it. The Chan monk assented, bowed, and took his leave, and thereupon went to dwell among the thatch
(that is, cutting grass to build a hut)
on Mount Nanyue.]
Zhuan (
zhuān

)yu Heng, the Chan monk, first relied on Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai, hearing and studying the scriptures and treatises. After studying in this way for a long while, he resolved to lay it all down, take up a single thought, and earnestly investigate the matter of seeing his own nature. He traveled a great distance southward seeking the Way, passed through Caoxi, and called on the Elder to request instruction. The Elder said: In this matter (the upward path), if one does not put down body and mind and grind the investigation with bitter effort to the place where the waters run dry and the mountains end, there will in the end be no landing place. Even having reached the place where waters run dry and mountains end, it is only what the ancients called ‘still, sunken, dead water,’ and again named ‘the burrow of the mysterious and wondrous.’ If one does not turn the head and shift the brain, then what stands before one is like an iron wall and a silver mountain: it is only the time of gaining power, not the place of use. The ancients’ use of mind was not to die all the way to the bottom; one must come alive within death — the key lies in turning the mechanism and shifting the position. Therefore it is said: ‘The one who does not move at the top of a hundred-foot pole, though he may enter, has not attained the ultimate; let him step forward once more from the top of the hundred-foot pole, and the great thousand-world will appear in his body.’ When a student reaches this, he should simply turn around and walk another road; only so will he not be obstructed by it. The Chan monk respectfully assented, bowed, and took his leave, going to Mount Nanyue to cut the wild grass and build a thatched hut for cultivation.

[The one who does not move] ‘Not moving’ means that thoughts do not move (no thought arises) — that is, not a single thought arises. ‘The one who does not move’ is a person in whom not a single thought arises.

[Before long the Elder too came leaning on his staff. On inquiring after the Chan monk, he learned that the monk had been troubled by the demon of illness and had already gone to Baoqing for medical treatment. Hearing this, the Elder sighed: ‘The Chan gate is in decline; students who truly take birth and death to heart are the hardest to find. And now this man has this illness — surely the dragons and devas have grown weary of this Dharma gate!’ In the spring of the bingchen year, on the first day of the third month, at midnight amid wind and rain, the Chan monk suddenly arrived, braving the rain and slogging through the mud. When the Elder saw him he was overjoyed and said: How could a sick man do this? Looking at his brow and countenance, brimming with clear, brisk spirit, he knew the illness was eight or nine parts cured.]

Before long the Elder (myself) also came leaning on a staff to Mount Nanyue. Asking after the Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng, he learned that the monk had been troubled by the demon of illness and had gone to Baoqing for medical treatment. The Elder sighed on hearing it: ‘The Chan gate is in decline; students who truly take birth and death to heart are the hardest to find. Now this man suffers this illness — is it not that the dragons and devas disdain this Dharma gate and withhold their protection?’ In the spring of the bingchen year, on the first day of the third month, in the middle of the night amid a raging storm, the Chan monk Zhuanyu Heng suddenly arrived, braving the rain and slogging through mud. The Elder met him and said with great joy: How is this a sick man? Looking at his brow and countenance, brimming with clear, brisk spirit, he therefore knew that his illness was already eight or nine parts cured.

[He therefore again offered incense and asked for instruction, and the Elder specially told him: Your demon of illness is your great good friend, a contributing condition for the Way — do you understand? Indeed, the illness of sentient beings lies in having a self. Because they cling to a self, all afflictions and manifold illnesses arise from it. When illness arises, suffering must follow. From ancient times to the present, there is no one who is not sick with this. Only the person who understands illness as illness is not ill. Moreover, the four great elements are a false union: whatever gathers must scatter — even if one is not ill, how is one ever not ill? If one understands the one who is not ill within illness, then illness cannot make one ill. You know today’s illness, but you do not know the illness of many lives, kalpa after kalpa, that has been ailing up to today. If you do not understand today’s illness, then from now on you will never know where illness ends.]

He therefore again offered incense and asked for instruction, and the Elder specially told him: Your demon of illness is your great good friend, a contributing condition for the Way — do you know this? The illness of sentient beings lies in having a self. Because of clinging to a self, all afflictions and manifold illnesses arise. When illness arises, suffering must follow. From ancient times to now, there is no one who is not ill from this. Only one who knows why illness is illness will not be made ill by illness. Moreover, the four great elements are a false union; whatever gathers must scatter — even if one is not ill, how is one ever not ill? If one understands that the root of illness is the self, and does not cling to the self, then sickness cannot make one sick. You know today’s illness, but you do not know the illness of many lives, kalpa upon kalpa of the illness of ‘having a self,’ up to today. If you do not understand today’s illness of ‘having a self,’ then from now on you will never know how to put an end to illness.
[Illness as illness] The first ‘illness’ is a verb; the second ‘illness’ is its object.

[You know the illness of birth and death, but you do not know the illness of wanting to escape birth and death — which is far greater than the illness of birth and death itself. Why is this? The ancients held that when Chan practice does not go beyond the realm of the aggregates and falls into the trap of consciousness and emotion, then even a wonderful awakening becomes a view of self. When one clings to the four elements as the self, the illness can still be cured; but now, having left the four elements behind, one again clings to there being a self — this illness leaves even the King of Physicians helpless, the hardest of all to treat. All the Buddhas and patriarchs came into the world expressly to cure this one terminal disease; though they spent untold effort of mind, how many are there who are willing to take the medicine and be cured?]

You know only the illness of birth and death, but you do not know that the practice for escaping birth and death is itself also diseased — and far more serious and harder to cure. Why? The ancients held that if Chan practice does not go beyond the realm of the aggregates and falls into the trap of consciousness and emotion, then even a wonderful awakening only builds up a view of self. Because one clings to the four elements as the self, the illness can still be treated; but now, having left the four elements behind, one again clings to there being a self — this illness leaves even the King of Physicians with no recourse, the hardest of all to treat. All the Buddhas and patriarchs came into the world expressly to cure this one terminal disease. Though they spent immeasurable effort of mind, how many are there who are willing to take the medicine and be cured?

[The realm of the aggregates (yīn jiè)] The five aggregates and the eighteen elements. The five aggregates are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. The eighteen elements are the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, together with the six dusts of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects, and the six consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. [A disease beyond cure (gāo huāng zhī bìng)] A terminal illness. [To be cured (
chài
To recover from illness.

[The Chan monk’s bodily illness is cured; on no account may he be invaded by the illness of Chan. Yunmen said that the dharma-body has two kinds of illness. His words ‘penetrating the dharma-body’ — if attachment to dharmas is not forgotten and one’s own views still remain, that too is illness — are an emphatic statement of the illness of clinging and grasping. Let the Chan monk spit out together all the mysterious words and wondrous sayings he previously accumulated, along with the merit he guarded and clung to in Chan practice, until not a trace of evil perception or evil habit remains; then he will certainly not let them grow into a root of illness, and will straightaway leave the Buddhas and patriarchs no place to stand. Have you not seen Sudhana, who journeyed south through a hundred cities and studied under fifty-three great good friends, each granting him one Dharma gate, and in the end came away only with something equal to the Dharma realm and equal to empty space — was there ever any real dharma tied to him? And have you not seen Vairocana, whose dharma-body is no body, but who takes the wonderful practice of Samantabhadra as his body? Samantabhadra has no practice; he takes the practice of sentient beings as his practice. Therefore it is said: That on which bodhi depends is suffering sentient beings; if there were no sentient beings, there would be no bodhi. This is the true model of the Buddhas and patriarchs of former times coming into the world.]

Chan monk (you), your bodily illness is cured; by no means may you be invaded by the illness of Chan. Yunmen (Chan Master Wenyan) said the dharma-body has two kinds of illness: in penetrating the dharma-body, if attachment to dharmas is not forgotten and one’s own views still remain, that too is illness — this is his utmost statement on the illness of clinging and grasping. You must cast away (spit out) all the mysterious words and wondrous sayings you previously accumulated, along with the fruits of merit (gōng xūn) you guarded and clung to in Chan practice, until not a trace of evil perception or evil habit remains; then you will certainly not let them grow into a root of illness, and will straightaway leave the Buddhas and patriarchs no place to stand. Have you not seen Sudhana, who journeyed south through a hundred cities and studied under fifty-three great good friends, each granting him one Dharma gate, and in the end came away only with something equal to the Dharma realm and equal to empty space — was there ever any real dharma tied to him? And have you not seen Vairocana Buddha, whose dharma-body is no body, but who takes the wonderful practice of Samantabhadra as his body? Samantabhadra has no practice; he takes the practice of sentient beings as his practice. Therefore it is said: That on which bodhi depends is suffering sentient beings; if there were no sentient beings, there would be no bodhi. This is the true model of the Buddhas and patriarchs of former times coming into the world.

[The two kinds of illness of the dharma-body] Yunmen said: “The dharma-body likewise has two kinds of illness: attaining the dharma-body, yet not forgetting attachment to dharmas and still holding one’s own views, is falling beside the dharma-body — that is one; even if one penetrates it thoroughly, one must not let it go. Examining it carefully, whatever breath or trace remains is also illness.” [Merit (gōng xūn)] The fruits of practice. [Vairocana] Vairocana is the dharmakāya Buddha, Locana the saṃbhogakāya Buddha, and Śākyamuni the nirmāṇakāya Buddha. Among the “ten Buddha names” there is: “Vairocana Buddha, pure dharmakāya; Locana Buddha, perfect saṃbhogakāya; Śākyamuni Buddha, transformation body in hundreds of thousands of millions.” [The ten Buddha names] The names of the Buddhas chanted at the two meals of porridge and rice each day, also called “the ten recitations at mealtime.” “Ten Buddhas” is an approximate number; in practice more than ten are chanted. [The three bodies] Dharmakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and nirmāṇakāya. The dharmakāya is also called the body of self-nature, or the body of dharma-nature: it is the permanent, indestructible true nature that everyone originally possesses; it is only that we sentient beings are deluded and do not manifest it, while the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. The saṃbhogakāya is formed from the Buddha’s wisdom and merit, and is divided into the saṃbhogakāya for his own enjoyment and the saṃbhogakāya for others’ enjoyment: the former is the body in which the Buddha himself enjoys the bliss of inner realization, the latter the body manifested to teach the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The nirmāṇakāya is also called the body of response and transformation, or the body of transformation: the Buddha-body manifested in response to the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.

[The Elder therefore said to the Chan monk: The diseased body of the four elements can only be cured by the demon of illness; the illness of Chan that pierces the heart can only be cured by sentient beings. From today on, simply make the body equal to the great earth, and the demon of illness will hide its traces. Make the mind equal to sentient beings, and the view of self will not stand. When the view of self does not stand, the illness of Chan dissolves of itself. Because the mind does not mind itself, it is originally unborn. Being unborn, not a single dharma is established. If not a single dharma is established, what dharma is there to become an obstruction of views? The ancients said: To renounce emotion is easy; to renounce dharmas is hard. The Chan monk renounces the body, which is to renounce emotion; renounces views, which is to renounce dharmas. With emotion and dharmas both forgotten, is he not a person of great, unobstructed liberation? Alas, I am old, and to meet again will be hard. Strive on, Chan monk.]

The Elder therefore said to the Chan monk: As for the illness of this diseased body of the four elements, apart from the demon of illness there is no curing it; as for the illness of Chan that pierces the heart, apart from sentient beings there is no curing it. From today on, simply make the body equal to the great earth, and the demon of illness will hide its traces. Make the mind equal to sentient beings, and the view of self will not stand. When the view of self does not stand, the illness of Chan dissolves of itself. Because the mind arises dependent on form and cannot exist independently, it is originally unborn. Being unborn, not a single dharma is established. If not a single dharma is established, what dharma is there to become an obstruction of views? The ancients said: To renounce emotion is easy; to renounce dharmas is hard. The Chan monk renounces the body, which is to renounce emotion; renounces views, which is to renounce dharmas. With emotion and dharmas both forgotten, is he not a person of great, unobstructed liberation? Alas, I am old, and to meet again will be hard. Strive on, Chan monk.

[The diseased body of the four elements can only be cured by the demon of illness] As for the illness of this diseased body of the four elements, apart from the demon of illness there is no curing it. For the demon of illness makes one realize that the body of form is illusory and is not oneself, while the root of the diseased body of the four elements is the deluded clinging to the body of form as “I” (as a self). Just as Master Hanshan taught earlier: “Your demon of illness is your great good friend, a contributing condition for the Way — do you know this? Indeed, the illness of sentient beings lies in having a self. Because they cling to a self, all afflictions and manifold illnesses arise from it.” [Because the mind does not mind itself, it is originally unborn] The mind arises dependent on form and cannot exist independently, and so is originally unborn. Mazu said: “Whatever form is seen is the seeing of mind; the mind does not mind itself — it exists because of form.” (Wudeng Huiyuan)

blocks.text: 37. Inscription on Clarifying the Mind

inline.s: (The Dream-Wandering Collection
Inscription on Clarifying the Mind, for Ding Youwu)
The key to clarifying the mind is the absence of the mark of self.
[The true nature, deep and serene, like water stilled and clear; struck by hate and love, waves of affliction appear.]
The original nature is serene and profound, like stilled, limpid water; when hate and love stir it, waves of affliction rise.
[Stirred without cease, the self-nature turns unclear; affliction and ignorance but deepen, unaware.]

Stirred without cease, the self-nature therefore grows turbid (the self-nature falls into a state of dullness); and because the self-nature is turbid (dull), affliction and ignorance only increase while one remains unaware.
[Increasing while unaware] They increase while one is unaware. If one were aware, affliction and ignorance could not increase.
[Grasping the other through the I, like mud mixed into water; letting the other stir the I, like oil that feeds the fire.]

Once the mark of self is established, “this” and “that” appear: it is like mud mixed into pure water, and the self-nature grows all the more turbid. Letting love and hate for the other stir me is like adding oil to fire, making the fire of affliction and ignorance fiercer and more blazing.
[Oil] Lamp oil. [The other] Other people and outer objects.
[The other troubles my true nature; the trouble springs from ‘I.’ If ‘I’ is never born, the kalpa-fire freezes to ice.]
The other disturbs my true nature (original nature); in fact the disturbance is born of the “I” (the mark of self). If the “I” is not born, the fire of the kalpa turns to ice.
[The kalpa burning] The great conflagration that occurs at the time of the destruction kalpa, burning up to the heaven of the first dhyāna, reducing everything to ashes.
[Therefore the sage first empties the mark of self; the mark of self once empty, from where can the other obstruct?]

For this reason, the sage (the person of the highest attainment) first empties out the mark of self; if the mark of self is empty, how can the other (other people and outer objects) become an obstruction?
[The sage (zhì rén)] A person who has reached the highest realm.
[To forget the self, hold firm and patiently endure; the moment habit stirs, wake suddenly and sure.]
Doing the work of forgetting the self depends on firm and patient endurance; the moment a habitual tendency arises, one wakes with a sudden start.
[Where one wakes is awareness: a single thought turns back its light, sweeping away all traces, leaving no track in sight; and in that very instant, all is cool and bright.]

The place where one wakes is awareness itself: with a single thought of turning the light back to shine within, habitual tendencies are swept away without trace, and one is immediately cool and clear.

[Where one wakes is awareness] The Diamond Sutra says: “All that has marks is deceptive.” “No mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a life span.” “All bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, nor on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; they should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all.” First one should take these three as the outline and earnestly do the work of wisdom’s contemplation, seeing through and letting go. Chan Master Guifeng said: “Awaken to all marks as empty, and the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, be aware; being aware, it is at once gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies nowhere else.” (Preface to the Collected Writings on the Sources of Chan) The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Knowing the illusory, one at once departs from it, without resort to means; departing from the illusory is itself awakening, with no gradual stages.”
[Cool, still, and quiet; upright, standing alone; calm and joyous in spirit — no thing can be its foe.]
Cool, still, and quiet; upright and standing alone (keeping no company with the ten thousand dharmas); tranquil and serene, gladdening the spirit — no thing can be its match.

[Things] People and circumstances other than oneself. [No thing can match it] Since one no longer stands opposed to things, one is naturally not defeated by them. This is the state that transcends the ten thousand things (keeping no company with the ten thousand dharmas).

blocks.text: 38. Song of Wasted Idleness

inline.s: Fei’ means spending effort and time; ‘xian’ means useless. Feixian, then, is to spend energy and time without any real result — what is commonly called doing useless work. In the Song of Wasted Idleness, Master Hanshan points out the pitfalls in practice where effort and time are squandered, and how to step out of them.

[To preach the Way is easy, to embody it hard; if stray thoughts are not cleared, all practice is marred. When worldly toil and dust still snag the breast, then sitting deep in mountains is but wasted rest.]

It is easy to preach the Way to others but hard to practice it oneself; if stray thoughts are not cleared away, everything is idle (effort wasted); if worldly toil and dust constantly snag the mind, then sitting in quiet in deep mountains is in vain.

[To embody the Way] To practice (personally carry out) the right Way. To preach the Way without personally walking it means one cannot truly realize the Way; and if one misleads students, it brings great evil consequences for both others and oneself. [Zongshi] All of it. [All is idle] All of it is useless. [In vain] To no purpose, futilely; for example: to waste effort to no purpose.

[To leave home is easy, to keep the rule is hard; with neither faith nor vow, all effort is marred. The pure precepts unkept, one labours but in vain; though one has shaved one’s head, it is but loss and pain.]

Leaving home is easy, but keeping the precepts and rules is hard; with no faith or vow at all, everything is idle; if the pure precepts are not kept, one labours in vain; though one shaves one’s head and leaves home, it is still futile.
[To practice is easy, to find a teacher hard; lacking a true teacher, all effort is marred. Clever in one’s own conceit, one toils in vain; blind and sightless practice is but loss and pain.]

Practice is easy, but meeting a teacher is hard; without meeting an illumined teacher, everything is idle; being clever in one’s own conceit is wasted effort; blind, sightless cultivation is also futile.

[To be stained is easy, to be free of stain is hard; if worldly toil is not cut off, all effort is marred. Clinging with passion and habit, one spends one’s strength in vain; the fruit of the Way unattained — it is but loss and pain.]

It is easy to be stained by dust but hard to get out of the dust; if worldly toil is not cut off, everything is idle; to cling and climb with passion and habit is wasted effort; failing to attain the fruit of the Way is also futile.

[Worldly toil (chén láo)] The mind toiling over the dusts of sense objects; another name for affliction. [Climbing with passion and habit] To climb after and fabricate things with emotional consciousness and habitual tendencies, mistaking it for practice.

[To hear is easy, to be true-hearted hard; to slight and scorn one’s teacher — all effort marred. Proud and puffed up, one spends one’s strength in vain; though wit outshine the world, it is but loss and pain.]

It is easy to hear the teachings but hard to practice them with a true heart; to slight and scorn one’s teacher is always idle; to be proud and arrogant is wasted effort; though one’s cleverness cover the world, it is also futile.
[Proud and high (gòng gāo)] To think oneself a cut above others.
[To study the Way is easy, to awaken to it hard; if no effort is made, all is idle, all is marred. To believe but not practice is strength spent in vain; mere empty talk is also loss and pain.]
Studying the Way is easy but awakening to the Way is hard; not putting in effort is always idle; being able to believe but not to practice is wasted effort; empty talk and discussion is also futile.

[To shut the gate is easy, to keep the gate is hard; if one refuses to practice, all effort is marred. Body within the gate, the mind outside — one toils in vain; a thousand years without emerging is but loss and pain.]

Secluding oneself is easy, but practicing earnestly inside the retreat is hard; refusing to practice steadily is always idle; with the body inside the gate and the mind outside, a thousand years without leaving the retreat is also futile.

[To recite the Buddha is easy, to have true faith is hard; with heart and mouth not one, all effort is marred. The mouth recites Amitābha, the mind is all astray; though the throat be shouted hoarse, it is but waste of day.]

Reciting the Buddha’s name is easy, but a faithful and true heart is hard; when heart and mouth are not one (the heart is not sincere: the mouth recites the Buddha while the mind thinks of other things) everything is idle (all wasted effort); to recite Amitābha with the mouth while the mind wanders is futile even if one shouts the throat raw.

[True and sincere] Honest, not deceitful. “A heart of faith” means a heart that is true and sincere; when heart and mouth are not one, that is falsehood. Hence the next line: “when heart and mouth are not one, all is idle.”

[To bow to the Buddha is easy, to revere is hard; when the intent is not devout, all effort is marred. The five limbs bowing empty, one toils in vain; though the skull be cracked open, it is but loss and pain.]

Bowing to the Buddha is easy, but a reverent heart is hard; when the intent is not devout, everything is idle; the five limbs (two hands, two knees, and the head) bowing hollowly (without reverence) is wasted effort; though the skull (the shell without a mind) be cracked open, it is also futile.

[To recite sutras is easy, to understand them hard; to chant with the mouth but not understand — all effort marred. To understand but not follow is strength spent in vain; though ten thousand scrolls be chanted daily, it is but loss and pain.]

Reciting sutras is easy but understanding them is hard; to recite with the mouth without understanding is always idle; to understand but not to practice is wasted effort; though one recites ten thousand scrolls a day, it is also futile.

blocks.text: 39. Turning Consciousness into Wisdom

inline.s: (From The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions for Zhou Yangru)

[Turning consciousness into wisdom] To turn the ordinary person’s defiled eight consciousnesses into the Buddha’s four wisdoms: that is, to turn the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the seventh (manas) into the Wisdom of Equality, the sixth (mental consciousness) into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and the first five (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness) into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done.

[Master Zhou asked for instruction on the essential purport of the Dharma-character school, and the Elder therefore brought up the Sixth Patriarch’s Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom: “The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature; the Wisdom of Equality is a mind without illness; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror. The fifth and eighth, the sixth and seventh, turn at the fruit and at the cause; but only the names turn — there is no real nature. If at the point of turning one keeps no attachment, then amid teeming activity one forever abides in nāga samādhi.”]

Master Zhou requested instruction on the essential purport of the Dharma-character school, so the Elder brought up the Sixth Patriarch’s Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom: “The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature; the Wisdom of Equality is a mind without illness; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror. The fifth and eighth, the sixth and seventh, turn at the fruit and at the cause; but only the names turn — there is no real nature. If at the point of turning one keeps no attachment, then amid teeming activity one forever abides in nāga samādhi.”

[Master Zhou] “Zi” was an ancient honorific for a person. [The Dharma-character school] One of the eight great schools of the Mahāyāna; because it exhaustively clarifies the nature and characteristics of the ten thousand dharmas, it is called the Dharma-character school. Since it relies on the Consciousness-Only treatises to clarify the principle that the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only, it is also called the Consciousness-Only school. [The eight schools] The Vinaya school, the Huayan school, the Tiantai school, the Three-Treatise school (the Dharma-nature school), the Dharma-character school (the Consciousness-Only school), the Mantra school, the Chan school, and the Pure Land school.
