To make Master Hanshan’s teaching below easier to understand, the Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom that the Sixth Patriarch set forth in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch are first explained as follows:

[The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature; the Wisdom of Equality is a mind without illness; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror.]

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature; the Wisdom of Equality is a mind free of illness; the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation perceives without effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror.

[The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure in nature] The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is what the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) turns into. The ālaya stores immeasurable karmic seeds and exerts a defiling influence on feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Now, with consciousness turned into wisdom, it no longer defiles, and so it is said to be “pure in nature.” [The Wisdom of Equality is a mind without illness] The Wisdom of Equality is what the seventh consciousness (manas) turns into. The chief function of manas is to think, measure, and calculate, which is the great illness that brings about birth and death. Now, with consciousness turned into wisdom, it no longer thinks, measures, and calculates, and so it is said to be “a mind without illness.” [The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort] The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation is what the sixth consciousness (mental consciousness) turns into. The chief function of the mental consciousness is to exercise discrimination when the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body) meet the corresponding five dusts (form, sound, smell, taste, and touch). Now, with consciousness turned into wisdom, it merely observes and no longer discriminates, and so it is said that “seeing is without effort” (in seeing there is likewise no function of discrimination). [The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is like a round mirror] The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done is what the first five consciousnesses turn into; once they become wisdom, they merely reflect the objects before them without discriminating, and so it is said to be “like a round mirror.”

[The fifth and eighth, the sixth and seventh, turn at the fruit and at the cause; but it is only names that turn — there is no real nature. If at the point of turning one keeps no attachment, then amid teeming activity one forever abides in nāga samādhi.]

The sixth and seventh consciousnesses turn on the level of cause, while the first five and the eighth are naturally accomplished on the level of fruit (at the time of becoming Buddha). This turning (turning the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms) merely turns their names and characteristics (their state); the essence is not two (it has no real nature). If at the point where (the sixth and seventh consciousnesses) turn from consciousness into wisdom one keeps no attachment, turning decisively and resolutely (this is precisely where the work is done in daily life), then even amid the swirling red dust of the world one is like a dragon hidden in the deep pool, coiled and unmoving, forever abiding in nāga samādhi.

[The level of fruit] As opposed to “the level of cause”: the fruition attained by practicing on the level of cause. Here the fruition means the fruit of Buddhahood. [Teeming activity (fán xīng)] Arising in great number; here it means the myriad phenomena in their profusion. [Nāga samādhi] “Nāga” is translated as “dragon.” “Nāga samādhi” is “dragon samādhi” — like a dragon lurking in a deep pool, coiled and unmoving. [If at the point of turning one keeps no attachment] Turning with not the slightest stagnation, like a poisonous snake biting one’s finger: cut it off at once. [Amid teeming activity one forever abides in nāga samādhi] Though placed amid the swirling red dust of the world with its myriad phenomena (teeming activity), one forever abides in dragon samādhi.
The main text of this chapter now continues:

[These eight lines lay bare the very heart and marrow of the Buddhas and patriarchs and reveal the root source of nature and characteristics. Yet those who count another’s treasures and tally grains of sand, greedy for much and unable to chew what they bite off, generally regard this as idle furniture and have never once looked at it with a true eye — how greatly to be pitied!]

These eight lines of the Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom lay bare the very heart and marrow of the Buddhas and patriarchs and reveal the root source of nature and characteristics. Yet those who circle endlessly among names and characteristics without true practice (those who count treasures and tally sand), greedy for much and unable to chew what they bite off (never tasting the true flavor within), all regard this as idle furniture and have never once looked at it closely with a true eye — truly a great pity.

[Counting treasures] Counting another’s treasures; it refers to those who do not truly practice according to the teachings but merely show off with their lips. [Tallying sand] To enter the sea and, instead of gathering treasures, go about counting grains of sand; it refers to those who sink into names and characteristics instead of awakening to the Way through practice.

[People all say the Sixth Patriarch was illiterate and unlearned in the teachings — how could he speak of this? They little know that the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and patriarchs is fully contained, with nothing left over, in just eight words: “The three realms are mind only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only.” Because they are mind only, the three realms are quiescent, utterly without a thing; because they are consciousness only, the ten thousand dharmas stand in profusion. For the ten thousand dharmas are merely manifested from consciousness only, and when one seeks them in one’s own mind, the self-nature is utterly unattainable. That is why the Buddhas and patriarchs, in teaching people, said only that outside the mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable — which is precisely what Huangmei brought forth at midnight as “originally there is not a single thing.” In this one phrase, all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times and all the patriarchs of successive generations are contained; it cannot be broken apart, and so the robe and bowl were entrusted to him. Even the two branches and five houses all derive from this one phrase — where was there ever a division into the nature school and the characteristics school?]

They imagine that since the Sixth Patriarch was illiterate and unlearned in the scriptures, how could he reveal the root source of nature and characteristics? They little know that the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and patriarchs is fully contained, with nothing left over, in just eight words: “The three realms are mind only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only.” Because they are mind only, the three realms are quiescent, utterly without a thing; because they are consciousness only, the ten thousand dharmas stand in ordered profusion. Since the ten thousand dharmas are all manifested from consciousness, when one seeks them in one’s own mind, the essence of the ten thousand dharmas (the self-nature) is utterly unattainable. Therefore what the Buddha and the patriarchs taught people was nothing more than that outside the mind not a fragment of anything is obtainable — which is precisely Huineng’s “originally there is not a single thing.” In this one phrase, all that the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times and the patriarchs of successive generations said is contained; this is an irrefutable truth, and therefore the Fifth Patriarch transmitted the robe and bowl to him. Even the two branches and five houses all evolved from this one phrase — when was there ever a division between the nature school and the characteristics school?
[For the ten thousand dharmas are merely manifested from consciousness only] The Dream-Wandering Collection
Master Hanshan’s own preface and chronological record says:
“Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Depending on consciousness, one is defiled; depending on wisdom, one is pure. Defilement has birth and death; purity has no Buddhas.”

[Huangmei at midnight brought forth “originally there is not a single thing”] When Huineng spoke this essential purport of the Buddhadharma, “originally there is not a single thing,” the Fifth Patriarch thereupon transmitted the patriarch’s seat to him at midnight. Hence the saying: on Mount Huangmei at midnight a patriarch of “originally there is not a single thing” suddenly popped up. [Huangmei] Mount Huangmei, where the East Chan Monastery of Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch of Chan, was located. [The two branches] Under the Fifth Patriarch there were two branches: the Northern school of Shenxiu and the Southern school of Huineng. The watershed between these two branches is whether or not one has awakened to the truth “originally there is not a single thing.” [The five houses] Under the Sixth Patriarch there were five houses (also called the five families): the Weiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan houses. [The nature school and the characteristics school] That is, the Dharma-nature school and the Dharma-character school. 1. The Dharma-nature school (the Three-Treatise school among the eight schools), abbreviated as the nature school: it breaks through the marks of the ten thousand dharmas and reveals their true nature of emptiness and quiescence. 2. The Dharma-character school (the Consciousness-Only school), abbreviated as the characteristics school: it traces the arising of the ten thousand dharmas back to the ālaya-vijñāna, takes the ālaya-vijñāna as the root of all defiled and pure cause and effect, and extensively distinguishes the names and meanings of the dharmas it produces; hence it is called the Dharma-character school.

[Then, looking into the Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom, I annotated and broke them open a little. If one takes it as “the three realms are mind only,” then there is no place to set one’s mouth. Because one is deluded about this mind and it transforms into consciousness, it loses the name of true suchness and is merely called ālaya-vijñāna, also called the storehouse consciousness; this consciousness is what the whole of true suchness transforms into. It is precisely what is meant by “born of the union of the born-and-destroyed with the unborn-and-undestroyed” — the root of the real and the false, of delusion and awakening, the basis of birth and death, of ordinary beings and sages. The Laṅkāvatāra says: “The ocean of the storehouse consciousness is forever abiding; moved by the wind of objects, great waves surge through the dark abyss, with never a moment of cessation.” Since it says the storehouse consciousness is the ālaya, and yet says it is forever abiding, then it is fundamentally unmoving. What moves, then, is not the storehouse consciousness but only the wind of objects.]

Now the Verses on Consciousness and Wisdom are used to elucidate the principle that “the three realms are mind only and the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only.” If one takes it in terms of “the three realms are mind only” (all that the three realms contain is simply one mind), then there is no place to set one’s mouth. Because one is deluded about this mind (true suchness) and it transforms into consciousness, it loses the name of true suchness and is merely called ālaya-vijñāna, also called the storehouse consciousness; this consciousness is what the whole of true suchness transforms into. This is precisely what is meant by “born of the union of the born-and-destroyed with the unborn-and-undestroyed” — the root of the real and the false, of delusion and awakening, the basis of birth and death, of ordinary beings and sages. The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “The ocean of the storehouse consciousness is forever abiding; moved by the wind of objects, great waves surge through the dark abyss, with never a moment of cessation.” In the scripture, since it speaks of the storehouse consciousness (that is, the ālaya-vijñāna) and also says it is forever abiding, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally unmoving. Therefore what moves is not the storehouse consciousness but the wind of objects.

[The verse says, “If the object before is absent, the mind too is absent.” If so, then what grasps objects is not the storehouse consciousness but the mind of birth and death. This mind of birth and death is provisionally named the seventh consciousness; in fact it is the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness, what is called the vital impulse. Once this impulse is stilled, the objects before one are at once empty, and though the sixth consciousness is able to discriminate, it has nothing to fasten on. As for the first five consciousnesses, they have no separate substance of their own; they are merely the functioning of the storehouse consciousness in response to conditions, able only to reflect objects and unable to discriminate — hence “like a round mirror.” What discriminates the five dusts is not the five consciousnesses but the mental consciousness arising at the same moment as them; hence it is credited with the merit. If it does not give rise to discrimination, then “seeing is without effort.”]

The verse says: “If the object before is absent, the mind too is absent.” Therefore what grasps objects is not the storehouse consciousness but the mind of birth and death. This mind of birth and death is tentatively named the seventh consciousness (manas); in fact it is the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness (the storehouse consciousness), what is called the vital impulse. Once this vital impulse (the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness) is stilled, the objects before one are at once empty, and even though the sixth consciousness (the mental consciousness) is able to discriminate, it has nothing to fasten on (there is nothing for it to discriminate). As for the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness), they have no separate substance; they are merely the functioning of the storehouse consciousness in response to conditions. These first five consciousnesses can only reflect the dusts of objects, not discriminate them — hence “like a round mirror.” What discriminates the five dusts (form, sound, smell, taste, and touch) is not the first five consciousnesses but the sixth consciousness (the mental consciousness) arising at the same moment as them; hence it is said that the sixth consciousness is credited with the merit. If it (the sixth consciousness) does not give rise to discrimination, then “seeing is without effort.”

[Once this impulse is stilled] Once this vital impulse (the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness) is stilled. The passage above says, “in fact it is the stirring of thought of the eighth consciousness, what is called the vital impulse.” “Impulse” (jī) is that from which the changes of things arise.

[Seen in this way, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally real, and so it is said to be pure in nature; its fault lies in a single thought giving rise to mind, and this is the illness of the mind. Where there is birth there is destruction; this very birth-and-destruction is like the flowing of water — there is no separate flow apart from the water. Yet the water’s nature of not abiding is what makes the mark of flowing appear; and where there is flowing, it is clear that it is not the water of a deep, still pool. Hence the Laṅkāvatāra speaks of two kinds of arising, abiding, and destruction: the arising, abiding, and destruction of marks, and the arising, abiding, and destruction of outflowing. These two kinds of birth and destruction both belong to the storehouse consciousness. If birth and destruction are not destroyed, then the first seven consciousnesses arise; if birth and destruction are destroyed, then only a single pure reality remains, and the nature of true suchness is restored from that point on. When it is restored, consciousness is no longer called consciousness but wisdom; hence it is said to be “a mind without illness.”]

Seen in this way, the storehouse consciousness is fundamentally real, and so it is said to be pure in nature; its fault lies in a single thought giving rise to mind, and this is the illness of the mind. Where there is birth there is destruction; this very birth-and-destruction is like the flowing of water — there is no separate flow apart from the water. But this water has the nature of not abiding, and so the mark of flowing appears; where there is flowing, it is clear that it is not the still water of a deep pool. Hence the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra speaks of two kinds of arising, abiding, and destruction for the consciousnesses: the arising, abiding, and destruction of marks, and the arising, abiding, and destruction of outflowing. These two kinds of birth and destruction both belong to the storehouse consciousness. If birth and destruction are not destroyed, the first seven consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mental, and manas consciousness) arise; if birth and destruction are destroyed, the first seven consciousnesses cease, and only the storehouse consciousness, this single pure reality, remains, and the nature of true suchness is restored from then on. Once restored, consciousness is no longer called consciousness but wisdom; hence it is said to be “a mind without illness.”

[What the Sixth Patriarch set forth in his verses concerns the turning of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is what the storehouse consciousness turns into, the Wisdom of Equality what the seventh consciousness turns into, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation what the sixth consciousness turns into, and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done what the first five consciousnesses turn into; because the false is the functioning of the storehouse consciousness, the true too is like a round mirror. Yet the sixth and seventh consciousnesses turn first on the level of cause, while the first five and the eighth, being one body, are perfected only at the level of fruit. Looked at in this way, consciousness is fundamentally unreal, and falsely has two functions; hence it is said that only the names turn — the name changes but not the substance. Moreover, this substance does not lie in Chan concentration and practice, but only in all the activities of daily life, where sage and ordinary turn it at the same time, and where the only difference lies in whether one keeps attachment or not; hence the distinction between sage and ordinary, delusion and awakening. Master Zhou, if you have set your will on this, earnestly fix your eye on where the turning happens in daily life, and try to settle it clearly.]

The verses composed by the Sixth Patriarch speak of turning the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is what the storehouse consciousness turns into, the Wisdom of Equality what the seventh consciousness (manas) turns into, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation what the sixth consciousness (mental consciousness) turns into, and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done what the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body) turn into; because the first five consciousnesses are the false functioning of the storehouse consciousness, when they are now turned into wisdom they are, together with the wisdom into which the storehouse consciousness is turned, the same round mirror. Yet the sixth and seventh consciousnesses turn first on the level of cause, while the first five and the eighth, being one body, turn into wisdom only on the level of fruit (at the time of becoming Buddha). Looked at in this way, the eight consciousnesses are fundamentally unreal, and falsely possess the two functions of birth-and-destruction and non-birth-and-destruction; hence it is said that only the name turns — the name changes but not the substance. Moreover, the transformation of this substance does not lie in Chan concentration and practice, but only in every arising of thought and movement of mind in daily life. Ordinary beings and sages (bodhisattvas above the first ground) alike turn it where thought arises and mind moves; ultimately, whether one is turning wisdom into consciousness or consciousness into wisdom depends only on whether one keeps attachment, and from this come the distinctions between ordinary and sage, deluded and awakened. Master Zhou, since you have set your will on this, earnestly fix your eye on where the turning happens in daily use, and look closely: are you turning rightly (turning consciousness into wisdom) or turning backwards (turning wisdom into consciousness)?

[Only the names turn — the name changes but not the substance] This means that the eight consciousnesses and the four wisdoms are two states of one substance, just as ice and water seem utterly different and so bear the names “ice” and “water,” when in fact they are only
H₂O
in two states — one substance, two states. When ice melts into water the name changes, but the substance is still
H₂O

, and so it is “only the names turn — the name changes but not the substance.” [Sage and ordinary turn it at the same time; the only difference lies in whether one keeps attachment] The sages, being awakened, keep no attachment toward greed, hatred, and delusion, and so are turning consciousness into wisdom; ordinary beings, being deluded, have not let go their attachment (keep attachment) toward greed, hatred, and delusion, and so do the opposite, turning wisdom into consciousness. [Sage] From the ordinary person’s practice to the attainment of Buddhahood there are fifty-two stages in all: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of dwelling, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal awakening, and wondrous awakening. Among them, the bodhisattvas of the ten dwellings, ten practices, and ten dedications have only cut off the delusions of views and thoughts, and still have the delusions of dust-and-sand and of ignorance; they are called “worthy.” Bodhisattvas from the first ground upward have stilled the false and merged with the real, meeting the true; they are called “sages.”

blocks.text: 40. The Vajra Precious Precepts

inline.s: (From The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions for the Chan monk Dongwen Fasheng)

[Dongwen Fasheng was long since endowed with a superior root. Having just left worldly ties, he met the Water-Flood Crane. After a while he saw that this was not right, and so abandoned him. He entered Mount Tianmu and, with the chief seat Xingrong and others, built a hut and dwelt there, polishing among themselves the matter beneath their own feet, enduring firmly for several years. He then studied under Chan Master Daguan, staying close to him for some time. Because his mind of loathing clamor and seeking stillness was not yet forgotten, he took his leave and hid himself at Luoxi. Now he has come specially to call on the Elder in this miasmal region, seeking the Dharma gate of the mind-ground.]

The Chan monk Dongwen Fasheng was long since endowed with a superior root. When he first left home he took Lanfeng as his teacher. Before long he discovered that what this man taught was not the right Dharma, and so he abandoned him and left. He entered Mount Tianmu and, with the chief seat Xingrong and others, built a hut and dwelt there, polishing among themselves the matter beneath their own feet (the great matter of birth and death), enduring firmly for several years. He also studied under Master Zibai, staying close to him for some time. Because his mind of loathing clamor and seeking stillness was not yet forgotten, he took his leave and hid himself at Luoxi. Now he has come specially to call on the Elder in this miasmal region, seeking the Dharma gate of the mind-ground.

[The Elder, following the Brahmā Net Sutra, conferred on him the Vajra Precious Precepts. Fasheng threw himself down in full prostration like Mount Tai collapsing — such was his diligence for the Dharma. Because the Elder had long drunk the miasmal mists and the four elements were impaired, he closed the gate and withdrew his traces, cultivating stillness to rest. Fasheng too bowed and returned to the mountain, having requested the conferral of the precepts.]

The Elder, following the Brahmā Net Sutra, conferred on him the Vajra Precious Precepts. Fasheng prostrated himself with the five limbs to the ground like Mount Tai collapsing — such was his diligence for the Dharma. Because the Elder had long drunk the miasmal mists and the four elements were out of harmony and impaired (he was ill), he closed the gate and withdrew his traces, cultivating stillness to rest and recover. Fasheng likewise took his leave and returned to the mountain, and so requested the conferral of the precepts.

[Water-Flood Crane] This refers to Iron-Beak Lanfeng. The original note at the end of this text says: “Dongwen first took Iron-Beak Lanfeng as his teacher. The ‘Water-Flood Crane’ mentioned here refers to Lanfeng.” [Vajra Precious Precepts] That is, the Mahāyāna bodhisattva precepts set forth in the Brahmā Net Sutra. Also called the single-mind vajra precepts. They are the intrinsically possessed, uncreated precepts of the one mind: once obtained, never lost, possessing incomparable great function. The Brahmā Net Sutra says: “The Vajra Precious Precepts are the source of all Buddhas, the source of all bodhisattvas.” [Precepts] That which guards the body and mind against transgression.

[He therefore taught him, saying: The Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all sentient beings — scaled, shelled, and feathered — down to those in the hells and the three evil paths, and even those utterly dispersed and sunk in emptiness: none of them are not joined eyebrow to eyebrow, not separated by the least hair. What they share is the vajra mind-ground; what differs is only thought, emotion, love, and hate. Because the Buddhas and patriarchs make good use of their minds, they turn a defiled land into a Pure Land and transform a mountain of knives into a treasured grove, so that even the bitterest suffering and acrid pain all become the true realm of ultimate bliss. This is no other technique than that within this mind, thought and emotion are not born and love and hate find no lodging. It is like a clear eye that sees the open sky through and through — how then could there be inverted, illusory flowers arising and perishing of themselves? Sentient beings turn away from this, and no wonder they fall into all kinds of inversion and bring the fault upon themselves.]

He therefore taught him, saying: The Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all sentient beings, birds and beasts, down to the three evil paths of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, as well as formless sentient beings — none of them are not joined eyebrow to eyebrow, without the least hair of difference. What they share is the vajra mind-ground; what differs is only thought, emotion, love, and hate. Because the Buddhas and patriarchs make good use of their vajra mind, they turn a defiled land into a Pure Land and transform a mountain of knives into a treasured grove; even the bitterest suffering and acrid pain all become the true realm of ultimate bliss. This is no other technique than that within this mind, thought and emotion are not born and love and hate find no lodging. It is like a clear eye that sees the open sky through and through — how then could it see inverted illusory flowers, arising and perishing of themselves? Sentient beings are entirely the opposite, taking thought, emotion, love, and hate as their mind; no wonder they fall into all kinds of confusion and inversion and falsely see illusory flowers arising and perishing — this is bringing the fault upon themselves.

[Emptied, scattered, dissolved, and sunk] This refers to formless sentient beings. The formless have no shape or color. Because of the delusion of inversion that scatters and dissolves them, such beings give rise to the karma of hidden, chaotic thought. Delusion and karma being dark and obscure, they are rewarded with this form of birth — that is, the class of the emptied, scattered, dissolved, and sunk. [Joined eyebrow to eyebrow] Joined as one body. The Gateless Gate says: “Chan Master Zhaozhou, asked by a monk, ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ answered, ‘No.’ Wumen (that is, the Chan monk Wumen Huikai, author of the book The Gateless Gate) said: In Chan practice one must pass through the patriarch’s gate, and in wondrous awakening one must exhaust the paths of mind. If the patriarch’s gate is not passed and the paths of mind are not cut off, one is nothing but a spirit clinging to grass and trees. But what is the patriarch’s gate? Just this one word No is a gate of the school. Hence he named it the gateless gate of Chan. One who passes through it not only sees Zhaozhou in person, but can walk hand in hand with the patriarchs of successive generations, joined eyebrow to eyebrow, seeing with the same eye and hearing with the same ear — is that not cause for rejoicing!” [The Gateless Gate] Wumen Huikai, a Chan monk of the Song dynasty, was asked for instruction by students, and so took the ancients’ public cases and made them into a tile for knocking at the gate, guiding students according to their capacities. He wrote them down as they came, and before he knew it they had become a collection. The book sets forth forty-eight famous public cases of old, together with verses and commentaries. [Vajra mind] That is, the original nature. Master Hanshan’s The Dream-Wandering Collection

Postface to the Vow of Bodhi Mind says: “All sages and ordinary beings alike are originally dwelling in the vajra mind-ground, complete with the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wisdom.” In his commentary on the Diamond Sutra (Resolving the Doubts of the Diamond Sutra), Master Hanshan says: “The vajra mind is the fundamental mind with which the Buddha practiced the cause and realized the fruit. Now, coming into the world to teach sentient beings, he uses this mind entirely. He now teaches bodhisattvas to take the vajra mind as the root of their practice, as the first gate of entering the Mahāyāna.” “Now, to lead those formerly of the small vehicle to bring forth the Mahāyāna mind, he takes this vajra mind-ground as the root of practice.” [Illusory flowers] That is, flowers in empty space, a metaphor for illusions. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “What is ignorance? Good sons! All sentient beings, from beginningless time, fall into all kinds of inversion, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy traces of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a person with a diseased eye who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons! The sky truly has no flowers; the sick person falsely clings to them. Because of this false clinging, he is not only confused about the nature of empty space but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From these false existences comes the turning round in birth and death; hence it is called ignorance.”

[The Buddhas and patriarchs, pitying such beings, came into the world expressly, and had no surplus dharma to give anyone: they did nothing but point directly at this mind, causing all sentient beings to know their home at once. Thus Vairocana, the Old One, when he first sat on the bodhi seat, likewise did no more than proclaim this precept-dharma of all the Buddhas of the past, the ten directions, and the three times. On the thousand-petal platform, Śākyamuni in every leaf and every world likewise did no more than declare this mind of all the Buddhas and proclaim this precept-dharma. Even the forty-nine years of wagging lips and flapping tongue, bustling here and there, bending and turning for people’s sake, did no more than cause all sentient beings universally to believe and accept this precept-dharma. And when at the very end he held up a flower, and gods and humans stared without understanding, they too were only deluded about this mind-precept. The golden-hued ascetic’s face broke into a smile, and so it passed through twenty-eight transmissions, hand to hand in succession; and when Bodhidharma came from the West and Shenguang stood in the snow, there were no words and no speech — all likewise a clear, direct pointing at this mind-precept.]

The Buddhas and patriarchs, pitying these inverted and deluded beings, came into the world expressly to teach, and had no other dharma to give anyone: they did nothing but point directly at this vajra mind, causing all sentient beings to know their home at once. Thus Vairocana Buddha, when he first sat on the bodhi seat, did no more than proclaim this vajra precious precept of all the Buddhas of the past, the ten directions, and the three times. On the thousand-petal platform, in each leaf a world, the Śākyamuni Buddha of each world likewise did no more than declare this mind of all the Buddhas and proclaim this precept-dharma. Even the forty-nine years of expounding sutras and preaching the Dharma, guiding with wholehearted care and explaining again and again for people’s sake, did no more than cause all sentient beings universally to believe and accept this precept-dharma. And when at the very end he held up a flower before the assembly, and gods and humans stared without understanding, they too were only deluded about this mind-precept (the vajra precious precepts). The golden-hued ascetic (Mahākāśyapa) broke into a smile, and so it passed through twenty-eight transmissions of Chan in the West, handed down in each generation; and when Bodhidharma (the first patriarch of Chan in China) came from the West and Shenguang (the second patriarch) stood in the snow and cut off his arm, there were no words and no speech — all were likewise a clear, direct pointing at this mind-precept.

[Holding up a flower] The Sutra of the Great Brahmā King Questioning the Buddha about Resolving Doubts says: The Brahmā King came to Vulture Peak and offered a golden utpala flower to Śākyamuni Buddha, requesting him to teach the Dharma. The World-Honored One held up the flower before the assembly and said nothing. At that moment a million humans and gods all failed to understand his meaning; only the Venerable Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: I have the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the formless mark of reality, the subtle and wondrous Dharma gate, which is not established on words and is transmitted outside the teachings. I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa. Śākyamuni Buddha first transmitted it to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa: this is the beginning of the Chan school.

[Transmitted in turn through six generations, it reached Old Lu, the common fellow, who, beneath his load of firewood, heard the Diamond Sutra say, “Give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all,” and at once awakened to this precept — not obtained from others, not conferred by a teacher, but the nature itself complete. What is so extraordinary about that? When he came to Huangmei for confirmation, he at once said, “Originally there is not a single thing — where could dust cling?” Therefore the old man of Huangmei could do nothing with him either, and could only return to the abbot’s quarters without a word. Even the secret transmission at the third watch was very like swapping a man’s eyes for black beans — what was so extraordinary beyond this?]

Transmitted in turn through six generations in Chinese Chan, it reached Huineng, who beneath his load of firewood heard the Diamond Sutra say, “Give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all,” and thereupon at once awakened to this precept — not obtained from others, not conferred by a teacher, the self-nature being originally complete. What was so extraordinary beyond this? When he came to Huangmei (the Fifth Patriarch) for confirmation, he at once said, “Originally there is not a single thing — where could dust cling?” Therefore the Fifth Patriarch could do nothing with him either, and could only return to the abbot’s quarters without a word. Even the secret transmission of the robe and bowl at the third watch was very like swapping a man’s eyes for black beans — what was so extraordinary beyond this?
[Old Lu, the common fellow] That is, the Sixth Patriarch Huineng. Huineng’s secular surname was Lu, and at that time he had not yet left home, so he was called a common fellow.

[From this time on, sons and grandsons filled the eye and spread throughout the realm; those who obtained it died, those who lost it lived; the seventeen hundred (the seventeen hundred public cases), piping and playing, did no more than mutually illuminate one another in this mind-ground Dharma gate — how could it be that outside this mind one should seek a wondrous awakening elsewhere? If one seeks elsewhere apart from this, one falls into the crooked paths of outside teachings. Hence the Brahmā Net Sutra says: “The mind-ground of Vairocana Buddha, recited in the first arising of the mind, is named the Precept of Radiant Vajra Precious Precepts; it is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all bodhisattvas, the seed of Buddha-nature. All sentient beings have Buddha-nature; all consciousness, form, and mind, whatever is feeling and whatever is mind, all enter the precept of Buddha-nature.” It also says: “When sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they at once enter the rank of all Buddhas; their rank being equal to great awakening, they are truly the sons of the Buddhas.” Therefore in the fifty-five stages of progressive practice, one who has not seen Buddha-nature still falls upon the road
(the character is a variant of “road”)

of stages. Only when at the very end, in the stage of equal awakening, does it say: “This person first obtains the vajra mind, the initial stage of dry wisdom, and arriving here enters directly into the ocean of Buddha-nature.”]

From this time on (beginning with the Sixth Patriarch), Chan’s sons and grandsons filled the eye and spread throughout the world; those who obtained it had their thought and emotion die, those who lost it had ignorance arise; the seventeen hundred (referring to the seventeen hundred public cases), piping and playing, did no more than mutually illuminate one another in this mind-ground Dharma gate — where was it that outside this mind one should seek a wondrous awakening? If one seeks elsewhere apart from this, one falls into the crooked paths of outside teachings. Hence the Brahmā Net Sutra says: “The mind-ground of Vairocana Buddha, recited in the first arising of the mind, is named the Precept of Radiant Vajra Precious Precepts; it is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all bodhisattvas, the seed of Buddha-nature. All sentient beings have Buddha-nature; all consciousness, form, and mind, whatever is feeling and whatever is mind, all enter the precept of Buddha-nature.” It also says: “When sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they at once enter the rank of all Buddhas; their rank being equal to great awakening, they are truly the sons of the Buddhas.” Therefore in the fifty-five stages of progressive practice, one who has not seen Buddha-nature falls upon the road of stages. Only when at the very end, in the stage of equal awakening, does it say: “This person first obtains the vajra mind, the initial stage of dry wisdom, and arriving here enters directly into the ocean of Buddha-nature.” [The fifty-five stages of progressive practice] That is, the fifty-five Mahāyāna stages: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of dwelling, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the four preparatory practices, the ten grounds, and equal awakening. [The four preparatory practices] In the course of Mahāyāna practice, between the ten dedications and the ten grounds one must still pass through the four preparatory practices as preparation for entering the first ground. The so-called four preparatory practices are the cultivation of the four investigations, by which the four kinds of true wisdom are obtained. “Preparatory practice” means that when one is about to enter the proper stage of cultivation, one must add a stretch of effort to one’s practice. [Piping and playing (gǔ huáng)] To blow the sheng. The huáng is the copper reed in the pipes of a sheng, and by extension the sheng itself; it is used as a metaphor for clever words and fine argument. [The stage of dry wisdom] The first of the “ten common grounds of the three vehicles” among the bodhisattva stages of practice; on this ground there is wisdom but no concentration, and so it is called the stage of dry wisdom.

[Seen in this way, apart from this vajra mind, is there any other essential dharma for going from ordinary to sage, for becoming a Buddha and a patriarch? Know then that these precepts are not easy to awaken to: to awaken is to be named the stage of dwelling. They are not easy to practice: to practice is to be named the stage of practice. They are not easy to penetrate: to penetrate is to be named the stage of dedication. They are not easy to purify: to purify is to be named the stage of the grounds. They are not easy to forget: to forget is to be named the stage of entering Buddhahood.]

Seen in this way, apart from this vajra mind, what other path is there for going from ordinary to sage and becoming a Buddha and a patriarch? Know then that these precepts are not easy to awaken to: to awaken is to be named the stage of the ten dwellings. They are not easy to practice: to practice is to be named the stage of the ten practices. They are not easy to penetrate: to penetrate is to be named the stage of the ten dedications. They are not easy to purify: to purify is to be named the stage of the ten grounds. They are not easy to forget: to forget is to be named the stage of entering Buddhahood.

[The fifty-two stages] From ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages in all: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of dwelling, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten grounds, equal awakening, and wondrous awakening (Buddhahood).

[Fasheng, today you should truly examine yourself: with what mind did you leave home? With what mind do you call on teachers and visit friends? With what mind do you delight in seeking the Buddhadharma? With what mind are you willing to receive these precepts? If you get at that mind, then the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all sentient beings together will emit light and shake the earth from the tip of a single hair of the Elder, and then in the twelve periods of the day you will be joined eyebrow to eyebrow with all sages and ordinary beings. This is what is called truly upholding the precepts. Otherwise there is danger, and where there is danger one falls. Investigate! Investigate! Investigate! (Original note: Dongwen first took Iron-Beak Lanfeng as his teacher. The “Water-Flood Crane” mentioned here refers to Lanfeng.)]

Fasheng, today you should earnestly search your own heart: with what mind did you leave home? With what mind do you call on teachers and visit friends? With what mind do you delight in seeking the Buddhadharma? With what mind are you willing to receive these precepts? If you get at that mind, then the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all sentient beings together will emit light and shake the earth from the tip of a single hair of the Elder, and then in the twelve periods of the day you will be joined eyebrow to eyebrow with all sages and ordinary beings. This is what is called truly upholding the precepts. Otherwise there is danger, and where there is danger one falls. Investigate! Investigate! Investigate!

[The tip of a single hair] The Avataṃsaka Sutra says: “Entering right concentration within a single pore, from that concentration emerging through all pores; entering right concentration through all pores, from that concentration emerging at the tip of a single hair.” This is the state of “manifesting a Buddha-land at the tip of a single hair, turning the great Dharma wheel within a single mote of dust.” Master Hanshan’s The Dream-Wandering Collection

Record of the Restoration of the Stupa Court of Master Wan at Shijing Mountain in Zhuozhou says: “Thus our Buddha, the World-Honored One, throughout vast kalpas gazed upon the worlds of the ten directions, and there was not so much as a mustard seed’s worth where he did not give up body and life for sentient beings’ sake, seeking the place of this Dharma; and having just sought and obtained it, he manifests a Buddha-land at the tip of a single hair and turns the great Dharma wheel within a single mote of dust.”

blocks.text: 41. No Quarrel Between Chan and Pure Land

inline.s: The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan monk Huijing Xin

[Our Buddha taught the Dharma with the one mind as the core. No matter how many hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates there are, none is other than a practice for realizing the one mind. The most essential of them are simply Chan practice and Buddha-recitation. Chan practice is the method for awakening to the mind established by the patriarchs of former times in this land; the gate of Buddha-recitation is what our Buddha revealed to the bodhisattvas of the three worthy ranks and the ten grounds, for whom Buddha-recitation is in every case the essential means of becoming a Buddha. The bodhisattvas of the ten grounds have already realized true suchness — are they not awakened? Yet they all say: never apart from recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, and recollection of the Saṃgha.]

Our Buddha taught the Dharma with the one mind as the core. No matter how many hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates there are, none is other than a practice for realizing the one mind. The most essential of them are simply Chan practice and Buddha-recitation. Chan practice is the method for awakening to the mind established by the patriarchs of former times in this land; the gate of Buddha-recitation is what our Buddha revealed to the bodhisattvas of the three worthy ranks and the ten grounds — in short, taking Buddha-recitation as the essential means of becoming a Buddha. The bodhisattvas of the ten grounds have already realized true suchness — are they not awakened? Yet they all say: never apart from recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, and recollection of the Saṃgha.

[The three worthy ranks] In the course of Mahāyāna practice, among the fifty-two stages from ordinary being to sage, the bodhisattvas of the ten dwellings, ten practices, and ten dedications have cut off only the delusions of views and thoughts and still have the delusions of dust-and-sand and of ignorance; they have not entered the sage stage of the ten grounds, and so are called only the “three worthy ranks,” or “bodhisattvas before the grounds.” [The three delusions] The delusion of views and thoughts, the delusion of dust-and-sand, and the delusion of ignorance. The delusion of views and thoughts is the delusion of ordinary beings: the delusion of views within it is error in understanding and views, such as the five wrong views of view of body, extreme views, and so on; the delusion of thoughts is error in thought, such as the five afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. If those on the paths of the voice-hearers and the solitary realizers cut off these two delusions, they realize the fruit of arhatship and escape the three realms. The delusion of dust-and-sand is the delusion of bodhisattvas: if a bodhisattva who transforms and saves sentient beings does not master the immeasurable Dharma gates, as numerous as dust and sand, he cannot complete the work of teaching sentient beings; hence it is called the delusion of dust-and-sand. The delusion of ignorance is fundamental ignorance, which obscures the principle of the middle way and true reality; when it is cut off entirely, one becomes a Buddha. Among the three delusions, the delusion of views and thoughts is coarse, the dust-and-sand is middling, and ignorance is subtle.

[Sudhana visited fifty-three good friends; the first, the monk Deyun, granted him solely the Dharma gate of liberation through Buddha-recitation. And at the very end, when he visited Samantabhadra, the good friend for entering wondrous awakening, he dedicated it exclusively toward the Pure Land of the West, saying: “Beholding the Tathāgata’s immeasurable light, may he bestow on me the bodhi prediction face to face.” Seen in this way, even though the Avataṃsaka is the highest single vehicle, and its practice is called the practice of the Dharma realm, it is from first to last never apart from Buddha-recitation. Sages of the ten grounds, having already realized true suchness, are still not apart from Buddha-recitation — and yet deluded people of the Dharma-ending age dare to slander Buddha-recitation as an inferior practice! How then can one doubt that Chan practice and Buddha-recitation are in conflict? It is a want
(a variant of the character for “want”)
of broad learning, not knowing the Buddha’s intent, that gives rise to false discrimination.]

Sudhana visited fifty-three good friends; the first, the monk Deyun, granted him solely the Dharma gate of liberation through Buddha-recitation. At the very end he visited Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Samantabhadra, the good friend for entering wondrous awakening, dedicated exclusively toward the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, saying: “Beholding the Tathāgata’s immeasurable light, may he bestow on me the bodhi prediction face to face.” Seen in this way, even if the Avataṃsaka samādhi is the highest single vehicle, and its method of practice is called the gate of practice of the Dharma realm, it is likewise from first to last never apart from Buddha-recitation. Sages of the ten grounds, having already realized true suchness, are still not apart from Buddha-recitation — and yet deluded people of the Dharma-ending age dare to slander Buddha-recitation as an inferior practice! How then can one doubt that Chan practice and Buddha-recitation are in conflict? It is only that they are poorly informed, not knowing the Buddha’s intent, and so give rise to false discrimination.

[Avataṃsaka samādhi] An abbreviation of the Buddha-Avataṃsaka samādhi. Also called Avataṃsaka concentration, it is the Chan concentration entered by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. This samādhi is the great samādhi that encompasses the Dharma realm and contains all Buddhadharmas. [The practice of the Dharma realm] In explaining the essence of Avataṃsaka samādhi, the Record of Profound Investigation of the Avataṃsaka says: “The gate of practice of the Dharma realm takes the ocean of mind as its substance. Through meditative equipoise it is vast and limitless.”

[If one speaks in terms of the Pure Land of mind only, then when the mind is pure the land is pure. Therefore, when one first practices Chan and has not yet awakened, without Buddha-recitation there is no way to purify one’s own mind; yet when the mind is pure, that is awakening to the mind. Bodhisattvas, having awakened, do not abandon Buddha-recitation; so without Buddha-recitation there is no way to perfect enlightenment. How then do we know that the patriarchs did not awaken to the mind through Buddha-recitation? If one recites the Buddha’s name to the point of single-mindedness, with afflictions dissolved and one’s own mind clearly understood, that is named awakening; in that case Buddha-recitation is precisely Chan practice. And as with the bodhisattvas, it means not abandoning Buddha-recitation after awakening. Hence the patriarchs of former times all did not abandon the Pure Land. In this way, Buddha-recitation is precisely Chan practice, and Chan practice is precisely birth in the Pure Land. This has been an unresolved doubt through the ages; now that this explanation has broken it open completely, the view that separates Chan from Pure Land is entirely dissolved. Even if the Buddhas were to appear in the world, they would not speak differently from this. If one sets this aside and gives rise to other wild opinions, all such talk is the talk of demons, not the Buddhadharma.]

If one speaks in terms of the Pure Land of mind only, then when the mind is pure the land is pure. Therefore, when one first practices Chan and has not yet awakened, without Buddha-recitation there is no way to purify one’s own mind; yet when the mind is pure, that is awakening to the mind. Bodhisattvas, having awakened, do not abandon Buddha-recitation; thus without Buddha-recitation there is no way to become a Buddha. How then do we know that the patriarchs did not awaken to the mind through Buddha-recitation? If one recites the Buddha’s name to the point of single-mindedness, with afflictions dissolved and one’s own mind clearly understood, that is named awakening; in that case Buddha-recitation is precisely Chan practice. And as with the bodhisattvas, it means not abandoning Buddha-recitation even after awakening. Hence the patriarchs of former times all did not abandon the Pure Land. In this way, Buddha-recitation is precisely Chan practice, and Chan practice is precisely birth in the Pure Land. The quarrel between Chan and Pure Land has been an unresolved case through the ages. By what has been said above this doubt is thoroughly broken, and the view that separates Chan from Pure Land is from then on entirely dissolved. Even if the Buddhas were to appear in the world, they would have no different teaching. If one sets this aside and gives rise to other wild opinions, all such talk is the talk of demons, not the Buddhadharma.

blocks.text: 42. Life Is a Dream

inline.s: The Dream-Wandering Collection
Reply to the Military Commander Yang Yuanru

[The ancients said, “In the field of feverish confusion, a cool eye is hard to withstand.” Because the three realms are without safety, like a burning house, none who come and go within them are not scorched and boiled. If one would find a patch of coolness amid the blazing flames, none but a cool-eyed person can obtain it. If one can in a single thought be cool, at once seeing the whole earth as ice, one will naturally no longer take the world of body and mind as a refuge. This is how the people of great strength from of old, playing in the field of birth and death, can turn worldly toil into Buddha-work and transform affliction into bodhi: they rely solely on that one cool eye and that one cool-hearted disposition of theirs — what need is there of any further spiritual powers and wondrous functions?]

The ancients said, “In the field of feverish confusion, though everything churns the mind, it cannot withstand being looked at with a cool eye.” Because the three realms are without safety, like a burning house, none who come and go within them are not scorched and boiled. If one would find a patch of coolness amid the blazing flames, only a cool-eyed person can manage it. If one can look upon the world with a cool eye until a single thought is cool, then at once one sees the whole earth as ice, and naturally will not take the world of body and mind as a refuge. From of old, the people of great strength who play in the field of birth and death and can turn worldly toil into Buddha-work and transform affliction into bodhi rely precisely on that one cool eye and that one cool-hearted disposition of theirs — what further spiritual powers and wondrous functions could there be?

[The three realms are without safety, like a burning house] The Lotus Sutra says: “The three realms are without safety, like a burning house, filled with many sufferings, most terrifying; there are always the sorrows of birth, aging, sickness, and death; such fires blaze without cease.” [They rely solely on that one cool eye and that one cool-hearted disposition] This means: when the mind is empty the object is empty of itself; the ten thousand dharmas bind nothing, and are originally liberated. The Diamond Sutra says: “All that has marks is deceptive.” “Not grasping at marks, one is thus, unmoving.” Of these two lines, “all that has marks is deceptive” is the cool eye; “not grasping at marks, one is thus, unmoving” is the cool heart. In the phrase above, “that” renders the pronoun qu, meaning “he.”

[These words are very easy to know, but very hard to see. Take the case of the Buddhas and patriarchs, who took the single phrase “all dharmas are like a dream” as the essential road out of the world. Yet the wise and the foolish of the world alike can all say, “Life is a dream.” Their words may be alike, but their meaning is not. In fact they have never truly, with one glance, seen through life as a dream. If one really saw through it, one would naturally, at every pass of honor and disgrace, gain and loss, right and wrong, swing one’s arms and walk away — who would dare cross swords with such a one?]

These words (“in the field of feverish confusion, a cool eye is hard to withstand”) are very easy to know, but their true meaning is very hard to see. Just as the Buddhas and patriarchs took the single phrase “all dharmas are like a dream” as the essential road out of the world — but how many see its true meaning? And the wise and the foolish of the world alike can all say, “Life is a dream.” Though the words are the same phrase, “life is a dream,” the meaning in the mouths of the wise and the foolish is entirely different. The foolish say it with their lips, but in fact have never truly, with one glance, seen through life as a dream. If one really saw through it, one would naturally be able to turn and walk away at every pass of honor and disgrace, gain and loss, right and wrong — and who could hold one back? (The carp slips off the golden hook and goes, wagging its head and tail, never to return.)
[Swinging the arms (diào bì)] To swing one’s arms and walk off — to depart without a backward look.

[In fact there is nothing very mysterious in it. As for the first step, however, there is no lack of a method. When we live in the world, we should first take the affairs of the dream and hold them up before our eyes, observing them closely. We must truly and distinctly look until we cannot help but burst into a great laugh. At that point we will suddenly feel that the ordinary saying “like a dream” has a meaning utterly different from before. Then, taking that place of laughter, turn a single thought to the objects before us and place them within the dream, observing closely. When we see them hazy and heavy and upside down, suddenly we wake with a start. In this way, looking back over our life, every kind of object we have ever passed through, when we truly seek it, is utterly unattainable. That place of utter unattainability is precisely the first gate through which the Buddhas and patriarchs leave birth and death.]

In fact there is nothing very mysterious in it. As for taking the first step, there is no lack of a method. The method is this: when we live in the world, we should first take the affairs of the dream and hold them up before our eyes, observing them closely. We must look truly and distinctly, until we cannot help bursting into a great laugh. At that point we will suddenly feel that the ordinary saying “life is a dream” has an utterly different meaning. Then, taking that place of laughing awakening, turn a single thought toward the objects before us and place them within the framework of “life is a dream,” observing closely. When we see them hazy and heavy and upside down, suddenly we wake with a start. In this way, looking back over our life, every kind of object we have ever passed through — even if we wish to take them as real, they are utterly unattainable (we simply cannot manage it). That place of utter unattainability is precisely the first gate through which the Buddhas and patriarchs leave birth and death.
[Looking until one cannot help but burst into a great laugh] Master Hanshan’s Song of Awakening the World says:

‘In life a thousand, ten thousand schemes one spends; in death one leaves an empty pair of hands. Joy, sorrow, parting, meeting — clamor day by day; long life or early death, success or failure — busy day by day. Do not strive for strength and fight to win: a hundred years are all a stage of play. In a moment the gong and drum fall still — who knows where one’s home village lies
(who knows how it will end)

[Do not strive to be strong and fight for victory] A person’s life is like a white colt glimpsed through a crack, gone in the blink of an eye. The result is that “the ten thousand things cannot be taken along; only karma follows the body”: after death the two hands are empty, yet the retribution of the evil karma created by striving for strength and fighting for victory follows like a shadow into future lives. Therefore, do not strive to be strong and fight for victory; rather, use the energy and time spent on such striving for practice, so as to settle birth and death. [A hundred years are wholly a stage of play] A hundred years of life are entirely a play. [In a moment the gong and drum fall silent] In a moment the play is sung out (the gong and drum fall silent).

blocks.text: 43. A Single Thought Turns the Mind Around

inline.s: The Dream-Wandering Collection
To Liu Cunchi

[We have for many lives and accumulated kalpas been sunk in the mud of the five desires and burned by the karmic fire of the seven emotions — deep and fierce indeed. There are no heroes who are not drowned and boiled by them. To seek a single thought that turns the mind around is utterly unattainable, let alone hoping that they will give rise to a mind of detachment, seek the way out of suffering, and single-mindedly rest their minds on the Pure Land in Buddha-recitation. This is not merely a lotus emerging from mud, but a root sending forth from within fire. What joy could be greater!]

From many lives and accumulated kalpas, we have been sunk in the mud of the five desires and burned by the karmic fire of the seven emotions — deep and fierce indeed. There are no heroes who are not drowned and boiled by them. Even to obtain a single thought that turns the mind around is unattainable, let alone hoping that they will give rise to a mind of detachment, seek the way out of suffering, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and rest their minds on the Pure Land. But that you can single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and rest your mind on the Pure Land means it is not merely a red lotus emerging from the mud of the five desires, but a root planted within the karmic fire of the seven emotions. How greatly this rejoices one!

[The five desires] The craving for form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form means beautiful appearances; sound means melodious sounds; smell means fragrant scents; taste means delicious flavors; touch means pleasant tactile pleasures. [The seven emotions] Joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, and desire.

[We who wish to escape birth and death must know the root of birth and death. You wish to seek the root of the Pure Land, but you little know that the root of the Pure Land is precisely the root of birth and death. It lies in this mind’s turning around in a single thought — in the span
(the text writes this character for “span”)

between, sparing no effort. May you earnestly fix your eye in advance on the objects before you in daily life: at the time of the reunion of wife and children, in the intervals of dealings with friends, at the point where right and profit attack each other, before joy and anger have arisen — truly and distinctly, clearly and exactly, see what the root of birth and death is, and then at once pull it out with all your might.]

We who wish to escape birth and death must certainly know the root of birth and death. In your letter you say you wish to know the root of cultivating the Pure Land; you little know that the root of cultivating the Pure Land is precisely the pulling out of the root of birth and death. And pulling out the root of birth and death lies in sparing no effort in the interval of a single thought’s turning of this mind! May you carefully fix your eye in advance on the objects before you in daily life: at the time of the reunion of wife and children, in the intervals of dealings with friends, at the point where right and profit attack each other, before joy and anger have arisen — truly and distinctly, clearly and exactly, see what the root of birth and death is, and immediately pull it out with all your might.
[The root of birth and death] Master Hanshan’s The Dream-Wandering Collection

Instructions for Feng Yanling says: “A student who turns toward the Way must first fear birth and death, and second must know the root of birth and death. The root of birth and death is simply the various hatred and love, taking and rejecting, self-conceit, and karma of greed, hatred, and delusion that appear before one in daily life. Since this is the bitter root of birth and death, if one resolves to cut it off there is no other technique: one need only illuminate it the moment it arises and firmly refuse to let it arise.” [Reunion (tuán
luán
)] To come together. [Clearly and exactly] Distinctly.

[Yet our mind is originally pure; what makes it defiled and turbid is in truth the foul grime of this root and stem. If one can uproot it with force, then the Pure Land comes without being sought. What is called “once one root returns to the source, the six faculties are all liberated” refers precisely to this. If one sees through the single fundamental thought, then every matter in daily life is a field of liberation, all returning to the realm of ultimate bliss. Truly, though the body has not yet entered the lotus, the mind is sent ahead to the heaven of ultimate bliss.]

Yet our mind is originally pure; what makes it defiled and turbid is in truth the foul grime of this root of birth and death. If one can uproot it with force, then the Pure Land comes without being sought. What is called “once one root returns to the source, the six faculties are all liberated” refers precisely to this. If one sees through the single fundamental thought, then every single matter in daily life is a field of liberation, all returning to the realm of ultimate bliss. This is truly: though the body has not yet entered the lotus, the mind is sent ahead to the heaven of ultimate bliss.

[Once one root returns to the source, the six faculties are all liberated] From the Śūraṃgama Sutra. It means that among the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), as long as one of them returns to the source, the whole of the six faculties is liberated. Here it is a metaphor for this: as soon as the root of birth and death is pulled out, the whole is liberated.

blocks.text: 44. Do Not Fall into the Illness of Letting Things Be

inline.s: The Dream-Wandering Collection · To Master Xiu Liuyi, Keeper of the Retreat

[The confusion of the past few days, I imagine, has already settled. This matter cannot be done with admixtures; one must lay hold right where the root of life is cut off and simply go on doing it. Do not concern yourself with how he is or how I am: the moment a hairsbreadth remains in the breast, you are toyed with by it. This present karmic opportunity is one that could not be sought in a hundred thousand kalpas; had this opportunity come earlier, you would not have wandered until today. Now that you are fortunate enough to have this great karmic opportunity, how could you lightly let it pass?]

The confusion of late (referring to the “seeing ghosts in broad daylight” mentioned below), I imagine, has already settled. This matter (the retreat) cannot be done with admixtures; one must lay hold right where the root of life is cut off and simply go on doing it. Do not concern yourself with how he is or how I am: the moment the slightest stray thought remains in the breast, you are toyed with by it. This present opportunity of retreat could not be sought in a hundred thousand kalpas; had this opportunity come earlier, you would not have wandered until today. Now that you are fortunate enough to have this one great karmic opportunity, how could you lightly let it pass?
[The pronoun tuō] It indicates the third person.

[A hundred years of time is but a moment; steal these three years of work, and they pass in the blink of an eye. Set your teeth and clench your jaw, and a turn of the head is all it takes. Do what you can while you can. After three years, let it be as it will: even if you do not awaken to the Way, you will at least have fulfilled the original intent with which you began to study the Way. This is the first step out of birth and death — how can you beat the retreat drum the moment you step out the door? From now on, truly put it down and pay no more heed to how it goes. Even amid swords and spears one must let go of body and life — how much more so when, on level ground in broad daylight, one sees ghosts and gives rise to inverted thoughts? Do not doubt; you must simply cut it off. Rouse your spirit; do not be entangled by it.]

A hundred years of time is but a moment; to draw out three years for retreat passes in the blink of an eye. Whatever difficulties you meet, set your teeth and clench your jaw — a turn of the head (a change of heart) is all it takes. Do what you can while you can, and only leave the retreat when the three years are up; let it be as it will. Even if you do not awaken to the Way, you will have fulfilled the original intent with which you began to study the Way. This is the first step out of birth and death — how can you beat the retreat drum the moment you step out the door? From now on, truly put it down and pay no more heed to how it goes. Even amid swords and spears one must lay down body and life — how much more so when, on level ground in broad daylight, one sees ghosts and gives rise to inverted thoughts? Do not doubt; you must simply cut it off (the doubt). Rouse your spirit; do not be entangled by it.
[To steal (tōu)] To draw out time; for example: to steal a moment of leisure, to snatch spare time, to steal leisure.

[Again: the long rains oppress one, and I have not been able to send word; this mind of mine has never for a single thought let you go. I know that you dwell at ease in quiet and that body and mind are peaceful, so that stray thoughts have long since of themselves melted away. But in the midst of stray thoughts melting away there comes of itself a lightness and ease and happiness — and one must not take that lightness and ease as the thing to be enjoyed. If you take it as attainment, then from that point you fall into the illness of letting things be, seeking only a dim, continuous vacancy and taking having nothing to do as wonderful. You little know that this illness is the most poisonous of all: if you hold to it long, there will be no progress at all; ignorance will secretly grow, karmic consciousness will flow on, the root of life will not be cut off, and in the end it is like wiping quicksilver with spittle — utterly useless.]

Again: the long rains oppress one and news is cut off; this mind of mine has never for a single thought let you go. I know that you dwell at ease in quiet and that body and mind are peaceful, so that stray thoughts have long since melted away. In the midst of stray thoughts melting away there comes of itself a lightness and ease and happiness, but one must by no means take that lightness and ease as the thing to be enjoyed. If you take it as attainment, then from that point you fall into the illness of letting things be, seeking only a dim, continuous vacancy and taking having nothing to do as wonderful. You little know that this illness is the most poisonous of all: if you hold to it long, there will be no progress at all; ignorance will secretly grow, karmic consciousness will flow on, the root of life will not be cut off, and in the end it is like wiping quicksilver with spittle — utterly useless.

[The illness of letting things be] The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Second, the illness of letting things be. If there is a person who speaks thus — ‘We now do not cut off birth and death, nor seek nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa and birth and death have no thought of arising or ceasing; let everything be as it will, following the nature of all dharmas’ — and wishes thereby to seek perfect enlightenment: because the nature of perfect enlightenment is not something that comes from letting be, this is called an illness.” On this Master Hanshan comments: “This sets forth the illness of letting things be. This illness of letting be belongs to people of wild understanding, who drift on in heedless self-will, indulging body and mind, claiming that they are without things and without obstruction and have attained great liberation, and who further borrow the words that originally there is no birth and death to cut off and no nirvāṇa to realize, making them provision for self-indulgence. They are not good friends of true knowledge and view. If one follows such people, one falls into wild delusion; hence it is said that self-willed letting be is an illness.” (Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment) [Wiping quicksilver with spittle] This is the so-called “secret formula” of the elixir of immortality, which in fact has no efficacy; hence Master Hanshan uses it here as a metaphor for something utterly useless.

[When stray thoughts melt away, that is precisely the time to put forth effort and take up the huatou, investigating earnestly and laying on the mass of doubt afresh. If the mass of doubt gains power and you hold firmly to the huatou, examining it day and night, investigating more and more deeply, there will at last come the time when cold ashes burst into beans. If you settle on having nothing to do and do not raise the mass of doubt, it is in the end not true practice. The Recorded Sayings of Gaofeng is just the right teacher — and do not take it as a mysterious principle. Strive on! Strive on!]

When stray thoughts melt away, that is precisely the time to put forth effort and take up the huatou, investigating earnestly and laying on the mass of doubt afresh. If the mass of doubt gains power and you hold firmly to the huatou, examining it day and night, investigating more and more deeply, there will at last come the time when cold ashes burst into beans (when the black lacquer barrel is smashed and the original face is seen through). If you settle on having nothing to do and do not raise the mass of doubt, it is in the end not true practice. The Recorded Sayings of Gaofeng is just the right teacher — but do not take it as a mysterious principle. Strive on! Strive on!

[Chan Master Gaofeng] His posthumous name was Yuanmiao. He was born in the wuxu year of the Jiaxi era of the Song dynasty, and attained the Dharma under Yunyan Qin at Beijian. In the jimao year of the Zhiyuan era of Kublai Khan, he went up the West Peak of Mount Tianmu and entered Zhanggong Cave, inscribing it “the Death Barrier”; he did not go out of doors for fifteen years. Students came to consult him without a single day’s gap. His Recorded Sayings of Gaofeng circulates widely in the world.

blocks.text: 45. A Single Thought Is Unborn

inline.s: From Master Hanshan’s Dream-Wandering Collection: To Bao Zhongsu of the Ministry of Rites
[You have written to tell me that in your recent practice you have gradually found an entry into your original ground, and that you would like a single secret phrase to serve as a shortcut.]

You have written that in your recent practice you have gradually found an entry into your original ground, and that you hope I will tell you a single secret phrase to serve as a shortcut to seeing your own nature.

[Original ground (běn dì)] As against the manifested transformation body, the source from which it is manifested is called the original ground. Here it means the original nature, what the Chan school calls one’s original face.

[Fundamentally this matter is originally neither secret nor not secret; it depends only on working at the single thought of the person concerned. Even the one device of watching the huatou is used only because there is no other way. One need only see through, with all one’s strength, the mind of perception that appears before one in daily life — it is all the working of deluded thought. Even if there are mysterious and wondrous views and understandings, they are all shadows of the spirit of consciousness, all matters on the side of mind, consciousness, and ideation. In short, one has never understood the one device of transcending mind, consciousness, and ideation; hence every movement of mind and arising of thought falls into the old trap of deluded thought. Therefore the Buddha said: All sentient beings, because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, employ various deluded thoughts; these thoughts being untrue, they turn round in birth and death. This is also what Aśvaghoṣa said: All sentient beings, from the very beginning, have never been apart from thought.]

Fundamentally, this matter (seeing one’s own nature) is originally neither secret nor not secret; the key is to work at one’s own single present thought. Even the one device of watching the huatou is used only because there is no other way. One need only see through, with all one’s strength, the mind of perception that appears before one in daily life — it is all the working of deluded thought. Even if there are mysterious and wondrous views and understandings, they too are all shadows of the spirit of consciousness, all matters on the side of mind, consciousness, and ideation. In short, one has never understood the one device of transcending mind, consciousness, and ideation; hence every movement of mind and arising of thought falls into the old trap of deluded thought. So in the Śūraṃgama Sutra the Buddha says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the pure and luminous substance of the nature (all because they do not know this pure and luminous substance of the nature that permanently abides in the true mind), and employ various deluded thoughts (and instead follow deluded thoughts); these thoughts being untrue, they turn round in birth and death.” This is also what Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa says in the Awakening of Faith: all sentient beings, from the very beginning, have never been apart from thought.

[Mind, consciousness, and ideation] “Mind” means collecting and giving rise to, and refers to the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna). “Consciousness” (yì) means thinking and measuring, and refers to the seventh consciousness (manas). “Ideation” (shí) means distinguishing, and refers to the sixth consciousness (mental consciousness). [The old trap (kē jiù)] An old pattern, a worn rut. [The pure and luminous substance of the nature] The luminous, wondrous substance whose nature is originally pure.
